All of Mount Sinai smoked, because Yahweh descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
When the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice.
Yahweh came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. Yahweh called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.

sessions.readWhy: Before the Ten Commandments comes this: 'I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you to myself.' The law follows the rescue, not the other way round. Israel is to be 'a kingdom of priests', a people standing between God and all the nations, which is Abraham's promise again.

think.why: The Exodus became the defining story for enslaved Christians in the Americas, who sang of Moses and Pharaoh and knew exactly whom they meant.

learn.why: These words were given to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai for the priests to speak over the people (Numbers 6), and they are still said at the end of many services today.

music.why: Its verses call on God by names from Israel's story; one asks the 'Lord of might', who gave the law 'on Sinai's height', to come again.

look.why: Wtewael paints people and animals gathered round a shallow pool in a wooded landscape, under the title Moses Striking the Rock. It is the last stop before Sinai: at Rephidim, where there was no water, God gave it from a rock (Exodus 17), and today's chapter begins with Israel setting out from there.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: the law at Sinai was given to people who had just been set free. Find one organisation near you that helps people out of trafficking or forced labour, and give it an hour of your time or some money.
sessions.reflect: What have you been set free from, and what might that freedom be for?

sessions.title: Kings, prophets and exile
sessions.line: Israel gets its kings, its temple and a promise to David, then loses everything, and the prophets insist the story is not over.
sessions.why: With the covenant given, the question is whether Israel can keep it. The long answer, told in the books of Samuel and Kings and the prophets, is no; and yet the promise survives the ruin.

read.author: John Milton
read.who: English poet and pamphleteer (1608–1674), who was completely blind by 1652 and dictated Paradise Lost, a retelling of Genesis 1 to 3, in twelve books of blank verse.
paras:
Mean while they, in their earthly Canaan placed,
Long time shall dwell and prosper, but when sins
National interrupt their publick peace,
Provoking God to raise them enemies;
From whom as oft he saves them penitent
By Judges first, then under Kings; of whom
The second, both for piety renowned
And puissant deeds, a promise shall receive
Irrevocable, that his regal throne
For ever shall endure; the like shall sing
All Prophecy, that of the royal stock
Of David (so I name this king) shall rise
A Son, the Woman's seed to thee foretold,
Foretold to Abraham, as in whom shall trust
All nations; and to kings foretold, of kings
The last; for of his reign shall be no end.

But first, a long succession must ensue;
And his next son, for wealth and wisdom famed,
The clouded ark of God, till then in tents
Wandering, shall in a glorious temple enshrine.
Such follow him, as shall be registered
Part good, part bad; of bad the longer scroll;
Whose foul idolatries, and other faults
Heaped to the popular sum, will so incense
God, as to leave them, and expose their land,
Their city, his temple, and his holy ark,
With all his sacred things, a scorn and prey
To that proud city, whose high walls thou sawest
Left in confusion; Babylon thence called.
There in captivity he lets them dwell
The space of seventy years; then brings them back,
Remembering mercy, and his covenant sworn
To David, stablished as the days of Heaven.

Returned from Babylon by leave of kings
Their lords, whom God disposed, the house of God
They first re-edify; and for a while
In mean estate live moderate; till, grown
In wealth and multitude, factious they grow;
But first among the priests dissention springs,
Men who attend the altar, and should most
Endeavour peace: their strife pollution brings
Upon the temple itself: at last they seise
The scepter, and regard not David's sons;
Then lose it to a stranger, that the true
Anointed King Messiah might be born
Barred of his right; yet at his birth a star,
Unseen before in Heaven, proclaims him come;
And guides the eastern sages, who inquire
His place, to offer incense, myrrh, and gold:
His place of birth a solemn Angel tells
To simple shepherds, keeping watch by night;
They gladly thither haste, and by a quire
Of squadroned Angels hear his carol sung.
A virgin is his mother, but his sire
The power of the Most High: He shall ascend
The throne hereditary, and bound his reign
With Earth's wide bounds, his glory with the Heavens.

He ceased, discerning Adam with such joy
Surcharged, as had like grief been dewed in tears,
Without the vent of words; which these he breathed.
O prophet of glad tidings, finisher
Of utmost hope! now clear I understand
What oft my steadiest thoughts have searched in vain;
Why our great Expectation should be called
The seed of Woman: Virgin Mother, hail,
High in the love of Heaven; yet from my loins
Thou shalt proceed, and from thy womb the Son
Of God Most High: so God with Man unites!

sessions.readWhy: In the last book of Paradise Lost, before Adam leaves Eden, the archangel Michael tells him what is to come. In under seventy lines Milton gives the whole of this act: the judges and kings, God's promise to David of a throne 'for ever', the long scroll of bad kings, Babylon and seventy years of captivity, the return, and the birth of the promised Son. Notice Adam at the end, finally understanding the promise he heard in the garden.

think.why: The prophets' charge against Israel was moral: injustice, contempt for the poor, worship of lesser things. This depth explains the belief in a moral law written on every heart, which Jeremiah promised God would one day write anew (Jeremiah 31:33).

learn.why: Addressed to a people in exile who had run out of strength, these lines promise strength renewed, not to the strong but to those who wait.

music.why: The hymn comes from Lamentations, a book of grief over Jerusalem destroyed by Babylon. In the middle of the ruins it says: 'his compassion doesn't fail. They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.'

look.why: Duccio paints a woman resting under a wooden shelter in a rocky cave, surrounded by angels, and in the narrow side panels two standing men, the prophets Isaiah and Ezekiel. The prophets stand either side of the birth they looked towards, which is where Milton's passage ends.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: exiles are people far from home. Get to know one person living a long way from where they grew up, a neighbour, a colleague or someone at a local refugee group, and ask them what they miss.
sessions.reflect: Have you known a time when what you relied on was taken away? What, if anything, survived?

sessions.title: Christ at the centre
sessions.line: Jesus claims that the whole story was about him. Is that true, or did his followers make it so?
sessions.why: Everything so far has been promise: an offspring, a blessing for all nations, a king for ever, a law written on the heart. Christians believe Jesus is where the promises meet, and this is the place to face the hardest objection: that the Bible is not one story at all, but many books by many hands over a thousand years, made into one plot by Christians reading Jesus back into texts that meant something else.

paras: As they said these things, Jesus himself stood among them, and said to them, “Peace be to you.”
But they were terrified and filled with fear, and supposed that they had seen a spirit.
He said to them, “Why are you troubled? Why do doubts arise in your hearts?
See my hands and my feet, that it is truly me. Touch me and see, for a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”
When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his feet.
While they still didn’t believe for joy, and wondered, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?”
They gave him a piece of a broiled fish and some honeycomb.
He took them, and ate in front of them.
He said to them, “This is what I told you, while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled.”
Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures.
He said to them, “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead the third day,
and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all the nations, beginning at Jerusalem.
You are witnesses of these things.
Behold, I send out the promise of my Father on you. But wait in the city of Jerusalem until you are clothed with power from on high.”
He led them out as far as Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them.
While he blessed them, he withdrew from them, and was carried up into heaven.
They worshiped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy,
and were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.

sessions.readWhy: The risen Jesus eats fish in front of his frightened friends, then 'opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures': everything written about him 'in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms'. Luke ends his Gospel with the claim this course rests on, and with Jesus lifting his hands to bless them as he is carried up into heaven. Read it beside the objection: for two thousand years Jewish readers have read the same scriptures with great care and not found Jesus there, and in the Jewish order the Hebrew Bible ends not with a prophet promising Elijah, as most Christian Bibles do, but with a call to go up and rebuild Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 36:23). If you have not yet read a Gospel through, the course on who Jesus was walks through Mark.

think.why: Athanasius and the Council of Chalcedon set out what Christians came to believe about the one at the centre: truly God and truly human, God become one of us so that we could share in the life of God.

listen.why: Bart Ehrman, a former evangelical who became an agnostic scholar, explains to Sam Harris how he thinks the Bible was written and why historians cannot follow the Gospels all the way. It is the sceptic's case at its most informed, and its fairest.

learn.why: John's Gospel opens with the first words of Genesis, 'In the beginning', and says the Word through whom the world was made has come into it: the whole story folded into five lines.

music.why: A medieval meditation on the crucified Christ, sung to the melody Bach harmonised: the death at the centre of the story, which Luke's risen Jesus says 'was necessary'.

look.why: Koerbecke paints twelve men and a woman kneeling either side of a green rock, gazing up at a man on a black cloud against a gold sky. It is the last scene of today's reading: 'he withdrew from them, and was carried up into heaven.'

sessions.practice: Live it this week: ask one person who reads the Bible differently from you, a Jewish friend, a sceptic, a Christian from another church, how they read it. Listen to the end without arguing, and thank them.
sessions.reflect: Does the claim that Jesus is the key to the whole story seem to you more like a discovery or an imposition? Why?

sessions.title: The Church and the end
sessions.line: We live in the sixth act. The Bible's last pages promise what comes after it.
sessions.why: Jesus sends his friends to 'all the nations', and Abraham's blessing at last goes out to every family on earth. The Church lives between his rising and the promised end, when God says 'I am making all things new' (Revelation 21:5).

read.author: Augustine of Hippo
read.who: North African bishop and theologian (354–430), a teacher of rhetoric who became a Christian at 31, and whose writings shaped Western Christianity for more than a thousand years.
paras: How great shall be that felicity, which shall be tainted with no evil, which shall lack no good, and which shall afford leisure for the praises of God, who shall be all in all! For I know not what other employment there can be where no lassitude shall slacken activity, nor any want stimulate to labour. I am admonished also by the sacred song, in which I read or hear the words, "Blessed are they that dwell in Thy house, O Lord; they will be still praising Thee." All the members and organs of the incorruptible body, which now we see to be suited to various necessary uses, shall contribute to the praises of God; for in that life necessity shall have no place, but full, certain, secure, everlasting felicity. For all those parts of the bodily harmony, which are distributed through the whole body, within and without, and of which I have just been saying that they at present elude our observation, shall then be discerned; and, along with the other great and marvellous discoveries which shall then kindle rational minds in praise of the great Artificer, there shall be the enjoyment of a beauty which appeals to the reason. What power of movement such bodies shall possess, I have not the audacity rashly to define, as I have not the ability to conceive. Nevertheless I will say that in any case, both in motion and at rest, they shall be, as in their appearance, seemly; for into that state nothing which is unseemly shall be admitted. One thing is certain, the body shall forthwith be wherever the spirit wills, and the spirit shall will nothing which is unbecoming either to the spirit or to the body. True honour shall be there, for it shall be denied to none who is worthy, nor yielded to any unworthy; neither shall any unworthy person so much as sue for it, for none but the worthy shall be there. True peace shall be there, where no one shall suffer opposition either from himself or any other. God Himself, who is the Author of virtue, shall there be its reward; for, as there is nothing greater or better, He has promised Himself. What else was meant by His word through the prophet, "I will be your God, and ye shall be my people," than, I shall be their satisfaction, I shall be all that men honourably desire,—life, and health, and nourishment, and plenty, and glory, and honour, and peace, and all good things? This, too, is the right interpretation of the saying of the apostle, "That God may be all in all." He shall be the end of our desires who shall be seen without end, loved without cloy, praised without weariness. This outgoing of affection, this employment, shall certainly be, like eternal life itself, common to all.

There shall be accomplished the words of the psalm, "Be still, and know that I am God." There shall be the great Sabbath which has no evening, which God celebrated among His first works, as it is written, "And God rested on the seventh day from all His works which He had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it; because that in it He had rested from all His work which God began to make." For we shall ourselves be the seventh day, when we shall be filled and replenished with God's blessing and sanctification. There shall we be still, and know that He is God; that He is that which we ourselves aspired to be when we fell away from Him, and listened to the voice of the seducer, "Ye shall be as gods," and so abandoned God, who would have made us as gods, not by deserting Him, but by participating in Him. For without Him what have we accomplished, save to perish in His anger? But when we are restored by Him, and perfected with greater grace, we shall have eternal leisure to see that He is God, for we shall be full of Him when He shall be all in all. For even our good works, when they are understood to be rather His than ours, are imputed to us that we may enjoy this Sabbath rest. For if we attribute them to ourselves, they shall be servile; for it is said of the Sabbath, "Ye shall do no servile work in it." Wherefore also it is said by Ezekiel the prophet, "And I gave them my Sabbaths to be a sign between me and them, that they might know that I am the Lord who sanctify them." This knowledge shall be perfected when we shall be perfectly at rest, and shall perfectly know that He is God.

This Sabbath shall appear still more clearly if we count the ages as days, in accordance with the periods of time defined in Scripture, for that period will be found to be the seventh. The first age, as the first day, extends from Adam to the deluge; the second from the deluge to Abraham, equalling the first, not in length of time, but in the number of generations, there being ten in each. From Abraham to the advent of Christ there are, as the evangelist Matthew calculates, three periods, in each of which are fourteen generations,—one period from Abraham to David, a second from David to the captivity, a third from the captivity to the birth of Christ in the flesh. There are thus five ages in all. The sixth is now passing, and cannot be measured by any number of generations, as it has been said, "It is not for you to know the times, which the Father hath put in His own power." After this period God shall rest as on the seventh day, when He shall give us (who shall be the seventh day) rest in Himself. But there is not now space to treat of these ages; suffice it to say that the seventh shall be our Sabbath, which shall be brought to a close, not by an evening, but by the Lord's day, as an eighth and eternal day, consecrated by the resurrection of Christ, and prefiguring the eternal repose not only of the spirit, but also of the body. There we shall rest and see, see and love, love and praise. This is what shall be in the end without end. For what other end do we propose to ourselves than to attain to the kingdom of which there is no end?

I think I have now, by God's help, discharged my obligation in writing this large work. Let those who think I have said too little, or those who think I have said too much, forgive me; and let those who think I have said just enough join me in giving thanks to God. Amen.

sessions.readWhy: Augustine wrote The City of God over some thirteen years, and in its very last chapter he imagines the end the Bible promises. Then he counts history as a week: Adam to the flood, the flood to Abraham, Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to Christ, a sixth age 'now passing', and a seventh, 'our Sabbath', God's rest. Notice how he closes the circle with Genesis 3: we shall be, by sharing God's life, what we grabbed at when we listened to 'Ye shall be as gods'. Read Revelation 21:1–7 beside it if you can: the Bible's own last act.

think.why: Christian hope, this depth explains, is not souls floating off to the clouds but the resurrection of the body and a renewed creation: the end the whole story has been moving towards.

listen.why: Tom Holland argues that the Christian story, carried by the Church for two thousand years, reshaped what even secular people now take for granted, and Sam Harris, an atheist, presses him on it. It is the sixth act seen from the outside.

learn.why: Julian asked why sin had to happen at all, and was told that it 'behoved' to be, but that all shall be well: the story from garden to city in a single line.

music.why: Heber's hymn is drawn from the worship of heaven in Revelation 4. The end of the story is not silence but praise, as Augustine says.

look.why: In Thomas Cole's The Return we look down from a height on a stone church with stained-glass windows and spires, framed by copper and bronze trees in low, honey-gold light. A picture of homecoming, and of the place where the story is told until its end.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: the Church is the people who carry the story on. Go once to a service near you, evensong if there is one, and listen for which act of the story each reading comes from.
sessions.reflect: If the story ends like this, what difference does it make to how you live in the middle of it?

closing.title: The seventh act
closing.prompt: Augustine called the last age 'our Sabbath', the act still to come. You have read the story from a garden to a city, and heard the case that it is not one story at all. Now tell it in your own words, in seven sentences: one for each act, and the seventh for the ending that has not happened yet. Then, if you wish, add an eighth: where, if anywhere, do you find yourself in it?
closing.practice: Over the next seven weeks, reread one passage from each act, one a week, and once in that time tell the whole story aloud to someone who asks: a child, a friend, anyone curious.

title: Can I trust the Bible?
question: Can a thinking person today trust the Bible?
line: Seven sessions that test the Bible the way you would test any old story: what it is, where both Testaments came from, whether it has been copied faithfully, what archaeology and Roman and Jewish writers say, the strongest case against it, and the verdict.
why: Before walking through the Bible's story, you need to know what kind of thing it is and whether it deserves a hearing. This journey weighs the evidence the way a historian would: the writers' own claims, the formation of both Testaments and how the churches' Bibles differ, the eyewitness question, archaeology and the Roman and Jewish writers, the manuscripts and the canon. Then it gives the sceptic the floor at full strength, and ends with Augustine on how to read honestly. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year theology paper introducing the study of the Bible: its formation, canon, text and interpretation, with the historical-critical method and its critics.
outcomes: Explain what the Bible is, and exactly how Jewish, Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and views of its authority differ.
Describe how the Old Testament came together and why Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Bibles differ.
Explain why 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 matters for the history of Jesus, and weigh the debate about eyewitnesses behind the Gospels.
Set out the evidence from archaeology and from Roman and Jewish writers, for both Testaments, and say honestly where it is silent.
Say what the manuscript evidence is for both Testaments, what textual variants are, and how the New Testament canon was recognised.
State Spinoza's case against the traditional authorship of the Pentateuch at full strength, and say which parts of it are now widely accepted and which conclusions do not follow.
Use Augustine's principles and the four senses to read a passage of Scripture carefully and honestly.

glossary.def: The study of the past through what people left behind: buildings, objects, inscriptions.
Words carved or written on stone, metal or clay, often the most direct evidence from the ancient world.
A fixed pattern of Bible readings for worship through the year.
In the Catholic Church, the teaching office of the pope and bishops, which gives the authoritative interpretation of Scripture and Tradition.
The view of some scholars that the Old Testament tells us little about the history of early Israel.
A stone box for the bones of the dead, used by Jews in Jerusalem in Jesus' time.
Writing under someone else's name; scholars debate how far it was accepted in the ancient world.
Reading a text as pointing to a further meaning beyond the literal, as when Jerusalem stands for the Church.
Books in the Greek Old Testament but not the Hebrew, such as Tobit and the Maccabees. Catholics and Orthodox call them deuterocanonical and include them.
From the Greek for a measuring rod: the list of books accepted as Scripture.
A book with pages, as opposed to a scroll. Christians adopted it early and widely.
A short summary of belief, from the Latin credo, 'I believe'.
About 900 manuscripts found near Qumran from 1947, including the oldest known copies of Old Testament books.
The theory that the Pentateuch combines four sources, J, E, D and P; given its classic form by Wellhausen in 1878.
Drawing out the meaning of a text by careful study.
Someone who saw the events; in Gospel study, those whose testimony stands behind the accounts.
The medieval way of reading Scripture: literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical.
A family of second-century movements teaching salvation by secret knowledge and often that matter is evil.
Old English 'good news', translating the Greek euangelion; also each of the four accounts of Jesus.
Studying the Bible as historians study any ancient text: asking who wrote, when, for whom and from what sources.
The belief that God worked through the human writers of Scripture: 'God-breathed' (2 Timothy 3:16).
A handwritten copy of a text.
The standard Hebrew text of the Old Testament, fixed with vowels and notes by the Masoretes, about AD 600–1000.
Teaching and stories passed on by word of mouth before, and alongside, writing.
Writing material made from Egyptian reeds; the earliest New Testament fragments are on papyrus.
Greek for 'five scrolls': Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, the Torah.
A professional writer and copyist; in Judaism also a teacher of the law.

Matthew, Mark and Luke, which 'see together' and share much material.

sessions.title: What the Bible is
sessions.line: A library of many books, and why the churches' Bibles differ.
sessions.plain: The Bible is not one book but a library: law, history, poetry, prophecy, letters and biographies, written by many people over more than a thousand years. Jews, Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox Christians do not even agree on exactly which books it contains. Before asking whether it can be trusted, you need to know what it is.
sessions.why: Most arguments about the Bible go wrong at the start, because people treat it as one book of one kind. This session gives you the map: what is in the library, how the churches' Bibles differ, and what the biblical writers themselves claimed.
answers: What exactly is the Bible?
Why are Jewish, Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles different?
How do the churches differ on the Bible's authority?
What did the biblical writers claim for their own work?
before: Each of these writers says something about how their words came to be. What does each one claim?
Does anyone here claim to be a neutral observer?
What is the Bible said to be for?
sessions.readWhy: Four short passages in which biblical writers tell us what they were doing: a letter on the many ways God has spoken, a historian explaining his method, a Gospel writer stating his purpose, and a teacher describing what the Scriptures are for. Before anyone else judges the Bible, hear how it describes itself.

paras: God, having in the past spoken to the fathers through the prophets at many times and in various ways,
has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds.
Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative concerning those matters which have been fulfilled among us,
even as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us,
it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write to you in order, most excellent Theophilus;
that you might know the certainty concerning the things in which you were instructed.
Therefore Jesus did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book;
but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.
But you remain in the things which you have learned and have been assured of, knowing from whom you have learned them.
From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith, which is in Christ Jesus.
Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness,
that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

parts.title: God spoke in many ways
parts.context: The opening of the Letter to the Hebrews, written in elegant Greek by an unknown early Christian, probably before AD 70, to Jewish believers tempted to drift back from their new faith. Its first sentence is a summary of the whole Bible.

commentary.on: at many times and in various ways
commentary.text: The writer knows the Scriptures are not one voice from the sky. They came over many centuries, through many people, in many forms: law, story, song, prophecy. Hold on to this phrase; it is the key to this whole session. The Bible is a library, and its variety is not an embarrassment but part of how it says God spoke.

commentary.on: through the prophets
commentary.text: In the Bible a prophet is not mainly a fortune-teller. A prophet is a spokesman, someone who speaks for God to his own generation, often to rebuke kings and call the people back to justice.

commentary.on: has at the end of these days spoken to us by his Son
commentary.text: Here is the Christian claim in a sentence. God's speaking reaches its climax not in a book but in a person. That is why Christians read the whole library, Old Testament included, as leading up to Jesus. It also means that, for a Christian, trusting the Bible is in the end about trusting him.

parts.title: A historian's preface
parts.context: The first four verses of Luke's Gospel, written in the later first century by a companion of Paul who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles. In Greek it is one long, polished sentence, in the style of the historians of the day.

commentary.on: many have undertaken to set in order a narrative
commentary.text: Luke is not the first to write about Jesus, and he says so. Written accounts were already circulating. Most scholars think Mark's Gospel was one of them, since Luke uses much of it.

commentary.on: those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word delivered them to us
commentary.text: Luke does not claim to have seen the events himself. He claims something more modest and more checkable: that his sources go back to people who were there from the start. 'Delivered' is a technical word for handing on a tradition carefully. Session 3 tests this claim.

commentary.on: having traced the course of all things accurately from the first
commentary.text: This is the language of research. Luke presents himself as a careful investigator, and in session 5 you will see how his details about rulers and places hold up against archaeology.

commentary.on: that you might know the certainty
commentary.text: His purpose is not entertainment but confidence. Theophilus ('friend of God') has already been taught the faith; Luke wants him to know it rests on solid ground. Notice that the Bible's own writers thought evidence mattered.

parts.title: Written that you may believe
parts.context: Near the end of John's Gospel, probably the last of the four to be written, in the 90s AD. The writer pauses to tell us why he wrote.

commentary.on: many other signs ... which are not written in this book
commentary.text: John admits he has been selective. Every historian selects; the question is whether the selection distorts. John's honesty about it is worth noticing.

commentary.on: these are written, that you may believe
commentary.text: John is open about his purpose: not neutral reporting but testimony meant to persuade. Sceptics sometimes say this makes the Gospels worthless as history. But a witness with a purpose can still be telling the truth; a survivor who writes to warn the world is no less reliable for wanting to warn it. The question is not whether a writer has a point of view, but whether the testimony is true.

parts.title: What the Scriptures are for
parts.context: From a letter to Timothy, Paul's younger colleague, presented as Paul's last letter before his execution in Rome in the mid-60s AD. (Many modern scholars think it was written by a follower in Paul's name; session 6 explains why.)

commentary.on: From infancy, you have known the holy Scriptures
commentary.text: Timothy's mother was Jewish and his father Greek (Acts 16:1). He grew up with the Jewish Scriptures, our Old Testament. When this letter says 'Scripture', that is chiefly what it means: the New Testament was still being written.

commentary.on: Every Scripture is God-breathed
commentary.text: One Greek word, theopneustos, found only here. It says the Scriptures come from God as breath comes from a mouth. Christians have understood this in different ways, but most have held that God worked through the human writers, with their own styles and knowledge, rather than dictating to them like a secretary.

commentary.on: profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness
commentary.text: Notice what inspiration is for. Not to answer every question we might ask, about science, say, but to form a person: to teach, to correct and to train in right living. Judge the Bible by what it says it is for.

paras: I resolved then to bend my mind to the holy Scriptures, that I might see what they were. But behold, I see a thing not understood by the proud, nor laid open to children, lowly in access, in its recesses lofty, and veiled with mysteries; and I was not such as could enter into it, or stoop my neck to follow its steps. For not as I now speak, did I feel when I turned to those Scriptures; but they seemed to me unworthy to be compared to the stateliness of Tully: for my swelling pride shrunk from their lowliness, nor could my sharp wit pierce the interior thereof. Yet were they such as would grow up in a little one. But I disdained to be a little one; and, swollen with pride, took myself to be a great one.

parts.title: Unworthy of Cicero?
parts.context: Augustine of Hippo (354–430), later a bishop and the most influential thinker of the Latin West, wrote his Confessions around 397–400 as a prayer to God telling the story of his life. Here he looks back to the age of nineteen, when he was a brilliant young teacher of rhetoric in Carthage.
parts.author: Augustine of Hippo

commentary.on: the stateliness of Tully
commentary.text: 'Tully' is Cicero, Marcus Tullius Cicero, the master of Latin prose. Augustine had just been bowled over by Cicero's call to love wisdom. Next to Cicero, the Latin Bible of the day, a rough translation, seemed clumsy and provincial.

commentary.on: lowly in access, in its recesses lofty
commentary.text: This is the older Augustine's verdict, and one of the best descriptions of the Bible ever written. It is simple enough at the door for a child to walk in, and deep enough inside that no scholar reaches the end of it.

commentary.on: I disdained to be a little one
commentary.text: Augustine's problem, he now thinks, was not the Bible's style but his own pride. You need not agree with him. But notice that first impressions of the Bible can mislead, and that he changed his mind after years of reading it. You will meet him again in the last session.

parts.plain: Augustine says: when I was young and proud, I tried reading the Bible, but it seemed plain and clumsy next to the great Roman writer Cicero. I didn't see that it is easy to walk into but very deep inside. I was too proud to become like a child and learn from it.

compare.author: Augustine of Hippo
compare.why: One of the cleverest men of the fourth century describes his first attempt to read the Bible. He found it crude next to Cicero's polished Latin, and gave up. Many readers today will recognise the feeling.
compare.title: A clever man's first reaction

paras: Our word Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, 'the books', a plural. That is the first thing to know. The Bible is a library bound in one cover: in a Protestant Bible, 39 books in the Old Testament and 27 in the New, 66 in all.

These books were written over more than a thousand years by kings, prophets, priests, fishermen, a tax collector, a doctor and a tentmaker, in three languages: Hebrew, a little Aramaic, and Greek. They include law codes, family stories, royal chronicles, love poetry, hymns, proverbs, prophetic visions, four biographies of Jesus and a collection of letters.
sections.key: The Bible is a library of many books, by many writers, in three languages, over more than a thousand years.

sections.h: Read each book as what it is
paras: Because the Bible holds so many kinds of writing, the first rule is to ask what kind you are reading. A psalm is a poem: when it says 'Let the rivers clap their hands' (Psalm 98:8), nobody is meant to look for palms. A proverb is a general truth, not a guarantee. A letter answers questions we have to reconstruct. A history tells what happened, selected and shaped to show what it meant.

Many arguments for and against the Bible go wrong here. Sceptics sometimes read poetry as if it were a science textbook and find it absurd; believers sometimes do the same and end up defending what the writer never claimed.
sections.key: The first rule of reading is to ask what kind of writing you are reading.

paras: The Old Testament is the Bible of Israel, which Jews call the Tanakh, from the initials of its three parts: the Torah (the Law, the five books of Moses), the Nevi'im (the Prophets) and the Ketuvim (the Writings). Jesus and his first followers were Jews, and this was their Bible.

The New Testament was written by Christians in Greek within about seventy years of Jesus' death: four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, letters, and the Revelation to John. 'Testament' means covenant: the old covenant with Israel, and what Christians believe is the new covenant in Jesus, promised by the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 31:31).
sections.key: The Old Testament was Israel's Bible and Jesus' own; the New was written by his followers within about seventy years.

sections.h: Whose Bible? How the canons differ
paras: Here is something many Christians never learn: the churches do not have the same list of books. The differences are all in the Old Testament. Jews and Protestants follow the Hebrew collection. Catholics and the Orthodox also accept books that were in the Greek translation used by the first Christians, the Septuagint, which you will meet in the next session.
The New Testament's 27 books are the same in almost every church. The table shows the main differences.

rows: 24 books: the same text as the Protestant 39, counted differently

sections.h: Who has the last word? How the churches differ on authority
paras: The churches also differ on how the Bible relates to the Church's teaching. All agree that Scripture is inspired. They disagree about who interprets it and whether anything stands beside it.
These differences go back to the Reformation of the sixteenth century, and you will meet them again in Hall VI. For now, it is enough to see them side by side.

Every believer may read it, and it is clear on what is needed for salvation
King James Version, New International Version, English Standard Version

sections.key: Protestants hold Scripture alone as final; Catholics hold Scripture and Tradition together under the Church's teaching office; the Orthodox read Scripture within Holy Tradition.

paras: Notice what the passages you read claim, and what they do not. Hebrews says God spoke in many ways. Luke claims careful research and sources going back to eyewitnesses. John claims testimony with an open purpose. The letter to Timothy claims that the Scriptures are God-breathed and useful for forming a life. None claims to be a neutral observer, and none claims to answer every question we might put to it.

Most Christians have held that God worked through the human writers rather than dictating to them. That is why Luke can say he researched, why each Gospel sounds like its author, and why the Bible can be studied as human writing without ceasing, for believers, to be the word of God. Muslims believe something different about the Qur'an: that it was dictated word for word.
sections.key: The writers claim research, testimony and inspiration, not neutrality; most Christians believe God worked through their human voices.

debate.question: Is the Bible one book or a library?

positions.name: One Word
positions.who: Most of the Christian tradition
positions.view: Behind the many human writers stands one divine author, so the Bible can be read as a single, coherent message, each part interpreting the others.
positions.evidence: The unity of its story from creation to new creation; the way the New Testament reads the Old; Jesus' own reading in Luke 24.

positions.name: Many voices
positions.who: Many modern historians of the Bible
positions.view: The Bible is an anthology of very different writings from different times, which sometimes disagree. Its unity was imposed later by the communities that collected it.
positions.evidence: Differences of language, date, theology and detail between books, such as the four Gospels.

positions.name: Both at once
positions.who: Many theologians today, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant
positions.view: God speaks through real human voices, with all their variety. The diversity is part of the message, and the unity lies in the story they tell together rather than in uniformity.
positions.evidence: The early Church chose to keep four Gospels rather than one harmonised account.

debate.agree: All agree that each book must be read for what it is, and that the Bible has shaped the West more than any other text.

look.why: For most of history people heard the Scriptures read aloud. Carpaccio, around 1505, painted Mary reading a small book alone, which was becoming possible for more people as printing made books cheaper.

One finger kept between the pages, as if she will come back to her place.
Behind a low white wall, a yellow meadow runs down to pale blue water, with hills, a few white buildings and a tower beyond.
At the left edge, a shoulder, an elbow and a foot of someone in midnight blue: a hint that the painting was once part of a larger picture.

learn.why: The Bible's shortest answer to what it is for: light for the next step, not a map of everything.

check.q: A Catholic and a Protestant compare their Bibles. What is the real difference?
options: The Protestant Bible leaves out some of the Psalms
The Catholic Old Testament has seven more books, and longer Esther and Daniel, from the Greek Bible
The Catholic Bible includes Gospels written after AD 300
They have different New Testaments
check.why: Both share the same 27 New Testament books. The difference is the deuterocanonical books of the Septuagint, which Protestants call the Apocrypha.

check.q: A Jewish friend calls her Bible the Tanakh; a Christian friend calls the same books the Old Testament. Why the different names?
options: They are completely different books
Christians believe God made a new covenant in Jesus, so they call the earlier Scriptures the 'old' covenant; Jews do not accept the New Testament
The Torah is only for rabbis
Christians do not read these books
check.why: Same books, different order and different names, because Jews and Christians read them in different lights.

check.q: What does Luke claim in his preface, and what does he not claim?
options: He claims to have seen the events himself
He claims to have researched accounts handed down from eyewitnesses, not to have been one
He claims that God dictated the text to him
He claims to be the first to write about Jesus

check.q: Why is it a mistake to quote 2 Timothy 3:16 ('Every Scripture is God-breathed') as the New Testament's claim about itself?
options: The verse was added in the Middle Ages
When it was written, 'Scripture' meant chiefly the Jewish Scriptures; the New Testament was still being written
Paul did not believe in inspiration
'God-breathed' only means 'poetic'

options: The Hebrew Masoretic text
The Greek Septuagint
Jerome's Latin Vulgate
The King James Version
check.why: The Septuagint was the Bible of the Greek-speaking first Christians, and Orthodox churches still use it.

check.q: On authority, what really separates the Protestant principle from the Catholic one?
options: Protestants reject all tradition; Catholics do not read the Bible
Protestants hold Scripture to be the final judge of all teaching; Catholics hold Scripture and Tradition together, interpreted by the Church's teaching office
Only Catholics believe the Bible is inspired
Protestants accept more books than Catholics
check.why: Both hold Scripture inspired; they differ on whether anything stands beside it and who interprets it.

check.q: A sceptic quotes 'Let the rivers clap their hands' as proof the Bible is unscientific. What is the best reply?
options: The verse is a mistranslation
It is a poem, and mistaking its genre is the sceptic's error
Rivers did once make that sound
The Psalms are not really part of the Bible
check.why: Reading poetry as a science textbook is the commonest mistake about the Bible, made by sceptics and believers alike.

tutorial.question: Is it fair to call the Bible 'a library, not a book'? What follows for how it should be read, and for the differences between the churches?
tutorial.approach: Describe its variety (writers, centuries, languages, kinds of writing). Explain why Christians have nevertheless read it as one story. Use Luke and John to show what the writers claimed. Then explain the differences in canon and authority between Jews, Protestants, Catholics and the Orthodox, and say what they have in common.
strong: Shows the real variety: dates, authors, languages, genres.
Explains the unity Christians find: one story from creation to new creation.
Uses the writers' own claims (Luke's research, John's purpose).
Explains accurately why the canons differ (the Septuagint and the deuterocanonical books).
Explains the difference between sola scriptura, Scripture and Tradition, and Holy Tradition.
Draws practical rules: read by genre; ask what the writer claimed; read the parts in the light of the whole.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: read one whole short book of the Bible in a single sitting (Ruth, Jonah, Mark or Philippians), the way it was meant to be heard, and tell someone what kind of writing it was.
sessions.reflect: What did you assume the Bible was before this session? What, if anything, has changed?
takeaways: The Bible is a library: many writers, three languages, more than a thousand years; each book must be read for what it is.
Jews and Protestants follow the Hebrew canon; Catholics and the Orthodox also accept books from the Greek Bible; the New Testament is shared.
Its writers claim research, testimony and inspiration, not neutrality; whether to trust them is what the rest of the journey weighs.
sessions.finding: The Bible is a library of many books. Christians agree on the New Testament and differ only over a few Old Testament books.

background.h: If you have never read the Bible
paras: That is fine. Most people today haven't, and this journey assumes nothing. You do not need to believe anything to follow it. You only need to be willing to look at the evidence.

The Bible is the sacred book of Christians, and its first and larger part is also the sacred book of Jews. It is not one book but a collection of sixty-six or more books, written over a very long time. Christians divide it into two parts: the Old Testament, written before Jesus, and the New Testament, written by his followers after his death.
background.key: The Bible is a collection of books: the Old Testament before Jesus, the New Testament after him.

paras: The Old Testament opens with God creating the world and human beings, and humans turning away from him. It then follows one family, Abraham's, to whom God promises a land and a blessing for all nations. Abraham's descendants, the Israelites, become slaves in Egypt and are led out by Moses, who receives God's law at Mount Sinai. They settle in Canaan (roughly modern Israel and Palestine), are ruled by kings such as David and Solomon, and are warned by prophets when they turn to injustice and other gods. Their kingdoms are destroyed by the empires of Assyria and Babylon, and many are taken into exile. Some return, rebuild Jerusalem and its Temple, and wait for God to act again.

The New Testament tells of Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher born into that waiting people under Roman rule. He preached, healed, was crucified by the Romans in Jerusalem, and his followers proclaimed that God had raised him from the dead. It then follows the first Christians as the message spread across the Roman Empire, through their letters, and ends with a vision of a renewed creation.
background.key: Creation, Abraham, Moses, the kings and prophets, exile and return; then Jesus, and the first Christians.

background.h: Torah, Hebrew Bible, Old Testament: what's the difference?
paras: These names confuse almost everyone, so here they are simply. The Torah (Hebrew for 'teaching' or 'instruction') is the first five books of the Bible: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. They tell the story from creation to the death of Moses, and contain the law God gave Israel at Mount Sinai. They are also called the Law of Moses or the Pentateuch ('five scrolls').

The Torah is the heart of Judaism. In every synagogue it is handwritten on a scroll, kept in a cabinet called the ark, and read aloud in portions week by week until the whole of it has been read in a year. Jews live by its commandments, as interpreted over centuries by the rabbis in the Talmud. But the Jewish Bible is bigger than the Torah: it adds the Prophets and the Writings (Psalms, Proverbs and others). Jews call the whole thing the Tanakh, or the Hebrew Bible.

Christians call those very same books the Old Testament. 'Testament' means covenant, a binding agreement between God and people. Christians believe that in Jesus God made the 'new covenant' that the prophet Jeremiah had promised (Jeremiah 31:31), so they call the earlier Scriptures the Old Testament and the writings about Jesus the New Testament. 'Old' means earlier, not out of date: the Old Testament is about three-quarters of the Christian Bible. Jews do not use the name, because they do not accept the New Testament, and many scholars say 'Hebrew Bible' to stay neutral.

So do both honour it? Yes. Jews and Christians both treat these books as God's word: the Psalms are prayed in synagogues and churches every day. The difference is how they read them. Jews read them through the Torah and the rabbis' teaching, and keep the Torah's laws, such as the Sabbath and the food laws. Christians read them through Jesus, who said of the law and the prophets, 'I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill' (Matthew 5:17). The first Christians decided that non-Jewish believers need not keep the Jewish ritual laws (Acts 15), but Christians keep the Torah's moral heart: the Ten Commandments, and the two commands Jesus called the greatest, both quoted from the Torah: love God (Deuteronomy 6:5) and love your neighbour as yourself (Leviticus 19:18).

rows: The first five books, Genesis to Deuteronomy
Jews (and everyone, for these five books)
Torah + Prophets + Writings: the whole Jewish Bible
The same books, in a different order (plus a few more for Catholics and Orthodox)
Gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation, about Jesus and his first followers

background.key: The Torah is the first five books; the Tanakh is the whole Jewish Bible; Christians call the same books the Old Testament. Both honour them, reading them in different lights.

paras: Here are the main landmarks, so that every passage in this journey has a place. Dates before about 1000 BC are traditional and debated; later ones are firm. BC means 'before Christ', counting down to the year 1; AD (Anno Domini, 'in the year of the Lord') counts up from it. Many historians write BCE and CE for the same years.

timeline.text: Abraham, by tradition
Moses and the Exodus from Egypt, by a common dating
King David; Solomon builds the Temple in Jerusalem
Assyria destroys the northern kingdom of Israel
Assyria besieges Jerusalem under King Hezekiah
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the Temple; exile
Persia conquers Babylon; exiles begin to return
Ezra reads the Law in Jerusalem

Rome takes control
