Rome destroys Jerusalem and the Temple

paras: Imagine your family has an old story, handed down for generations, about something that happened to a great-great-grandparent. How would you decide whether to believe it? You would ask a few simple questions, one after another. This journey asks the same questions of the Bible, one per session.

First, what exactly is it (this session)? Second and third, where did it come from, and were the people who wrote it close to what they describe (sessions 2 and 3)? Fourth, has it been passed down without being changed (session 4)? Fifth, does anything outside the story back it up (session 5)? Sixth, what do the people who doubt it say, at their strongest (session 6)? And last, putting it all together, what should we conclude, and how should we read it (session 7)? At the start of each session you will see the case so far.
background.key: Six checks, as for any old family story: what it is, where it came from, faithful copies, outside evidence, the doubters, the verdict.

background.h: Why we start with these passages
paras: Before asking whether the Bible can be trusted, it is only fair to ask what it claims for itself. So this session begins with four short passages, chosen because in each a biblical writer steps back and tells us what he is doing: one says how God spoke through many voices, one explains how he researched, one says why he wrote, and one says what the Scriptures are for.

They come from the New Testament, written in the first century AD, but they look back on the whole library. Each has a short introduction telling you who wrote it and when, then the text, then a commentary walking you through it. Take them slowly: they are short.
background.key: We start with what the Bible's own writers claim, before testing those claims.

sessions.title: How the Old Testament came together
sessions.line: We cannot watch the books being written. But we can catch them in use, at three moments in history.
sessions.plain: Nobody filmed the Old Testament being written, and its books do not come with dates on them. What historians can do is find moments where we see these books existing and being treated as sacred, and the oldest physical copies. This session follows three such moments, 622 BC, 445 BC and AD 95, and the oldest surviving fragments, to answer a simple question: is the Old Testament we read really the ancient book of ancient Israel, or something put together much later?
sessions.why: Session 1 showed what the Bible is. Before we can trust any part of it, we need to know that it is genuinely old, and that it has not been invented or rewritten since. We begin with the Old Testament, the older and larger half.
answers: Who wrote the Old Testament, and when?
How do we know these books are really ancient, and not invented later?
When did they become a fixed collection, and who decided?
Why do Jewish, Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments differ?
before: In each scene, a book is read aloud. What book, and how do people react?
What does each scene tell you about how old the book already was, and how much authority it had?
In the comparison, what does Josephus say about how many books there were, and how his people treated them?
sessions.readWhy: Two scenes, about 180 years apart, where we can watch the Law of Moses being read aloud to the whole people: first under King Josiah in 622 BC, then under Ezra in about 445 BC. Then, in the comparison, a Jewish historian in AD 95 describes the finished collection. Three snapshots of the Old Testament taking shape.

paras: Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the book of the law in Yahweh’s house.” Hilkiah delivered the book to Shaphan, and he read it.

Shaphan the scribe came to the king, and brought the king word again, and said, “Your servants have emptied out the money that was found in the house, and have delivered it into the hands of the workmen who have the oversight of Yahweh’s house.”
Shaphan the scribe told the king, saying, “Hilkiah the priest has delivered a book to me.” Then Shaphan read it before the king.
When the king had heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes.
The king commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Achbor the son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying,

“Go inquire of Yahweh for me, and for the people, and for all Judah, concerning the words of this book that is found; for great is Yahweh’s wrath that is kindled against us, because our fathers have not listened to the words of this book, to do according to all that which is written concerning us.”
The king sent, and they gathered to him all the elders of Judah and of Jerusalem.

The king went up to Yahweh’s house, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with him, with the priests, the prophets, and all the people, both small and great; and he read in their hearing all the words of the book of the covenant which was found in Yahweh’s house.

The king stood by the pillar, and made a covenant before Yahweh, to walk after Yahweh, and to keep his commandments, his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and all his soul, to confirm the words of this covenant that were written in this book; and all the people agreed to the covenant.

All the people gathered themselves together as one man into the wide place that was in front of the water gate; and they spoke to Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which Yahweh had commanded to Israel.
Ezra the priest brought the law before the assembly, both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding, on the first day of the seventh month.

He read from it before the wide place that was in front of the water gate from early morning until midday, in the presence of the men and the women, and of those who could understand. The ears of all the people were attentive to the book of the law.

Ezra the scribe stood on a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people (for he was above all the people), and when he opened it, all the people stood up.
Then Ezra blessed Yahweh, the great God.
All the people answered, “Amen, Amen,” with the lifting up of their hands. They bowed their heads, and worshiped Yahweh with their faces to the ground.

Also Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites, caused the people to understand the law; and the people stayed in their place.
They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading.

Nehemiah, who was the governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who taught the people, said to all the people, “Today is holy to Yahweh your God. Don’t mourn, nor weep.” For all the people wept when they heard the words of the law.

Then he said to them, “Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared, for today is holy to our Lord. Don’t be grieved, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.”
So the Levites calmed all the people, saying, “Hold your peace, for the day is holy. Don’t be grieved.”
All the people went their way to eat, to drink, to send portions, and to celebrate, because they had understood the words that were declared to them.

parts.title: Snapshot 1, 622 BC: a book found in the Temple
parts.context: Jerusalem, 622 BC, in the eighteenth year of King Josiah of Judah. Workmen are repairing the Temple, which Solomon had built about 350 years earlier. During the repairs the high priest finds something. This is the first time the Bible describes a book of God's law being read, and it is about 35 years before the Babylonians destroy the city.

commentary.on: I have found the book of the law in Yahweh's house
commentary.text: A book of the law is found in the Temple. Most scholars, ancient and modern, think it was some form of Deuteronomy, the fifth book of Moses, because what Josiah does next, abolishing worship outside Jerusalem and destroying idols (2 Kings 23), follows Deuteronomy's commands closely.

commentary.on: Shaphan the scribe
commentary.text: Notice the scribe. Writing and reading were specialist skills, and royal scribes kept and copied documents. Shaphan's son and grandson appear in Jeremiah 36, which you will read in session 4, and a clay seal of 'Gemaryahu son of Shaphan' has been found in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: When the king had heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes
commentary.text: The king treats the book as carrying God's authority, and is horrified at how far the nation has strayed from it. So by 622 BC there is a written law, believed to be ancient, with power to judge a king.

commentary.on: our fathers have not listened to the words of this book
commentary.text: Here is the great debate. Josiah and the writer of Kings believe this was an old book that had been neglected and lost. Many modern scholars think Deuteronomy, in the form found, was in fact written not long before, perhaps by reforming priests, and 'found' to give their reforms authority. Others think it preserved much older law. Either way, this scene is a fixed point: a written book of the Law existed and was treated as Scripture by 622 BC.

commentary.on: he read in their hearing all the words of the book of the covenant
commentary.text: The king reads the book to everyone, 'small and great', and the people commit themselves to it. The pattern of a nation ordering its life by a written covenant begins here.

parts.title: Snapshot 2, about 445 BC: the Law read at the Water Gate
parts.context: About 180 years later. In between, Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the Temple (587 BC) and took its leaders into exile; Persia conquered Babylon (539 BC) and let the exiles go home. A small, poor community has rebuilt the Temple and, under Nehemiah, the city walls. Now Ezra, a priest and scribe who has come from Persia, brings out 'the book of the law of Moses'.

commentary.on: they spoke to Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses
commentary.text: This time the book is not a surprising discovery: everyone knows it, and the people ask for it. Most scholars think 'the book of the law of Moses' here means the Torah, the five books from Genesis to Deuteronomy, in something close to their final form. So by about 445 BC the heart of the Old Testament existed as a finished, recognised book.

commentary.on: both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding
commentary.text: The Law is read to the whole community, women included. A people who had lost their king, their independence and their Temple found their identity in a book. That is why they guarded it so carefully, and why this matters for trust: a community that lives by a text has every reason to preserve it exactly.

commentary.on: all the people stood up
commentary.text: They stand when the book is opened. Jews still stand when the Torah scroll is brought out in the synagogue, and many Christians stand for the Gospel. You are watching a practice that is about 2,500 years old.

commentary.on: they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading
commentary.text: The Levites explain the text, perhaps translating it from Hebrew into Aramaic, which many returned exiles now spoke better. From the start the Bible came with teaching. This verse matters later: in session 6, the sceptic Spinoza uses it to argue that Ezra didn't just read the Law but edited it.

parts.title: From tears to a feast
parts.context: The same morning. Hearing the Law after years of neglect, the people are overcome.

commentary.on: all the people wept when they heard the words of the law
commentary.text: They recognise themselves in the text and are grieved by how far they have strayed, just as Josiah was. Two scenes, 180 years apart, with the same reaction: this book was felt to speak with God's voice.

commentary.on: send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared
commentary.text: The leaders turn grief into a feast, and the feast must include the poor. The verse you will learn by heart.

paras: 8. For we have not an innumerable multitude of books among us, disagreeing from and contradicting one another, [as the Greeks have,] but only twenty-two books, [8] which contain the records of all the past times; which are justly believed to be divine; and of them five belong to Moses, which contain his laws and the traditions of the origin of mankind till his death. This interval of time was little short of three thousand years; but as to the time from the death of Moses till the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, who reigned after Xerxes, the prophets, who were after Moses, wrote down what was done in their times in thirteen books. The remaining four books contain hymns to God, and precepts for the conduct of human life. It is true, our history hath been written since Artaxerxes very particularly, but hath not been esteemed of the like authority with the former by our forefathers, because there hath not been an exact succession of prophets since that time; and how firmly we have given credit to these books of our own nation is evident by what we do; for during so many ages as have already passed, no one has been so bold as either to add any thing to them, to take any thing from them, or to make any change in them;

but it is become natural to all Jews immediately, and from their very birth, to esteem these books to contain Divine doctrines, and to persist in them, and, if occasion be willingly to die for them. For it is no new thing for our captives, many of them in number, and frequently in time, to be seen to endure racks and deaths of all kinds upon the theatres, that they may not be obliged to say one word against our laws and the records that contain them; whereas there are none at all among the Greeks who would undergo the least harm on that account, no, nor in case all the writings that are among them were to be destroyed; for they take them to be such discourses as are framed agreeably to the inclinations of those that write them; and they have justly the same opinion of the ancient writers, since they see some of the present generation bold enough to write about such affairs, wherein they were not present, nor had concern enough to inform themselves about them from those that knew them; examples of which may be had in this late war of ours, where some persons have written histories, and published them, without having been in the places concerned, or having been near them when the actions were done; but these men put a few things together by hearsay, and insolently abuse the world, and call these writings by the name of Histories.

parts.title: Twenty-two books
parts.context: Flavius Josephus (about 37–100) was a Jewish priest and general who fought Rome in the war of 66–70, was captured, changed sides and spent the rest of his life writing history in Rome. Against Apion, written around 95, defends the Jewish people against an Egyptian-Greek writer who had attacked them. Here he contrasts Jewish sacred books with the many conflicting histories of the Greeks.
parts.author: Flavius Josephus

commentary.on: only twenty-two books
commentary.text: Josephus' twenty-two are the same as the thirty-nine of the Protestant Old Testament, counted differently: the twelve minor prophets count as one book, Samuel, Kings and Chronicles as one each, Ezra and Nehemiah together, and so on. He does not include the extra books found in the Greek Bible, which is why Protestants leave them out.

commentary.on: five belong to Moses ... the prophets ... wrote down what was done in their times in thirteen books. The remaining four books contain hymns to God
commentary.text: The three-part shape that Jews still use: the Law (Genesis to Deuteronomy), the Prophets, and the Writings (Psalms, Proverbs and the like). Josephus describes it as something every Jew knew.

commentary.on: the reign of Artaxerxes
commentary.text: Artaxerxes I ruled Persia in the fifth century BC, the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. Josephus says later books exist but lack the same authority, because 'there hath not been an exact succession of prophets since that time'. In other words, he believed the collection closed in Ezra's age, the second snapshot.

commentary.on: no one has been so bold as either to add any thing to them, to take any thing from them
commentary.text: A large claim, and he is arguing a case. But the Dead Sea Scrolls, copied in the centuries just before Josephus, bear out the care with which these books were copied (session 4).

commentary.on: willingly to die for them
commentary.text: This is not exaggeration: in the persecution of 167 BC under the Greek king Antiochus IV, Jews were killed for keeping copies of the Law, as 1 Maccabees records. People do not die for books they think anyone can rewrite.

commentary.on: they see some of the present generation bold enough to write about such affairs, wherein they were not present
commentary.text: Josephus attacks Greek historians who wrote without having been there or asked those who were. Ancient readers already knew the difference between testimony and hearsay. Keep that in mind for session 3.

parts.plain: Josephus says: unlike the Greeks, who have endless history books that contradict each other, we Jews have only twenty-two sacred books: five by Moses, thirteen by the prophets, and four of songs and wise sayings. Books written after the time of Ezra are not equal to them. No one has ever dared to change them, and Jews would rather die than speak against them. The Greeks, by contrast, write histories of things they never saw.

compare.author: Flavius Josephus
compare.why: About 540 years after Ezra, a Jewish historian writing in Rome describes his people's sacred books as a fixed set of twenty-two, the same books as the Protestant Old Testament, and says no one has dared add to them or take from them. It is our clearest ancient witness to the finished collection.
compare.title: Snapshot 3, AD 95: a closed collection

sections.h: Why the origins matter for trust
paras: If the Old Testament had been invented or heavily rewritten late, say by Christians, or by rabbis after Jesus, then whatever it says about ancient Israel would be suspect. If instead its books were already old, treasured and fixed long before Jesus, and copied with great care, then what we read is genuinely what ancient Israel read.

That is what this session tests. It doesn't yet ask whether the events the books describe really happened; that is session 5. It asks a prior question: is the book itself ancient, and has it come down to us intact?
sections.key: Before asking whether the Old Testament is true, we ask whether it is genuinely ancient and intact.

paras: The Old Testament's books mostly do not name their authors. Jewish and Christian tradition assigned them: Moses for the first five books, David for many psalms, Solomon for Proverbs, the prophets for their books, Ezra for Chronicles and Ezra–Nehemiah. Most modern scholars think the books grew over centuries, through collecting, writing and editing by priests, prophets, royal scribes and their disciples, many unnamed.

Both views agree on something important: the books preserve traditions much older than their final form, and they reached that form before the time of Jesus. Where they differ is in how early, and how much, Moses and the prophets themselves wrote. Session 6 sets out that debate in full.
sections.key: Tradition names authors; most scholars see long growth by many hands. Both agree the books were complete before Jesus.

paras: Because the books carry no dates, historians look for moments where they can be seen in use. This session's readings give three. The table puts them together.

rows: A written book of God's Law, probably a form of Deuteronomy, exists and has authority over the king and the nation
The Law of Moses, probably the whole Torah, is a recognised book read to the entire people
A Jewish writer speaks of 'the law, the prophets and the other books'
Jesus speaks of 'the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms' as Scripture
A closed collection, the same books as the Protestant Old Testament

sections.key: From 622 BC to AD 95 we can watch the Old Testament take shape: first the Law, then the Prophets and Writings, then a closed collection.

paras: Snapshots in texts are one kind of evidence. Physical objects are another. The oldest surviving words of the Bible are on two tiny silver scrolls, found in 1979 in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, dated to around 600 BC, in Josiah's century. Rolled up as amulets, they carry the priestly blessing from Numbers 6:24–26, 'Yahweh bless you, and keep you', in almost the same words as our Bibles.

Then come the Dead Sea Scrolls, found from 1947 in caves near Qumran: about 900 manuscripts copied between about 250 BC and AD 68, including parts of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. They prove that all these books existed, and were being copied as Scripture, before Jesus. Session 5 shows how closely they match the text we read today.
sections.key: Silver amulets from about 600 BC and the Dead Sea Scrolls from before Jesus show the books are genuinely ancient.

paras: No council decided. The Torah was settled first, as the snapshots show; the Prophets were recognised next; the Writings last, with debate about a few books, such as Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, continuing into the first century AD. An old theory said the rabbis fixed the list at a council in Jamnia (Yavneh) around AD 90; most scholars now doubt any such decision was made. The collection was settled by centuries of use in worship and study.
Jesus treated this same collection as the word of God, 'the Scripture can't be broken' (John 10:35), and argued with other teachers about what it meant, never about whether it was Scripture.
sections.key: The collection was settled by long use, not by a council; Jesus treated it as Scripture.

paras: In the third and second centuries BC, Jews in Alexandria translated the Scriptures into Greek. This Septuagint was the Bible of most of the first Christians, and the New Testament usually quotes it. It also included books that were not in the Hebrew collection: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, the Maccabees and others.

Christians disagreed about these books for centuries. At the Reformation Protestants followed the Hebrew list, the one Josephus describes; Catholics, at the Council of Trent in 1546, affirmed the extra books; the Orthodox kept the Septuagint. That is the origin of the different Old Testaments you saw in session 1.
sections.key: The Greek Septuagint's extra books explain why the churches' Old Testaments differ.

paras: The Old Testament was not invented by the Church or by a late council. Its Law can be seen in use by 622 BC, as a finished book by about 445 BC, its three parts by about 130 BC, and a closed collection by AD 95. Its words survive on silver from about 600 BC and on scrolls from before Jesus. It was the Scripture of a people who built their life round it, and who, as Josephus says, would die rather than change it.
This shows the book is ancient and was treasured. It does not yet show that what it says happened, happened. That is the next step, in sessions 3 and 5.
sections.key: The Old Testament is genuinely ancient and was carefully kept; whether its history is true is tested next.

refs: 2 Kings 22–23; Nehemiah 8; the prologue to Sirach (about 130 BC); Luke 24:44; John 10:35; 1 Maccabees 1:56–57.

On Josiah's book and Deuteronomy: W. M. L. de Wette (1805), the classic identification; Ronald Clements, Deuteronomy (1989); for an earlier dating, K. A. Kitchen, On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003).
Josephus, Against Apion I.8 (about AD 95).
Ketef Hinnom: Gabriel Barkay et al., 'The Amulets from Ketef Hinnom: A New Edition and Evaluation', BASOR 334 (2004).
On Jamnia: Jack P. Lewis, 'What Do We Mean by Jabneh?', Journal of Bible and Religion 32 (1964); Lee Martin McDonald, The Formation of the Biblical Canon (2017).
Council of Trent, Session IV (8 April 1546).

debate.question: When was the Old Testament written down?

positions.name: Early
positions.who: Traditional Jewish and Christian views; scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen
positions.view: Much of the Law goes back to Moses, and many books were written close to the events they describe; Josiah's book was a genuinely old law rediscovered.
positions.evidence: The books' own claims; ancient Near Eastern parallels to the Law's forms; the Ketef Hinnom amulets.

positions.name: Late
positions.who: Some 'minimalist' scholars, such as Philip Davies and Niels Peter Lemche
positions.view: Most of the Old Testament was written in the Persian or Greek periods, after the exile, and tells us more about those times than about early Israel.
positions.evidence: The lack of outside evidence for early periods; the post-exile setting of the final editing.

positions.name: Over centuries
positions.who: Most scholars today
positions.view: Written traditions began under the kings, grew through the seventh century (Josiah's reign) and the exile, and were completed in the Persian period; the books preserve older memories within later editions.
positions.evidence: Josiah's book, Ezra's Torah and the long editing visible in the books themselves.

debate.agree: All agree that the Law was recognised Scripture by Ezra's time, that the collection was largely complete before Jesus, and that it was copied with great care.

look.why: For centuries the Scriptures were kept alive in households as well as in synagogues and churches. Rembrandt and his workshop painted this woman in 1637 with a heavy book in her lap.
points: A woman in a black dress with a wide starched white collar and white cuffs.
She sits in a wooden chair against a dark brown background.
Her face is lined; she looks away to our left rather than down.
In her lap, a thick book fastened with metal clasps, her hand resting on it, holding a pair of spectacles.

music.why: Psalm 23 in the Scottish metrical psalter, sung to Crimond: the Old Testament as ordinary people have carried it, by heart and in song.

think.why: Jerusalem is the West's first root. This depth sets it beside Athens.

learn.why: Said to a people weeping over the law they had broken: the reading was meant to end in a feast shared with the poor.

check.q: Why does this session start with scenes of the Law being read, rather than with the writing of the books?
options: Because the books were never written down
Because the books carry no dates, so historians look for datable moments when we can see them existing and in use
Because Ezra wrote the whole Old Testament
Because reading is more important than writing
check.why: Snapshots of use give us latest possible dates for the books' existence and authority.

check.q: What does the scene under King Josiah in 622 BC establish, whatever view one takes of Deuteronomy's origin?
options: That Moses wrote Deuteronomy
That a written book of God's Law existed and had authority over king and people by 622 BC
That the Old Testament was complete
That the book was forged
check.why: Scholars debate whether it was old or recent; all agree on the fixed point.

check.q: Josephus counts twenty-two sacred books; the Protestant Old Testament has thirty-nine. What explains the difference?
options: Josephus had lost seventeen books
They are the same books, counted differently
Protestants added books in the sixteenth century
Josephus left out the Prophets
check.why: The twelve minor prophets count as one book, Samuel, Kings and Chronicles as one each, and so on.

check.q: What is the significance of the Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls?
options: They contain the whole Torah
They carry the priestly blessing of Numbers 6 from about 600 BC, the oldest surviving words of the Bible
They prove the Exodus
They were written by Ezra
check.why: Physical evidence that at least part of the Torah's text existed in Josiah's century.

check.q: Why do Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments contain books that Jewish and Protestant ones do not?
options: Medieval popes wrote them
They were in the Greek Septuagint used by the first Christians but not in the Hebrew collection Josephus describes
They were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls
Luther removed them from the Hebrew Bible
check.why: Protestants followed the Hebrew list; Catholics and Orthodox kept the Greek.

check.q: What does this session's evidence NOT show?
options: That the Old Testament is ancient
That it was treasured and carefully kept
That the events it describes really happened
That it was largely complete before Jesus
check.why: An ancient, faithfully kept book could still be mistaken; sessions 3 and 5 test the history.

tutorial.question: Is the Old Testament we read today genuinely the ancient book of ancient Israel, or something assembled much later?
tutorial.approach: Explain why the origins matter for trust. Use the three snapshots (Josiah, Ezra, Josephus) and the oldest copies (Ketef Hinnom, the Dead Sea Scrolls). Give the strongest case for late composition. Then say what the evidence establishes, and what it leaves for later sessions.
strong: Explains why origins matter for trust, and distinguishes 'ancient and intact' from 'true'.
Uses 2 Kings 22–23 accurately, including the debate about Deuteronomy.
Uses Nehemiah 8 and Josephus as later snapshots.
Cites the physical evidence: Ketef Hinnom and the Dead Sea Scrolls.
States the late-composition case fairly.
Explains the Septuagint and why the churches' Old Testaments differ.

reading.author: John Barton
reading.title: A History of the Bible
reading.why: Clear chapters on how the Old Testament was formed.

reading.author: Konrad Schmid
reading.title: The Old Testament: A Literary History
reading.why: How scholars now reconstruct the writing of the books, period by period.

reading.author: Lee Martin McDonald
reading.title: The Formation of the Biblical Canon
reading.why: The standard detailed study of how the collection was fixed.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: read a psalm aloud with someone else, at a meal or before bed, the way the people listened to Ezra. Ask each other which line stays with you.
sessions.reflect: The people wept when they heard the law, and were told to rejoice. What would make a text bring you to tears, and then to joy?
takeaways: The Old Testament's books carry no dates, so historians trace them through moments of use: Josiah (622 BC), Ezra (about 445 BC) and Josephus (AD 95).
The oldest copies, silver amulets from about 600 BC and the Dead Sea Scrolls, show the books are genuinely ancient and were complete before Jesus.
The collection was settled by long use, not a council; the churches' Old Testaments differ because of the Greek Septuagint's extra books.
sessions.finding: The Old Testament is genuinely ancient: its Law was in use by 622 BC, a finished book by about 445 BC, and the collection was closed by AD 95.

paras: If you pick up a modern book, the first pages tell you who wrote it and when it was printed. The books of the Old Testament have nothing like that. Most do not name their author, and none carries a date. So how can anyone know how old they are, or whether they were made up much later?

Historians do what detectives do. They look for moments in history where we can see these books already existing and being used, and for the oldest physical copies. Each moment tells us: 'by this date, at the latest, this book existed and people treated it as sacred.'
background.key: The books carry no dates, so we look for moments in history where we can see them in use.

paras: Here is the history you need, in brief. Around 1000 BC Israel became a kingdom with Jerusalem as its capital, and King Solomon built a Temple there. After Solomon the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south, around Jerusalem. The Assyrian empire destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC.

Judah survived another 135 years. In 622 BC its king, Josiah, set out to reform the nation's worship; that is our first reading. Then in 587 BC the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple and took its leaders into exile in Babylon (in modern Iraq). In 539 BC the Persians conquered Babylon and let the exiles go home. A small community rebuilt Jerusalem, and in about 445 BC the scribe Ezra read them the Law; that is our second reading.

timeline.text: Kingdom under David and Solomon
Northern kingdom destroyed by Assyria
King Josiah: a book of the Law found (reading 1)
Jerusalem destroyed; exile in Babylon
Exiles allowed home by Persia
Ezra reads the Law to the people (reading 2)
Josephus describes the closed collection (comparison)

background.key: Kingdom, Josiah's reform, exile in Babylon, return: our readings sit at two turning points.

paras: The three texts in this session are three snapshots of the Old Testament taking shape. In 622 BC, under King Josiah, a book of God's Law is found and read to the nation: the first time the Bible shows a sacred book being read. About 180 years later, around 445 BC, Ezra reads the whole Law of Moses to the people as their recognised Scripture. And in AD 95 the historian Josephus describes a finished collection of sacred books that no one dared to change.

Why does this matter for trust? If these books had been invented late, by Christians or by rabbis after Jesus, we could not rely on them to tell us about ancient Israel. These snapshots, and the oldest copies described in the lecture, show they are genuinely ancient, and were treasured and fixed long before Jesus.
background.key: Three snapshots, 622 BC, 445 BC and AD 95, show the Old Testament is genuinely ancient.

sessions.title: Where the New Testament came from
sessions.line: Who wrote it, how soon after Jesus, and who chose the twenty-seven books.
sessions.plain: The New Testament was written by Jesus' followers within about seventy years of his death. Paul's letters are the earliest; the four Gospels came a little later. This session asks how close they stand to the events, who wrote them, and how the Church came to recognise these twenty-seven books and not others.
sessions.why: Session 2 showed that the Old Testament is genuinely ancient. Now the same question for the New: where did it come from, and were its writers in a position to know?
answers: When were the Gospels and letters written, and by whom?
What is the earliest Christian evidence we have?
What about the differences between the four Gospels?
Who chose the twenty-seven books? Did Constantine?
before: Paul says he 'delivered' what he 'received'. What exactly did he receive, and from whom might he have received it?
Whom does Paul name as witnesses, and why would he mention that most are still alive?
What do the Galatians passage and the end of John add?
sessions.readWhy: Paul's first letter to Corinth, written about AD 53–55, quotes a short summary of the faith which he says he had received earlier, and names witnesses. His letter to Galatia says when he met Peter and James in Jerusalem. Together they are the earliest written evidence about what the first Christians claimed.

paras: Now I declare to you, brothers, the Good News which I preached to you, which also you received, in which you also stand,
by which also you are saved, if you hold firmly the word which I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,
that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep.
Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles,
and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.
But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.
Whether then it is I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.
Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days.
But of the other apostles I saw no one except James, the Lord’s brother.
Now about the things which I write to you, behold, before God, I’m not lying.
Then I came to the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
I was still unknown by face to the assemblies of Judea which were in Christ,
but they only heard: “He who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy.”
So they glorified God in me.
Then after a period of fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also with me.
I went up by revelation, and I laid before them the Good News which I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who were respected, for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain.
This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things. We know that his witness is true.
There are also many other things which Jesus did, which if they would all be written, I suppose that even the world itself wouldn’t have room for the books that would be written.

parts.title: What I also received
parts.context: Paul writes from Ephesus, about AD 53–55, to the church he had founded in Corinth, a busy Greek port. Some there doubt that the dead are raised. Paul reminds them of the message he gave them when he first came, around AD 50.

commentary.on: I delivered to you first of all that which I also received
commentary.text: 'Delivered' and 'received' are the technical words Jewish teachers used for passing on tradition carefully, word for word. Paul is signalling that what follows is not his own composition. He is quoting.

commentary.on: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day
commentary.text: Read verses 3 to 5 aloud and you will hear the rhythm of a formula: four short clauses, each beginning 'that'. Scholars across the spectrum, sceptical ones included, think Paul received it within a few years of the crucifixion, most likely when he visited Peter and James in Jerusalem (the next passage). That makes it perhaps the oldest Christian text we have.

commentary.on: he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve
commentary.text: Cephas is Peter's name in Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke. Its appearance here is a fingerprint of the early, Aramaic-speaking church in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: most of whom remain until now
commentary.text: This is the most remarkable line. Paul is in effect saying: if you doubt me, go and ask them. You do not invite people to check with living witnesses unless you are confident of what they will say.

commentary.on: I persecuted the assembly of God
commentary.text: Paul had been a persecutor of the movement. Whatever we make of his experience, his change of side is one of the best-attested facts of early Christianity, and it cost him dearly.

parts.title: Fifteen days with Peter
parts.context: Paul writes to churches in Galatia (central Turkey), around AD 48–55, to insist that his message is not second-hand. He gives a dated account of his contacts with the leaders in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days
commentary.text: Three years after his conversion, which most date to the early 30s, so this visit is about AD 35–37, within five or six years of the crucifixion. The Greek word for 'visit' (historēsai, from which 'history' comes) can mean to get to know someone and learn from them.

commentary.on: James, the Lord's brother
commentary.text: Paul met Jesus' own brother. James had not followed Jesus in his lifetime (John 7:5) but later led the church in Jerusalem; the creed you just read says the risen Jesus appeared to him. Josephus, the Jewish historian, also mentions 'the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James' (session 5).

commentary.on: before God, I'm not lying
commentary.text: Paul takes an oath, which tells you that his opponents disputed his account. Ancient readers expected witnesses to swear to what mattered.

commentary.on: I laid before them the Good News which I preach
commentary.text: Fourteen years later he checks his message with the leaders in Jerusalem. The earliest Christians cared that what was taught matched what the first witnesses said.

parts.title: We know that his witness is true
parts.context: The last verses of John's Gospel, probably added by the community that published it in the 90s AD.

commentary.on: This is the disciple who testifies about these things, and wrote these things
commentary.text: The Gospel claims to rest on the testimony of 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', an eyewitness who is never named. Tradition identifies him with John, son of Zebedee; some scholars think he was another disciple in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: We know that his witness is true
commentary.text: A group speaks here, vouching for the witness. Whether or not you accept their claim, this is how ancient testimony worked: a named community standing behind a named source.

commentary.on: the world itself wouldn't have room for the books
commentary.text: A deliberate exaggeration, a common ancient way of ending a book. It reminds us again that the Gospels are selective portraits, not complete records.

paras: For we didn’t follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty.
For he received from God the Father honor and glory when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”
We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.

parts.title: We were eyewitnesses
parts.context: From the Second Letter of Peter, which presents itself as Peter's farewell. It is the New Testament letter whose authorship is most widely doubted: many scholars, including some conservative ones, date it after Peter's death (session 6 explains pseudonymity). Read it as a statement of what the early Church believed about its own message.

commentary.on: we didn't follow cunningly devised fables
commentary.text: The Greek word is mythos, myth. The writer knows the Greek and Roman myths of gods visiting the earth, and insists the Christian story is a different kind of thing: not a tale about the distant past, but a report about a recent man that people saw and heard.

commentary.on: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty
commentary.text: The writer refers to the Transfiguration (Mark 9:2–8), when three disciples saw Jesus shining on a mountain. The claim is extraordinary, and you may doubt it. But notice its form: not 'it is said' but 'we saw'.

commentary.on: We heard this voice come out of heaven when we were with him
commentary.text: Whether this letter is by Peter or by a follower writing in his name, it shows that by the end of the first century Christians defended their faith as testimony, not as myth or philosophy. That is why the historical questions in this journey matter to Christianity in a way they would not to a religion of myths.

compare.why: A short passage that insists the Christian message is not myth but eyewitness testimony. Ancient readers knew the difference between a myth and a report, and so did the first Christians.
compare.title: Not cunningly devised fables

paras: Jesus was crucified around AD 30. Paul's letters, the earliest Christian writings we have, date from about AD 48 to the early 60s. Most scholars date Mark's Gospel around 65–70, Matthew and Luke in the 80s, and John in the 90s; some date them earlier. The Gospels were written while people who had known Jesus, or known those who had, were still alive.
How does that compare? The table sets the main sources for Jesus beside the sources for some other famous ancient figures.

rows: Plutarch (about AD 100) and Arrian (2nd century AD), drawing on lost earlier works
Plato and Xenophon, his own pupils
table.note: The point is not that early sources must be true, but that the Gospels are as close to their subject as the sources historians rely on for most of antiquity, and closer than many.

sections.key: The Gospels were written within living memory, closer to Jesus than many ancient biographies are to their subjects.

paras: The most important passage for historians is the one you read first. Paul wrote in the mid-50s, but he is quoting something earlier, with the marks of an oral formula and an Aramaic name for Peter. His visit to Peter and James in Jerusalem, about three years after his conversion, is the likeliest moment he received it.

Scholars across the spectrum date it to within a few years of the crucifixion. Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist New Testament scholar, put it within three years; Bart Ehrman, an agnostic, agrees it is very early. Whatever one makes of its claim, belief that Jesus had been raised and had appeared to named people was not a legend that grew up over generations. It was there at the start.
sections.key: Paul quotes a summary of the faith that scholars of every view date to within a few years of the crucifixion.

paras: Between Jesus and the written Gospels lie two or three decades of oral tradition: sayings and stories told and retold. How reliable was that stage? In the twentieth century, form critics such as Rudolf Bultmann argued that stories changed freely as communities used them, so that much in the Gospels reflects the early Church more than Jesus.

Other scholars point out that teaching in Jewish and ancient settings was often memorised; that Jesus' sayings are shaped for memory, with parallelism, rhythm and vivid images; and that named people who had known Jesus, Peter, James and John among them, led the communities for decades. Psychologists of memory add a caution on both sides: memory keeps the gist better than the details.
sections.key: Scholars debate whether the oral stage changed the stories freely or kept their substance stable.

paras: The Gospels do not name their authors in the text. The titles 'according to Matthew', 'Mark', 'Luke' and 'John' are attested in the second century, and no rival names were ever attached to them. Around AD 120 Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor, reported that Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down what Peter remembered. Around 180 Irenaeus of Lyons named all four.

Many modern scholars doubt that Matthew and John were written by apostles in their present form, while accepting that they draw on early tradition; others defend the traditional names. Mark and Luke, who were not apostles, are names nobody would invent to give a book authority.
sections.key: The traditional names are attested early and unchallenged; two of them are names nobody would invent.

paras: The Gospels differ. Matthew mentions one angel at the empty tomb, Luke two. Matthew and Luke give different genealogies for Jesus. John places the cleansing of the Temple at the start of Jesus' ministry, the others at the end. Sceptics have long counted these as contradictions.

Historians see them differently. Independent witnesses always differ in detail, and identical accounts suggest copying. Ancient biographers also arranged material by theme rather than strict order, as Plutarch admits. Some differences can be reconciled; some cannot easily be. But none touches the core: that Jesus taught, healed, was crucified under Pilate, and that his followers proclaimed him risen. The early Church had the chance to merge the four into one tidy account (Tatian did so around 170) and chose to keep all four, differences included.
sections.key: The Gospels differ in detail as independent witnesses do; the differences do not touch the core of the story.

paras: How did the Church decide which books belonged in the New Testament? Not by a vote at a single council, but over about three centuries, by recognising books already being read in worship across the churches. The tests, roughly, were apostolic origin (written by an apostle or someone close to one), agreement with the faith handed down, and wide and long use.

The four Gospels and Paul's letters were accepted very early; Irenaeus, around 180, defends the four Gospels against rivals. A few books, such as Hebrews, James, 2 Peter and Revelation, were debated longer. In 367 Athanasius of Alexandria, in his thirty-ninth Festal Letter, listed exactly our twenty-seven books, the first list we have to do so. Councils at Hippo (393) and Carthage (397) in North Africa confirmed the list for the West.
sections.key: The canon was recognised over three centuries from books the churches already read, not chosen by a single decision.

paras: A popular story, repeated by Voltaire and in Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code (2003), says that the Emperor Constantine or the Council of Nicaea in 325 decided which books went into the Bible and suppressed the rest. There is no evidence for this. The Council of Nicaea met to settle the dispute over Arius' teaching about Christ and the date of Easter; none of its surviving decisions mentions the canon.

Constantine did do one thing for the Bible: around 331 he ordered fifty copies of the Scriptures from Eusebius of Caesarea for the churches of his new capital (Eusebius, Life of Constantine IV.36). By then the four Gospels and Paul's letters had been read as Scripture for nearly two centuries.
sections.key: Neither Constantine nor the Council of Nicaea chose the books of the Bible; the core was settled long before.

paras: Other early writings were not accepted. Some were respected but late, like the Shepherd of Hermas, which some churches read for a time. Others, such as the Gospel of Thomas, the Gospel of Peter or the Gospel of Judas, were rejected because they taught a different faith, often the 'gnostic' belief that salvation comes through secret knowledge and that the material world is evil. Most date from the second century or later; a few scholars date parts of Thomas earlier.

Marcion, around 140, accepted only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul and rejected the Old Testament altogether. The Church's response, insisting on the Jewish Scriptures and on four Gospels, shaped the canon we have.
sections.key: The 'lost gospels' were mostly later, and were left out because they taught a different faith.

sections.h: What this evidence shows, and what it does not
paras: The evidence shows that the claims about Jesus, including the extraordinary claim that he was raised, were made very early, by people who named witnesses, some of them leaders of the movement. It shows that the Gospels were written within living memory, and that the Church kept four distinct accounts rather than one harmonised story.

It does not, by itself, show that every detail is accurate, or that the miracles happened. And so far all our witnesses are Christians. Two more checks follow: whether the text has been copied faithfully since (session 4), and what evidence from outside the Bible says (session 5).
sections.key: The evidence shows early, named testimony and a canon recognised over time; the next checks are the copies and the outside evidence.

debate.question: How close are the Gospels to the eyewitnesses?

positions.name: Very close
positions.who: Richard Bauckham and others
positions.view: The Gospels were written within living memory and rest on the testimony of named eyewitnesses, such as Peter behind Mark, which the authors signal deliberately.
positions.evidence: 1 Corinthians 15 and Galatians 1; Papias on Mark; the naming of minor characters who could be checked.

positions.name: Shaped by communities
positions.who: Rudolf Bultmann and the form critics; Bart Ehrman in a modern form
positions.view: Stories about Jesus circulated orally for decades and changed as they were retold, so the Gospels show us the faith of the early Church more than the facts about Jesus.
positions.evidence: Differences between the Gospels; studies of how memories change in retelling.

positions.name: Remembered Jesus
positions.who: James D. G. Dunn and many others
positions.view: The tradition was flexible in wording but stable in substance, because communities kept and checked the memory of Jesus together. We meet Jesus as he was remembered, which is how we meet any historical figure.
positions.evidence: The mix of stable core and varied detail in the synoptic Gospels.

debate.agree: All agree that Jesus existed, that the Gospels were written in the first century, and that belief in his resurrection goes back to the earliest days.

look.why: Simone Cantarini, in the 1640s, painted the old tradition of Matthew writing his Gospel with an angel's help: the Church's way of saying that inspiration came through a real human author.
points: A balding, grey-bearded man holding open a book with black writing on its pages.
His forehead deeply lined; he looks down at the page.
An angel, seen from behind, with braided blond hair tied with a red bow and snowy white wings.
The angel holds a white feather pen and an inkwell, as if handing the writer his tools.

music.why: Bach set Matthew's account of the Passion word for word in Luther's German. In his hands the Gospel is sung as testimony, by an Evangelist who narrates and a crowd that answers.

think.why: How historians weigh the Gospels as sources.

learn.why: Perhaps the oldest words of Christian faith we have, handed on within a few years of the events they describe.

check.q: Why do historians value 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 even more than the Gospels' dates would suggest?
options: Paul was an eyewitness of the crucifixion
Paul is quoting a formula he received earlier, which takes the evidence back to within a few years of the events
It is the longest account of the resurrection
It was written before the crucifixion
check.why: 'I delivered what I also received': the letter is from the 50s, but the creed is older.

check.q: What is the significance of Paul's remark that 'most' of the five hundred 'remain until now'?
options: It proves the resurrection happened
It invites his readers to check with living witnesses, which a writer confident of his facts would do
It shows the five hundred were all dead
It was added by a later copyist
check.why: It doesn't prove the claim, but it shows Paul expected the witnesses to confirm it.

check.q: Why do historians not count differences between the Gospels as evidence of invention?
options: There are no differences
Independent witnesses always differ in detail, while identical accounts suggest copying
The Church forbade comparing them
One author wrote all four
check.why: And the core events are the same in all four.

check.q: Which statement about the Gospels' authors is most accurate?
options: All four name their authors in the text
The traditional names are attested in the second century and never rivalled, though scholars debate how direct the apostolic link is
The names were first given at the Reformation
No one knew who wrote them until the nineteenth century
check.why: Papias (about 120) and Irenaeus (about 180) give the names; modern scholars disagree about Matthew and John.

check.q: What did the Council of Nicaea (325) decide about the books of the Bible?
options: It chose the four Gospels and burned the rest
Nothing: it dealt with Arius' teaching about Christ and the date of Easter
It added the Book of Revelation
It removed the Apocrypha
check.why: The story that Nicaea chose the canon has no basis in the sources.

check.q: Which best describes how the New Testament canon was formed?
options: An emperor's decree
A gradual recognition, over about three centuries, of books already read across the churches, judged by apostolic origin, faithfulness and wide use
A single vote at Jerusalem in AD 50
The choice of Martin Luther
check.why: Athanasius' list of 367 and the African councils of 393 and 397 recorded a consensus already largely formed.

tutorial.question: Where did the New Testament come from, and were its writers in a position to know?
tutorial.approach: Start with dates, comparing other ancient sources. Use 1 Corinthians 15 and Galatians 1 as your earliest evidence. Set out the case for and against eyewitness testimony, and deal honestly with the differences between the Gospels. Then explain how the twenty-seven books were recognised, and answer the claim that Constantine chose them.
strong: Gives realistic dates and compares other ancient sources.
Explains why 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 is so important and how early it is.
States the form critics' case and the eyewitness reply fairly.
Treats the differences between the Gospels as historians would.
Explains canon as recognition over three centuries, with Athanasius in 367.
Corrects the Nicaea myth and explains why the 'lost gospels' were left out.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: ask an older relative or friend to tell you about an event they witnessed long ago. Notice what stays fixed in their telling and what varies, and thank them for it.
sessions.reflect: Whose testimony do you trust most in your own life, and why?
takeaways: The New Testament was written within living memory; Paul quotes a creed from within a few years of the crucifixion.
The Gospels differ in detail as independent witnesses do; how close they stand to eyewitnesses is debated.
The twenty-seven books were recognised over three centuries; Athanasius first listed them in 367; Constantine and Nicaea did not choose them.
sessions.finding: The New Testament was written within living memory of Jesus, by people who named their witnesses; its books were recognised over time, not picked by an emperor.

background.h: From the Old Testament to the New
paras: Between the last books of the Old Testament and the time of Jesus lie about four centuries. Alexander the Great conquered the region in 332 BC, and Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean. In 63 BC Rome took control. By Jesus' day Judea was ruled by Roman governors and local client kings such as Herod, and many Jews longed for God to free them, perhaps through an anointed king, the 'Messiah' (in Greek, 'Christ').

Jesus was born around 4 BC and crucified in Jerusalem around AD 30. His followers claimed he had been raised from the dead and began to spread the message, first among Jews and then among non-Jews across the Roman Empire.
background.key: Jesus lived under Roman rule, among Jews hoping for a Messiah; his followers spread their message across the Empire.

paras: Paul (also called Saul) was a Jew from Tarsus, in modern Turkey, trained as a strict Pharisee, who at first persecuted the Christians. A few years after Jesus' death he had an experience he describes as seeing the risen Jesus, and he became the movement's most energetic missionary. Between about AD 48 and his execution in Rome in the 60s, he travelled around the eastern Mediterranean founding churches, and wrote them letters.

Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry his name. Scholars agree that at least seven are certainly his, including the two you will read today, 1 Corinthians and Galatians. They are the earliest Christian writings that survive.
background.key: Paul, once a persecutor, became the leading missionary; his letters are the earliest Christian writings.

background.h: Why we read Paul before the Gospels
paras: You might expect a session about the Gospels to start with a Gospel. But the Gospels were written later than Paul's letters, between about AD 65 and 100. If we want to know how close the written record comes to Jesus, the earliest evidence is the place to start.

In 1 Corinthians, Paul quotes a short summary of the faith that he says he had been given, and lists people who saw the risen Jesus. In Galatians he tells us exactly when he met Jesus' closest followers. Then a passage from the end of John's Gospel shows how a Gospel described its own source.
The lecture then asks the other half of the question: how, over the next three centuries, the Church came to recognise these twenty-seven books, and not the 'lost gospels', as its New Testament.
background.key: We start with Paul because his letters are older than the Gospels and take us closest to the events.

sessions.title: Has it been copied faithfully?
sessions.line: No originals survive. So how do we know what was written?
sessions.plain: Before printing, every book was copied by hand, and copies of copies can drift. None of the Bible's original pages survives, and none of any other ancient book. But we have far more, and far older, copies of the Bible than of any other ancient writing, and scholars compare them to work out what was first written. This session shows how that works, what has changed, and what has not.
sessions.why: Sessions 2 and 3 showed where the books came from. But a book written long ago is only useful if what we read today is what was written then. That is the next check.
answers: Has the Bible been changed over the centuries?
How many copies are there, and how old?
What did the Dead Sea Scrolls show?
Isn't a modern Bible a translation of a translation of a translation?
before: What happens to Jeremiah's scroll, and what happens next?
What does Baruch do, and why does it matter for how Scripture survived?
In the comparison, why do the writers warn against adding or taking away?
sessions.readWhy: The only story in the Bible about a biblical book being written, destroyed and written again. A king cuts up the prophet's scroll and burns it piece by piece; the prophet dictates it again, with more added. It is a parable of how fragile, and how persistent, the written word has been.

paras: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying,

“Take a scroll of a book, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against Israel, and against Judah, and against all the nations, from the day I spoke to you, from the days of Josiah, even to this day.
It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I intend to do to them; that they may each return from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.”
Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah; and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all Yahweh’s words, which he had spoken to him, on a scroll of a book.
Jeremiah commanded Baruch, saying, “I am restricted. I can’t go into Yahweh’s house.

Therefore you go, and read from the scroll which you have written from my mouth, Yahweh’s words, in the ears of the people in Yahweh’s house on the fast day. Also you shall read them in the ears of all Judah who come out of their cities.
It may be they will present their supplication before Yahweh, and will each return from his evil way; for Yahweh has pronounced great anger and wrath against this people.”
Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book Yahweh’s words in Yahweh’s house.

Now in the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, all the people in Jerusalem, and all the people who came from the cities of Judah to Jerusalem, proclaimed a fast before Yahweh.

Then Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the book in Yahweh’s house, in the room of Gemariah the son of Shaphan, the scribe, in the upper court, at the entry of the new gate of Yahweh’s house, in the ears of all the people.
When Micaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all Yahweh’s words,

he went down into the king’s house, into the scribe’s room: and behold, all the princes were sitting there, Elishama the scribe, Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, Elnathan the son of Achbor, Gemariah the son of Shaphan, Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.
Then Micaiah declared to them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people.

Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, to Baruch, saying, “Take in your hand the scroll in which you have read in the ears of the people, and come.”
So Baruch the son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand, and came to them.
They said to him, “Sit down now, and read it in our hearing.”
So Baruch read it in their hearing.
Now when they had heard all the words, they turned in fear one toward another, and said to Baruch, “We will surely tell the king of all these words.”
They asked Baruch, saying, “Tell us now, how did you write all these words at his mouth?”
Then Baruch answered them, “He dictated all these words to me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.”
Then the princes said to Baruch, “You and Jeremiah go hide. Don’t let anyone know where you are.”
They went in to the king into the court; but they had laid up the scroll in the room of Elishama the scribe. Then they told all the words in the hearing of the king.

So the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll; and he took it out of the room of Elishama the scribe. Jehudi read it in the hearing of the king, and in the hearing of all the princes who stood beside the king.
Now the king was sitting in the winter house in the ninth month; and there was a fire in the brazier burning before him.
When Jehudi had read three or four leaves, the king cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was in the brazier, until all the scroll was consumed in the fire that was in the brazier.
The king and his servants who heard all these words were not afraid, and didn’t tear their garments.
Moreover Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the scroll; but he would not listen to them.
The king commanded Jerahmeel the king’s son, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet; but Yahweh hid them.
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah, after the king had burned the scroll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying,
“Take again another scroll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first scroll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah has burned.

Concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, ‘Yahweh says: “You have burned this scroll, saying, “Why have you written therein, saying, ‘The king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land, and will cause to cease from there man and animal?’ ” ’
Therefore Yahweh says concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: “He will have no one to sit on David’s throne. His dead body will be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.

I will punish him, his offspring, and his servants for their iniquity. I will bring on them, on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and on the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them, but they didn’t listen.” ’ ”

Then took Jeremiah another scroll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah, who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire; and many similar words were added to them.

parts.title: The prophet dictates a scroll
parts.context: Jerusalem, 605–604 BC, the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. Babylon has just defeated Egypt at Carchemish and is about to become master of the region. Jeremiah has been warning for twenty years that disaster is coming.

commentary.on: Take a scroll of a book, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you
commentary.text: Here is the moment spoken prophecy becomes a written book. Jeremiah had preached for over twenty years; now his words are collected on a scroll so they can be read where he cannot go.

commentary.on: Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah
commentary.text: Baruch son of Neriah is a professional scribe, and the first named 'secretary' of a biblical book. Many books of the Bible came into being like this: a prophet or teacher speaking, a scribe writing. That is why it makes sense to speak of human authors and editors without denying that the words are, as believers say, God's.

commentary.on: I am restricted. I can't go into Yahweh's house
commentary.text: Jeremiah has been banned from the Temple for his preaching. The written word goes where the prophet cannot. That is one reason books matter: they outlive bans, prisons and deaths.

parts.title: The scroll is read in the Temple
parts.context: A year later, on a public fast day, Baruch reads the scroll aloud in the Temple. The royal officials hear of it.

commentary.on: in the room of Gemariah the son of Shaphan, the scribe
commentary.text: A detail worth noticing: a clay seal impression reading 'Gemaryahu son of Shaphan' was found in the City of David in Jerusalem in the 1980s, in a layer burned in the Babylonian destruction of 587 BC. Whether it belonged to this very man cannot be proved, but the name, the father's name and the period fit.

commentary.on: how did you write all these words at his mouth?
commentary.text: The officials ask about the process of writing. Baruch's answer, 'He dictated ... and I wrote them with ink in the book', is the clearest description in the Bible of how one of its books was made.

commentary.on: You and Jeremiah go hide
commentary.text: The officials know the king will be furious. Writing that challenges power has always been dangerous.

parts.title: The king burns it
parts.context: Winter, in the palace. The scroll is read to King Jehoiakim beside a brazier.

commentary.on: When Jehudi had read three or four leaves, the king cut it with the penknife
commentary.text: A scribe's penknife was used for trimming reed pens. The king uses the tool of writing to destroy writing, column by column, as it is read. It is a calculated act of contempt.

commentary.on: were not afraid, and didn't tear their garments
commentary.text: Compare the people in Nehemiah 8, who wept when they heard the Law. Tearing one's garments was a sign of grief and repentance; the king and his servants show none. The writer wants us to notice the contrast.

commentary.on: but Yahweh hid them
commentary.text: The writer's comment. The prophet and the scribe survive, and so will the words.

parts.title: Written again, with more
parts.context: After the burning, Jeremiah is told to write the scroll again.

commentary.on: Take again another scroll, and write in it all the former words
commentary.text: The destroyed text is restored, from memory and dictation. This is how ancient texts survived disaster: through people who knew them and copied them again.

commentary.on: many similar words were added to them
commentary.text: Honest and important. The book grew, under the prophet's own direction. Ancient books were often expanded and re-edited. In fact the Greek translation of Jeremiah is about one-eighth shorter than the Hebrew and arranged differently, and the Dead Sea Scrolls contain copies of both forms. Textual scholars study exactly this kind of growth.

paras: Now, Israel, listen to the statutes and to the ordinances which I teach you, to do them; that you may live, and go in and possess the land which Yahweh, the God of your fathers, gives you.
You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it, that you may keep the commandments of Yahweh your God which I command you.
I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book, if anyone adds to them, may God add to him the plagues which are written in this book.
If anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, may God take away his part from the tree of life, and out of the holy city, which are written in this book.

parts.title: Moses' warning
parts.context: From Deuteronomy, presented as Moses' farewell speeches to Israel before they enter the promised land.

commentary.on: You shall not add to the word which I command you, neither shall you take away from it
commentary.text: Ancient law codes and treaties often ended with curses on anyone who altered them; the Babylonian Code of Hammurabi does. Here the warning protects the commandments themselves. It shows how seriously the text's integrity was taken, and also, by implication, that people knew texts could be tampered with.

parts.title: John's warning
parts.context: The last verses of the last book of the Bible, the Revelation to John, written in the 90s AD.

commentary.on: if anyone adds to them ... If anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy
commentary.text: The warning applies to 'this book', the Revelation, not to the whole Bible, which had not yet been collected. It is a copyist's curse, aimed at scribes who might change a text as they copied it. It is a fitting end to the Bible all the same: a reminder that every generation receives the text from those before it, and is responsible for handing it on intact.

compare.why: The first and last books of the Bible to say it warn against adding to or taking from the words. Such warnings were common in the ancient world; they show that copyists were expected to be faithful, and also that people knew texts could be changed.
compare.title: Do not add, do not take away

paras: No original manuscript of any biblical book survives, nor of any classical book: not Plato, not Caesar, not Virgil. Ancient texts were written on papyrus or parchment, which decay, and were copied by hand. What we have are copies of copies, and copyists make mistakes: they skip a line, misread a letter, or 'correct' what they think is an error.

The question is not whether the copies differ (they do) but whether we can recover what was written. That is the work of textual criticism, a discipline developed first for the Greek and Latin classics and then applied to the Bible. How does the Bible compare?

rows: Papyri from the 3rd century BC; complete manuscripts from the 10th century AD
Over a thousand, mostly papyrus fragments
Papyri from the 2nd–3rd centuries; complete Bibles from the 4th century
About 5,800 Greek, plus over 10,000 in Latin and thousands in other early languages
Over many centuries to about the 2nd century BC
Dead Sea Scrolls, 3rd century BC to 1st century AD; complete codices about AD 930 and 1008
Hundreds of scrolls and thousands of medieval manuscripts
table.note: Manuscript counts for classical works are approximate and change as catalogues are revised.

sections.key: No ancient book survives in its original, but the Bible is far better attested than any other.

paras: Because there are so many manuscripts, there are also very many variants, places where the manuscripts differ: hundreds of thousands, more than the number of words in the New Testament. Bart Ehrman made this point famous in Misquoting Jesus (2005).

Most variants are trivial: spelling, word order (which matters little in Greek), obvious slips. A small number matter. The longer ending of Mark (16:9–20) and the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11) are absent from the earliest manuscripts, as is the angel stirring the pool in John 5:4, which you will meet in session 5. A verse on the Trinity in some older English Bibles (1 John 5:7) is a late addition. Modern Bibles mark all of these. Ehrman himself has said that no essential Christian belief depends on a disputed reading; his argument is about what the variants show of the copyists, not that the text is lost.
sections.key: There are many variants, but most are trivial and the significant ones are known and marked in modern Bibles.

sections.h: How scholars work out the original
paras: Imagine a letter copied by hand a hundred times, by different people in different towns, and each copy copied again. Every copy has a few slips, but different slips in different places. If you gather many copies and lay them side by side, the mistakes stand out, because most copies agree where one goes wrong. That, in essence, is textual criticism.

Scholars also use a few rules of thumb. Older copies are usually closer to the original. A reading found in copies from several different regions is more likely original than one found in only one region. And where copies differ, the harder or shorter reading is often the original, because copyists tended to smooth out difficulties and add explanations, as with the angel in John 5:4.
sections.key: Lay many copies side by side, and the slips stand out; older, widespread and harder readings are usually original.

sections.h: Check it in your own Bible
paras: You do not have to take any of this on trust. Open almost any modern Bible at Mark 16:9 or John 7:53 and you will find a note or brackets saying the passage is missing from the earliest manuscripts. Many Bibles add footnotes elsewhere saying 'some manuscripts read…'. Those notes are the work of textual critics, shown openly to every reader.
A tradition that wanted to hide changes in its book would not print them on the page. The openness of modern Bibles about their own text is itself part of the answer to the question of this session.
sections.key: Modern Bibles show their doubtful passages openly in notes and brackets: you can check them yourself.

paras: For the Old Testament, the great discovery came in 1947, when Bedouin shepherds found jars of scrolls in caves near Qumran by the Dead Sea. Over the next decade, around 900 manuscripts were recovered, including parts of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther, most of them copied between about 250 BC and AD 68.

The most famous, the Great Isaiah Scroll, was copied around 125 BC, about a thousand years earlier than the oldest Hebrew manuscript of Isaiah known before. Comparing them showed two things at once. Some books circulated in more than one form, as Jeremiah did. And yet the text of Isaiah had been copied with remarkable faithfulness across a millennium: the differences are overwhelmingly matters of spelling and small wording.
sections.key: The Dead Sea Scrolls showed the Hebrew text copied with remarkable care across a thousand years, alongside some variety of editions.

paras: A common claim is that today's Bible is like a game of Chinese whispers: Hebrew into Greek into Latin into English, changing at every step. This is simply not how modern Bibles are made. Since the Reformation, translators have worked directly from the Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, using the best manuscripts available. Today's translations draw on the Dead Sea Scrolls and on Greek manuscripts that the King James translators of 1611 never saw.

Translations do differ, in method rather than in text. Some aim to follow the original word for word (the King James, the English Standard Version); others aim to render the meaning in natural modern English (the New International Version, the New Living Translation). Comparing two of them is one of the best ways to see where the original is difficult.
sections.key: Modern Bibles are translated directly from the Hebrew and Greek, from better manuscripts than ever before.

Bart D. Ehrman, Misquoting Jesus (2005), and the interview in the 2007 paperback edition.
