debate.question: Who wrote the Torah?

positions.name: Moses
positions.who: Traditional Jewish and Christian teaching
positions.view: Moses wrote the five books, apart from a few later notes such as the account of his death, as Jesus and the New Testament assume.
positions.evidence: The books' own statements that Moses wrote (Exodus 24:4, Deuteronomy 31:9); the unanimous ancient tradition.

positions.name: Four documents
positions.who: Julius Wellhausen and the classical critics
positions.view: The Pentateuch combines four sources (J, E, D, P) written over five centuries and joined after the exile; Moses wrote none of it.
positions.evidence: Different divine names, doublets and styles; later place names and perspectives.

positions.name: A long growth
positions.who: Most scholars today, believing and not
positions.view: The Pentateuch grew over centuries from older traditions, perhaps around an ancient core linked to Moses, and reached its final form in or after the exile. The details are hotly debated.
positions.evidence: The breakdown of the four-source theory; comparisons with other ancient Near Eastern texts.

debate.agree: All agree that the Pentateuch contains some material from after Moses and that it was edited over time; they disagree on how much, when and by whom.

look.why: Painted in Rembrandt's workshop in Amsterdam around 1653, possibly by his pupil Willem Drost, in the same city and decade in which the young Spinoza was expelled from the synagogue. It shows not a scholar at his books but a man thinking.
points: A gaunt man with a trimmed brown beard and a large, soft brown beret.
His hands are folded at the bottom of the picture; he leans over them.
His head turns to our left; his deep-set eyes look away, as if at a thought.
A robe banded with rust red and gold, and a heavy gold chain across his chest.

music.why: Brahms chose his own texts from Luther's Bible for this Requiem, leaving out the creeds and even the name of Christ: an honest, searching reading of Scripture by a man unsure what he believed.

think.why: Underneath the argument about the Bible lies the argument about God. This depth sets out the strongest cases on both sides.

listen.why: Bart Ehrman, the best-known sceptical scholar of the New Testament, explains his case. Listen for what he accepts as well as what he rejects.

check.q: Which of Spinoza's clues is strongest against Moses writing the whole Pentateuch?
options: That Moses could not write
Passages such as 'the Canaanite was then in the land' and 'to this day', which look back from a later time
That the Pentateuch is in Greek
That Moses never existed
check.why: Spinoza never denies Moses existed or wrote something; his clues are later perspectives in the text.

check.q: What was genuinely new in Spinoza's approach?
options: Noticing that Moses' death is described in Deuteronomy
The principle that the Bible should be studied with the same historical methods as any other book
Translating the Bible into Dutch
Denying that the Bible was ever read in synagogues
check.why: The Talmud and ibn Ezra had noticed some problems; the method was Spinoza's contribution.

check.q: Which of these is a philosophical assumption rather than a historical finding?
options: That ancient writers used sources
That the Pentateuch was edited over time
That miracles cannot happen
That Deuteronomy 34 was written after Moses' death
check.why: No study of texts can settle whether miracles are possible.

check.q: What is the state of Wellhausen's documentary hypothesis today?
options: Universally accepted in its 1878 form
Its classic four-source form has broken down; scholars agree on growth over time but disagree widely on how
Disproved by the Dead Sea Scrolls
Never taken seriously
check.why: Many now speak of fragments, supplements or a long process of editing.

check.q: Spinoza cites Nehemiah 8:8 ('gave the sense') as evidence. For what?
options: That Ezra was illiterate
That Ezra expounded and, he thinks, compiled and edited the books
That Nehemiah wrote Genesis
That the people could not understand Hebrew
check.why: The same verse can be read as reverent explanation or as a clue to editing.

tutorial.question: Does the critical case against the traditional authorship of the Bible show that it cannot be trusted?
tutorial.approach: First state Spinoza's evidence fully and fairly. Then show how his method developed into the documentary hypothesis and the modern sceptic's case. Then separate the questions: who wrote the books, how they were composed, whether they are historically reliable, and whether they are true. Say which points are now widely accepted and which conclusions do not follow.
strong: States Spinoza's evidence accurately (third person, death of Moses, 'then', 'to this day', later names).
Notes his debt to ibn Ezra and the Talmud.
Explains historical criticism, the documentary hypothesis and its later breakdown.
States the modern case at full strength, including pseudonymity and archaeology.
Separates authorship, composition, reliability and truth.
Identifies the philosophical assumptions in the strongest sceptical case.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: find someone who doubts the Bible and ask them why, then listen without arguing until you could state their case so well that they would agree with your summary.
sessions.reflect: Which part of the sceptic's case unsettled you most? What would you need to know to answer it?
takeaways: Spinoza argued from the text that Moses did not write the Pentateuch, and that the Bible must be studied like any other book.
His method led to historical criticism, the documentary hypothesis and the modern sceptic's case.
Some of the case is widely accepted; that the Bible cannot be trusted does not follow from it.
sessions.finding: The sceptic's best case is serious: the books were written and edited over time by many hands. But that does not make them untrustworthy, and its strongest step rests on an assumption, not evidence.

paras: The first five books of the Bible, Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, are called the Torah (Hebrew for 'teaching' or 'law') or the Pentateuch (Greek for 'five scrolls'). They run from the creation of the world to the death of Moses, just before the Israelites enter the promised land. Jewish and Christian tradition held for two thousand years that Moses himself wrote them.
This session examines the most famous challenge to that tradition, and through it the whole modern critical approach to the Bible.
background.key: Tradition held that Moses wrote the first five books; this session tests that belief.

paras: Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) was born in Amsterdam to a family of Portuguese Jews who had fled persecution. Amsterdam was then the freest city in Europe, a refuge for religious minorities and a centre of printing. At 23 Spinoza was expelled from his synagogue for his opinions. He lived quietly, grinding lenses for a living, and became one of the great philosophers of the modern age.

Europe in his lifetime had just been through decades of wars between Catholics and Protestants. Spinoza believed that if people read the Bible as a historical book, they would stop killing each other over it. In 1670 he published his argument anonymously.
background.key: Spinoza wrote in the freest city in Europe, after decades of religious war, to argue for freedom of thought.

paras: Every journey on Rose Window includes the strongest objection at full strength, before any reply. For the Bible, the strongest objection is that its books were not written by the people tradition names, were edited long after the events, and must be read like any other ancient book. Spinoza's treatise is where that case was first made openly and in detail, and he makes it from the text itself.
You will read his chapter in six short passages, each with a commentary. Then you can test three of his key verses yourself in the comparison.
background.key: Spinoza's chapter is the founding statement of the case against the traditional view, made from the text itself.

sessions.title: The verdict, and how to read it
sessions.line: So, can I trust it? And how should I read it?
sessions.plain: If the Bible was written by many people over centuries and handed down through fallible copies, how should a thinking person read it? Augustine, who knew its difficulties well, argued that a text may hold more than one true meaning and that the test of a good reading is love. The road to Emmaus shows the Christian key to the whole library.
sessions.why: We have weighed the evidence and heard the sceptic. The last question is practical: not only whether the Bible can be trusted, but how to read it so that trust is honest.
answers: So, can a thinking person trust the Bible?
How should it be read today?
Does a passage have one meaning or many?
What, for Christians, is the key to the whole Bible?
before: What does Augustine say when someone insists, 'Moses meant what I say'?
What rule does Augustine give for deciding between readings?
In Luke 24, what makes the two disciples' hearts burn?
sessions.readWhy: At the end of the Confessions Augustine argues with readers who insist that only their interpretation of Genesis is right. His answer is a short masterpiece on interpretation: humble about our grasp of an author's mind, confident that truth is shared, and governed by love.

paras: But which of us shall, among those so many truths, which occur to enquirers in those words, as they are differently understood, so discover that one meaning, as to affirm, "this Moses thought," and "this would he have understood in that history"; with the same confidence as he would, "this is true," whether Moses thought this or that? For behold, O my God, I Thy servant, who have in this book vowed a sacrifice of confession unto Thee, and pray, that by Thy mercy I may pay my vows unto Thee, can I, with the same confidence wherewith I affirm, that in Thy incommutable world Thou createdst all things visible and invisible, affirm also, that Moses meant no other than this, when he wrote, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth? No. Because I see not in his mind, that he thought of this when he wrote these things, as I do see it in Thy truth to be certain. For he might have his thoughts upon God's commencement of creating, when he said In the beginning; and by heaven and earth, in this place he might intend no formed and perfected nature whether spiritual or corporeal, but both of them inchoate and as yet formless. For I perceive, that whichsoever of the two had been said, it might have been truly said; but which of the two he thought of in these words, I do not so perceive. Although, whether it were either of these, or any sense beside (that I have not here mentioned), which this so great man saw in his mind, when he uttered these words, I doubt not but that he saw it truly, and expressed it aptly.

Let no man harass me then, by saying, Moses thought not as you say, but as I say: for if he should ask me, "How know you that Moses thought that which you infer out of his words?" I ought to take it in good part, and would answer perchance as I have above, or something more at large, if he were unyielding. But when he saith, "Moses meant not what you say, but what I say," yet denieth not that what each of us say, may both be true, O my God, life of the poor, in Whose bosom is no contradiction, pour down a softening dew into my heart, that I may patiently bear with such as say this to me, not because they have a divine Spirit, and have seen in the heart of Thy servant what they speak, but because they be proud; not knowing Moses' opinion, but loving their own, not because it is truth, but because it is theirs. Otherwise they would equally love another true opinion, as I love what they say, when they say true: not because it is theirs, but because it is true;

and on that very ground not theirs because it is true. But if they therefore love it, because it is true, then is it both theirs, and mine; as being in common to all lovers of truth. But whereas they contend that Moses did not mean what I say, but what they say, this I like not, love not: for though it were so, yet that their rashness belongs not to knowledge, but to overboldness, and not insight but vanity was its parent. And therefore, O Lord, are Thy judgements terrible; seeing Thy truth is neither mine, nor his, nor another's; but belonging to us all, whom Thou callest publicly to partake of it, warning us terribly, not to account it private to ourselves, lest we be deprived of it. For whosoever challenges that as proper to himself, which Thou propoundest to all to enjoy, and would have that his own which belongs to all, is driven from what is in common to his own; that is, from truth, to a lie. For he that speaketh a lie, speaketh it of his own.

Hearken, O God, Thou best judge; Truth Itself, hearken to what I shall say to this gainsayer, hearken, for before Thee do I speak, and before my brethren, who employ Thy law lawfully, to the end of charity: hearken and behold, if it please Thee, what I shall say to him. For this brotherly and peaceful word do I return unto Him: "If we both see that to be true that Thou sayest, and both see that to be true that I say, where, I pray Thee, do we see it? Neither I in thee, nor thou in me; but both in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our souls." Seeing then we strive not about the very light of the Lord God, why strive we about the thoughts of our neighbour which we cannot so see, as the unchangeable Truth is seen: for that, if Moses himself had appeared to us and said, "This I meant"; neither so should we see it, but should believe it. Let us not then be puffed up for one against another, above that which is written: let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind: and our neighbour as ourself. With a view to which two precepts of charity, unless we believe that Moses meant, whatsoever in those books he did mean, we shall make God a liar, imagining otherwise of our fellow servant's mind, than he hath taught us. Behold now, how foolish it is, in such abundance of most true meanings, as may be extracted out of those words, rashly to affirm, which of them Moses principally meant; and with pernicious contentions to offend charity itself, for whose sake he spake every thing, whose words we go about to expound.

parts.title: Can we know what Moses meant?
parts.context: The last books of the Confessions (about 397–400) are a meditation on the first verse of Genesis, 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.' Augustine has set out several possible meanings and now asks whether anyone can be sure which one Moses intended. The whole book is addressed to God.
parts.author: Augustine of Hippo

commentary.on: this Moses thought
commentary.text: Augustine distinguishes two claims: 'this is true' and 'this is what Moses meant'. He thinks we can often be sure of the first and rarely of the second. That distinction is the beginning of humility in reading any text.

commentary.on: Because I see not in his mind
commentary.text: We cannot see into another person's mind, least of all one who lived long ago. Modern scholars say the same about 'authorial intention'. Augustine reached it in 400.

commentary.on: I doubt not but that he saw it truly, and expressed it aptly
commentary.text: But he is no sceptic. He trusts that Moses saw truly, even if we cannot be sure exactly what Moses saw. Trust in the author and humility about our interpretation go together.

parts.plain: Augustine says: the first verse of Genesis can be understood in several true ways. I can be sure what is true, but I can't see inside Moses' mind to know which meaning he intended, though I'm sure he meant something true.

parts.title: Not mine, not yours, but the truth's
parts.context: Augustine turns to readers who say, 'Moses meant what I say, not what you say.'
parts.author: Augustine of Hippo

commentary.on: not because it is truth, but because it is theirs
commentary.text: Augustine's diagnosis of quarrels over the Bible: people love their own interpretation because it is theirs, not because it is true. Anyone who has watched a religious argument, or an argument about anything, will recognise this.

commentary.on: as being in common to all lovers of truth
commentary.text: Truth belongs to no one. If a reading is true, it is yours and mine alike. This is one of the deepest ideas in Western thought about inquiry: truth is a common good, not private property.

commentary.on: For he that speaketh a lie, speaketh it of his own
commentary.text: An echo of John 8:44. The person who claims truth as his own possession has already turned it into a lie, because he has made it about himself.

parts.plain: Augustine says: people who insist 'Moses meant what I say, not what you say' are often proud. They love their opinion because it is theirs, not because it is true. But truth belongs to everyone who loves it, not to any one person.

parts.title: The rule of love
parts.context: Augustine ends the argument by appealing to the two great commandments.
parts.author: Augustine of Hippo

commentary.on: but both in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our souls
commentary.text: When two people both see that something is true, where do they see it? Not in each other's minds, says Augustine, but in the truth itself, which stands above both of them. That is why argument can be peaceful: both parties are looking at the same thing.

commentary.on: let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind: and our neighbour as ourself
commentary.text: Jesus' summary of the Law (Matthew 22:37–40). For Augustine this is the purpose of all Scripture. In another book, On Christian Doctrine, he says that anyone whose reading builds up this double love is not dangerously mistaken, even if he misses the author's exact meaning; and anyone whose reading does not build it up has not yet understood the Bible.

commentary.on: with pernicious contentions to offend charity itself, for whose sake he spake every thing
commentary.text: The final irony: to fight bitterly over what the Bible means is to defeat the very purpose for which it was written. A reading that leads to hatred is wrong, however clever or literal.

parts.plain: Augustine says: if we both see that something is true, we see it in the truth itself, not in each other's minds. So let us not quarrel. The whole point of the Bible is love of God and of our neighbour, and fighting over its meaning betrays that point.

paras: Behold, two of them were going that very day to a village named Emmaus, which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem.
They talked with each other about all of these things which had happened.
While they talked and questioned together, Jesus himself came near, and went with them.
But their eyes were kept from recognizing him.
He said to them, “What are you talking about as you walk, and are sad?”
One of them, named Cleopas, answered him, “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem who doesn’t know the things which have happened there in these days?”
He said to them, “What things?”
They said to him, “The things concerning Jesus, the Nazarene, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people;
and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him up to be condemned to death, and crucified him.
But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel. Yes, and besides all this, it is now the third day since these things happened.
Also, certain women of our company amazed us, having arrived early at the tomb;
and when they didn’t find his body, they came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who said that he was alive.
Some of us went to the tomb, and found it just like the women had said, but they didn’t see him.”
He said to them, “Foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken!
Didn’t the Christ have to suffer these things and to enter into his glory?”
Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.
They came near to the village where they were going, and he acted like he would go further.
They urged him, saying, “Stay with us, for it is almost evening, and the day is almost over.”
He went in to stay with them.
When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them.
Their eyes were opened and they recognized him, then he vanished out of their sight.
They said to one another, “Weren’t our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?”
They rose up that very hour, returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them,
saying, “The Lord is risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon!”
They related the things that happened along the way, and how he was recognized by them in the breaking of the bread.
He said to them, “This is what I told you, while I was still with you, that all things which are written in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms, concerning me must be fulfilled.”
Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures.

parts.title: A stranger on the road
parts.context: The evening of the first Easter Sunday. Two followers of Jesus, one named Cleopas, are walking from Jerusalem to Emmaus, a village about seven miles away, after the crucifixion.

commentary.on: But we were hoping that it was he who would redeem Israel
commentary.text: The saddest line in the Gospels. They had hoped Jesus would free Israel; his death ended their hope. They know the facts, even the report of the empty tomb, but cannot make sense of them.

commentary.on: Beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself
commentary.text: The stranger gives them a Bible study. The facts make sense only when they are read within the whole story of Scripture. This is how Christians have read the Old Testament ever since: as a long story leading to Christ.

parts.title: Recognised in the breaking of bread
parts.context: They reach the village at evening and invite the stranger in.

commentary.on: Their eyes were opened and they recognized him
commentary.text: They recognise him at a meal, as he breaks bread. Christians have always seen here the pattern of their worship: the Scriptures explained, then the bread broken.

commentary.on: Weren't our hearts burning within us, while he spoke to us along the way, and while he opened the Scriptures to us?
commentary.text: The verse you will learn by heart. Reading the Bible well, Luke suggests, is not only an intellectual exercise; it is an encounter. Even before they knew who he was, something in them responded.

parts.title: The law, the prophets and the psalms
parts.context: Later that night, Jesus appears to the gathered disciples in Jerusalem.

commentary.on: the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms
commentary.text: The three parts of the Hebrew Bible, named by their largest books, exactly as you met them in session 2. Jesus claims the whole collection points to him.

commentary.on: Then he opened their minds, that they might understand the Scriptures
commentary.text: Luke's last word on reading the Bible: understanding is a gift as well as an achievement. That is the believer's claim. A thinking person can test the evidence, as this journey has done; trusting the God it speaks of is a further step.

compare.why: The risen Jesus walks with two disciples and explains 'in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself'. This is the key with which Christians have read the whole library: the story finds its centre in Christ.
compare.title: The key on the road

paras: Put the six checks together. The Bible is a library, read for what each book is. Its Old Testament is genuinely ancient and its New Testament was written within living memory. Its text has been copied more faithfully, and is better attested, than any other ancient book. Outside evidence often confirms its people and places, though some early stories have none. And the strongest case against it shows that its books grew and were edited, not that they are untrustworthy.

So a thinking person can trust the Bible as a collection of ancient writings, close to what they describe and faithfully handed down. Whether to trust what it says about God is a different kind of question. History can show that the witnesses were in a position to know; it cannot make you believe them. That last step, as the two disciples found on the road to Emmaus, is taken another way.
sections.key: The Bible can be trusted as ancient, close and faithfully copied; trusting its God is a further step.

paras: You met Augustine in the first session, disappointed by the Bible's plain style. By the time he wrote these chapters, about twenty years later, he was a bishop who preached on the Scriptures several times a week and had spent years on the first chapters of Genesis alone.

He had come to think that the Bible's plainness was deliberate: it is 'lowly in access, in its recesses lofty', open to the simplest reader and deep enough for the cleverest. And he had come to think its difficulties are part of its purpose, because they make us search, and humble us.
sections.key: Augustine came to see the Bible's plainness as deliberate and its difficulties as part of its purpose.

paras: We cannot see into another person's mind, Augustine says, so we should be slow to claim we know exactly what Moses intended. But we can know whether a reading is true. If two readings are both true, why fight over which one Moses had in mind? Perhaps he meant both, or God, who inspired him, did.

This is not relativism. Augustine thinks some readings are false, and that truth is one. But he thinks a great text can hold more truth than any single reader can see, and that arrogance about interpretation is itself a failure to read rightly.
sections.key: We cannot see an author's mind, but we can ask whether a reading is true; a great text holds more than one truth.

paras: What, then, is the test? Augustine's answer, here and at length in On Christian Doctrine, is the double commandment: love of God and of neighbour. The whole of Scripture, he says, aims at this. Whoever reads it in a way that builds up love, even if he misses the author's meaning, is mistaken in a good direction, like a traveller who leaves the road but still reaches the destination; but he should be corrected, lest he get used to leaving the road.
It is a principle with consequences. A reading that leads to hatred of others is wrong, however literal.
sections.key: For Augustine a reading that does not build up love of God and neighbour has not yet understood the Bible.

paras: Christians developed a rich method from this. The early theologian Origen, and later the Middle Ages, spoke of four senses of Scripture: the literal (what happened, what the words say), the allegorical (what it shows about Christ and the Church), the moral (how we should live) and the anagogical (what it shows of our final hope). Jerusalem was the standard example: literally a city, allegorically the Church, morally the soul, anagogically heaven.

But the literal sense came first. Augustine warned in his Literal Meaning of Genesis that Christians who talk nonsense about the natural world, claiming the Bible's authority, bring the Scriptures into contempt among educated unbelievers. Thomas Aquinas held that all the other senses rest on the literal one.
sections.key: The four senses rest on the literal sense, which must not be twisted into nonsense.

paras: You saw in session 1 that the churches differ on the Bible's authority. They also differ in how they read it, though less than they once did.

Protestants, following Luther and Tyndale, stress the plain sense of the text and the right of every believer to read it, with preaching at the centre of worship. Catholics, following the Second Vatican Council's Dei Verbum (1965), read Scripture together with Tradition and the Church's teaching, and encourage both historical study and spiritual reading; since 1943 they have embraced modern scholarship. The Orthodox read the Bible above all in worship, through the Fathers and the liturgy, where most of the Psalter is sung every week. In practice all three now share much of the same scholarship, and many of the same translations.
sections.key: Protestants stress the plain sense and personal reading; Catholics, Scripture with Tradition; the Orthodox, Scripture in worship and the Fathers.

paras: For most Christians the Bible has never been mainly a private book. It is read aloud in worship, often in a lectionary, a pattern of readings that in many churches takes people through much of the Bible every few years. The psalms are sung. The Gospel is often carried in procession, and people stand to hear it, as the people stood for Ezra.

Reading this way teaches something that private study can miss: the Bible was written to be heard by a community, and much of it was first spoken. Paul's letters were read to whole churches. To hear it read well, in a quiet church, is still one of the best ways to meet it.
sections.key: The Bible was written to be heard, and most Christians still meet it read aloud in worship.

paras: So how can a thinking person read the Bible well? Some practical rules follow from this journey. Read each book for what it is. Read it whole, not in fragments. Learn what scholars know of its history and text, without fear; truth cannot contradict truth. Hear the sceptic out, and know which of his claims are evidence and which are assumptions. Read it with others, past and present. And read it, as Augustine did, with the double love he thought was its purpose.

Can you trust the Bible? You now know that its writers were close to the events, that outside evidence often confirms their world, that the text has reached us faithfully to a remarkable degree, that the hard questions are real, and that the Church's best readers knew them. Whether you trust the God it speaks of is a further step, which no history can take for you.
sections.key: Read by genre, read whole, learn the scholarship without fear, hear the sceptic, read with others and with love.

refs: Augustine, Confessions III.5 and XII.18–32; On Christian Doctrine I.35–36 (the rule of love; the traveller, I.36.41); The Literal Meaning of Genesis I.19.39.
Origen, On First Principles IV; the four senses with Jerusalem as example: John Cassian, Conferences XIV.8; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10.
Pius XII, Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943); Dei Verbum (1965), §§12, 21–25.
Henri de Lubac, Medieval Exegesis (1959–64); John Barton, The Nature of Biblical Criticism (2007).

debate.question: How should the Bible be read?

positions.name: The plain sense
positions.who: The Reformers, and many Protestants since
positions.view: Scripture interprets Scripture, and its plain meaning is clear enough for any reader to grasp what is needed for salvation; it is the final authority.
positions.evidence: Luther's and Tyndale's insistence on the literal sense and on Bibles in the people's language.

positions.name: With the Church's tradition
positions.who: Catholic and Orthodox teaching
positions.view: The Bible was written, collected and recognised within the Church, and is best read within its living tradition, which keeps the spiritual senses alongside the literal.
positions.evidence: The canon itself was recognised by the Church; the Fathers' four senses; the liturgy.

positions.name: Historically first
positions.who: Modern historical critics
positions.view: The first task is to recover what each text meant in its own time, using every tool of history and language; later theological meanings must not be read back into it.
positions.evidence: The gains of textual and historical study since Spinoza.

debate.agree: All agree that the literal and historical sense matters and that the Bible should be read whole and with care. Most now accept that the three approaches can learn from one another.

look.why: An American painter of the 1720s shows the road itself: the moment before recognition, while the stranger is still explaining the Scriptures and the travellers' hearts are burning.
points: Three barefoot men walking towards us on a dirt path between two stretches of water.
The central figure, long-haired and bearded, in a pink robe.
His two companions in brown robes and blue cloaks, one with a cane; they look at one another.
A broken wooden fence along the path, tall trees behind, and far off a town with red roofs.

music.why: An old Irish prayer, put into English verse in the early twentieth century: a reader asking that the Word become the light he sees by.

think.why: Augustine's warning about Christians talking nonsense on nature is still the best starting point for faith and science.

learn.why: The disciples' words on the road to Emmaus: the experience Christians hope for when they read.

check.q: Augustine distinguishes 'this is true' from 'this is what Moses meant'. Why?
options: Because Moses was often wrong
Because we can often know whether a reading is true, but cannot see into the author's mind to be sure what he intended
Because only bishops can know what Moses meant
Because Genesis has no meaning
check.why: Humility about intention, confidence about truth: that is his principle.

check.q: What does Augustine say about a reader who misses the author's meaning but builds up love of God and neighbour?
options: He is a heretic
He is mistaken in a good direction, like a traveller who leaves the road but reaches the destination, though he should be corrected
He has understood perfectly
He should stop reading
check.why: On Christian Doctrine I.36. The rule of love governs, but accuracy still matters.

check.q: Why did Augustine warn Christians against talking nonsense about the natural world on the Bible's authority?
options: Because the Bible contains no truth about nature
Because it brings the Scriptures into contempt among educated unbelievers and misreads what the Bible is for
Because science is forbidden
Because Genesis was written by Greeks
check.why: The Literal Meaning of Genesis I.19.39, written about 401–415.

check.q: In Luke 24, why are the facts not enough for the two disciples?
options: They had not heard of the empty tomb
They know the facts but cannot make sense of them until they are read within the whole story of Scripture
They did not know Jesus
They could not read
check.why: They report the empty tomb themselves; understanding comes when the Scriptures are opened.

check.q: Which describes a real difference between how Catholics and Orthodox, on the one hand, and many Protestants, on the other, read the Bible?
options: Catholics and Orthodox do not read the Bible
Catholics and Orthodox read it within the Church's Tradition and worship; many Protestants stress its plain sense and every believer's right to interpret it
Protestants reject the literal sense
Only Protestants use the four senses
check.why: Though today all three share much of the same scholarship.

tutorial.question: Can a thinking person today trust the Bible, and how should they read it?
tutorial.approach: Draw on the whole journey: what the Bible is, how both Testaments came together, how close the sources are, the outside evidence, the copies and canon, and the sceptic's case. Then give your own rules for reading, using Augustine and Luke 24, and say what trust in the Bible can and cannot rest on.
strong: Draws on all seven sessions, not just this one.
Uses specific evidence: the creed in 1 Corinthians 15, Tacitus, the Dead Sea Scrolls, archaeology.
Faces the sceptic's strongest points honestly.
Explains Augustine's 'many true meanings' without making it relativism, and the rule of love.
Shows how Luke 24 gives the Christian key.
Distinguishes historical trust in the sources from faith in the God they speak of.

reading.title: Confessions
reading.why: Read Books I–IX for his story, and XI–XIII for his reading of Genesis.

reading.title: Scripture and the Authority of God
reading.why: How the Bible can be an authority, by a leading New Testament scholar.

reading.why: The great study of the four senses.
