reading.title: The Nature of Biblical Criticism
reading.why: What historical criticism is, and is not, by a leading Oxford critic.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: read Luke 24 slowly with one other person, over a meal if you can. Ask each other where your hearts 'burned', or where they did not.
sessions.reflect: What would it take for you to read the Bible not only as evidence, but as something that speaks to you?
takeaways: Augustine taught humility about an author's meaning and confidence that truth is shared by all who love it.
The test of a reading is whether it builds up love of God and neighbour; the literal sense comes first and must not be twisted.
Christians read the whole library in the light of Christ, as on the road to Emmaus; trusting the God it speaks of is a further step no history can take for you.
sessions.finding: The verdict: the Bible's writers were close to what they describe, knew their world, and have reached us faithfully. Trusting the God they speak of is a further step that evidence can open but not take for you.

paras: You have now seen what the Bible is, where both Testaments came from, how faithfully it has been copied, what outside evidence says, and the strongest case against it. This last session puts the case together and gives a verdict, then asks the practical question: how should a thinking person read it?
For that we turn to two guides. One is a man you met in session 1, who once dismissed the Bible as beneath him. The other is Jesus himself, in one of the last scenes of Luke's Gospel.
background.key: The verdict, and then how to read the Bible well.

paras: Augustine (354–430) was born in what is now Algeria, in Roman North Africa. Brilliant and ambitious, he became a professor of rhetoric in Carthage, Rome and Milan, and for years was attracted to philosophy and to a religion called Manichaeism. In 386, in a garden in Milan, he was converted to Christianity. He became bishop of Hippo, a port in North Africa, and wrote more than almost any ancient author: the Confessions, The City of God and hundreds of sermons and letters.

His Confessions, written around 397–400, tell his life story as a prayer addressed to God. In the last books he turns to the first verse of the Bible, 'In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth', and asks how anyone can know what it means.
background.key: Augustine, the great North African bishop, wrote on how to read the Bible after years of studying it.

paras: Augustine's chapters are about a problem every reader meets: what to do when people disagree about what a passage means. His answer, humility about our own interpretations and love as the test of a good reading, has shaped Christian reading for sixteen centuries.

The comparison is the story of the road to Emmaus. Two of Jesus' followers, walking away from Jerusalem after his death, meet a stranger who explains the Scriptures to them. It is the passage Christians have always used to explain how they read the whole Bible: as a story whose centre is Christ.
background.key: Augustine on disagreement and love; Emmaus on the key to the whole story.

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: Can you trust the Bible? Make the case in about 300 words: why should a thinking person today read the Bible and take it seriously, and what is the strongest objection you must answer?
closing.practice: Choose one Gospel and read it through over the next month, a chapter a day. Before each chapter, ask what kind of writing it is; after it, ask what it asks of you.
synthesis: This journey asked one question, can a thinking person trust the Bible, and tested it the way you would test any old family story: what is it, where did it come from, has it been passed down faithfully, does anything else back it up, what do the doubters say, and so what do we conclude? Here are the short answers.

What is the Bible? A library, not a book: sixty-six books in a Protestant Bible, seventy-three in a Catholic one and about seventy-six in an Orthodox one, written over more than a thousand years in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, in every kind of writing from law to love poetry. The churches differ only on some Old Testament books from the Greek Bible; the New Testament is shared. They also differ on authority: Scripture alone for Protestants, Scripture and Tradition under the Church's teaching office for Catholics, Scripture within Holy Tradition for the Orthodox.

Who wrote the Old Testament, and when was it fixed? It grew over centuries. By Ezra's time, around 445 BC, Jewish life was organised round the public reading of the Law; by about 130 BC the three parts, Law, Prophets and Writings, were familiar; by the first century AD Josephus could count twenty-two sacred books that his people would die rather than alter. Jesus treated the same collection as Scripture.

How close are the Gospels to the events? Within living memory. Paul's letters date from the 50s, and he quotes a summary of the faith that scholars of every persuasion date to within a few years of the crucifixion, naming witnesses who could be asked. The Gospels followed within decades, closer to Jesus than many ancient biographies are to their subjects. They differ in detail as independent witnesses do.

Who chose the books? No one person or council. The churches recognised, over about three centuries, the books they were already reading. Athanasius first listed the twenty-seven in 367. Constantine and the Council of Nicaea did not choose them. The 'lost gospels' were mostly later and taught a different faith.

Has the text been changed? It has been copied by hand for centuries, and copies differ. But we have more and earlier manuscripts of the New Testament than of any other ancient book, and the Dead Sea Scrolls showed Isaiah copied faithfully across a thousand years. The significant variants are few, known and marked. Modern Bibles are translated directly from the Hebrew and Greek, not from earlier translations.

Is there evidence outside the Bible? Yes, a good deal, with honest gaps. From the ninth century BC, Israel's kings appear in the records of their neighbours: the House of David on the Tel Dan Stele, Hezekiah's tribute on Sennacherib's prism, his tunnel still under Jerusalem. In the New Testament, Pilate, Caiaphas, Gallio, the pools of Bethesda and Siloam have all been found. Tacitus and Josephus, neither a Christian, confirm that Jesus lived and was executed under Pilate. But the patriarchs, the Exodus and the conquest have little or no outside confirmation, and some puzzles, such as Quirinius' census, remain.

What is the strongest case against it? Spinoza's, developed by two centuries of criticism: the books were written, edited and re-edited by many hands, often long after the events; some carry false names; they contradict one another in details; the earliest periods lack outside evidence; their miracles are what legend produces. Some of this is now accepted by many believing scholars. But composition from sources does not make a text untrustworthy, outside evidence often confirms the Bible's world, and the assumption that miracles cannot happen is philosophy, not history.

So, can you trust it? The evidence allows you to say that the Bible's writers were, on the whole, close to what they describe and knew their world; that their words have reached us with a reliability no other ancient text can match; and that the hard questions are real and were known long before the modern age. What no history can do is make you trust the God the Bible speaks of. That is a further step, taken not by argument alone.

How should it be read? Augustine's answer still serves. Ask what kind of writing it is; read it whole; be humble about what an author meant and confident that truth is shared; let the literal sense come first; and remember that the test of a reading is whether it builds up love of God and neighbour. Christians read the whole library in the light of Christ, as the two disciples did on the road to Emmaus.

One more thing. The habits this journey asked of you, reading carefully, weighing evidence, hearing the other side at full strength, distinguishing what a text says from what you wish it said, were formed in the West largely by people reading this book. The universities began as schools for studying it; textual criticism was perfected on it; even Spinoza learned his method from a rabbi's commentary. To read the Bible well is to learn to read anything well.
exam: 'A library, not a book.' Discuss the implications for how the Bible should be read, and for the differences between the churches' Bibles.
How and when did the Old Testament become a fixed collection? Use Josephus and at least one other source.
What is the significance of 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 for the historical study of Jesus?
How far does archaeology confirm the Bible? Discuss with reference to both Testaments, and to the limits of the evidence.
What do non-Christian writers of the first and early second centuries tell us about Jesus?
'We don't have the originals, so we can't know what the Bible said.' Assess this claim.
State and evaluate Spinoza's case against the Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch.
'The test of a good reading is love.' Is Augustine's principle of interpretation adequate?

next.place: See the evidence for yourself: the Lachish reliefs and the Taylor Prism in the British Museum in London; the Codex Sinaiticus in the British Library; the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Pilate Stone in the Israel Museum in Jerusalem; or the early papyri at the Chester Beatty in Dublin. Many of these are online.
next.book: John Barton, A History of the Bible (2019), and Peter J. Williams, Can We Trust the Gospels? (2018), read side by side.

title: Why beauty matters
question: What is beauty for?
line: A psalm, a philosopher, a saint, a naturalist, a book of craftsmen and a Victorian critic: six ways into the question of why beautiful things stop us, and what they are for.
why: Almost everyone has been stopped by something beautiful: a face, a forest, a building, a song. This course asks what that moment is for. It begins with the Bible's great hymn of creation and Plato's ladder of love, tests them against Darwin's case that beauty is an evolved charm, and ends in the workshop, with the people who make beautiful things. You will come away with a way of looking, and an answer of your own.
outcomes: By the end you'll be able to say what the Psalms, Plato, Augustine, Exodus and Ruskin each thought beauty is for, and where they agree and differ.
You'll know what science has found about awe, shared taste and the pull of attractive faces, and what Darwin's theory of sexual selection does and does not explain.
You'll have looked closely at six paintings and listened to six pieces of music, and be able to say in your own words whether beauty points beyond itself.

sessions.title: The world is charged
sessions.line: Begin where everyone begins: being stopped by the beauty of the world.
sessions.why: Every question about beauty starts with an experience. This first session puts the Bible's great hymn of creation beside what psychologists have learned about awe, and asks what happens to us when something is too vast or too lovely to take in.

paras:
Bless Yahweh, my soul.
Yahweh, my God, you are very great.
You are clothed with honor and majesty.

He covers himself with light as with a garment.
He stretches out the heavens like a curtain.

He lays the beams of his rooms in the waters.
He makes the clouds his chariot.
He walks on the wings of the wind.

He makes his messengers winds,
and his servants flames of fire.

He laid the foundations of the earth,
that it should not be moved forever.

You covered it with the deep as with a cloak.
The waters stood above the mountains.

At your rebuke they fled.
At the voice of your thunder they hurried away.

The mountains rose,
the valleys sank down,
to the place which you had assigned to them.

You have set a boundary that they may not pass over,
that they don’t turn again to cover the earth.

He sends springs into the valleys.
They run among the mountains.

They give drink to every animal of the field.
The wild donkeys quench their thirst.

The birds of the sky nest by them.
They sing among the branches.

He waters the mountains from his rooms.
The earth is filled with the fruit of your works.

He causes the grass to grow for the livestock,
and plants for man to cultivate,
that he may produce food out of the earth:

wine that makes the heart of man glad,
oil to make his face to shine,
and bread that strengthens man’s heart.

Yahweh’s trees are well watered,
the cedars of Lebanon, which he has planted;

where the birds make their nests.
The stork makes its home in the cypress trees.

The high mountains are for the wild goats.
The rocks are a refuge for the rock badgers.

He appointed the moon for seasons.
The sun knows when to set.

You make darkness, and it is night,
in which all the animals of the forest prowl.

The young lions roar after their prey,
and seek their food from God.

The sun rises, and they steal away,
and lie down in their dens.

Man goes out to his work,
to his labor until the evening.

Yahweh, how many are your works!
In wisdom, you have made them all.
The earth is full of your riches.

There is the sea, great and wide,
in which are innumerable living things,
both small and large animals.

There the ships go,
and leviathan, whom you formed to play there.

These all wait for you,
that you may give them their food in due season.

You give to them; they gather.
You open your hand; they are satisfied with good.

You hide your face; they are troubled.
You take away their breath; they die and return to the dust.

You send out your Spirit and they are created.
You renew the face of the ground.

Let Yahweh’s glory endure forever.
Let Yahweh rejoice in his works.

He looks at the earth, and it trembles.
He touches the mountains, and they smoke.

I will sing to Yahweh as long as I live.
I will sing praise to my God while I have any being.

Let my meditation be sweet to him.
I will rejoice in Yahweh.

Let sinners be consumed out of the earth.
Let the wicked be no more.
Bless Yahweh, my soul.
Praise Yah!

sessions.readWhy: Psalm 104 walks through the world from the sky to the sea: springs in the valleys, birds singing in the branches, wine and oil and bread, young lions roaring at night, people going out to work until evening, and Leviathan, 'whom you formed to play there'. It never says the world is God. It says the world is God's, made 'in wisdom', and it prays: 'Let the Lord rejoice in his works.'

think.why: The short answer sets out how psychologists define awe, as the response to something vast that makes the mind stretch, and why the findings so far are promising rather than proven.

listen.why: Dacher Keltner, who helped found the science of awe, describes a study of awe stories gathered in many languages; listen for what people found awe-inspiring most often, and whether it was what you expected.

evidence.why: Keltner and Haidt defined awe in 2003. Later experiments found that brief moments of awe made people feel they had more time and act a little more generously, and a large 2025 review finds a consistent link between awe and helping others. Most studies are short laboratory tasks, some samples are small, and the size of the average effect hints at publication bias, so treat this as promising rather than settled.

learn.why: Hopkins, a Jesuit, wrote this sonnet in 1877; its last lines, the Holy Ghost brooding over the bent world, echo Psalm 104:30, where God sends out his Spirit and renews the face of the ground.

music.why: Eleanor Farjeon wrote these words in 1931 for a hymn book, to an old Gaelic melody, and Cat Stevens made them a hit in 1971. The whole song gives thanks for one ordinary morning. Listen to how plain it is, and let it do what Psalm 104 does: notice, and say thank you.

look.why: Look slowly. Asher Durand paints cool light filtering through a thick forest: high canopies of celery, matcha and olive green, moss carpeting the trunks of five trees that loom over us from across a narrow brook, and dead sienna-brown limbs, sharp and broken. Find the brook, count the five trees, and notice that he paints the dead branches too. It is the psalm's 'trees well watered' (verse 16), seen by one patient eye.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: each day, notice one beautiful thing that someone else made or tends, a garden, a well-kept shop, a meal, a tidy workshop, and tell them specifically what you saw.
sessions.reflect: When were you last stopped in your tracks by something beautiful, and what did it ask of you?

sessions.title: The ladder of love
sessions.line: In Plato's Symposium, Socrates recalls a wise woman who taught him that every beautiful thing is a step on a stair.
sessions.why: Last time beauty stopped us. Now we ask where it leads. Plato's answer, later taken up by many Christian thinkers, is that beauty is meant to draw our love upward: from one face, to every good thing, and at last to Beauty itself.

read.author: Plato
read.ref: 210a–212b: Diotima's teaching, as Socrates recalls it
read.who: Athenian philosopher (about 428–348 BC), pupil of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle, whose dialogues shaped Christian thinking about beauty and the soul.
paras: 'These are the lesser mysteries of love, into which even you, Socrates, may enter; to the greater and more hidden ones which are the crown of these, and to which, if you pursue them in a right spirit, they will lead, I know not whether you will be able to attain. But I will do my utmost to inform you, and do you follow if you can. For he who would proceed aright in this matter should begin in youth to visit beautiful forms; and first, if he be guided by his instructor aright, to love one such form only—out of that he should create fair thoughts; and soon he will of himself perceive that the beauty of one form is akin to the beauty of another; and then if beauty of form in general is his pursuit, how foolish would he be not to recognize that the beauty in every form is and the same! And when he perceives this he will abate his violent love of the one, which he will despise and deem a small thing, and will become a lover of all beautiful forms; in the next stage he will consider that the beauty of the mind is more honourable than the beauty of the outward form. So that if a virtuous soul have but a little comeliness, he will be content to love and tend him, and will search out and bring to the birth thoughts which may improve the young, until he is compelled to contemplate and see the beauty of institutions and laws, and to understand that the beauty of them all is of one family, and that personal beauty is a trifle; and after laws and institutions he will go on to the sciences, that he may see their beauty, being not like a servant in love with the beauty of one youth or man or institution, himself a slave mean and narrow-minded, but drawing towards and contemplating the vast sea of beauty, he will create many fair and noble thoughts and notions in boundless love of wisdom; until on that shore he grows and waxes strong, and at last the vision is revealed to him of a single science, which is the science of beauty everywhere. To this I will proceed; please to give me your very best attention:

'He who has been instructed thus far in the things of love, and who has learned to see the beautiful in due order and succession, when he comes toward the end will suddenly perceive a nature of wondrous beauty (and this, Socrates, is the final cause of all our former toils)—a nature which in the first place is everlasting, not growing and decaying, or waxing and waning; secondly, not fair in one point of view and foul in another, or at one time or in one relation or at one place fair, at another time or in another relation or at another place foul, as if fair to some and foul to others, or in the likeness of a face or hands or any other part of the bodily frame, or in any form of speech or knowledge, or existing in any other being, as for example, in an animal, or in heaven, or in earth, or in any other place; but beauty absolute, separate, simple, and everlasting, which without diminution and without increase, or any change, is imparted to the ever-growing and perishing beauties of all other things. He who from these ascending under the influence of true love, begins to perceive that beauty, is not far from the end. And the true order of going, or being led by another, to the things of love, is to begin from the beauties of earth and mount upwards for the sake of that other beauty, using these as steps only, and from one going on to two, and from two to all fair forms, and from fair forms to fair practices, and from fair practices to fair notions, until from fair notions he arrives at the notion of absolute beauty, and at last knows what the essence of beauty is. This, my dear Socrates,' said the stranger of Mantineia, 'is that life above all others which man should live, in the contemplation of beauty absolute; a beauty which if you once beheld, you would see not to be after the measure of gold, and garments, and fair boys and youths, whose presence now entrances you; and you and many a one would be content to live seeing them only and conversing with them without meat or drink, if that were possible—you only want to look at them and to be with them. But what if man had eyes to see the true beauty—the divine beauty, I mean, pure and clear and unalloyed, not clogged with the pollutions of mortality and all the colours and vanities of human life—thither looking, and holding converse with the true beauty simple and divine? Remember how in that communion only, beholding beauty with the eye of the mind, he will be enabled to bring forth, not images of beauty, but realities (for he has hold not of an image but of a reality), and bringing forth and nourishing true virtue to become the friend of God and be immortal, if mortal man may. Would that be an ignoble life?'

Such, Phaedrus—and I speak not only to you, but to all of you—were the words of Diotima; and I am persuaded of their truth. And being persuaded of them, I try to persuade others, that in the attainment of this end human nature will not easily find a helper better than love: And therefore, also, I say that every man ought to honour him as I myself honour him, and walk in his ways, and exhort others to do the same, and praise the power and spirit of love according to the measure of my ability now and ever.

sessions.readWhy: At a dinner where each guest makes a speech in praise of love, Socrates reports what Diotima, a wise woman from Mantinea, once taught him. Love begins with one beautiful person, she says, but should not stop there: it climbs to all beautiful bodies, to beautiful souls, to good laws and knowledge, until it sees a beauty that never grows or fades. The dialogue takes for granted the Athenian custom of older men courting youths; Diotima's point is that love must not settle on any one body.

think.why: Plato was not a Christian, so why do Christians read him? This depth tells how Justin Martyr and Augustine decided to take the best of pagan learning, as the Israelites took gold out of Egypt.

listen.why: The Irish poet and philosopher John O'Donohue speaks of beauty not as prettiness but as something that makes us more alive and asks more of us; hear it as a Christian echo of Diotima's ladder.

learn.why: In the Republic Plato says education does not put sight into blind eyes but turns the whole soul towards the light: the ladder is climbed by turning, not by cleverness.

music.why: Hildegard of Bingen, a twelfth-century German abbess, wrote this chant to Wisdom, pictured with three wings: one flies on high, one toils on the earth, and one flies everywhere. Listen to the single line of melody climb and circle back, and hear how a Christian could rise like Diotima without leaving the earth behind.

look.why: Diotima's ladder starts with one face. Leonardo da Vinci paints the head and shoulders of a young woman in a square portrait: her body is angled to our right but her face turns to us, her skin smooth and chalk-white. Behind her a spiky bush fills most of the background, and on the right a landscape opens into the deep distance. Look at the face first, then let your eye travel past the bush into the far distance, and notice where it comes to rest.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Diotima says love of beauty should bring forth 'fair thoughts'. Each day, tell one person something good you have noticed in them: not their looks, but their character or their work.
sessions.reflect: Which beautiful thing in your life has led you towards something higher, and which has kept you stuck on the first rung?

sessions.title: Loving what passes
sessions.line: Augustine loved beautiful things, and asks why none of them could hold him.
sessions.why: Plato's ladder can be climbed, but it can also be clung to at the first rung. Augustine, who read the Platonists before he became a Christian, tells what it was like to love beautiful things that pass away, and what he came to think they were for.

read.author: Augustine of Hippo
read.who: North African bishop and philosopher (AD 354–430), who in his twenties taught rhetoric and wrote a book on beauty, years before he became a Christian.
paras: Turn us, O God of Hosts, show us Thy countenance, and we shall be whole. For whithersoever the soul of man turns itself, unless toward Thee, it is riveted upon sorrows, yea though it is riveted on things beautiful. And yet they, out of Thee, and out of the soul, were not, unless they were from Thee. They rise, and set; and by rising, they begin as it were to be; they grow, that they may be perfected; and perfected, they wax old and wither; and all grow not old, but all wither. So then when they rise and tend to be, the more quickly they grow that they may be, so much the more they haste not to be. This is the law of them. Thus much has Thou allotted them, because they are portions of things, which exist not all at once, but by passing away and succeeding, they together complete that universe, whereof they are portions. And even thus is our speech completed by signs giving forth a sound: but this again is not perfected unless one word pass away when it hath sounded its part, that another may succeed. Out of all these things let my soul praise Thee, O God, Creator of all; yet let not my soul be riveted unto these things with the glue of love, through the senses of the body. For they go whither they were to go, that they might not be; and they rend her with pestilent longings, because she longs to be, yet loves to repose in what she loves. But in these things is no place of repose; they abide not, they flee; and who can follow them with the senses of the flesh? yea, who can grasp them, when they are hard by? For the sense of the flesh is slow, because it is the sense of the flesh; and thereby is it bounded. It sufficeth for that it was made for; but it sufficeth not to stay things running their course from their appointed starting-place to the end appointed. For in Thy Word, by which they are created, they hear their decree, "hence and hitherto."

If bodies please thee, praise God on occasion of them, and turn back thy love upon their Maker; lest in these things which please thee, thou displease. If souls please thee, be they loved in God: for they too are mutable, but in Him are they firmly stablished; else would they pass, and pass away. In Him then be they beloved; and carry unto Him along with thee what souls thou canst, and say to them, "Him let us love, Him let us love: He made these, nor is He far off. For He did not make them, and so depart, but they are of Him, and in Him. See there He is, where truth is loved. He is within the very heart, yet hath the heart strayed from Him. Go back into your heart, ye transgressors, and cleave fast to Him that made you. Stand with Him, and ye shall stand fast. Rest in Him, and ye shall be at rest. Whither go ye in rough ways? Whither go ye? The good that you love is from Him; but it is good and pleasant through reference to Him, and justly shall it be embittered, because unjustly is any thing loved which is from Him, if He be forsaken for it. To what end then would ye still and still walk these difficult and toilsome ways? There is no rest, where ye seek it. Seek what ye seek; but it is not there where ye seek. Ye seek a blessed life in the land of death; it is not there. For how should there be a blessed life where life itself is not?

"But our true Life came down hither, and bore our death, and slew him, out of the abundance of His own life: and He thundered, calling aloud to us to return hence to Him into that secret place, whence He came forth to us, first into the Virgin's womb, wherein He espoused the human creation, our mortal flesh, that it might not be for ever mortal, and thence like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, rejoicing as a giant to run his course. For He lingered not, but ran, calling aloud by words, deeds, death, life, descent, ascension; crying aloud to us to return unto Him. And He departed from our eyes, that we might return into our heart, and there find Him. For He departed, and lo, He is here. He would not be long with us, yet left us not; for He departed thither, whence He never parted, because the world was made by Him. And in this world He was, and into this world He came to save sinners, unto whom my soul confesseth, and He healeth it, for it hath sinned against Him. O ye sons of men, how long so slow of heart? Even now, after the descent of Life to you, will ye not ascend and live? But whither ascend ye, when ye are on high, and set your mouth against the heavens? Descend, that ye may ascend, and ascend to God. For ye have fallen, by ascending against Him." Tell them this, that they may weep in the valley of tears, and so carry them up with thee unto God; because out of His spirit thou speakest thus unto them, if thou speakest, burning with the fire of charity.

These things I then knew not, and I loved these lower beauties, and I was sinking to the very depths, and to my friends I said, "Do we love any thing but the beautiful? What then is the beautiful? and what is beauty? What is it that attracts and wins us to the things we love? for unless there were in them a grace and beauty, they could by no means draw us unto them." And I marked and perceived that in bodies themselves, there was a beauty, from their forming a sort of whole, and again, another from apt and mutual correspondence, as of a part of the body with its whole, or a shoe with a foot, and the like. And this consideration sprang up in my mind, out of my inmost heart, and I wrote "on the fair and fit," I think, two or three books. Thou knowest, O Lord, for it is gone from me; for I have them not, but they are strayed from me, I know not how.

sessions.readWhy: These chapters come straight after Augustine's account of losing a close friend in his youth. Beautiful things, he says, 'rise, and set': they are good and they come from God, but they cannot bear the whole weight of our love. 'If bodies please thee, praise God on occasion of them.' The extract ends with his younger self asking his friends, 'Do we love any thing but the beautiful?', and writing a book, now lost, on 'the fair and fit'.

think.why: Augustine's mistake, as he came to see it, was to love beautiful things as if they were God; this depth explains the Christian claim that God is not one more thing in the world but the source of all that is good and beautiful in it.

learn.why: The first page of the same book: 'Thou awakest us to delight in Thy praise.' Augustine thought our delight in beauty is a restlessness that only comes to rest in God.

music.why: Mozart wrote this short motet in June 1791 for the feast of Corpus Christi at Baden, near Vienna, months before he died. Its forty-six bars greet the 'true body' born of Mary, the same 'true Life' that Augustine says 'came down hither'. Listen to how little it does, and how it ends almost before it has begun.

look.why: Vincent van Gogh paints a profusion of white roses bursting from the neck of a tan jug, so many that they almost fill the height of the canvas. Look closely at the white: the petals are tinged with denim and aquamarine blue, sage green, mauve pink, teal and butter yellow, among emerald-green leaves. Cut roses last a few days. Augustine would say: praise God for them, and do not ask them to last.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: Augustine says, 'carry unto Him along with thee what souls thou canst.' Give someone flowers, or something beautiful you have made, with a short note saying why you thought of them.
sessions.reflect: What beautiful thing have you asked to carry more weight than it can bear?

sessions.title: Only in the eye?
sessions.line: The strongest case against: beauty is an evolved charm, a matter of taste, and a tool for anyone who wants to sway us.
sessions.why: Three sessions have treated beauty as a signpost. Now we must ask whether it points anywhere at all. Darwin thought the beauty of birds was shaped by their mates' preferences, and that our own taste comes from the same source; others add that beauty is in the eye of the beholder, and that it is used every day to sell, flatter and persuade.

read.author: Charles Darwin
read.work: The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex
read.ref: Chapter XIII (the Argus pheasant) and Chapter XXI, from the general summary (shortened)
read.who: English naturalist (1809–1882), who studied at Cambridge intending to become a clergyman, sailed round the world on HMS Beagle and set out evolution by natural selection in On the Origin of Species (1859).
paras: The Argus pheasant affords a much more remarkable case. The immensely developed secondary wing-feathers are confined to the male; and each is ornamented with a row of from twenty to twenty-three ocelli, above an inch in diameter. These feathers are also elegantly marked with oblique stripes and rows of spots of a dark colour, like those on the skin of a tiger and leopard combined. These beautiful ornaments are hidden until the male shows himself off before the female. He then erects his tail, and expands his wing-feathers into a great, almost upright, circular fan or shield, which is carried in front of the body. The neck and head are held on one side, so that they are concealed by the fan; but the bird in order to see the female, before whom he is displaying himself, sometimes pushes his head between two of the long wing-feathers (as Mr. Bartlett has seen), and then presents a grotesque appearance. This must be a frequent habit with the bird in a state of nature, for Mr. Bartlett and his son on examining some perfect skins sent from the East, found a place between two of the feathers which was much frayed, as if the head had here frequently been pushed through. Mr. Wood thinks that the male can also peep at the female on one side, beyond the margin of the fan.

The ocelli on the wing-feathers are wonderful objects; for they are so shaded that, as the Duke of Argyll remarks, they stand out like balls lying loosely within sockets. When I looked at the specimen in the British Museum, which is mounted with the wings expanded and trailing downwards, I was however greatly disappointed, for the ocelli appeared flat, or even concave. But Mr. Gould soon made the case clear to me, for he held the feathers erect, in the position in which they would naturally be displayed, and now, from the light shining on them from above, each ocellus at once resembled the ornament called a ball and socket. These feathers have been shown to several artists, and all have expressed their admiration at the perfect shading. It may well be asked, could such artistically shaded ornaments have been formed by means of sexual selection? But it will be convenient to defer giving an answer to this question until we treat in the next chapter of the principle of gradation.

The foregoing remarks relate to the secondary wing-feathers, but the primary wing-feathers, which in most gallinaceous birds are uniformly coloured, are in the Argus pheasant equally wonderful. They are of a soft brown tint with numerous dark spots, each of which consists of two or three black dots with a surrounding dark zone. But the chief ornament is a space parallel to the dark-blue shaft, which in outline forms a perfect second feather lying within the true feather. This inner part is coloured of a lighter chestnut, and is thickly dotted with minute white points. I have shewn this feather to several persons, and many have admired it even more than the ball and socket feathers, and have declared that it was more like a work of art than of nature. Now these feathers are quite hidden on all ordinary occasions, but are fully displayed, together with the long secondary feathers, when they are all expanded together so as to form the great fan or shield.

The case of the male Argus pheasant is eminently interesting, because it affords good evidence that the most refined beauty may serve as a sexual charm, and for no other purpose. We must conclude that this is the case, as the secondary and primary wing-feathers are not at all displayed, and the ball and socket ornaments are not exhibited in full perfection until the male assumes the attitude of courtship. The Argus pheasant does not possess brilliant colours, so that his success in love appears to depend on the great size of his plumes, and on the elaboration of the most elegant patterns. Many will declare that it is utterly incredible that a female bird should be able to appreciate fine shading and exquisite patterns. It is undoubtedly a marvellous fact that she should possess this almost human degree of taste. He who thinks that he can safely gauge the discrimination and taste of the lower animals may deny that the female Argus pheasant can appreciate such refined beauty; but he will then be compelled to admit that the extraordinary attitudes assumed by the male during the act of courtship, by which the wonderful beauty of his plumage is fully displayed, are purposeless; and this is a conclusion which I for one will never admit.

Although we have some positive evidence that birds appreciate bright and beautiful objects, as with the bower-birds of Australia, and although they certainly appreciate the power of song, yet I fully admit that it is astonishing that the females of many birds and some mammals should be endowed with sufficient taste to appreciate ornaments, which we have reason to attribute to sexual selection; and this is even more astonishing in the case of reptiles, fish, and insects. But we really know little about the minds of the lower animals. It cannot be supposed, for instance, that male birds of paradise or peacocks should take such pains in erecting, spreading, and vibrating their beautiful plumes before the females for no purpose. We should remember the fact given on excellent authority in a former chapter, that several peahens, when debarred from an admired male, remained widows during a whole season rather than pair with another bird.

Nevertheless I know of no fact in natural history more wonderful than that the female Argus pheasant should appreciate the exquisite shading of the ball-and-socket ornaments and the elegant patterns on the wing-feather of the male. He who thinks that the male was created as he now exists must admit that the great plumes, which prevent the wings from being used for flight, and which are displayed during courtship and at no other time in a manner quite peculiar to this one species, were given to him as an ornament. If so, he must likewise admit that the female was created and endowed with the capacity of appreciating such ornaments. I differ only in the conviction that the male Argus pheasant acquired his beauty gradually, through the preference of the females during many generations for the more highly ornamented males; the aesthetic capacity of the females having been advanced through exercise or habit, just as our own taste is gradually improved. In the male through the fortunate chance of a few feathers being left unchanged, we can distinctly trace how simple spots with a little fulvous shading on one side may have been developed by small steps into the wonderful ball-and-socket ornaments; and it is probable that they were actually thus developed.

Everyone who admits the principle of evolution, and yet feels great difficulty in admitting that female mammals, birds, reptiles, and fish, could have acquired the high taste implied by the beauty of the males, and which generally coincides with our own standard, should reflect that the nerve-cells of the brain in the highest as well as in the lowest members of the Vertebrate series, are derived from those of the common progenitor of this great Kingdom. For we can thus see how it has come to pass that certain mental faculties, in various and widely distinct groups of animals, have been developed in nearly the same manner and to nearly the same degree.

sessions.readWhy: Darwin studies the Argus pheasant, whose wing feathers carry rows of eye-spots so finely shaded that artists admired them, and concludes that 'the most refined beauty may serve as a sexual charm, and for no other purpose.' He is answering writers such as the Duke of Argyll, who saw such ornament as beauty made for its own sake. Darwin does not sneer: he calls the female bird's taste a marvel. But his conclusion is the heart of the objection: our own sense of beauty may have the same humble origin as hers.

think.why: This depth states the objections fairly: that beauty is in the eye of the beholder and shaped by culture, and that Christians themselves have feared beauty could become an idol, to the point of stripping their churches bare.

evidence.why: The evidence cuts both ways. A large review found that people agree strongly about which faces are attractive, even across cultures, and that attractive people are judged and treated better: real evidence that beauty sways us, often unfairly. Another study found that people share taste for faces and landscapes far more than for buildings and paintings, which fits an inherited origin for some of our taste and a learned one for the rest. A small brain-scan study found the same region active for beautiful paintings and beautiful music. None of this settles whether beauty points beyond itself: the sceptic and the believer can both read it.

learn.why: Herbert's poem answers the objection in a single line. When the guest protests that he cannot bear to look at Love, Love takes his hand, smiles and asks, 'Who made the eyes but I?'

music.why: Morten Lauridsen set this old Christmas text in 1994; it marvels that animals should see the newborn Lord lying in a manger. After Darwin's birds, listen to slow, rich chords that linger over animals and a child, and ask whether what you feel is only a charm.

look.why: Look closely before deciding anything. Martin Johnson Heade paints a petal-pink and amethyst-purple orchid growing from a mossy branch close to us, and three jewel-toned hummingbirds gathered round a nest, against a distant, hazy forest. He painted it in 1871, the year The Descent of Man appeared, and Darwin wrote about hummingbirds in it. Is your delight in these birds only an old preference, or a glimpse of something real?

sessions.practice: Live it this week: the research shows that looks sway how we treat people. Each day, give your full, kind attention to someone easily overlooked because of their looks, age or clothes: learn their name and use it.
sessions.reflect: If your sense of beauty was shaped by evolution, does that make it less trustworthy, or only older than you thought?

sessions.title: Filled to make
sessions.line: In the wilderness God calls a craftsman by name and fills him with his Spirit.
sessions.why: If beauty can be used to take things from people, the Bible's answer is not to give it up but to ask what it is for and who it serves. In Exodus, God fills a craftsman with his Spirit, and a whole people give so freely that they have to be told to stop.

paras: All the congregation of the children of Israel departed from the presence of Moses.

They came, everyone whose heart stirred him up, and everyone whom his spirit made willing, and brought Yahweh’s offering for the work of the Tent of Meeting, and for all of its service, and for the holy garments.

They came, both men and women, as many as were willing-hearted, and brought brooches, earrings, signet rings, and armlets, all jewels of gold; even every man who offered an offering of gold to Yahweh.
Everyone with whom was found blue, purple, scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, and sea cow hides, brought them.
Everyone who offered an offering of silver and bronze brought Yahweh’s offering; and everyone with whom was found acacia wood for any work of the service, brought it.
All the women who were wise-hearted spun with their hands, and brought that which they had spun: the blue, the purple, the scarlet, and the fine linen.
All the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom spun the goats’ hair.
The rulers brought the onyx stones and the stones to be set for the ephod and for the breastplate;
with the spice and the oil for the light, for the anointing oil, and for the sweet incense.
The children of Israel brought a free will offering to Yahweh; every man and woman whose heart made them willing to bring for all the work, which Yahweh had commanded to be made by Moses.
Moses said to the children of Israel, “Behold, Yahweh has called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
He has filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, in understanding, in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship;
and to make skillful works, to work in gold, in silver, in bronze,
in cutting of stones for setting, and in carving of wood, to work in all kinds of skillful workmanship.
He has put in his heart that he may teach, both he and Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan.

He has filled them with wisdom of heart to work all kinds of workmanship, of the engraver, of the skillful workman, and of the embroiderer, in blue, in purple, in scarlet, and in fine linen, and of the weaver, even of those who do any workmanship, and of those who make skillful works.

“Bezalel and Oholiab shall work with every wise-hearted man, in whom Yahweh has put wisdom and understanding to know how to do all the work for the service of the sanctuary, according to all that Yahweh has commanded.”
Moses called Bezalel and Oholiab, and every wise-hearted man, in whose heart Yahweh had put wisdom, even everyone whose heart stirred him up to come to the work to do it.

They received from Moses all the offering which the children of Israel had brought for the work of the service of the sanctuary, with which to make it. They kept bringing free will offerings to him every morning.
All the wise men, who performed all the work of the sanctuary, each came from his work which he did.
They spoke to Moses, saying, “The people have brought much more than enough for the service of the work which Yahweh commanded to make.”

Moses gave a commandment, and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp, saying, “Let neither man nor woman make anything else for the offering for the sanctuary.” So the people were restrained from bringing.
For the stuff they had was sufficient to do all the work, and too much.

sessions.readWhy: The Israelites, newly freed from slavery, make a tent where God will meet them. Everyone 'whose heart stirred him up' brings gold, wool, wood or skill; the skilled women spin with their hands; and Bezalel is 'filled with the Spirit of God' for work in gold, stone and wood, and given the gift to teach others. It ends with the craftsmen telling Moses that the people have brought 'much more than enough'. Here beauty is not a lure to take from people: it is what they give.

think.why: The tent Bezalel built was where God met his people; John says that in Jesus 'the Word became flesh, and lived among us', using a word that means he pitched his tent, and this depth explains why that lets matter, and so craft and art, carry holiness.

learn.why: The 'holy garments' in this reading were made for Aaron the priest, and these are the words that he and his sons were given to bless the people (Numbers 6:22–27).

music.why: Anton Bruckner, a cathedral organist and devout Catholic, wrote this short motet in 1869 for the consecration of a chapel in the new cathedral at Linz. Its Latin words, sung at the dedication of churches, begin: 'This place was made by God, a priceless mystery.' Listen to how quietly a whole building is offered back.

look.why: Exodus names the embroiderers and the women who 'spun with their hands'. Diego Velázquez paints a woman with rosy cheeks and brown hair pulled back, in a dark corset with white fabric over her shoulders, looking down at the needlework in her hands. The whole picture is her attention.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: make something by hand for someone else, bake bread, mend a garment, frame a photograph, copy out a poem in your best handwriting, and give it without saying how long it took.
sessions.reflect: What skill of yours could become an offering, and not only a job or a pastime?

sessions.title: The beauty of the imperfect
sessions.line: A Victorian critic looks at the rough carvings on an old cathedral and sees free men.
sessions.why: Exodus gave us a craftsman filled with the Spirit. Ruskin asks what becomes of beauty when workers are turned into machines. His answer brings the course home: the beauty worth having is not the flawless finish that sells, but the mark of living, thinking, imperfect people, and of a faith that lets them confess their faults without fear.

read.author: John Ruskin
read.ref: Volume II, chapter VI, 'The Nature of Gothic', from the section on 'Savageness' (shortened)
read.who: John Ruskin (1819–1900), English art critic and social thinker, brought up on daily Bible reading, who moved from writing about painting and architecture to writing about the lives of working people.
paras: But in the mediaeval, or especially Christian, system of ornament, this slavery is done away with altogether; Christianity having recognized, in small things as well as great, the individual value of every soul. But it not only recognizes its value; it confesses its imperfection, in only bestowing dignity upon the acknowledgment of unworthiness. That admission of lost power and fallen nature, which the Greek or Ninevite felt to be intensely painful, and, as far as might be, altogether refused, the Christian makes daily and hourly contemplating the fact of it without fear, as tending, in the end, to God's greater glory. Therefore, to every spirit which Christianity summons to her service, her exhortation is: Do what you can, and confess frankly what you are unable to do; neither let your effort be shortened for fear of failure, nor your confession silenced for fear of shame. And it is, perhaps, the principal admirableness of the Gothic schools of architecture, that they thus receive the results of the labour of inferior minds; and out of fragments full of imperfection, and betraying that imperfection in every touch, indulgently raise up a stately and unaccusable whole.

But the modern English mind has this much in common with that of the Greek, that it intensely desires, in all things, the utmost completion or perfection compatible with their nature. This is a noble character in the abstract, but becomes ignoble when it causes us to forget the relative dignities of that nature itself, and to prefer the perfectness of the lower nature to the imperfection of the higher; not considering that as, judged by such a rule, all the brute animals would be preferable to man, because more perfect in their functions and kind, and yet are always held inferior to him, so also in the works of man, those which are more perfect in their kind are always inferior to those which are, in their nature, liable to more faults and shortcomings. For the finer the nature, the more flaws it will show through the clearness of it; and it is a law of this universe, that the best things shall be seldomest seen in their best form. The wild grass grows well and strongly, one year with another; but the wheat is, according to the greater nobleness of its nature, liable to the bitterer blight. And therefore, while in all things that we see or do, we are to desire perfection, and strive for it, we are nevertheless not to set the meaner thing, in its narrow accomplishment, above the nobler thing, in its mighty progress; not to esteem smooth minuteness above shattered majesty; not to prefer mean victory to honourable defeat; not to lower the level of our aim, that we may the more surely enjoy the complacency of success. But, above all, in our dealings with the souls of other men, we are to take care how we check, by severe requirement or narrow caution, efforts which might otherwise lead to a noble issue; and, still more, how we withhold our admiration from great excellencies, because they are mingled with rough faults. Now, in the make and nature of every man, however rude or simple, whom we employ in manual labour, there are some powers for better things: some tardy imagination, torpid capacity of emotion, tottering steps of thought, there are, even at the worst; and in most cases it is all our own fault that they are tardy or torpid. But they cannot be strengthened, unless we are content to take them in their feebleness, and unless we prize and honour them in their imperfection above the best and most perfect manual skill. And this is what we have to do with all our labourers; to look for the thoughtful part of them, and get that out of them, whatever we lose for it, whatever faults and errors we are obliged to take with it. For the best that is in them cannot manifest itself, but in company with much error. Understand this clearly; You can teach a man to draw a straight line, and to cut one; to strike a curved line, and to carve it; and to copy and carve any number of given lines or forms, with admirable speed and perfect precision; and you find his work perfect of its kind: but if you ask him to think about any of those forms, to consider if he cannot find any better in his own head, he stops; his execution becomes hesitating; he thinks, and ten to one he thinks wrong; ten to one he makes a mistake in the first touch he gives to his work as a thinking being. But you have made a man of him for all that. He was only a machine before, an animated tool.

And observe, you are put to stern choice in this matter. You must either make a tool of the creature, or a man of him. You cannot make both. Men were not intended to work with the accuracy of tools, to be precise and perfect in all their actions. If you will have that precision out of them, and make their fingers measure degrees like cog-wheels, and their arms strike curves like compasses, you must unhumanize them. All the energy of their spirits must be given to make cogs and compasses of themselves. All their attention and strength must go to the accomplishment of the mean act. The eye of the soul must be bent upon the finger-point, and the soul's force must fill all the invisible nerves that guide it, ten hours a day, that it may not err from its steely precision, and so soul and sight be worn away, and the whole human being be lost at last—a heap of sawdust, so far as its intellectual work in this world is concerned; saved only by its Heart, which cannot go into the form of cogs and compasses, but expands, after the ten hours are over, into fireside humanity. On the other hand, if you will make a man of the working creature, you cannot make a tool. Let him but begin to imagine, to think, to try to do anything worth doing; and the engine-turned precision is lost at once. Out come all his roughness, all his dulness, all his incapability; shame upon shame, failure upon failure, pause after pause: but out comes the whole majesty of him also; and we know the height of it only when we see the clouds settling upon him. And, whether the clouds be bright or dark, there will be transfiguration behind and within them.

And, on the other hand, go forth again to gaze upon the old cathedral front, where you have smiled so often at the fantastic ignorance of the old sculptors: examine once more those ugly goblins, and formless monsters, and stern statues, anatomiless and rigid; but do not mock at them, for they are signs of the life and liberty of every workman who struck the stone; a freedom of thought, and rank in scale of being, such as no laws, no charters, no charities can secure; but which it must be the first aim of all Europe at this day to regain for her children.

The second reason is, that imperfection is in some sort essential to all that we know of life. It is the sign of life in a mortal body, that is to say, of a state of progress and change. Nothing that lives is, or can be, rigidly perfect; part of it is decaying, part nascent. The foxglove blossom,—a third part bud, a third part past, a third part in full bloom,—is a type of the life of this world. And in all things that live there are certain irregularities and deficiencies which are not only signs of life, but sources of beauty. No human face is exactly the same in its lines on each side, no leaf perfect in its lobes, no branch in its symmetry. All admit irregularity as they imply change; and to banish imperfection is to destroy expression, to check exertion, to paralyze vitality. All things are literally better, lovelier, and more beloved for the imperfections which have been divinely appointed, that the law of human life may be Effort, and the law of human judgment, Mercy.

sessions.readWhy: Ruskin argues that the Greek master builder allowed his workmen no imperfection, while the Gothic builders let every carver think for himself and accepted rough results, because Christianity recognises 'the individual value of every soul' and confesses imperfection without fear. 'You must either make a tool of the creature, or a man of him.' His last sentence is a law for art and for people alike: 'that the law of human life may be Effort, and the law of human judgment, Mercy.'

think.why: Ruskin's choice between a tool and a person is our question too; this short answer says that a person is worth more than what he or she produces.

learn.why: Few of the carvers Ruskin praised are known by name. Thomas à Kempis's 'love to be thyself unknown' is the spirit in which much of the beauty of the old churches was made.

music.why: Ralph Vaughan Williams, who edited The English Hymnal, took a psalm tune that Thomas Tallis wrote in 1567 and built this work for strings for Gloucester Cathedral, where it was first played in 1910. Two string orchestras, one large and one small, and a string quartet answer one another like voices across a nave. Listen to how an old, plain tune grows until it seems to fill the stone.

look.why: Hans Memling paints a young woman holding a baby on her lap, seated on a curving gold chair between two kneeling angels, under an ornately carved stone arch. Ruskin did not despise fine finish: elsewhere in this chapter he praises the great masters who 'finished with the most exquisite care'. Look at the carved arch and the gold, and ask his question: is this finish serving a thought, or only showing off?

sessions.practice: Live it this week: when someone's work is rough but honest, a child's drawing, a colleague's first attempt, a meal that did not quite work, look for the thought in it and praise that first, specifically.
sessions.reflect: Where do you demand a perfection of yourself or others that is really a kind of slavery?

closing.title: Your answer
closing.prompt: You have read a psalm, Plato, Augustine, Darwin, Exodus and Ruskin, and looked closely at six paintings. What do you now think beauty is for: a charm, a pleasure, a signpost, a gift, or something else? And what will you do with it?
closing.practice: Once a week, give something beautiful away: a piece of music sent with a note, a meal laid with care, an afternoon in a gallery with someone who would not go alone.

title: Light, stone and glass
question: Can a building lead you to God?
line: Six sessions inside the great cathedrals: how they were built, how to read their glass and stone, why some Christians hated them, and what they were for.
why: Millions of people who never pray still walk into cathedrals and fall silent. This journey asks why. It follows the idea of a house for God from Solomon's Temple to Saint-Denis and Chartres, teaches you to read stained glass, stone and sound as their makers meant them to be read, and gives full voice to the monk who said the money should have gone to the poor. It is written at the depth of a first-year university course, for anyone.
follows: A first-year history of art paper on Gothic architecture and its makers, with elements of a theology paper on Christianity and the transformation of culture.
outcomes: Explain why the first Christians had no sacred buildings, and why they later built basilicas and called them pictures of heaven.
Say what was new at Saint-Denis in the 1140s, how pointed arches, rib vaults and buttresses let walls become glass, and why historians argue about Suger's theology of light.
Read a medieval stained-glass window pane by pane, and explain how it was made.
State Bernard of Clairvaux's case against costly church art at full strength, and weigh the best answers to it.
Explain how cathedral music, from plainchant to evensong, was shaped by the buildings and the hours of prayer.
Walk into almost any old church and read it: its orientation, its storeys, its windows, its saints and its history.

glossary.def: A walkway round the back of the altar, so that pilgrims can circulate without disturbing services.
Leading upward: Suger's word for the way material beauty lifts the mind to God.
The rounded end of a church, usually at the east, behind the altar.
A row of arches on columns; in a nave, the lowest storey, opening into the aisles.
A lower passage running alongside the nave, behind a row of columns.
A Roman public hall: long, with a tall central space and lower sides. The model for most churches.
A carved stone where the ribs of a vault meet.
A mass of stone built against a wall to resist the outward push of the vault.
Both the singers and the part of the church east of the crossing where they sing the services.
A monk of the reformed order founded at Cîteaux in 1098, vowed to poverty and simplicity.
The 'clear storey': the row of high windows in the upper wall of the nave.
A great Benedictine abbey in Burgundy, famous for its rich worship and huge church.
Where the nave and the transepts meet, often under a tower.
The service that consecrates a church to God, with readings and chants of its own.
The daily round of prayer at set hours, sung chiefly from the Psalms.
The evening service of the Church of England, made by Cranmer in 1549 from Vespers and Compline.
A buttress that reaches over the side aisle on an arch to support the upper walls.
The basin used for baptism, often placed near the west door.
The style begun in France in the 1140s, with pointed arches, rib vaults and large windows. Named later as an insult.
Clear or greyish glass painted or leaded in patterns, without coloured pictures; favoured by the Cistercians.
The destruction of religious images, as in parts of the Reformation.
A remission of the punishment due for sin, granted by the Church; their sale for building St Peter's sparked Luther's protest.
A chapel dedicated to Mary, often at the east end of an English cathedral.
A tall, narrow window with a pointed top.
The strip of lead, H-shaped in section, that holds the pieces of glass in a window.
A window made of framed scenes (circles, squares, quatrefoils), read in order.
The main body of a church, from the west door to the crossing. From the Latin for 'ship'.
Early harmony: one or more voices added above a plainchant melody.
Single-line, unaccompanied sung prayer, also called Gregorian chant.
An arch of two curves meeting at a point; it can be made taller or narrower at will.
Small chapels opening off the ambulatory around the apse.
The lingering of sound in a space after its source stops.
A stone ceiling with arched ribs that carry its weight down to a few points.
The style of the 11th and 12th centuries, with round arches and thick walls.
A great round window, usually in a west front or transept, filled with tracery and glass.
The stonework that divides a window: pierced through a slab (plate) or built of thin bars (bar).
The arms of a cross-shaped church, reaching north and south.
The narrow middle storey of a nave wall, often a walkway in the wall's thickness.
Reading Old Testament events as foreshadowing the New, often shown side by side in glass.
The main entrance front of a church, usually with portals, towers and a rose.

sessions.title: A house for God?
sessions.line: A king builds God a house, then admits no house could ever hold him.
sessions.plain: Before there were cathedrals there was a question: can God live in a building at all? This session follows that question from Solomon's Temple to the first Christian churches. By the end you will see why Christians built at all, and why, one day, they built so high.
sessions.why: Every cathedral begins with a prayer that contradicts itself. Before we look at stone and glass, we need the question the builders were answering, and it is three thousand years old.
before: Solomon builds God a house and then says no house can hold God. Which does he really believe?
Notice what Solomon asks the house to be for. Is it for God's sake, or for the people's?
In the comparison passage, where has the temple gone?

paras: Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel, with all the heads of the tribes, the princes of the fathers’ households of the children of Israel, to king Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of Yahweh’s covenant out of David’s city, which is Zion.
All the men of Israel assembled themselves to king Solomon at the feast, in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month.
All the elders of Israel came, and the priests picked up the ark.
They brought up Yahweh’s ark, the Tent of Meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the Tent. The priests and the Levites brought these up.
King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who were assembled to him, were with him before the ark, sacrificing sheep and cattle, that could not be counted or numbered for multitude.
The priests brought in the ark of Yahweh’s covenant to its place, into the inner sanctuary of the house, to the most holy place, even under the cherubim’s wings.
For the cherubim spread their wings out over the place of the ark, and the cherubim covered the ark and its poles above.
The poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the holy place before the inner sanctuary; but they were not seen outside. They are there to this day.
There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets which Moses put there at Horeb, when Yahweh made a covenant with the children of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt.
It came to pass, when the priests had come out of the holy place, that the cloud filled Yahweh’s house,
so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for Yahweh’s glory filled Yahweh’s house.
Then Solomon said, “Yahweh has said that he would dwell in the thick darkness.
I have surely built you a house of habitation, a place for you to dwell in forever.”
The king turned his face around, and blessed all the assembly of Israel; and all the assembly of Israel stood.
He said, “Blessed is Yahweh, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David your father, and has with his hand fulfilled it, saying,

‘Since the day that I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel to build a house, that my name might be there; but I chose David to be over my people Israel.’
“Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel.
But Yahweh said to David my father, ‘Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart.
Nevertheless, you shall not build the house; but your son who shall come out of your body, he shall build the house for my name.’

Yahweh has established his word that he spoke; for I have risen up in the place of David my father, and I sit on the throne of Israel, as Yahweh promised, and have built the house for the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel.
There I have set a place for the ark, in which is Yahweh’s covenant, which he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.”
Solomon stood before Yahweh’s altar in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven;

and he said, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above, or on earth beneath; who keeps covenant and loving kindness with your servants, who walk before you with all their heart;
who has kept with your servant David my father that which you promised him. Yes, you spoke with your mouth, and have fulfilled it with your hand, as it is today.

Now therefore, may Yahweh, the God of Israel, keep with your servant David my father that which you have promised him, saying, ‘There shall not fail from you a man in my sight to sit on the throne of Israel, if only your children take heed to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.’
“Now therefore, God of Israel, please let your word be verified, which you spoke to your servant David my father.
But will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
Yet have respect for the prayer of your servant, and for his supplication, Yahweh my God, to listen to the cry and to the prayer which your servant prays before you today;
that your eyes may be open toward this house night and day, even toward the place of which you have said, ‘My name shall be there;’ to listen to the prayer which your servant prays toward this place.
Listen to the supplication of your servant, and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. Yes, hear in heaven, your dwelling place; and when you hear, forgive.

notes.text: The seventh month is in the autumn, the time of the harvest festival of Tabernacles, when Israel remembered living in tents in the desert. The house of God is dedicated at the feast of the tent.
The ark, the gold-covered chest at the heart of the Temple, held only the two stone tablets of the law. The holiest object in Israel was a container for words.
The cloud is the sign of God's presence, the same cloud that filled the tent in the desert (Exodus 40:34). Christians later called this presence 'the glory'.
'Thick darkness': in Solomon's Temple God dwells in the dark of the inner room. Keep this in mind for the next session, when a French abbot builds for light.
The key verse of this session, and perhaps of the whole journey.
Solomon asks God to hear prayers made 'toward this place'. Jews still pray facing Jerusalem, and most churches face east, towards the rising sun, for a similar reason: prayer has a direction.

sessions.readWhy: This is the first great dedication of a house of God in the Bible, and every church dedication since has echoed it. Solomon's prayer holds the whole paradox of sacred building in one verse: heaven cannot contain God, how much less this house.

paras: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s farming, God’s building.
According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds on it. But let each man be careful how he builds on it.
For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.
But if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or stubble,
each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is.
If any man’s work remains which he built on it, he will receive a reward.
If any man’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, but as through fire.
Don’t you know that you are a temple of God, and that God’s Spirit lives in you?
If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him; for God’s temple is holy, which you are.
compare.why: Paul, writing to a young church that owned no building at all, moves the temple from stone to people. 'You are God's building.' Every church since has had to hold these two passages together.

paras: Solomon has spent seven years building. The Temple is finished, the ark has been carried in, the cloud has filled the house so thickly that the priests cannot stand to do their work. It is the greatest moment of his reign. And at the very height of it he says something that seems to undo the whole project: 'Will God in very deed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens can't contain you; how much less this house that I have built!'

This is not modesty. It is theology. The God of Israel is not a local god who lives in a shrine and needs feeding. He made heaven and earth. So why build at all? Solomon's answer, in the rest of the prayer, is careful. The house is not where God is trapped; it is where God has chosen to put his name, a place 'toward' which people pray, and where God promises to hear. The building is a meeting place and a direction, not a container.

Hold on to that distinction. Every argument in this journey, from the abbot who filled his church with coloured light to the monk who said the money should have gone to the poor, is an argument about what a building for God can and cannot do.
sections.key: A house for God is not a container for God, but a place to pray towards, where God promises to hear.

sections.h: From the Temple to the upper room
paras: The first Christians had no temples. For nearly three centuries they met in houses: a large room lent by a richer member, a courtyard, sometimes a hired hall. The best evidence we have is a house at Dura-Europos, a Roman frontier town on the Euphrates, in modern Syria. Around AD 232 one of its houses was adapted for Christian worship, with a room set aside for baptism and painted with scenes of the Good Shepherd, Christ walking on the water and the women at the tomb. The town was destroyed by the Persians in about 256, and the house was buried, which is why it survived.

This was not only because Christians were poor or persecuted, though they were often both. It was also a conviction. When Paul tells the Corinthians that they are 'God's building' and 'a temple of God', he is saying something radical: the presence that once filled Solomon's house now lives in a community of ordinary people. In John's Gospel Jesus tells a Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when people will worship 'neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem', but 'in spirit and truth'.
So the first Christian answer to the question 'Where does God live?' was: among us. Christianity began as a faith without sacred buildings.
sections.key: For nearly three centuries Christians had no sacred buildings: the people themselves were the temple.

paras: The Temple Solomon built was destroyed by the Babylonians in 587 BC, rebuilt after the exile, magnificently enlarged by Herod the Great, and destroyed again by the Romans in AD 70. Jesus prayed in it and taught in its courts. After its fall, Jewish life gathered round the synagogue, the 'assembly', a place not of sacrifice but of reading, prayer and teaching, and Jews prayed facing the place where the Temple had stood.

The early Church inherited both. From the Temple it took the idea of a holy place and of sacrifice, now understood as Christ's once-for-all offering, remembered at the altar. From the synagogue it took the gathering to read Scripture, sing psalms and pray. A cathedral holds both inheritances in one building: the altar at the east end, the pulpit and the lectern in the nave. When you see them, you are seeing the Temple and the synagogue side by side.
sections.key: A church holds two inheritances side by side: the Temple's altar and the synagogue's reading and prayer.

sections.h: The basilica: borrowing Rome's public hall
paras: That changed with the Emperor Constantine, who ended the persecution in 313 and began to build churches on an imperial scale: the Lateran in Rome, and in the 320s and 330s the great church over the tomb of St Peter. Christians did not copy pagan temples, which were small houses for a god's statue, with the worship outside. They needed room for a crowd inside. So they borrowed the basilica, the Roman public hall used for law courts and business.

A basilica is a long rectangle: a tall central space, the nave, lit by windows high up, with lower aisles on either side behind rows of columns, and at the far end a rounded recess, the apse, where a magistrate once sat. In the Christian basilica the bishop sat there, with the altar in front of him. Almost every great church in Europe, including every Gothic cathedral, is a descendant of this plan. When you walk up a nave towards an altar, you are walking up a Roman hall of justice.
sections.key: Christians copied the Roman public hall, not the pagan temple, because they needed room for a crowd inside.

paras: Once Christians had buildings, they needed to say what they were. The answer they gave, again and again, came from the last book of the Bible: the church is an image of the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of God that comes down out of heaven in Revelation 21. When a church was consecrated, the service read that chapter, and from about the seventh century the hymn sung at a dedication began 'Urbs beata Ierusalem', 'Blessed city, heavenly Jerusalem'.

The other text read at a dedication was Jacob's cry when he woke from his dream of the ladder: 'How awesome this place is! This is none other than God's house, and this is the gate of heaven' (Genesis 28:17). Its Latin opens the chant for the anniversary of a church's dedication, 'Terribilis est locus iste', and a related chant, 'Locus iste', 'This place was made by God', is the text of the music in this session.

Notice what has happened. Paul said the people are the temple. The dedication rites keep that, but add something: the building is a sign of the people, and of the city they are travelling towards. It is a picture of heaven you can walk into.
sections.key: Once Christians had buildings, they explained them as pictures of the heavenly Jerusalem.

paras: Around the year 1000 Europe began building churches in stone on a scale not seen since Rome. A Burgundian monk, Rodulfus Glaber, writing around 1030, said it was as though the whole world were throwing off its old age and clothing itself in a white robe of churches. Historians call the style Romanesque, 'Roman-like', because it used the round arch and heavy masonry of Roman building.

Romanesque churches were often vast, built for monks and for pilgrims coming to see the relics of saints. But round arches and stone vaults are heavy. They push outwards as well as down, so the walls had to be thick and the windows small. The light inside a great Romanesque church is dim, solemn and beautiful, rather like the 'thick darkness' of Solomon's inner room.
