sessions.title: Where did everything come from?
sessions.line: The Bible's first page, and the Babylonian story it answers.
sessions.plain: The Bible opens with God making the world in seven days. Before asking whether that fits with science, which we will come to in session 6, we need to understand what this page meant to the people who first heard it. They lived surrounded by other creation stories, and the best way to see what Genesis is saying is to read it beside one of them.
sessions.why: This is the first session. It starts where the Bible starts, with the biggest question a child asks: where did everything come from?
answers: What does Genesis 1 actually say?
What kind of writing is it: science, history, poetry or something else?
Was Genesis copied from Babylonian myths?
What did this page mean to the people who first heard it?
sessions.finding: Genesis 1 says that one good God made an ordered, good world on purpose, and it says so deliberately against the myths of its neighbours.

background.h: If you are new to Genesis
paras: Genesis is the first book of the Bible. Its name is Greek for 'origin' or 'beginning'; in Hebrew it is called Bereshit, its first word, 'In the beginning'. It is the first of the five books of the Torah, the books of Moses (if you have taken Can I trust the Bible?, you met them there).

Genesis has two parts. Chapters 1 to 11 tell the story of the whole human race: creation, the first humans, the first murder, the flood and the tower of Babel. From chapter 12 the story narrows to one family, Abraham's, and stays with them. This journey is about those first eleven chapters, which scholars call the 'primeval history', the story of the beginning of everything.
background.key: Genesis 1–11 is the Bible's story of everyone, before it narrows to Abraham's family.

paras: Every child eventually asks the same questions. Where did everything come from? Who am I? Why do things go wrong? Why do people hurt each other? Will it all be all right? Why are there so many different people? Genesis 1–11 answers each of those questions in turn, in the form of stories. This journey takes them one at a time, a question a session.

Then, in session 6, we will ask the question an adult asks: does science prove these stories wrong? And in the last session we put it together. At the start of each session you will see the case so far.

timeline.text: Where did everything come from? (Genesis 1)
Who am I? (Genesis 2)
Why is the world broken? (Genesis 3)
Why do people hurt each other? (Genesis 4 and 6)
Will God give up on us? (the flood, Genesis 6–9)
Doesn't science say otherwise?
Why so many peoples? (Babel, Genesis 11) and the verdict

background.key: Six questions a child asks, one per session; then the question an adult asks; then the verdict.

background.h: The world it was written in
paras: Israel was a small people living between two great civilisations: Egypt to the south-west and Mesopotamia (modern Iraq) to the east, home of the Babylonians and Assyrians. Both had their own stories of how the world began, told in temples and at festivals. Most scholars think Genesis reached its final form in the sixth or fifth century BC, when many Israelites were living in exile in Babylon itself, surrounded by those stories; tradition holds that Moses wrote it much earlier. Either way, its first hearers knew the Babylonian stories well.

The most famous is called Enuma Elish, from its first words, 'When above'. It was recited every year at Babylon's New Year festival in honour of the city's god, Marduk. Its clay tablets were dug up at Nineveh in the 1840s and 1850s and first published in English in the 1870s.
background.key: Genesis was written among peoples with their own creation stories; Babylon's was Enuma Elish.

paras: The main reading is the Bible's first page, Genesis 1:1–2:3: seven days, from 'In the beginning' to God's rest. We read it in three parts, with a commentary after each.

Then, in the comparison, you will read three short extracts from Enuma Elish: how it begins, how its god makes the sky, and why it says human beings were made. Putting the two side by side is the quickest way to see what Genesis is claiming, and what it is arguing against.
background.key: Genesis 1 read beside Enuma Elish shows what Genesis is claiming, and what it is arguing against.

before: What is there before God speaks, and what is the first thing he makes?
Notice what is repeated, day after day. What pattern can you see?
In the comparison, how is the world made in the Babylonian story, and why are humans made?
sessions.readWhy: The first page of the Bible, read slowly in three parts: the world given its shape, the world filled with life, and the seventh day. Each part has a commentary.

paras: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters.
God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
God saw the light, and saw that it was good. God divided the light from the darkness.
God called the light “day”, and the darkness he called “night”. There was evening and there was morning, the first day.
God said, “Let there be an expanse in the middle of the waters, and let it divide the waters from the waters.”
God made the expanse, and divided the waters which were under the expanse from the waters which were above the expanse; and it was so.
God called the expanse “sky”. There was evening and there was morning, a second day.
God said, “Let the waters under the sky be gathered together to one place, and let the dry land appear;” and it was so.
God called the dry land “earth”, and the gathering together of the waters he called “seas”. God saw that it was good.
God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth;” and it was so.
The earth yielded grass, herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, with their seeds in it, after their kind; and God saw that it was good.
There was evening and there was morning, a third day.
God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs to mark seasons, days, and years;
and let them be for lights in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth;” and it was so.
God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. He also made the stars.
God set them in the expanse of the sky to give light to the earth,
and to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness. God saw that it was good.
There was evening and there was morning, a fourth day.
God said, “Let the waters abound with living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth in the open expanse of the sky.”
God created the large sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarmed, after their kind, and every winged bird after its kind. God saw that it was good.
God blessed them, saying, “Be fruitful, and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth.”
There was evening and there was morning, a fifth day.
God said, “Let the earth produce living creatures after their kind, livestock, creeping things, and animals of the earth after their kind;” and it was so.
God made the animals of the earth after their kind, and the livestock after their kind, and everything that creeps on the ground after its kind. God saw that it was good.

God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
God said, “Behold, I have given you every herb yielding seed, which is on the surface of all the earth, and every tree, which bears fruit yielding seed. It will be your food.
To every animal of the earth, and to every bird of the sky, and to everything that creeps on the earth, in which there is life, I have given every green herb for food;” and it was so.
God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. There was evening and there was morning, a sixth day.
The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished.
On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.

parts.title: Days 1 to 3: the world given its shape
parts.context: The opening of Genesis. Imagine it read aloud: it is written to be heard, with repeated refrains like a song. The world begins as 'formless and empty', and God speaks it into order.

commentary.on: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
commentary.text: The first sentence of the Bible. There is no story of where God came from, no battle, no rival. God simply is, and everything else is made. 'The heavens and the earth' is a Hebrew way of saying 'everything'.

commentary.on: The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep
commentary.text: 'Formless and empty' (in Hebrew, tohu wa-bohu) is the starting point: a dark, watery chaos. Remember these two words, because the next six days answer them. In the first three days God gives the world form; in the next three he fills it.

commentary.on: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
commentary.text: God creates by speaking. Nothing resists him and nothing has to be fought. Compare this with the Babylonian story you will read shortly, where the world is made out of a defeated monster.

commentary.on: God saw the light, and saw that it was good.
commentary.text: This refrain comes seven times in the chapter. The world is good, the light is good, the land, the plants, the animals are good. In many ancient religions matter was dark or tainted; Genesis says, again and again, that the physical world is good.

commentary.on: Let there be an expanse in the middle of the waters
commentary.text: The 'expanse' (older Bibles say 'firmament') divides the waters above from the waters below. Ancient peoples pictured the sky as a great dome holding back waters above, which is why rain was 'the windows of heaven' opening. Genesis speaks the language of its time about the shape of the world; its point is who made it, not its physics.

commentary.on: There was evening and there was morning, a third day.
commentary.text: Day one makes light, day two the sky and sea, day three the dry land and plants. These are three spaces, made ready like rooms in a house. Now they need filling.

parts.title: Days 4 to 6: the world filled with life
parts.context: The second half of the week. Watch how each day matches one of the first three days.

commentary.on: God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night.
commentary.text: Notice what is missing: the words 'sun' and 'moon'. In Hebrew, as in Babylonian, those words were also the names of gods (the Babylonian sun god was Shamash). Genesis refuses to name them. They are not gods; they are lamps, hung in the sky by God to mark the seasons. For ancient hearers this was a bold, almost cheeky, demotion.

commentary.on: God created the large sea creatures
commentary.text: The great sea monsters, which other peoples feared as gods of chaos, are simply creatures God made, and he calls them good. Nothing in creation is a rival to God.

commentary.on: Let's make man in our image, after our likeness.
commentary.text: The pattern breaks. For the first time God pauses to deliberate: 'Let us make'. Christians have heard the Trinity in the 'us'; Jewish commentators suggest God speaking with his heavenly court, or a royal 'we'. Either way, human beings are made with special care.

commentary.on: God created man in his own image. In God's image he created him; male and female he created them.
commentary.text: This is one of the most important sentences ever written. Every human being, male and female, carries the image of God. In the ancient world, a king set up statues of himself, his 'images', across his land to show who ruled it. Genesis says every person, not only kings, is God's image in the world. Session 2 will explore what this means.

commentary.on: Have dominion over the fish of the sea
commentary.text: Humans are given rule over the other creatures. In context this is the rule of a good king who cares for his land, not a licence to destroy it; the next chapter says the man was put in the garden 'to cultivate and keep it'.

commentary.on: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.
commentary.text: After making humans, 'good' becomes 'very good'. The world as God made it is not a mistake or a battlefield. That conviction, that the world is good and orderly and worth studying, would one day help to make modern science possible.

parts.title: The seventh day
parts.context: The last three verses of the story, which belong with chapter 1 although they are numbered as chapter 2 (the chapter numbers were added in the Middle Ages).

commentary.on: he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done
commentary.text: The week ends not with more making but with rest. God does not rest because he is tired; he rests because the work is complete and good. The Hebrew word for 'rested' is the root of 'Sabbath'.

commentary.on: God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy
commentary.text: The first thing in the Bible called holy is not a place or a person but a day. Israel's weekly Sabbath, a day of rest for everyone, servants and animals included (Exodus 20:11), is rooted here. The whole Western week, with its day of rest, goes back to this page.

parts.author: The Babylonian creation epic (Enuma Elish)
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1921)
parts.title: Before anything was named
parts.context: The opening lines. Apsu is the god of fresh water and Tiamat the goddess of the salt sea; their waters are mixed together, and from them the first gods are born. The numbers are the line numbers of the tablet. Words in square brackets are the translator's guesses where the clay is broken.
parts.plain: The Babylonian story says: in the beginning, before the sky or the earth had names, there were only two watery gods, Apsu and Tiamat, their waters mixed together. Nothing had been made or decided. Then, out of them, the other gods were born.

commentary.on: When the heavens above were yet unnamed
commentary.text: It begins much like Genesis: before anything existed, only water. But notice the difference at once. Here the water is itself divine: Apsu and Tiamat are gods. In Genesis the 'deep' is just water, and God is outside it.

commentary.on: The gods came into being in the midst of them.
commentary.text: In Babylon, the gods themselves are born, out of the primeval waters. In Genesis, God is never born and has no beginning: 'In the beginning, God'.

parts.author: The Babylonian creation epic (Enuma Elish)
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1921)
parts.title: The sky made from a defeated goddess
parts.context: Between the first and fourth tablets, war breaks out among the gods. Tiamat raises an army of monsters; the young god Marduk agrees to fight her if he is made king of the gods. He kills her. This is what he does next.
parts.plain: The Babylonian story says: Marduk crushed Tiamat's skull and cut her blood vessels, and the other gods celebrated. Then he split her body in two like a fish, and lifted one half up to make the sky, setting guards to stop her waters escaping.

commentary.on: With his unsparing club he clave her skull.
commentary.text: In Babylon, the world is made through violence: a war among the gods, and the murder of a goddess. Creation is the spoils of victory.

commentary.on: He slit Tiamat open like a flat (?) fish [cut into] two pieces,
commentary.text: The sky is made from half of Tiamat's body, the other half becoming the earth. Compare Genesis: God divides the waters with a word, and the 'deep' is not a monster but plain water. Many scholars think the Hebrew word for 'the deep' (tehom) is related to the name Tiamat, which would make Genesis's calm 'deep' a deliberate quiet reply.

parts.author: The Babylonian creation epic (Enuma Elish)
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1921)
parts.ref: Enuma Elish, Tablet VI, lines 1–6 and 23–27
parts.title: Why humans were made
parts.context: The war is won and Marduk is king. Now the lesser gods complain about their work. Marduk has a plan. Kingu, mentioned here, was Tiamat's general, captured in the battle.
parts.plain: The Babylonian story says: Marduk decided to make a creature called 'Man' out of blood and bone, so that humans could do the gods' work and the gods could rest. They blamed Tiamat's general Kingu for the war, killed him, and made mankind out of his blood, to serve the gods.

commentary.on: The service of the gods shall be established, and I will set them (i.e., the gods) free.
commentary.text: Here is the heart of the difference. In Babylon, human beings were made to be slaves: to do the gods' hard labour so the gods could rest. In Genesis, human beings are made in God's image to rule the world as his representatives, and it is God who rests and then gives rest to everyone.

commentary.on: From his blood he (i.e., Ea) fashioned mankind for the service of the gods
commentary.text: Humans are made from the blood of a defeated rebel. Compare Genesis: humans are made by a God who is pleased with them, and called 'very good'. Two pictures of what a human being is, and they could not be more different. The West inherited the second.

compare.author: The Babylonian creation epic (Enuma Elish)
compare.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1921)
compare.why: Enuma Elish was Babylon's great creation story, recited at its New Year festival. Read three short extracts: how it begins, how its god makes the sky, and why it says humans were made. Then compare them with what you have just read.
compare.title: Babylon's story of creation

sections.h: What kind of writing is Genesis 1?
paras: The first question to ask of any text is what kind of writing it is. Genesis 1 is not poetry in the way the Psalms are, but it is not ordinary prose either. It is carefully patterned: ten times 'God said', seven times 'it was good', a seven-day week, and a refrain closing each day. It is written to be heard and remembered, like a solemn hymn or a liturgy.

It is also clearly not a modern scientific report. It describes the world as it looks to the eye, in the language of its time, and it is far more interested in who made the world, and why, than in how or when. That does not make it untrue; it tells us what kind of truth to look for in it.
sections.key: Genesis 1 is a patterned, solemn account written to be heard, more interested in who and why than how and when.

paras: The days are arranged in two matching sets of three. Remember the world began 'formless and empty'. Days one to three give it form by separating: light from dark, sea from sky, land from sea. Days four to six fill the spaces just made: lights for the day and night, fish and birds for the sea and sky, animals and humans for the land.
Then the seventh day stands apart: the week is crowned not by more work but by rest and blessing.

rows: God blesses the day and makes it holy

sections.key: Days one to three give the world form; days four to six fill it; day seven is rest.

paras: When the Babylonian tablets were first read in the 1870s, some people concluded that Genesis had simply copied Babylon. Scholars now see it differently. There are real similarities: a watery beginning, the dividing of the waters, a sky that holds back water above, the making of humans last. These were the shared ideas of the ancient world, like a common vocabulary.

But what Genesis says with that vocabulary is almost the opposite of Enuma Elish. One God, not many. No birth of the gods. No battle, no murder, no monster's body. The sun and moon not gods but lamps. Humans not slaves made from a rebel's blood but royal images, blessed and called very good. Most scholars now read Genesis 1 as a deliberate answer to the myths around it, a polemic, not a copy.

rows: Many gods, born from the waters
Through war and the killing of Tiamat
By God's word, with nothing resisting
Unnamed lamps, 'the greater light' and 'the lesser light'
To do the gods' work so the gods can rest
To bear God's image and care for the world
For the gods, by making humans work
For God, and then for everyone, on the seventh day

sections.key: Genesis shares the ancient world's picture of the cosmos but says the opposite of Babylon about God, the world and humans.

paras: Genesis describes the world as ancient people saw it: a flat earth beneath a dome of sky, with waters above the dome and below the earth. When the flood comes, 'the fountains of the great deep burst open, and the sky's windows opened' (Genesis 7:11). This picture was shared by Egyptians, Babylonians and Israelites.

Should that worry a reader today? Christians have long said not. Augustine and John Calvin both taught that Scripture speaks about nature in the everyday language of ordinary people, because its purpose is to teach about God and salvation, not astronomy. Calvin, commenting on this chapter in 1554, said that Moses wrote in a popular way that ordinary people could understand, and that anyone who wants to learn astronomy should go elsewhere.
sections.key: Genesis uses the ancient picture of the world; Christians since Augustine have said its purpose is to teach about God, not astronomy.

paras: Put simply, Genesis 1 makes six claims. There is one God, before and beyond everything. He made everything that exists. He made it by his word, freely, not by fighting anyone. It is good, every part of it. Human beings, men and women alike, bear his image. And there is a rhythm of work and rest built into the world.

None of these is a scientific claim, and none can be proved or disproved by a telescope. But each one was revolutionary in its time, and each one shaped the West: the goodness of matter, the dignity of every person, the order of nature that invites study, and the week with its day of rest.
sections.key: Genesis 1 claims one God, a free and good creation, human dignity and a rhythm of rest: none of them scientific claims, all of them revolutionary.

paras: Jews and Christians of every tradition read this chapter as true and inspired. They differ over how literally to take the seven days. Some of the earliest Christian readers already took them as more than ordinary days: Origen in the third century asked how there could be 'evening and morning' before the sun was made on day four, and Augustine thought God made everything at once and the days were a way of teaching its order. Others, such as Basil of Caesarea in the fourth century, read the days more literally.

Later sessions will come back to this: session 6 will ask what science says, and session 7 will set out how the churches read Genesis today. For now, notice that the debate about how to read the days is not new: it is as old as the Church.
sections.key: From the start, Jews and Christians have disagreed about how literally to read the days, while agreeing on what they teach about God.

debate.question: What is Genesis 1 mainly about?

positions.name: A literal week
positions.who: Basil of Caesarea in part; modern young-earth creationists
positions.view: Genesis 1 describes what God did in six ordinary days, in that order, and should be read as straightforward history.
positions.evidence: The 'evening and morning' of each day; Exodus 20:11 grounds the Sabbath in a six-day creation.

positions.name: A picture of order
positions.who: Augustine; many modern scholars, such as Gordon Wenham
positions.view: The days are a literary frame, forming and filling, that teaches the order and goodness of creation rather than a timetable.
positions.evidence: The matching pattern of days 1–3 and 4–6; light before the sun; Augustine's 'all at once'.

positions.name: A cosmic temple
positions.who: John Walton and others
positions.view: Genesis 1 describes God giving the world its functions and taking up residence in it, as an ancient temple was inaugurated over seven days; it is about purpose, not material origins.
positions.evidence: Ancient temple-dedication texts lasting seven days; God's 'rest' as enthronement.

debate.agree: All agree that Genesis 1 teaches one sovereign God, a good creation and human dignity.

look.why: Frederic Edwin Church, an American painter fascinated by science and by the natural world, painted this tropical river in 1877. It is not a picture of Genesis, but it shows the kind of world Genesis calls 'very good': light, water, plants and creatures, in their places.
points: A wide, calm river running away from us between banks of dense tropical forest.
Trees covered in climbing vines, with gnarled, sprawling branches.
Two tiny black birds with cherry-red chests on a curving stem near us, on the left.
A line of white birds flying low over the water, and a small white sun in a hazy sky.
Far off on the river, barely visible, a person rowing a canoe.

music.why: Haydn's oratorio The Creation (1798) sets Genesis 1 to music. At 'and there was light' the whole orchestra and choir burst out fortissimo: one of the most famous moments in music.

think.why: A first look at how Christians have related faith and science.

learn.why: The first words of the Bible: everything begins with God, and with light.

listen.why: A psychologist and a mathematician discuss God and the stories of Genesis. Listen for how differently they read the same chapter.

check.q: Why does Genesis say 'the greater light' and 'the lesser light' instead of 'sun' and 'moon'?
options: Those words were also names of gods, and Genesis refuses to treat them as gods
It is a mistranslation
The writer did not know what they were
The Hebrew language had no words for them
check.why: In the ancient Near East the sun and moon were worshipped; Genesis makes them lamps.

check.q: What is the clearest difference between why humans are made in Enuma Elish and in Genesis?
options: In Enuma Elish humans are made from clay, in Genesis from water
In Genesis humans are made first
In Enuma Elish humans are made to do the gods' labour; in Genesis they are made in God's image to care for the world
There is no difference
check.why: Slaves from a rebel's blood, or royal images called 'very good'.

check.q: Days four to six match days one to three. What does that pattern suggest?
options: That the writer made a mistake
That the sun was made before light
That the chapter is carefully arranged to teach order (forming, then filling), not written as a lab report
That there were only three days
check.why: The structure is part of the message.

check.q: Most scholars now describe the relation of Genesis 1 to Babylonian myth as:
options: A deliberate answer that uses the shared picture of the world but says the opposite about God and humans
Completely unrelated
A Babylonian copy of Genesis
A word-for-word copy
check.why: Shared vocabulary, opposite message: polemic, not plagiarism.

check.q: Origen and Augustine noticed something about 'evening and morning' on days one to three. What?
options: That they were added later
That they mean exactly 24 hours
That they contradict the Hebrew
That there could be no evening and morning in the ordinary sense before the sun was made on day four
check.why: Debate about how to read the days is as old as the Church.

check.q: Which of these is a claim Genesis 1 makes?
options: The earth is 6,000 years old
The world is good, and every human being bears God's image
The sky is made of crystal
Birds evolved from dinosaurs
check.why: Its claims are about God, goodness and humanity, not about dates or physics.

tutorial.question: What is Genesis 1 claiming, and how does reading it beside Enuma Elish help us see it?
tutorial.approach: Describe the structure of the chapter (forming, filling, rest). Then set it beside Enuma Elish on the gods, the method of creation, the sun and moon, the purpose of humans and the meaning of rest. Say what kind of writing Genesis 1 is, and what its main claims are.
strong: Describes the seven-day structure and its pattern of forming and filling.
Uses specific details from both texts (the 'greater light', Tiamat's body, Kingu's blood).
Explains why most scholars read Genesis 1 as an answer to its neighbours, not a copy.
Explains the ancient picture of the world and why Christians have not been troubled by it.
States the chapter's main claims about God, goodness and human dignity.
Notes that Christians have disagreed from the start about how literally to take the days.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: keep one day as a real day of rest: no work, no shopping, time with people you love. Notice what it feels like to stop.
sessions.reflect: If the world is 'very good', what in your own life have you been treating as less than that?
takeaways: Genesis 1 is a carefully patterned account: three days of forming, three of filling, and a day of rest.
Read beside Enuma Elish, it answers its neighbours: one God, no battle, sun and moon not gods, humans made in God's image rather than as slaves.
Its claims are about God, the goodness of the world and human dignity; from the start, readers disagreed about how literally to take the days.

sessions.title: Who am I?
sessions.line: Dust and breath, the garden, and a man and a woman.
sessions.plain: Genesis tells the creation story a second time, close up: God shaping a man from dust, breathing life into him, planting a garden and making a woman. This session asks what Genesis says a human being is, and what 'made in God's image' means.
sessions.why: Session 1 showed that the world is good and that human beings bear God's image. Now Genesis zooms in, and we ask the second question a child asks: who am I?
answers: Why are there two creation stories in Genesis?
What does 'made in the image of God' mean?
What does Genesis say about men and women?
Why does any of this matter today?
sessions.finding: Genesis says every human being, man and woman, is made in God's image: dust and divine breath, made to work, to love and to belong to God.

paras: In session 1 you read the Bible's first page: the world made good in seven days, crowned by human beings made in God's image, male and female. Read beside the Babylonian story, it said something revolutionary: humans are not slaves of the gods but God's representatives in his world.
background.key: Session 1: one good God, a good world, and humans in his image.

paras: At Genesis 2:4 the style changes completely. God is now called 'Yahweh God', using his personal name (Yahweh, often printed 'the LORD'). Instead of a cosmic week we are in a garden, close up: God shapes a man from the earth like a potter, breathes into him, plants trees, brings him animals and makes a woman.

Why two accounts? Many scholars think they come from two different sources, later placed side by side (session 6 will explain this theory). Others see a deliberate design: first the wide shot, then the close-up, like a film. Either way, the editor who put them together saw no contradiction: the first tells us where humans stand in the universe, the second what a human being is like.
background.key: Genesis 2 retells creation close up; whether from two sources or by design, the two accounts are meant to be read together.

paras: The main reading is Genesis 2:4–25, in three parts: the man made from dust and breath, the garden and its one command, and the making of the woman. These few verses have shaped Western ideas of human nature, work and marriage more than almost any others.
The comparison is Psalm 8, a hymn that asks the question of this session out loud, 'What is man?', and answers it from Genesis 1.
background.key: Genesis 2 shows what a human being is; Psalm 8 asks 'What is man?' and answers from Genesis.

before: What two things is the man made from?
What is the man given to do in the garden, and what is he told not to do?
Why does God make the woman, and how does the man respond?
sessions.readWhy: The second creation story, in three parts, with a commentary after each.

paras: This is the history of the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that Yahweh God made the earth and the heavens.
No plant of the field was yet in the earth, and no herb of the field had yet sprung up; for Yahweh God had not caused it to rain on the earth. There was not a man to till the ground,
but a mist went up from the earth, and watered the whole surface of the ground.
Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.

Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
Yahweh God commanded the man, saying, “You may freely eat of every tree of the garden;
but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.”
Yahweh God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.”

Out of the ground Yahweh God formed every animal of the field, and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. Whatever the man called every living creature became its name.
The man gave names to all livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field; but for man there was not found a helper comparable to him.
Yahweh God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep. As the man slept, he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh in its place.
Yahweh God made a woman from the rib which he had taken from the man, and brought her to the man.
The man said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She will be called ‘woman,’ because she was taken out of Man.”
Therefore a man will leave his father and his mother, and will join with his wife, and they will be one flesh.
The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

parts.title: Dust and breath
parts.context: The second creation story begins. The earth is still bare, and there is no one to work it.

commentary.on: Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground
commentary.text: There is a pun in Hebrew: the man is adam, made from the adamah, the ground. We might say 'the earthling from the earth'. 'Formed' is the word for what a potter does with clay. Human beings are made of the same stuff as the world: we are part of nature, and we will return to it.

commentary.on: breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul
commentary.text: But we are not only dust. God breathes his own breath into the man, face to face, and he comes alive. Here is the Bible's picture of a human being: earth and breath together, body and spirit, never just one or the other.

commentary.on: Yahweh God planted a garden eastward, in Eden
commentary.text: Eden probably means 'delight' or 'abundance'. God is a gardener, and the first home of human beings is a garden full of trees 'pleasant to the sight, and good for food'. Beauty and usefulness together.

commentary.on: the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
commentary.text: Two trees are named. The first offers life; the second, 'knowledge of good and evil', will be the subject of session 3. 'Good and evil' may mean the right to decide for oneself what is good.

parts.title: Work and a single command
parts.context: Between verses 9 and 15 Genesis describes four rivers flowing out of Eden, two of them the real Tigris ('Hiddekel') and Euphrates of Mesopotamia. Then God gives the man his work.

commentary.on: put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it
commentary.text: Work comes before anything goes wrong. In Genesis, work is not a curse but part of being human: to 'cultivate' (literally 'serve') and 'keep' (guard, look after) the earth. Much later, these same two Hebrew words are used for the priests' work in the tabernacle, so some scholars see the garden as the first temple and the man as its priest.

commentary.on: You may freely eat of every tree of the garden
commentary.text: The first word God speaks to the man is permission, generous permission: every tree.

commentary.on: but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil
commentary.text: And one limit. Freedom in Genesis is not the absence of all limits; it is life within a good boundary set by someone who can be trusted. Whether that trust holds is the question of the next chapter.

parts.title: Not good to be alone
parts.context: For the first time something is 'not good'. Watch how God answers it.

commentary.on: It is not good for the man to be alone.
commentary.text: Everything in chapter 1 was 'good'. The first 'not good' in the Bible is loneliness. Human beings are made for relationship; a human being alone is incomplete.

commentary.on: I will make him a helper comparable to him.
commentary.text: 'Helper' (Hebrew ezer) does not mean a servant. The same word is used of God himself: 'My help comes from Yahweh' (Psalm 121:2). 'Comparable to him' means 'corresponding to him', a partner who matches, face to face.

commentary.on: The man gave names to all livestock
commentary.text: Naming the animals shows the man's intelligence and his care for creation, the 'dominion' of chapter 1 in action. But among them all there is no partner for him.

commentary.on: he took one of his ribs
commentary.text: The word translated 'rib' can also mean 'side'. A medieval saying puts it well: the woman was not taken from the man's head to rule over him, nor from his feet to be trampled by him, but from his side to be his equal, and near his heart to be loved.

commentary.on: This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.
commentary.text: The first words a human being speaks in the Bible are a poem of joy at meeting another person. At last, someone like me.

commentary.on: they will be one flesh
commentary.text: Marriage is rooted here. Jesus quoted this verse when asked about divorce (Mark 10:6–8), joining it to 'male and female he created them' from chapter 1.

commentary.on: The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
commentary.text: Nothing to hide, from each other or from God. This last line sets up the next chapter, where they will hide from both.

paras:
Yahweh, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!
You have set your glory above the heavens!

From the lips of babes and infants you have established strength,
because of your adversaries, that you might silence the enemy and the avenger.

When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers,
the moon and the stars, which you have ordained;

what is man, that you think of him?
What is the son of man, that you care for him?

For you have made him a little lower than the angels,
and crowned him with glory and honor.

You make him ruler over the works of your hands.
You have put all things under his feet:

All sheep and cattle,
yes, and the animals of the field,

the birds of the sky, the fish of the sea,
and whatever passes through the paths of the seas.

Yahweh, our Lord,
how majestic is your name in all the earth!

parts.title: A little lower than the angels
parts.context: Psalm 8 is headed 'a Psalm by David' in the Hebrew Bible. It was sung in the Temple, and it is the first psalm of praise in the book of Psalms.

commentary.on: When I consider your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars
commentary.text: The psalmist looks up at the night sky and feels tiny. Anyone who has stood under the stars knows the feeling. Modern astronomy, with its billions of galaxies, only makes it stronger.

commentary.on: what is man, that you think of him?
commentary.text: The great question. Next to all that, why should a human being matter?

commentary.on: you have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honor
commentary.text: The answer comes straight from Genesis 1: humans are crowned like kings, given rule over 'the works of your hands', sheep and cattle, birds and fish, the very list of creatures in Genesis 1. Small in size, great in dignity. The Hebrew can also mean 'a little lower than God'.

compare.why: A psalm, a song for worship, asks the question of this session aloud. It looks at the night sky, feels small, and then remembers Genesis 1.
compare.title: What is man?

sections.h: What is the image of God?
paras: 'Image of God' appears only a few times in the Old Testament, yet it has shaped Western thought more than almost any other phrase. What does it mean? Christians have given three main answers, and they can all be true together.

Some say it means something we have: reason, freedom, conscience, the ability to know God. Some say it means something we do: we represent God in the world, ruling and caring for it on his behalf, as Genesis 1:26 goes on to say. Some say it means a relationship: we are made to know and love God and each other, 'male and female'.

rows: Our reason, freedom and moral sense
Augustine, Aquinas: the mind that can know God
Our role as God's representatives, caring for the world
Our relationships with God and each other
Karl Barth: 'male and female he created them'

sections.key: The image of God has been read as what we are (reason), what we do (represent God) and whom we are with (relationship).

paras: The second answer has striking support from archaeology. In 1979, at Tell Fekheriye in Syria, a farmer found a statue of a ninth-century BC ruler with an inscription in two languages. It calls the statue the king's 'image' and 'likeness', using the very same pair of words as Genesis 1:26.

Ancient kings set up such statues across their territory to show who ruled there. Genesis takes that idea and gives it to everyone. Not only kings but every human being, every slave and every child, is God's image, set in the world to show who it belongs to.
sections.key: Kings set up images of themselves to show their rule; Genesis says every human being is such an image of God.

paras: If every human being bears God's image, then every human life has a dignity that no king, law or majority gave and none can take away. The Book of Genesis says it to the first humans, before there are any nations, races or classes.

That idea, worked out slowly and often betrayed, lies behind much of what the West values most: the worth of the poor, the disabled and the unborn; the equality of men and women before God; the argument against slavery; and the idea of universal human rights. You will follow that story in Hall III, in the journey on human dignity. It begins here.
sections.key: Because every person bears God's image, every person has a dignity no one gave and no one can take away.

sections.h: Dust and breath: what a human being is
paras: Genesis 2 adds a second picture. A human being is dust and breath: made of the same stuff as the earth, and alive with breath from God. Neither half is the whole person.

This matters because two errors have tempted people ever since. One says we are only dust, nothing but chemistry. The other says we are really souls trapped in bodies, and the body does not matter. Genesis rejects both. That is why Christianity has always cared about the body, and why its central hope is not escape from the body but the resurrection of the body.
sections.key: Genesis rejects both 'we are only matter' and 'the body does not matter': a person is dust and breath together.

paras: Both creation stories insist on man and woman together. Genesis 1 says God's image is 'male and female'. Genesis 2 says the woman is a 'helper comparable to him', using a word also used of God, and the man greets her with joy as his equal. In the ancient world, where women were often treated as property, this was remarkable.

Genesis 2 also founds marriage: a man leaves his parents and the two become 'one flesh'. Jesus later quoted it as God's design from the beginning. Christians have drawn from these chapters both the equal dignity of men and women and the meaning of marriage, though they have often failed to live up to the first.
sections.key: Genesis gives men and women equal dignity as God's image and roots marriage in creation.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read it
paras: Jewish tradition drew a famous lesson from the fact that God made one human being first: 'whoever destroys a single life is as if he destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves a single life is as if he saved a whole world' (Mishnah, Sanhedrin 4:5). It also taught that all people descend from one ancestor 'so that no one could say to another, my father is greater than yours'.

Christians add that Jesus is the perfect image of God (Colossians 1:15), and that the image damaged by sin is restored in him. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant teaching all affirm the image of God in every person; the Orthodox especially speak of growing from God's 'image' into his 'likeness', becoming more like him over a lifetime.
sections.key: Jews drew from Genesis the infinite worth of each life; Christians see the image of God restored in Jesus.

refs: Genesis 1:26–28; 2:4–25; 5:1–3; 9:6; Psalm 8; Psalm 121:2; Mark 10:6–8; Colossians 1:15.
Tell Fekheriye statue: A. Abou-Assaf, P. Bordreuil and A. R. Millard, La statue de Tell Fekherye (1982); discussed in J. Richard Middleton, The Liberating Image (2005).
Garden as sanctuary: Gordon Wenham, 'Sanctuary Symbolism in the Garden of Eden Story' (1986).
Mishnah, Sanhedrin 4:5.
The 'rib' saying: Peter Lombard, Sentences II.18 (twelfth century), later quoted by Matthew Henry.
On the image: Karl Barth, Church Dogmatics III/1 (1945); Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.6 (image and likeness).

debate.question: What does it mean to be made in God's image?

positions.name: Reason and freedom
positions.who: Augustine, Thomas Aquinas and much of the tradition
positions.view: The image is the rational soul: our capacity to think, choose and know God, which sets us apart from other animals.
positions.evidence: The unique human capacities for language, morality and worship.

positions.name: God's representatives
positions.who: Most Old Testament scholars today, such as J. Richard Middleton
positions.view: The image is a role: humans are God's royal representatives, set in the world to rule and care for it on his behalf.
positions.evidence: Genesis 1:26 links image and dominion; the Tell Fekheriye statue; ancient royal images.

positions.name: Made for relationship
positions.who: Karl Barth and others
positions.view: The image is relational: we image God, who is himself a communion of love, in our relationships with him and with each other, beginning with 'male and female'.
positions.evidence: 'Let us make'; 'male and female he created them'; 'It is not good for the man to be alone'.

debate.agree: All agree that the image of God gives every human being a unique dignity, and that it belongs to men and women alike.

look.why: Edward Hicks, a Quaker preacher in Pennsylvania, painted dozens of versions of this picture. Its subject is Isaiah's vision of a world at peace (Isaiah 11), a return to the harmony of Eden, when the wolf will lie down with the lamb and 'a little child will lead them'.
points: Three small children among a group of animals at rest: a bull, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, sheep, goats, bears and a jaguar.
One child stands with an arm around the tiger's shoulders; another touches the jaguar's nose.
In the distance on the left, a group of Native Americans in feathered headdresses meets a group of men in tricorn hats beside a river.
One of the men holds up a roll of cloth lifted from a chest.
A tree with olive-green, rust-red and yellow leaves at the right edge.

reading.title: The Liberating Image

sessions.practice: Live it this week: do one ordinary piece of work, at home or at your job, as if you were looking after God's garden: carefully, well, and for someone else's good.
sessions.reflect: Whom do you find it hardest to see as made in the image of God? What would change if you did?
takeaways: Genesis 2 retells creation close up: a human being is dust and divine breath, body and spirit together.
The 'image of God' has been read as reason, as a royal role and as relationship; ancient royal statues show the role clearly.
Every human being, man and woman, bears God's image, which became the root of the West's idea of human dignity.

sessions.title: Why is the world broken?
sessions.line: A serpent, a tree, and the question 'Where are you?'
sessions.plain: If God made the world very good, why is it so full of pain and wrong? Genesis answers with the story of a serpent, a forbidden tree and two people who hide from God. This session reads the story closely, alongside the greatest English poem about it, and asks what Christians mean by 'original sin', where the churches differ, and whether Adam and Eve were real people.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 and 2 described a good world and human beings made in God's image, living without shame. Now comes the third question a child asks: so why is everything broken?
answers: What happens in the story of the fall?
Was the serpent the devil?
What is original sin, and how do Catholics, Orthodox, Protestants and Jews differ about it?
Were Adam and Eve real people?
sessions.finding: Genesis says evil is not built into the world; it began when human beings distrusted God and grasped at being like him. Christians differ about how that first wrong affects us, and about whether Adam and Eve were two historical people.

paras: Session 1: one good God made a good world. Session 2: human beings, man and woman, are made in his image, dust and breath, given a garden to look after, one command, and each other. They were 'naked, and not ashamed'. Hold that picture: it is about to be broken.
background.key: A good world, human beings in God's image, one command, and no shame.

paras: Every religion and philosophy has to explain why the world is full of suffering and wrongdoing. Some say the world was made bad, or that matter itself is evil. Some say evil is an illusion. Genesis says something different: the world was made good, and it went wrong through a choice.

The story is short, only twenty-four verses, but it has shaped Western thought about freedom, temptation, guilt and shame more than almost any other text. It has also been read in very different ways, by Jews and Christians, and by different churches.
background.key: Genesis says the world was made good and went wrong through a human choice.

paras: The main reading is Genesis 3, in three parts: the temptation, God's questions, and the consequences. The commentary goes through it phrase by phrase.

The comparison is from Paradise Lost (1667), John Milton's great poem retelling the story. It is the most famous English telling of the fall, and it shaped how English-speaking people imagined it for three centuries, sometimes more than Genesis itself.
background.key: Genesis 3 read closely, then Milton's famous retelling.

before: What does the serpent say about God? Is it true?
When God asks questions, how do the man and woman answer?
What changes as a result, and what does God do for them before they leave?
sessions.readWhy: The story of the fall, in three parts, with a commentary after each.

paras: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?”
The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden,
but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’ ”
The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die,
for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.
They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.
Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?”
The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.”
God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?”
The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.”
Yahweh God said to the woman, “What have you done?”
The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”
Yahweh God said to the serpent,

“Because you have done this,
you are cursed above all livestock,
and above every animal of the field.
You shall go on your belly
and you shall eat dust all the days of your life.

I will put hostility between you and the woman,
and between your offspring and her offspring.
He will bruise your head,
and you will bruise his heel.”
To the woman he said,

“I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth.
You will bear children in pain.
Your desire will be for your husband,
and he will rule over you.”
To Adam he said,

“Because you have listened to your wife’s voice,
and ate from the tree,
about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’
the ground is cursed for your sake.
You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life.

It will yield thorns and thistles to you;
and you will eat the herb of the field.

You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the ground,
for you were taken out of it.
For you are dust,
and you shall return to dust.”
The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living.
Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
Yahweh God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever—”
Therefore Yahweh God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken.
So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.

parts.title: The temptation
parts.context: The same garden, some time after chapter 2. A new character appears.

commentary.on: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which Yahweh God had made.
commentary.text: The serpent is a creature God made, not a rival god. Genesis never calls it the devil; later Jewish and Christian writers identified it with Satan (Wisdom 2:24; Revelation 12:9 calls the devil 'the old serpent'). In Hebrew there is a pun: the couple were 'naked' (arummim), the serpent 'subtle' (arum).

commentary.on: Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?
commentary.text: The first temptation is a question that twists God's words. God had said 'every tree except one'; the serpent makes it sound like 'no tree'. Temptation often starts by making God seem stingy.

commentary.on: You won't really die, for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God
commentary.text: Now the serpent says God is lying, and keeping something good from them out of jealousy. The heart of the temptation is not fruit but mistrust: the suspicion that God is not good, and that we would do better to decide for ourselves what is good and evil.

commentary.on: good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise
commentary.text: Three attractions: appetite, beauty, and the wish to be wise. None of these is bad in itself; everything in the garden was good. The wrong lies in taking what was refused.

commentary.on: she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too
commentary.text: 'With her': the man was there all along, and said nothing. The Bible does not blame the woman alone; Paul's letters put the responsibility on Adam (Romans 5:12).

commentary.on: Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked.
commentary.text: The serpent was half right: their eyes were opened. But what they see is not divinity; it is their own exposure. The first result of mistrusting God is shame, and the first human invention is a covering.

parts.title: Where are you?
parts.context: Evening in the garden. God comes walking, as if this were his usual time to meet them.

commentary.on: the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden
commentary.text: Before, they were not ashamed. Now they hide, from God and, behind their fig leaves, from each other. Everything that was whole in chapter 2 is now divided.

commentary.on: Where are you?
commentary.text: God's first words after the fall are a question. God knows where they are; the question is for them. It is an invitation to come out and be honest. Many Jewish and Christian teachers have said it is the question God still asks every person.

commentary.on: The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.
commentary.text: The man blames the woman, and by implication God ('whom you gave'). The woman blames the serpent. The first effect of sin on relationships is blame. No one says sorry.

parts.title: Consequences, and a promise
parts.context: God speaks to each in turn: the serpent, the woman and the man. Some of this is written as poetry.

commentary.on: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.
commentary.text: Christians since Irenaeus in the second century have called this verse the 'first gospel' (protoevangelium): a promise that a descendant of the woman will one day crush the serpent, though wounded himself. They read it as pointing to Christ. Jewish readers take it more simply, of the lasting struggle between humans and evil.

commentary.on: Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.
commentary.text: Notice that this is described as a result of the fall, not God's design. In chapter 2 the man and woman were partners; now love becomes tangled with domination. Many readers see here not a command but a sad prediction of how relationships would go wrong.

commentary.on: the ground is cursed for your sake
commentary.text: The man is not cursed, but the ground is. Work, which was a joy in the garden, becomes toil with 'thorns and thistles'. Sin damages our relationship with the earth as well as with God and each other.

commentary.on: For you are dust, and you shall return to dust.
commentary.text: Death enters the story. The 'dust and breath' of chapter 2 will come apart. These words are still said in many churches on Ash Wednesday, as ash is marked on people's foreheads.

commentary.on: Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.
commentary.text: Before they leave, God himself makes them better clothes than their fig leaves. Even in judgement there is care. This small act of kindness runs through the whole Bible: God does not abandon the people who have turned from him.

commentary.on: to guard the way to the tree of life
commentary.text: They are sent out of the garden, east, and the way back to the tree of life is guarded. The Bible's last chapter returns to it: 'the tree of life' stands in the new city, open to all (Revelation 22:2). The whole Bible is the story of the way back.

paras:
Of Mans First Disobedience, and the Fruit
Of that Forbidden Tree, whose mortal tast
Brought Death into the World, and all our woe,
With loss of EDEN, till one greater Man
Restore us, and regain the blissful Seat,
Sing Heav'nly Muse, that on the secret top
Of OREB, or of SINAI, didst inspire
That Shepherd, who first taught the chosen Seed,
In the Beginning how the Heav'ns and Earth
Rose out of CHAOS: Or if SION Hill
Delight thee more, and SILOA'S Brook that flow'd
Fast by the Oracle of God; I thence
Invoke thy aid to my adventrous Song,
That with no middle flight intends to soar
Above th' AONIAN Mount, while it pursues
Things unattempted yet in Prose or Rhime.
And chiefly Thou O Spirit, that dost prefer
Before all Temples th' upright heart and pure,
Instruct me, for Thou know'st; Thou from the first
Wast present, and with mighty wings outspread
Dove-like satst brooding on the vast Abyss
And mad'st it pregnant: What in me is dark
Illumine, what is low raise and support;
That to the highth of this great Argument
I may assert th' Eternal Providence,
And justifie the wayes of God to men.

So saying, her rash hand in evil hour
Forth reaching to the Fruit, she pluck'd, she eat:
Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat
Sighing through all her Works gave signs of woe,
That all was lost.  Back to the Thicket slunk
The guiltie Serpent, and well might, for EVE
Intent now wholly on her taste, naught else
Regarded, such delight till then, as seemd,
In Fruit she never tasted, whether true
Or fansied so, through expectation high
Of knowledg, nor was God-head from her thought.
Greedily she ingorg'd without restraint,
And knew not eating Death: Satiate at length,

O fairest of Creation, last and best
Of all Gods Works, Creature in whom excell'd
Whatever can to fight or thought be found,
Holy, divine, good, amiable, or sweet!
How art thou lost, how on a sudden lost,
Defac't, deflourd, and now to Death devote?
Rather how hast thou yeelded to transgress
The strict forbiddance, how to violate
The sacred Fruit forbidd'n! som cursed fraud
Of Enemie hath beguil'd thee, yet unknown,
And mee with thee hath ruind, for with thee
Certain my resolution is to Die;
How can I live without thee, how forgoe
Thy sweet Converse and Love so dearly joyn'd,
To live again in these wilde Woods forlorn?
Should God create another EVE, and I
Another Rib afford, yet loss of thee
Would never from my heart; no no, I feel
The Link of Nature draw me: Flesh of Flesh,
Bone of my Bone thou art, and from thy State
Mine never shall be parted, bliss or woe.

parts.author: John Milton
parts.title: Of man's first disobedience
parts.context: John Milton (1608–1674) wrote Paradise Lost after the English Civil War, blind, dictating it to his daughters and assistants. It is in blank verse, unrhymed lines of ten syllables. The spelling is Milton's own. These are its famous opening lines.
parts.plain: Milton says: I am going to sing about the first time humans disobeyed God, by eating the forbidden fruit, which brought death and all our sorrow into the world and lost us Eden, until a greater Man, Christ, restores us. I call on God's Spirit, who inspired Moses and who brooded over the waters at creation, to help me, so that I can explain and justify God's ways to human beings.

commentary.on: Of Mans First Disobedience
commentary.text: Milton names the subject in the first line: disobedience. For him, the fall is about trust and obedience, not about sex or knowledge as such.

commentary.on: till one greater Man
commentary.text: From the very start Milton looks ahead to Christ, the 'greater Man' who will restore what Adam lost. This is how Christians have always read Genesis 3: as the beginning of a story that ends in rescue.

commentary.on: In the Beginning how the Heav'ns and Earth
commentary.text: Milton quotes Genesis 1:1, and calls Moses 'That Shepherd', following the tradition that Moses wrote Genesis.

commentary.on: Dove-like satst brooding on the vast Abyss
commentary.text: Milton echoes Genesis 1:2, where 'God's Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters', and pictures it as a bird brooding over eggs. He asks the same Spirit to inspire his poem.

commentary.on: And justifie the wayes of God to men.
commentary.text: Milton's famous aim: to show that God is just, even though he allowed the fall. That is the question this whole session raises: if God is good, why is the world broken?

parts.author: John Milton
parts.title: She pluck'd, she eat
parts.context: Book IX. Satan, disguised as the serpent, has persuaded Eve with a long, flattering speech. These lines describe the moment she eats.
parts.plain: Milton says: as she said this, Eve reached out and took the fruit and ate it, and the whole earth felt the wound and groaned that all was lost. The serpent slipped away. Eve was so absorbed in the taste and the hope of becoming wise, even godlike, that she ate greedily, not knowing she was eating death.

commentary.on: she pluck'd, she eat
commentary.text: Two short phrases, two stressed beats: the moment that changes everything is over in an instant. 'Eat' is Milton's past tense of 'eat', pronounced 'et'.

commentary.on: Earth felt the wound, and Nature from her seat
commentary.text: Milton makes the whole creation feel it. This picks up Genesis 3:17, 'the ground is cursed for your sake', and Paul's saying that 'the whole creation groans' (Romans 8:22).

commentary.on: nor was God-head from her thought
commentary.text: Eve is thinking of becoming divine: 'you will be like God'. Milton saw that the heart of the temptation was ambition, the wish to be God rather than to trust him.

commentary.on: And knew not eating Death
commentary.text: A brilliant line: she was eating death without knowing it. It echoes God's warning in Genesis 2:17.

parts.author: John Milton
parts.title: Flesh of flesh, bone of my bone
parts.context: Eve brings the fruit to Adam and tells him what she has done. He drops the garland of roses he had made for her. These are his first thoughts.
parts.plain: Milton says: Adam is horrified. Eve, the best of all God's works, is lost and doomed to die. He guesses some enemy has tricked her. But he decides at once that he will die with her: he cannot live without her, and even if God made him another wife, he would never stop grieving. She is flesh of his flesh, and he will share her fate.

commentary.on: O fairest of Creation, last and best
commentary.text: Adam's love for Eve is real and beautiful. Milton does not make the fall cartoonish: it comes from good things loved in the wrong order. (The word 'fight' in the third line is a printing error in this edition for 'sight'.)

commentary.on: Certain my resolution is to Die
commentary.text: In Milton, Adam is not deceived as Eve was; he eats knowingly, because he would rather die with her than live without her. Milton is following Paul's remark that 'Adam wasn't deceived' (1 Timothy 2:14).

commentary.on: Flesh of Flesh, Bone of my Bone thou art
commentary.text: Adam quotes his own words of joy from Genesis 2:23, now turned into a reason to share in her fall. The love that was the crown of creation becomes the occasion of its ruin. That is Milton's deepest insight: sin is often a good love put above love of God.

compare.author: John Milton
compare.why: John Milton's Paradise Lost (1667) is the greatest English poem about the fall. Read its opening lines, the moment Eve eats, and Adam's response. Notice what Milton adds to Genesis, and what he understands about it.
compare.title: Milton's Paradise Lost

paras: Strip the story to its bones and it says this. God gave good gifts and one limit. A voice suggested that God could not be trusted. The humans chose to decide good and evil for themselves. The result was shame, hiding, blame, toil, pain and death; and a world in which relationships with God, with each other and with the earth are all damaged.

Notice what Genesis does not say. It does not say the body is evil, or sex, or knowledge, or the world. It does not say evil is an equal power to God. It says that a good creation was spoiled by a misuse of freedom. That is why Christians call evil a 'privation', a lack or twisting of something good, rather than a thing in its own right.
sections.key: Genesis 3 says evil began as mistrust of God and a grasping at autonomy, spoiling a good creation.

paras: Genesis itself calls the serpent simply 'more subtle than any animal'. It never mentions Satan, a figure who appears only rarely in the Old Testament.

Later writers made the connection. The Wisdom of Solomon, written in Greek about a century before Christ, says that death entered the world through the devil's envy (2:24). The Book of Revelation calls the devil 'the old serpent' (12:9). Christian tradition and Milton followed. Jewish tradition often reads the serpent as a picture of the human inclination to do wrong.
sections.key: Genesis does not name the devil; later Jewish and Christian writers identified the serpent with Satan.

sections.h: Original sin: what Paul and Augustine said
paras: The phrase 'original sin' is not in the Bible. It comes from Augustine, around 400. It builds on Paul, who wrote that 'sin entered into the world through one man, and death through sin; so death passed to all men, because all sinned' (Romans 5:12), and that Christ, the new Adam, undoes what the first Adam did.

Augustine taught that the whole human race was somehow 'in Adam', so that every person is born both damaged by his sin and sharing in its guilt. That is why, he argued, even babies need baptism. His view shaped Western Christianity, Catholic and Protestant. Eastern Christianity, as the next screen shows, never fully accepted it.
sections.key: 'Original sin' is Augustine's term, building on Paul's teaching that sin and death came into the world through Adam.

paras: This is one of the clearest places where the churches differ, and where Judaism differs from Christianity. All agree that human beings are not what they were meant to be, and that everyone needs God's mercy. They differ about what we inherit from the first sin.

rows: Original sin: the loss of the holiness and justice of the first humans, 'contracted, not committed'; it is washed away in baptism
Human nature is wounded, not totally corrupted; we remain free and capable of good
Council of Trent (1546); Catechism of the Catholic Church 396–409
Ancestral sin: we inherit mortality and a tendency to sin, but not Adam's guilt; each person is guilty only of their own sins
Human nature is wounded and darkened, but the image of God remains intact
The Greek Fathers; usually traced to Cyril of Alexandria and earlier writers
Original sin as both inherited guilt and inherited corruption
'Total depravity': every part of human nature is affected, so we cannot save ourselves
Augsburg Confession (1530), Art. II; Westminster Confession (1646), ch. 6
No original sin; each person is born innocent and responsible for their own choices (Ezekiel 18:20)
Everyone has a good inclination and an evil inclination (yetzer tov and yetzer hara) and is free to choose

sections.key: Catholics speak of inherited loss, the Orthodox of inherited mortality without guilt, Protestants of inherited guilt and corruption; Jews of no inherited sin.

paras: The name Adam means 'human being' and Eve means 'life'. That alone shows the story is about all of us. But were they also two individual people? Christians give three main answers.

Some hold that Adam and Eve were the first two humans and sole ancestors of everyone, created a few thousand years ago. Some hold that they were real people chosen by God from among an early human population to be its representatives, so that their fall affected all. Others read the story as true about humanity without being about two individuals: Adam is 'Everyman'. Genetics bears on this question, and session 6 will return to it.

rows: The first two humans, from whom everyone descends
Real people, chosen from an early human population to stand for all
Many evangelical and Catholic thinkers today
A picture of every human being: the story is true of all of us

sections.key: Adam means 'human': the story is about everyone; Christians disagree about whether it is also about two historical individuals.

paras: You do not need to settle every question about Adam and Eve to see the truth of Genesis 3. Every person knows the voice that says 'God is holding out on you'; the hiding; the blame. The story names the pattern of human wrongdoing more exactly than any psychology textbook.

And it names the hope. God comes looking ('Where are you?'), clothes the guilty, and promises that the serpent will be crushed. Christians read the rest of the Bible as the story of that promise kept.
sections.key: Genesis 3 names the pattern of human wrongdoing exactly, and the hope of a God who comes looking.

refs: Genesis 3; Romans 5:12–19; Romans 8:22; 1 Timothy 2:14; Wisdom 2:24; Revelation 12:9; 22:2; Ezekiel 18:20.
Irenaeus, Against Heresies V.21.1 (Genesis 3:15 and Christ).
Augustine, On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins (412); City of God XIII–XIV.
Council of Trent, Session V (1546); Catechism of the Catholic Church 396–409 ('contracted and not committed', 404).
On ancestral sin: John Meyendorff, Byzantine Theology (1974), ch. 11.
Augsburg Confession (1530), Art. II; Westminster Confession (1646), ch. 6.
On Adam and Eve: Hans Madueme and Michael Reeves (eds), Adam, the Fall, and Original Sin (2014); John Walton, The Lost World of Adam and Eve (2015).

debate.question: What do we inherit from Adam?

positions.name: Inherited guilt and corruption
positions.who: Augustine; Lutheran and Reformed Protestants
positions.view: All humanity was 'in Adam'; everyone is born sharing his guilt and with a nature so corrupted that we cannot turn to God without his grace.
positions.evidence: Romans 5:12–19; Psalm 51:5 ('My mother conceived me in sin'); the universality of sin.

positions.name: Inherited loss
positions.who: Catholic teaching
positions.view: We are born without the original holiness of the first humans; this original sin is 'contracted, not committed', and our nature is wounded but not destroyed.
positions.evidence: Romans 5; the Council of Trent; the practice of infant baptism.

positions.name: Inherited mortality, not guilt
positions.who: Orthodox Christians; and, in a different form, Jewish teaching
positions.view: From Adam we inherit death and a tendency to sin, but each person is guilty only of their own sins.
positions.evidence: Ezekiel 18:20; the Greek reading of Romans 5:12; the Greek Fathers.

debate.agree: All agree that every human being needs God's mercy, and that human nature is not what it was meant to be.

look.why: Hendrick Goltzius, a Dutch engraver turned painter, painted this Fall of Man in 1616. Look for the serpent: Goltzius gives it a human face, following a medieval tradition.
points: Adam and Eve recline together under an apple tree, gazing into each other's eyes.
Eve holds up a small green and red apple with a bite taken out of it.
A snake winds round the tree trunk; it has a human face with flushed cheeks and blond hair, just above Eve's head, looking towards us.
A brown and white cat sits near Adam's hip and looks out at us.
Far off in the landscape, tiny animals: an elephant, two camels and others.

music.why: Allegri's setting of Psalm 51, the great psalm of repentance ('Have mercy on me, God'), sung in the Sistine Chapel in Holy Week: the human answer to 'Where are you?'

think.why: The story of Adam and Eve and what Christians believe about it.

learn.why: God's first words after the fall are not a sentence but a question, and an invitation.

check.q: What is the heart of the serpent's temptation?
options: Curiosity about animals
A wish to leave the garden
The suggestion that God is not good and is keeping something from them, so they should decide for themselves

check.q: Why do Christians call Genesis 3:15 the 'first gospel'?

It was the first verse written
They read it as the first promise that a descendant of the woman would defeat evil, pointing to Christ

check.q: Which statement best describes the Orthodox view of 'ancestral sin'?
options: Everyone is born guilty of Adam's sin
We inherit mortality and a tendency to sin, but not Adam's guilt
Only Adam's direct sons inherited sin

check.q: How does Milton's Adam differ from Milton's Eve in the fall?
options: They eat together at the same moment

Forgives them completely and lets them stay
Gives them a new garden

Adam means 'human being', so the story is about everyone, whatever one thinks of two historical individuals
It means 'first'

tutorial.question: What does Genesis 3 say about why the world is broken, and how far do Christians agree about it?
tutorial.approach: Read the story closely: the temptation, the hiding and blaming, the consequences and the signs of hope. Explain where the idea of original sin comes from, then set out the Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant and Jewish views fairly. Discuss whether Adam and Eve were historical, and say what the story teaches either way. Use Milton if it helps.
strong: Shows that the temptation is about trust, not fruit, with the serpent's words.
Traces the damage to every relationship: with God, each other and the earth.
Notes the signs of hope (the questions, the clothes, Genesis 3:15).
Explains original sin from Paul to Augustine, and the four traditions accurately.
Sets out the views on Adam and Eve's historicity fairly.
Says what the story teaches whichever view one takes.
