sessions.practice: Live it this week: when you are tempted to blame someone else for something that went wrong, stop and own your part, out loud if you can.
sessions.reflect: If God asked you 'Where are you?', what honest answer would you give?
takeaways: Genesis 3 says evil began with mistrust of God and the wish to decide good and evil for ourselves, damaging every relationship.
'Original sin' is Augustine's term; Catholics, Orthodox, Protestants and Jews differ about what we inherit from the first sin.
Christians disagree about whether Adam and Eve were two historical people; all agree the story is true of every human being.

sessions.title: Why do people hurt each other?
sessions.line: Cain and Abel, Lamech's boast, and a world filled with violence.
sessions.plain: Outside the garden, the very first children grow up, and one kills the other. Genesis then shows violence spreading, from one murder to a boast of seventy-sevenfold revenge to a whole world 'filled with violence'. This session asks what Genesis says about why people hurt each other, and how the Greek poet Hesiod told a strikingly similar story of decline.
sessions.why: Session 3 showed trust in God broken and relationships damaged. Now we see where that leads: the fourth question a child asks, why do people hurt each other?
answers: What happens between Cain and Abel, and why?
Am I my brother's keeper?
Who did Cain marry, and who were the Nephilim?
Did other ancient peoples tell a similar story?
sessions.finding: Once trust in God is broken, violence spreads from brother to brother to whole societies; yet Genesis insists each person is responsible, and God shows mercy even to a murderer.

paras: Session 1: one good God made a good world. Session 2: human beings, in his image, made for each other. Session 3: they mistrusted God, hid, blamed each other and were sent out of the garden, east of Eden. Now the story follows their children.
background.key: A good world, God's image, then mistrust and exile.

paras: Adam and Eve have two sons: Cain, a farmer, and Abel, a shepherd. Both bring offerings to God; God accepts Abel's and not Cain's, and Cain, furious, kills his brother. God punishes Cain but also protects him. Cain's descendants build the first city and invent music and metalwork; one of them, Lamech, boasts of killing a man. Chapter 5 lists the generations from Adam to Noah, with very long lifespans. Chapter 6 opens with a mysterious story about 'God's sons' and 'the Nephilim', and ends with God seeing that the earth is 'filled with violence'.
It is the story of how one wrong in a garden becomes violence in a family, and then in a whole civilisation.
background.key: From one murder to a world filled with violence: Genesis 4–6 traces the spread.

paras: The main reading has three parts: Cain and Abel (4:1–16), Lamech's song of revenge (4:23–24), and the corruption of the world before the flood (6:1–8).

The comparison is from Hesiod's Works and Days, written in Greece around 700 BC. Hesiod tells of five ages of humanity, each worse than the last, ending in an 'age of iron' when 'brother will not be dear to brother'. Read beside Genesis, it shows how both Athens and Jerusalem saw human history as a story of decline, and how differently they explained it.
background.key: Genesis 4–6 beside Hesiod: two ancient accounts of how humans grew violent.

before: What does God say to Cain before the murder? Could Cain have chosen differently?
What does God do for Cain after the murder?
In the comparison, what does Hesiod blame for the decline of the human race?
sessions.readWhy: The first murder, the first revenge song, and the world before the flood, in three parts.

paras: The man knew Eve his wife. She conceived, and gave birth to Cain, and said, “I have gotten a man with Yahweh’s help.”
Again she gave birth, to Cain’s brother Abel. Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground.
As time passed, Cain brought an offering to Yahweh from the fruit of the ground.
Abel also brought some of the firstborn of his flock and of its fat. Yahweh respected Abel and his offering,
but he didn’t respect Cain and his offering. Cain was very angry, and the expression on his face fell.
Yahweh said to Cain, “Why are you angry? Why has the expression of your face fallen?
If you do well, won’t it be lifted up? If you don’t do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.”
Cain said to Abel, his brother, “Let’s go into the field.” While they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.
Yahweh said to Cain, “Where is Abel, your brother?”
He said, “I don’t know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”
Yahweh said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground.
Now you are cursed because of the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand.
From now on, when you till the ground, it won’t yield its strength to you. You will be a fugitive and a wanderer in the earth.”
Cain said to Yahweh, “My punishment is greater than I can bear.
Behold, you have driven me out today from the surface of the ground. I will be hidden from your face, and I will be a fugitive and a wanderer in the earth. Whoever finds me will kill me.”
Yahweh said to him, “Therefore whoever slays Cain, vengeance will be taken on him sevenfold.” Yahweh appointed a sign for Cain, so that anyone finding him would not strike him.
Cain left Yahweh’s presence, and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.
Lamech said to his wives,

“Adah and Zillah, hear my voice.
You wives of Lamech, listen to my speech,
for I have slain a man for wounding me,
a young man for bruising me.

If Cain will be avenged seven times,
truly Lamech seventy-seven times.”
When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them,
God’s sons saw that men’s daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives.
Yahweh said, “My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years.”
The Nephilim were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when God’s sons came in to men’s daughters and had children with them. Those were the mighty men who were of old, men of renown.
Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.
Yahweh was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart.
Yahweh said, “I will destroy man whom I have created from the surface of the ground—man, along with animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky—for I am sorry that I have made them.”
But Noah found favor in Yahweh’s eyes.

parts.title: Cain and Abel
parts.context: The first story outside Eden. Adam and Eve's first two sons grow up, one a farmer, one a shepherd.

commentary.on: Yahweh respected Abel and his offering, but he didn't respect Cain and his offering.
commentary.text: Why? Genesis does not say directly, and readers have puzzled ever since. Notice that Abel brings 'the firstborn of his flock and of its fat', the best, while Cain brings simply 'an offering'. The letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered 'by faith' (Hebrews 11:4). The point seems to be the heart behind the gift.

commentary.on: If you don't do well, sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.
commentary.text: The first time the word 'sin' appears in the Bible, it is pictured as a wild animal crouching at the door, waiting to pounce. And God says Cain can master it. Before the murder, God warns him and gives him a choice. Genesis insists on human responsibility: no one is fated to do wrong.

commentary.on: Cain rose up against Abel, his brother, and killed him.
commentary.text: The word 'brother' is repeated seven times in this story. The first death in the Bible is not old age but murder, and it is a brother who is killed.

commentary.on: Am I my brother's keeper?
commentary.text: One of the most famous questions ever asked. Cain answers God's question with a lie and a shrug. The whole Bible answers yes: you are your brother's keeper. That conviction, that we are responsible for one another, is one of the foundations of Western ethics.

commentary.on: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground.
commentary.text: No murder goes unnoticed by God. The victim, though silenced, has a voice. Justice for the innocent dead is God's concern.

commentary.on: Yahweh appointed a sign for Cain, so that anyone finding him would not strike him.
commentary.text: God punishes Cain with exile, but protects him from revenge. Even a murderer remains within God's mercy. The 'mark of Cain', often imagined as a curse, is actually a sign of protection.

parts.title: Lamech's song
parts.context: Several generations later. Cain's descendant Lamech has built a family; his sons invent herding, music and metalwork (4:20–22). Then he sings this song to his two wives, the first poem in the Bible after Adam's words over Eve.

commentary.on: I have slain a man for wounding me
commentary.text: Lamech boasts of killing a man for wounding him: punishment far greater than the injury. Civilisation is advancing, with cities, music and tools, but so is violence.

commentary.on: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times.
commentary.text: God had protected Cain with a sevenfold warning; Lamech turns that mercy into a boast of unlimited revenge. Centuries later, when Peter asks Jesus how often he must forgive, Jesus answers 'until seventy times seven' (Matthew 18:22), turning Lamech's revenge into unlimited forgiveness.

parts.title: A world filled with violence
parts.context: The opening of the flood story. Between Lamech and here comes the long list of generations in chapter 5. These first verses are among the strangest in the Bible.

commentary.on: God's sons saw that men's daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives.
commentary.text: Who were 'God's sons'? Three main answers. Some ancient Jewish writers, such as the book of 1 Enoch, said they were angels who crossed the boundary between heaven and earth. Augustine and many others said they were the godly descendants of Seth, Adam's third son, marrying into Cain's line. Others think they were powerful kings who took 'any that they wanted'. Whatever they were, the point is boundaries broken and power abused.

commentary.on: The Nephilim were in the earth in those days
commentary.text: The Nephilim, perhaps 'fallen ones', were 'mighty men who were of old, men of renown': legendary heroes, like the Greek heroes Hesiod describes. Genesis mentions them briefly and moves on; it is not interested in them for their own sake.

commentary.on: every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was continually only evil
commentary.text: The diagnosis goes deep: not only actions but 'every imagination' of the heart. Genesis locates the problem inside people, not only in circumstances.

commentary.on: Yahweh was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart.
commentary.text: One of the most moving verses in the Bible. God is not a distant force; he grieves. The same word for 'grief' was used of the woman's pain in childbirth (3:16). The God who made the world very good is heartbroken by what it has become.

commentary.on: But Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes.
commentary.text: The last line turns the story. Even here, there is one person through whom God will begin again. That is where session 5 will begin.

paras: (ll. 109-120) First of all the deathless gods who dwell on Olympus made a golden race of mortal men who lived in the time of Cronos when he was reigning in heaven. And they lived like gods without sorrow of heart, remote and free from toil and grief: miserable age rested not on them; but with legs and arms never failing they made merry with feasting beyond the reach of all evils. When they died, it was as though they were overcome with sleep, and they had all good things; for the fruitful earth unforced bare them fruit abundantly and without stint. They dwelt in ease and peace upon their lands with many good things, rich in flocks and loved by the blessed gods.

(ll. 140-155) But when earth had covered this generation also--they are called blessed spirits of the underworld by men, and, though they are of second order, yet honour attends them also--Zeus the Father made a third generation of mortal men, a brazen race, sprung from ash-trees; and it was in no way equal to the silver age, but was terrible and strong. They loved the lamentable works of Ares and deeds of violence; they ate no bread, but were hard of heart like adamant, fearful men. Great was their strength and unconquerable the arms which grew from their shoulders on their strong limbs. Their armour was of bronze, and their houses of bronze, and of bronze were their implements: there was no black iron. These were destroyed by their own hands and passed to the dank house of chill Hades, and left no name: terrible though they were, black Death seized them, and they left the bright light of the sun.

(ll. 170-201) Thereafter, would that I were not among the men of the fifth generation, but either had died before or been born afterwards. For now truly is a race of iron, and men never rest from labour and sorrow by day, and from perishing by night; and the gods shall lay sore trouble upon them. But, notwithstanding, even these shall have some good mingled with their evils. And Zeus will destroy this race of mortal men also when they come to have grey hair on the temples at their birth. The father will not agree with his children, nor the children with their father, nor guest with his host, nor comrade with comrade; nor will brother be dear to brother as aforetime. Men will dishonour their parents as they grow quickly old, and will carp at them, chiding them with bitter words, hard-hearted they, not knowing the fear of the gods. They will not repay their aged parents the cost their nurture, for might shall be their right: and one man will sack another's city. There will be no favour for the man who keeps his oath or for the just or for the good; but rather men will praise the evil-doer and his violent dealing. Strength will be right and reverence will cease to be; and the wicked will hurt the worthy man, speaking false words against him, and will swear an oath upon them. Envy, foul-mouthed, delighting in evil, with scowling face, will go along with wretched men one and all. And then Aidos and Nemesis, with their sweet forms wrapped in white robes, will go from the wide-pathed earth and forsake mankind to join the company of the deathless gods: and bitter sorrows will be left for mortal men, and there will be no help against evil.

parts.author: Hesiod
parts.title: Gold, silver, bronze, heroes, iron
parts.context: Hesiod (about 700 BC) lived in Boeotia, in central Greece. His Works and Days is advice to his idle brother Perses, who had cheated him of his inheritance, mixed with myths about why life is hard. This is his story of the ages of humanity. The cuts marked '…' leave out the silver and heroic ages.
parts.plain: Hesiod says: the gods first made a golden race of humans, who lived like gods, without toil, sorrow or old age. Then came worse races: a bronze race who loved war and destroyed themselves. Now we live in the age of iron, full of toil and sorrow, when families fall apart, brothers no longer love each other, children dishonour their parents, might is right, and the wicked are praised. Shame and justice have left the earth.

commentary.on: a golden race of mortal men who lived in the time of Cronos
commentary.text: Like Genesis, Hesiod begins with a lost golden age when life was easy and there was no toil. Many peoples remembered, or imagined, a paradise at the beginning.

commentary.on: They loved the lamentable works of Ares and deeds of violence
commentary.text: Ares was the Greek god of war. The bronze race, like the generation before the flood, is filled with violence, and it destroys itself 'by their own hands'.

commentary.on: nor will brother be dear to brother as aforetime
commentary.text: Here is the closest echo of Genesis: the age of iron is the age of Cain, when brother turns against brother. Hesiod wrote this, probably, without ever having heard of Genesis.

commentary.on: might shall be their right
commentary.text: The age of iron is the age of Lamech: strength makes right, and revenge has no limit.

commentary.on: Aidos and Nemesis
commentary.text: Aidos is shame or modesty, the feeling that stops us doing wrong; Nemesis is righteous indignation at wrong. Hesiod pictures them as two goddesses leaving the earth. When no one is ashamed any more, he says, there is 'no help against evil'.

commentary.on: would that I were not among the men of the fifth generation
commentary.text: The great difference from Genesis: Hesiod's decline is simply fate, the gods making worse races one after another. There is no choice at the beginning, no warning like God's words to Cain, no grief in heaven, and no promise of a way back. Genesis explains decline by human choice, and keeps hope open.

compare.author: Hesiod
compare.why: Hesiod, a Greek farmer-poet writing around 700 BC, told of five races of humans, each worse than the one before. His picture of the last age, our own, is strikingly like Genesis 4–6. Read it, and notice both the likeness and the difference.
compare.title: Hesiod's ages of man

paras: Genesis 3 to 6 is carefully built to show sin spreading outwards. In chapter 3 it damages the relationship between humans and God, and between husband and wife. In chapter 4 it becomes murder between brothers. With Lamech it becomes boasting and revenge. By chapter 6 it fills the whole earth.

It also goes deeper: from an act to a habit to the 'imagination of the heart'. Genesis is not naive about human nature. It sees that wrongdoing grows, passes between generations and becomes part of a culture.
sections.key: Genesis shows wrongdoing spreading outwards, from a family to a society, and inwards, to the heart.

paras: And yet Genesis never says anyone had to do wrong. God warns Cain before the murder: 'sin crouches at the door… but you are to rule over it.' Cain is free and responsible. When God asks 'Where is Abel, your brother?', Cain is answerable.

This is one of the great differences between the Bible and its neighbours. In Hesiod, human decline is fate. In many ancient myths, humans are playthings of quarrelling gods. In Genesis, people choose, and are accountable. Western law, with its idea that every person is responsible for their own acts, owes much to this.
sections.key: Genesis insists that people choose and are accountable; decline is not fate.

paras: Cain's question has echoed through Western history. The answer the Bible gives, yes, became the root of a whole moral tradition: the Law's care for the stranger, the widow and the orphan; the prophets' demand for justice; Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan, which answers 'Who is my neighbour?'; the hospitals, schools and charities of Christendom.

Even the idea that a murder is a wrong against society, not just a private matter between families, grows from 'the voice of your brother's blood cries to me': God himself takes up the cause of the victim.
sections.key: The Bible's answer to Cain, yes, you are your brother's keeper, became a foundation of Western ethics.

paras: The most surprising thing in the story of Cain is that God protects him. Murder deserves punishment, and Cain is punished; but God sets a limit to it and forbids revenge. Lamech's song shows what happens without such limits: revenge escalates to seventy-sevenfold.

Ancient law codes later limited revenge with 'an eye for an eye', which was meant as a ceiling, not a demand. Jesus went further: forgive 'seventy times seven'. The story of Cain stands at the beginning of the long path from revenge to justice to mercy.
sections.key: God limits Cain's punishment and forbids revenge: the beginning of a path from revenge to justice to mercy.

paras: Who did Cain marry? Genesis does not say, because it is not interested in the question. It mentions later that Adam had 'other sons and daughters' (5:4); an ancient Jewish book, Jubilees, says Cain married his sister. Readers who take Adam and Eve as one couple among a larger early population, or as a picture of all humanity, see other people already present: Cain fears that 'whoever finds me will kill me', and he builds a city.

How did people live so long? Chapter 5 gives the generations from Adam to Noah enormous ages, such as Methuselah's 969 years. Babylonian king lists give their kings before the flood reigns of tens of thousands of years. Some read the numbers literally; many scholars think they are symbolic, marking the great age of the world's first people and, as they shrink after the flood, the growing distance from Eden.
sections.key: Genesis isn't interested in who Cain married; the long lifespans may be literal or, as many think, symbolic.

sections.h: Athens and Jerusalem on human decline
paras: Hesiod and Genesis agree on a great deal: an early paradise, a fall into toil and violence, brothers turning on each other, strength making right. Both were part of how the West understood itself: a civilisation that does not expect human beings to be naturally good.

But they explain it differently. For Hesiod, the gods simply made worse races; there is no reason, no responsibility and no hope beyond enduring. For Genesis, decline comes from human choice; God warns, grieves and protects; and the story is moving towards a new beginning. When the West later combined Greek realism about human nature with biblical hope for its redemption, it drew on both.
sections.key: Hesiod and Genesis both see human decline; Genesis explains it by choice and keeps hope open.

refs: Genesis 4–6; 5:4; Hebrews 11:4; Matthew 18:21–22; Luke 10:25–37; Exodus 21:23–25.
Jubilees 4:1–9 (Cain's wife); 1 Enoch 6–11 (the watchers); Augustine, City of God XV.22–23 (the sons of Seth).
Sumerian King List (antediluvian reigns): Thorkild Jacobsen, The Sumerian King List (1939).
Hesiod, Works and Days 106–201, tr. H. G. Evelyn-White (1914); M. L. West, Hesiod: Works and Days (1978).
On Genesis 4–11 as the spread of sin: Gerhard von Rad, Genesis (1956; English 1961); Claus Westermann, Genesis 1–11 (1974; English 1984).

debate.question: Who were the 'sons of God' in Genesis 6?

positions.name: Angels
positions.who: 1 Enoch; many early Jewish and Christian writers; many scholars today
positions.view: They were heavenly beings who crossed the boundary between heaven and earth, and their offspring were the Nephilim.
positions.evidence: 'Sons of God' means angels elsewhere (Job 1:6); 1 Enoch; Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4.

positions.name: The line of Seth
positions.who: Augustine, John Calvin and many Christian readers
positions.view: They were the godly descendants of Seth who married the ungodly descendants of Cain, so that faith was diluted.
positions.evidence: Genesis 4–5 sets the lines of Cain and Seth side by side; angels do not marry (Matthew 22:30).

positions.name: Tyrant kings
positions.who: Some Jewish commentators and modern scholars
positions.view: They were powerful rulers, 'sons of God' in the royal sense, who took any women they wanted: an abuse of power.
positions.evidence: Ancient kings were called sons of gods; 'they took any that they wanted'.

debate.agree: All agree that the passage describes boundaries broken and power abused, as the world slides towards the flood.

look.why: Benjamin West, an American who became President of the Royal Academy in London, painted the expulsion from Eden in 1791. Look at what he puts in the background: the violence of the world outside the garden.
points: An angel in a white robe with coral-red fabric raises his arms over a man and a woman being driven away.
The woman, in an animal-skin garment, kneels and looks up, grasping the man's arm; the man covers his face with his hand.
Thistles in the foreground, and a striped serpent lifting its head on the right.
Beyond them, a lion attacks two horses; in the sky an eagle swoops down on a heron.
A spear of light thrusts down from the clouds above the angel.

music.why: 'Dear Lord and Father of mankind, forgive our foolish ways': a Victorian hymn by the Quaker poet John Greenleaf Whittier, asking for the 'still small voice of calm' in a world of strife.

think.why: If we are our brother's keeper, where does that obligation come from?

learn.why: Cain's shrug, and God's answer: the victim's blood has a voice.

check.q: What does God say to Cain before the murder, and why does it matter?
options: That Cain is cursed already
That sin is crouching at the door but Cain can rule over it, showing that Cain was free and responsible
That Abel deserves to die
Nothing; Cain acts without warning
check.why: Genesis insists that wrongdoing is a choice, not a fate.

check.q: What is the 'mark of Cain'?
options: A tattoo identifying murderers
A sign of protection so that no one would kill him in revenge
The mark of Satan
A curse that made him evil
check.why: Even a murderer remains within God's mercy.

check.q: How does Jesus' 'seventy times seven' relate to Lamech's song?
options: It repeats Lamech's boast
It is unrelated
It reverses it: Lamech's unlimited revenge becomes unlimited forgiveness
It counts Lamech's descendants
check.why: Matthew 18:22 answers Genesis 4:24.

check.q: What is the biggest difference between Hesiod's ages of man and Genesis 4–6?
options: In Hesiod decline is fate, made by the gods; in Genesis it comes from human choice, and God warns, grieves and keeps hope open
Hesiod has no golden age
Hesiod blames women
Genesis has no violence
check.why: Both see decline; only Genesis explains it by responsibility and hope.

check.q: Who did Cain marry, according to Genesis?
options: A Nephilim
No one
Genesis does not say; it mentions Adam's 'other sons and daughters', and later Jewish tradition says his sister
A woman from Babylon
check.why: The question is not Genesis's interest; readers answer it differently depending on how they read Adam and Eve.

check.q: 'Yahweh was sorry that he had made man… and it grieved him in his heart.' What does this verse show about the God of Genesis?
options: That he hates human beings
That he is not a distant force but grieves over human violence
That he has no feelings
That he made a mistake he could not foresee
check.why: Genesis speaks of God in human terms to show that he cares.

tutorial.question: Why do people hurt each other, according to Genesis 4–6, and how does its answer compare with Hesiod's?
tutorial.approach: Trace the spread of violence from Cain to Lamech to the world before the flood. Explain what the story says about responsibility, the victim and mercy. Then compare Hesiod's ages of man: what they share and where they differ.
strong: Traces the spread of sin outward (family, society) and inward (the heart).
Explains God's warning to Cain and its importance for responsibility.
Explains 'Am I my brother's keeper?' and its legacy.
Notes the mercy shown to Cain and the contrast with Lamech, and Jesus' reversal.
Compares Hesiod accurately, especially fate versus choice.
Deals briefly and sensibly with Cain's wife, the Nephilim or the long lifespans.

reading.why: Superb chapters on Cain and Abel and the rise of civilisation.

reading.title: Genesis: Translation and Commentary
reading.why: A literary translation with notes on the Hebrew.

reading.author: Claus Westermann
reading.title: Genesis 1–11
reading.why: The great critical commentary on the primeval history.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: be your brother's (or sister's, or neighbour's) keeper in one concrete way: check on someone who may be struggling, and help them.
sessions.reflect: Where is 'sin crouching at the door' in your own life? What would it mean to rule over it?
takeaways: Genesis 4–6 shows violence spreading from one murder to a whole society, and deepening from acts to the heart.
God warns Cain before he acts and protects him afterwards: people are free and responsible, and mercy limits revenge.
Hesiod tells a similar story of decline, but as fate; Genesis explains it by choice and keeps hope open.

sessions.title: Will God give up on us?
sessions.line: The flood, the ark, the rainbow, and the Babylonian flood story found in 1872.
sessions.plain: Genesis says God sent a great flood and saved only Noah, his family and the animals in the ark, then promised never to destroy the earth again. In 1872 a young scholar at the British Museum found a much older Babylonian flood story with astonishing likenesses. This session reads both, asks what each says about God and about us, and what geology says about a worldwide flood.
sessions.why: Session 4 ended with the world 'filled with violence' and God grieving. The fifth question a child asks is whether it will all be all right: will God give up on us?
answers: What does the flood story actually say?
Was it copied from the Babylonian flood story?
Was there really a worldwide flood?
How can a good God send a flood?
sessions.finding: Genesis retells a flood story known across the ancient world, but makes it about God's grief at violence and his promise never to destroy the world again; geology finds no worldwide flood, so most readers today take it as a local flood or a theological story.

paras: Session 3: trust in God broken. Session 4: violence spreading, until God sees the earth 'filled with violence' and grieves that he made humans. But 'Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes'. The flood story begins there.
background.key: Violence everywhere, God grieving, and one righteous man.

background.h: A discovery at the British Museum
paras: In 1872 George Smith, a self-taught assistant at the British Museum who had started as a banknote engraver, was sorting clay tablets from the ruins of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital. He found one that told of a ship resting on a mountain and a dove sent out to find dry land. According to a colleague's later account, he was so excited that he began to undress in the room. On 3 December 1872 he read his translation to the Society of Biblical Archaeology in London, with the Prime Minister, William Gladstone, in the audience.

The tablet was the eleventh tablet of the Epic of Gilgamesh, a poem about a king who seeks to escape death. In it, an old man named Uta-Napishtim tells Gilgamesh how he survived the great flood. An even older Babylonian poem, Atrahasis, from about 1700 BC, tells the same story. Here was a flood story many centuries older than the earliest likely date of Genesis.
background.key: In 1872 George Smith found the Babylonian flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh, much older than Genesis.

paras: The main reading follows the flood in four parts: God's plan and the ark (6:9–22), the waters (7:17–24), the waters going down and the birds (8:1–12), and the covenant and the rainbow (9:8–17).

The comparison is three passages from Gilgamesh Tablet XI: the warning to build a ship, the storm, and the birds and the sacrifice. Read them side by side and you will see both how much the stories share and how differently they picture God.
background.key: Genesis's flood beside the Gilgamesh flood: shared story, different God.

before: Why does God send the flood, according to Genesis?
Which birds does Noah send out, and what happens?
What promise does God make afterwards, and to whom?
sessions.readWhy: The flood story, in four parts: the ark, the waters, the birds, and the rainbow.

paras: This is the history of the generations of Noah: Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God.
Noah became the father of three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.
God saw the earth, and saw that it was corrupt, for all flesh had corrupted their way on the earth.
God said to Noah, “I will bring an end to all flesh, for the earth is filled with violence through them. Behold, I will destroy them and the earth.
Make a ship of gopher wood. You shall make rooms in the ship, and shall seal it inside and outside with pitch.
This is how you shall make it. The length of the ship shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.
You shall make a roof in the ship, and you shall finish it to a cubit upward. You shall set the door of the ship in its side. You shall make it with lower, second, and third levels.
I, even I, will bring the flood of waters on this earth, to destroy all flesh having the breath of life from under the sky. Everything that is in the earth will die.
But I will establish my covenant with you. You shall come into the ship, you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you.
Of every living thing of all flesh, you shall bring two of every sort into the ship, to keep them alive with you. They shall be male and female.
Of the birds after their kind, of the livestock after their kind, of every creeping thing of the ground after its kind, two of every sort will come to you, to keep them alive.
Take with you some of all food that is eaten, and gather it to yourself; and it will be for food for you, and for them.”
Thus Noah did. He did all that God commanded him.
The flood was forty days on the earth. The waters increased, and lifted up the ship, and it was lifted up above the earth.
The waters rose, and increased greatly on the earth; and the ship floated on the surface of the waters.
The waters rose very high on the earth. All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered.
The waters rose fifteen cubits higher, and the mountains were covered.
All flesh died that moved on the earth, including birds, livestock, animals, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth, and every man.
All on the dry land, in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, died.

Every living thing was destroyed that was on the surface of the ground, including man, livestock, creeping things, and birds of the sky. They were destroyed from the earth. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship.
The waters flooded the earth one hundred fifty days.
God remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the livestock that were with him in the ship; and God made a wind to pass over the earth. The waters subsided.
The deep’s fountains and the sky’s windows were also stopped, and the rain from the sky was restrained.
The waters continually receded from the earth. After the end of one hundred fifty days the waters receded.
The ship rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on Ararat’s mountains.
The waters receded continually until the tenth month. In the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains were visible.
At the end of forty days, Noah opened the window of the ship which he had made,
and he sent out a raven. It went back and forth, until the waters were dried up from the earth.
He himself sent out a dove to see if the waters were abated from the surface of the ground,

but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned into the ship to him, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship.
He waited yet another seven days; and again he sent the dove out of the ship.
The dove came back to him at evening and, behold, in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf. So Noah knew that the waters were abated from the earth.
He waited yet another seven days, and sent out the dove; and she didn’t return to him any more.
God spoke to Noah and to his sons with him, saying,
“As for me, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you,
and with every living creature that is with you: the birds, the livestock, and every animal of the earth with you, of all that go out of the ship, even every animal of the earth.
I will establish my covenant with you: All flesh will not be cut off any more by the waters of the flood. There will never again be a flood to destroy the earth.”
God said, “This is the token of the covenant which I make between me and you and every living creature that is with you, for perpetual generations:
I set my rainbow in the cloud, and it will be a sign of a covenant between me and the earth.
When I bring a cloud over the earth, that the rainbow will be seen in the cloud,
I will remember my covenant, which is between me and you and every living creature of all flesh, and the waters will no more become a flood to destroy all flesh.
The rainbow will be in the cloud. I will look at it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is on the earth.”
God said to Noah, “This is the token of the covenant which I have established between me and all flesh that is on the earth.”

parts.title: Noah and the ark
parts.context: The story begins with Noah, a descendant of Adam's son Seth.

commentary.on: Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God.
commentary.text: In a world filled with violence, one man lives rightly. 'Walked with God' is said of only one other person, Enoch (5:24). Genesis does not say Noah was perfect (chapter 9 shows him drunk), but he trusted God when no one else did.

commentary.on: the earth was filled with violence
commentary.text: The reason for the flood is stated twice: violence and corruption. Remember this when you read the Babylonian version, where the reason is very different.

commentary.on: The length of the ship shall be three hundred cubits, its width fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits.
commentary.text: A cubit is about half a metre, the length of a forearm. So the ark is roughly 140 metres long, 23 wide and 14 high: a long box, built to float, not to sail. The Babylonian ship, by contrast, is a cube.

commentary.on: But I will establish my covenant with you.
commentary.text: The first use of the word 'covenant' in the Bible: a binding promise. Even before the flood, God's purpose is not to end the world but to begin it again through Noah.

parts.title: The waters
parts.context: Noah, his family and the animals are in the ark. The rain begins.

commentary.on: All the high mountains that were under the whole sky were covered.
commentary.text: Genesis describes the flood as covering everything 'under the whole sky'. Whether that means the whole planet as we know it, or the whole world the writer knew, is one of the main questions readers ask. The lecture comes back to it.

commentary.on: All flesh died that moved on the earth
commentary.text: The flood reverses creation. In Genesis 1 God separated the waters to make dry land; now the waters return and cover it, and the living creatures of day six die. The world goes back to the watery chaos of Genesis 1:2.

commentary.on: Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ship.
commentary.text: Out of the un-creation, a small remnant survives. The pattern of a faithful few through whom God begins again runs through the whole Bible.

parts.title: God remembered Noah
parts.context: The turning point of the story.

commentary.on: God remembered Noah
commentary.text: This is the exact centre of the flood story. In the Bible 'remember' does not mean God had forgotten; it means he acts on his promise. Everything turns here.

commentary.on: God made a wind to pass over the earth.
commentary.text: The Hebrew word for 'wind' is the same as 'Spirit' in Genesis 1:2, where 'God's Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters'. As at creation, God's wind moves over the waters, and dry land appears again. The flood is followed by a new creation.

commentary.on: The ship rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on Ararat's mountains.
commentary.text: Ararat is the region of Urartu, in modern eastern Turkey and Armenia, not necessarily the single mountain now called Mount Ararat. Many expeditions have searched for the ark; none has found it.

commentary.on: in her mouth was a freshly plucked olive leaf
commentary.text: The dove returns with an olive leaf: life is growing again. The dove with an olive branch became a symbol of peace across the Western world, still used today.

parts.title: The rainbow
parts.context: Noah has left the ark and offered a sacrifice. Now God speaks.

commentary.on: I establish my covenant with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you
commentary.text: The covenant is not only with Noah but with 'every living creature': birds, livestock, animals. God binds himself to the whole of creation. The first covenant in the Bible includes the animals.

commentary.on: There will never again be a flood to destroy the earth.
commentary.text: This is the answer to the session's question. God will not give up on the world. Whatever judgement means, it will never again mean the destruction of everything. The rest of the Bible's story is about how God will deal with evil without destroying the world.

commentary.on: I set my rainbow in the cloud
commentary.text: The Hebrew word for rainbow is the same as the word for a warrior's bow. Some scholars suggest an image of God hanging up his bow in the sky, pointed away from the earth: the weapon laid down.

commentary.on: I will remember my covenant
commentary.text: The rainbow is a reminder, says Genesis, not for people but for God. The promise is unconditional: it does not depend on humans behaving better.

parts.author: The Epic of Gilgamesh
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1920)
parts.title: Build a ship
parts.context: The tablet was copied for the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh in the seventh century BC; the story itself is much older. Uta-Napishtim, who has been given eternal life, tells his secret. Shurippak was a real Sumerian city on the Euphrates. Ea (Nin-igi-azag) is the god of wisdom and fresh water; Enlil is the chief of the gods.
parts.plain: Uta-Napishtim says: I will tell you a secret of the gods. In the old city of Shurippak, the great gods decided to send a flood. But the god Ea, who was in their council, warned me secretly, speaking to the reed walls of my house: tear down your house, build a ship, give up your wealth and save your life, and take into the ship the seed of every living thing.

commentary.on: Their hearts induced the great gods to make a wind-storm
commentary.text: Notice: no reason is given here for the flood. In the older poem Atrahasis, the gods send it because humans were making too much noise and disturbing their sleep. Compare Genesis: the reason is violence and corruption, a moral reason.

commentary.on: Nin-igi-azag, Ea, was with them [in council] and
commentary.text: The gods are divided. Ea secretly betrays the council's plan by whispering to the wall of Uta-Napishtim's reed house, so that he technically does not tell a human. In Genesis there is one God, and he speaks openly to Noah.

commentary.on: Throw down the house, build a ship
commentary.text: The same command as to Noah: build a boat and save life. The likeness is unmistakable.

commentary.on: The breadth and the length thereof shall be the same.
commentary.text: Uta-Napishtim's ship is a cube, about 60 metres on each side. Noah's ark is long and low, a shape that would actually float steadily.

parts.author: The Epic of Gilgamesh
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1920)
parts.title: The storm, and the frightened gods
parts.context: The flood comes. Adad is the storm god, Nergal and En-urta are gods of war and destruction, and the Anunnaki are the gods of the underworld. Ishtar is the goddess of love and war; here she is called 'the Lady of the Gods'.
parts.plain: Uta-Napishtim says: at dawn a black cloud came up and the storm gods brought the flood. Darkness covered everything; the water rose to the mountains and fell on the people like an army. Even the gods were terrified: they fled up to heaven and crouched like dogs. The goddess Ishtar wailed: why did I agree to destroy my own people?

commentary.on: The gods crouched like a dog and cowered by the wall.
commentary.text: An astonishing line. The gods who sent the flood lose control of it and cower in fear. In Genesis, God is never frightened or out of control; he sends the flood, he shuts the door of the ark (7:16), and he 'remembers' Noah.

commentary.on: Did I of myself bring forth my people
commentary.text: Ishtar regrets the flood, as God 'was sorry' in Genesis 6:6. But her regret is that she agreed to a rash decision of the divine council. God's grief in Genesis is over human violence, and it comes before the flood, not after.

parts.author: The Epic of Gilgamesh
parts.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1920)
parts.title: The birds and the sacrifice
parts.context: After seven days the storm ends. The ship has grounded on Mount Nisir, in the mountains east of the Tigris.
parts.plain: Uta-Napishtim says: after six days and nights the storm stopped; everyone else had turned to mud, and I wept. The ship came to rest on Mount Nisir. On the seventh day I sent out a dove, which came back, then a swallow, which came back, then a raven, which found food and did not return. Then I came out and offered a sacrifice, and the gods smelled it and gathered round like flies.

commentary.on: I brought out a dove and let her go free.
commentary.text: Here is the detail that so excited George Smith: birds sent out to find dry land. A dove and a raven in both stories; a swallow too in Gilgamesh. The likeness is too close to be chance.

commentary.on: The raven flew away, she saw the sinking waters.
commentary.text: In Gilgamesh the raven not returning is the sign. In Genesis the raven goes back and forth, and the dove's olive leaf is the sign. The stories share the motif and use it differently.

commentary.on: The gods gathered together like flies over him that sacrificed.
commentary.text: After the flood, the gods have had no offerings and are hungry; they swarm over the sacrifice 'like flies'. Compare Genesis 8:21: 'Yahweh smelled the pleasant aroma', and in response promises never again to curse the ground. In Babylon the gods need humans to feed them; in Genesis God needs nothing, and responds with a promise.

compare.author: The Epic of Gilgamesh
compare.translator: E. A. Wallis Budge, for the British Museum (1920)
compare.why: Three passages from Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, found by George Smith in 1872. The old man Uta-Napishtim tells the hero Gilgamesh how he survived the flood. Watch for the likenesses to Genesis, and then for the differences.
compare.title: The Babylonian flood

paras: The flood in Genesis is not mainly about water. It is about violence, judgement and a new beginning. God grieves over a world filled with violence. He undoes creation, letting the waters of chaos return, but preserves a remnant and two of every kind. Then he remembers Noah, sends his wind over the waters as at the beginning, and starts again, binding himself by a promise to every living creature never to do it again.
So the answer to this session's question is no: God will not give up on his world. The flood story establishes that whatever God does about evil from now on, it will not be by destroying the world.
sections.key: The flood is about violence, judgement and a new creation, ending in God's promise never to destroy the world again.

sections.h: The two flood stories side by side
paras: The likenesses between Genesis and Gilgamesh are too many and too specific to be chance. But the differences are just as important, and they are all about God.

paras: How are the stories related? Three main answers have been given. Some think Genesis adapted the Babylonian story, perhaps during the exile, deliberately rewriting it to say something new about God. Some think both go back to a common memory of a real, devastating flood in Mesopotamia, told in different ways. Some traditional readers hold that Genesis preserves the true account, and Gilgamesh a distorted one.

Whichever is right, the comparison shows the same pattern as Genesis 1 and Enuma Elish: Genesis uses the shared stories of the ancient world, and transforms what they say about God, about human beings and about why things happen.
sections.key: Genesis may adapt, share or preserve the flood story; either way it transforms what it says about God.

paras: Here science has something to say. Geologists find no evidence of a single flood covering the whole planet in the time of human history: no worldwide layer of flood deposits, and an unbroken record of ice layers, tree rings and sediments going back far further. That is the conclusion of virtually all geologists, including many Christians.

There is evidence of great local floods. In 1929 the archaeologist Leonard Woolley found a deep layer of flood silt at Ur in southern Iraq, and flood deposits at Shuruppak, Uta-Napishtim's city, date to around 2900 BC. Mesopotamia, a flat plain between two great rivers, was prone to catastrophic floods. Many think the stories remember such a disaster, which to those who lived through it was the whole world.
sections.key: Geology finds no worldwide flood, but great local floods in Mesopotamia, such as at Ur and Shuruppak, are well attested.

sections.h: Three ways Christians read the flood
paras: Christians read the flood in three main ways today. Some, especially young-earth creationists, hold that it was a global flood a few thousand years ago that laid down most of the world's rock layers; this 'flood geology' was popularised by The Genesis Flood (1961). Some hold that it was a real but local flood, covering the world the writer knew. Others read it as a theological story, using the ancient memory of a great flood to teach about judgement and grace.
All three agree on what the story teaches about God: that he takes evil seriously, grieves over violence, saves the faithful and binds himself to creation by a promise.

rows: A worldwide flood a few thousand years ago, which laid down most rock layers
A real, catastrophic flood in Mesopotamia; 'the whole earth' meant the known world
A story using an ancient memory to teach about judgement, grace and covenant
Most biblical scholars; many Catholic, Orthodox and mainline Protestant readers

sections.key: Christians read the flood as global, local or theological; all agree on what it teaches about God.

sections.h: How can a good God send a flood?
paras: Many readers today find the flood morally troubling: a God who drowns almost everyone, children included. This is a serious objection, and session 6 will give it its full weight.

Here it is worth noticing what Genesis itself does with it. It insists the flood was a response to violence, not a whim; that God grieved before he acted; that he saved those who trusted him; and that afterwards he bound himself never to do it again. The story is, in a sense, about God refusing the very thing it describes. Christians add that the Bible's final answer to evil is not a flood but the cross, where God takes judgement on himself.
sections.key: The flood troubles many readers; Genesis presents it as a response to violence that God grieves and promises never to repeat.

positions.who: Some historians and archaeologists

sessions.title: Doesn't science say otherwise?
sessions.line: The case against Genesis, at full strength, from 'Darwin's bulldog' and from today.
sessions.plain: Science says the universe is about 13.8 billion years old, that life evolved over billions of years, and that human beings share ancestors with apes. Many people think this simply disproves Genesis. This session lets the sceptic make that case at full strength: first in the words of Thomas Huxley, the Victorian scientist known as 'Darwin's bulldog', then in its modern form. Only after that do we weigh it.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 5 read Genesis 1–11 as its first hearers would. Now we ask the question a modern adult asks: doesn't science prove it wrong?
answers: What does science say about the age of the universe and the origin of life and humans?
Does evolution disprove Genesis?
What about Adam and Eve and genetics?
What is the strongest case against Genesis, and what does it actually prove?
sessions.finding: Science rules out reading Genesis as a scientific timetable; the strongest sceptical case shows that, but its further step, that Genesis is therefore untrue about God and humanity, does not follow, and most Christians do not take it.

paras: Five sessions have read Genesis 1–11 as its first hearers did: a good creation answering Babylon's myths, human beings in God's image, a fall, spreading violence, and a flood that ends in a promise. Along the way you have seen the ancient picture of the world and the evidence against a worldwide flood. Now the strongest objection gets its turn.
background.key: Five sessions read Genesis in its own world; now the strongest objection.

paras: In the nineteenth century geologists showed that the earth was immensely old, far older than the roughly 6,000 years that some had calculated by adding up the ages in Genesis (Archbishop James Ussher famously dated creation to 4004 BC). In 1859 Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, arguing that all living things descend from common ancestors by natural selection. In 1871 his The Descent of Man applied the theory to human beings.

Not all Christians resisted. Some leading churchmen accepted evolution early. But the idea of a war between science and religion took hold, helped by famous clashes. One of the sharpest was in 1885–86, when the former Prime Minister William Gladstone, a devout Christian, argued in a magazine that science confirmed the order of creation in Genesis 1, and the biologist Thomas Henry Huxley replied.

The Genesis Flood launches modern young-earth creationism

background.key: In the nineteenth century geology and Darwin made the earth ancient and life evolved; Huxley's reply to Gladstone is a classic of the debate.

paras: Thomas Henry Huxley (1825–1895) was a brilliant self-taught biologist, a fierce defender of Darwin (who nicknamed himself 'Darwin's bulldog') and the man who coined the word 'agnostic'. He believed science must be free from the control of the churches, and he enjoyed a fight.

Gladstone had claimed that Genesis's order of creation, sea creatures, then birds, then land animals, then humans, had been 'affirmed' by science. Huxley set out to show, from the fossil record, that it had not. Then, at the end of his essay, he said something more surprising about science and religion.
background.key: Huxley, Darwin's great defender and inventor of the word 'agnostic', answered Gladstone's claim that science confirmed Genesis.

paras: The main reading is Huxley's essay of 1885, in five short parts: his flat denial, his test, the fossil evidence, and then his own view of science and religion. Read it as the sceptic's case.
The comparison is from Darwin himself, the last pages of the Origin of Species. You may be surprised by what Darwin says about the Creator.
background.key: Huxley states the case; Darwin, surprisingly, does not see a contradiction with a Creator.

before: What exactly did Gladstone claim, and what does Huxley say is wrong with it?
Does Huxley think science and religion are enemies? What is he really against?
In the comparison, how does Darwin speak of the Creator?
sessions.readWhy: The sceptic's case in his own words: Huxley's reply to Gladstone, in five parts. A commentary follows each.

paras: For I can meet the statement in the last paragraph of the above citation with nothing but a direct negative. If I know anything at all about the results attained by the natural science of our time, it is "a demonstrated conclusion and established fact" that the "fourfold order" given by Mr. Gladstone is not that in which the evidence at our disposal tends to show that the water, air, and land-populations of the globe have made their appearance.

Now what I want to make clear is this: that if the terms "water-population," "air-population," and "land-population" are understood in the senses here defined, natural science has nothing to say in favour of the proposition that they succeeded one another in the order given by Mr. Gladstone; but that, on the contrary, all the evidence we possess goes to prove that they did not. Whence it will follow that, if Mr. Gladstone has interpreted Genesis rightly (on which point I am most anxious to be understood to offer no opinion), that interpretation is wholly irreconcilable with the conclusions at present accepted by the interpreters of nature--with everything that can be called "a demonstrated conclusion and established fact" of natural science. And be it observed that I am not here dealing with a question of speculation, but with a question of fact.

Either the geological record is sufficiently complete to afford us a means of determining the order in which animals have made their appearance on the globe or it is not. If it is, the determination of that order is little more than a mere matter of observation; if it is not, then natural science neither affirms nor refutes the "fourfold order," but is simply silent.

The water-population of vertebrated animals first appears in the Upper Silurian. Therefore, if we found ourselves on vertebrated animals and take "fowl" to mean birds only, or, at most, flying vertebrates, natural science says that the order of succession was water, land, and air-population, and not--as Mr. Gladstone, founding himself on Genesis, says--water, air, land-population. If a chronicler of Greece affirmed that the age of Alexander preceded that of Pericles and immediately succeeded that of the Trojan war, Mr. Gladstone would hardly say that this order is "understood to have been so affirmed by historical science that it may be taken as a demonstrated conclusion and established fact." Yet natural science "affirms" his "fourfold order" to exactly the same extent--neither more nor less.

The antagonism between science and religion, about which we hear so much, appears to me to be purely factitious--fabricated, on the one hand, by short-sighted religious people who confound a certain branch of science, theology, with religion; and, on the other, by equally short-sighted scientific people who forget that science takes for its province only that which is susceptible of clear intellectual comprehension; and that, outside the boundaries of that province, they must be content with imagination, with hope, and with ignorance.
"And what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"
If any so-called religion takes away from this great saying of Micah, I think it wantonly mutilates, while, if it adds thereto, I think it obscures, the perfect ideal of religion.

But what extent of knowledge, what acuteness of scientific criticism, can touch this, if any one possessed of knowledge, or acuteness, could be absurd enough to make the attempt? Will the progress of research prove that justice is worthless and mercy hateful; will it ever soften the bitter contrast between our actions and our aspirations; or show us the bounds of the universe and bid us say, Go to, now we comprehend the infinite? A faculty of wrath lay in those ancient Israelites, and surely the prophet's staff would have made swift acquaintance with the head of the scholar who had asked Micah whether, peradventure, the Lord further required of him an implicit belief in the accuracy of the cosmogony of Genesis!

The antagonism of science is not to religion, but to the heathen survivals and the bad philosophy under which religion herself is often well-nigh crushed. And, for my part, I trust that this antagonism will never cease; but that, to the end of time, true science will continue to fulfil one of her most beneficent functions, that of relieving men from the burden of false science which is imposed upon them in the name of religion.

parts.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
parts.work: The Interpreters of Genesis and the Interpreters of Nature
parts.title: Science says no
parts.context: Huxley answers Gladstone's claim that science has 'affirmed' Genesis's 'fourfold order': first sea creatures, then birds, then land animals, then humans. The quotation marks are Huxley quoting Gladstone's words back at him.
parts.plain: Huxley says: Gladstone claims science has proved Genesis's order of creation, sea creatures, birds, land animals, humans. I can only reply with a flat no. The fossil evidence shows the creatures did not appear in that order. So if Gladstone has read Genesis rightly, Genesis is irreconcilable with science. And this is a question of fact, not speculation.

commentary.on: I can meet the statement in the last paragraph of the above citation with nothing but a direct negative
commentary.text: Huxley's tone is crisp and combative. He is a professional scientist correcting an amateur who has claimed science's authority for his reading of the Bible.

commentary.on: if Mr. Gladstone has interpreted Genesis rightly (on which point I am most anxious to be understood to offer no opinion)
commentary.text: Read this carefully: it is the hinge of the whole argument. Huxley is attacking Gladstone's interpretation, which treated Genesis as a scientific timetable. If that interpretation is right, Genesis is wrong. Whether it is right, he says, he will not judge.

commentary.on: I am not here dealing with a question of speculation, but with a question of fact.
commentary.text: Huxley's point is fair: the order in which fossils appear in the rocks is something that can be observed, not a matter of opinion.

parts.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
parts.work: The Interpreters of Genesis and the Interpreters of Nature
parts.title: Water, land, air
parts.context: Huxley sets out what the rocks show. 'Vertebrated' means animals with backbones; the 'Silurian' and the 'Jurassic' are ages of the earth, about 440 and 200 million years ago in modern dating.
parts.plain: Huxley says: either the fossil record can tell us the order in which animals appeared, or it cannot. If it can, it shows sea creatures first, then land animals, and only much later birds. Genesis, as Gladstone reads it, puts birds before land animals. That is like a historian putting Alexander the Great before Pericles.

commentary.on: Either the geological record is sufficiently complete to afford us a means of determining the order in which animals have made their appearance on the globe or it is not.
commentary.text: A clean dilemma. Either the fossils can be read, or they cannot. If they can, they disagree with Gladstone; if they cannot, science neither confirms nor refutes him. Either way, Gladstone cannot claim science is on his side.

commentary.on: natural science says that the order of succession was water, land, and air-population
commentary.text: This is still the modern view: fish, then land animals (amphibians and reptiles), and birds much later, evolving from a group of dinosaurs. Genesis 1 puts birds on day five, before land animals on day six.

commentary.on: If a chronicler of Greece affirmed that the age of Alexander preceded that of Pericles
commentary.text: Pericles lived in the fifth century BC, Alexander in the fourth. Huxley's comparison: reading Genesis 1 as a sequence of natural history is like reading a history book with its eras in the wrong order.

parts.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
parts.work: The Interpreters of Genesis and the Interpreters of Nature
parts.title: The antagonism is 'purely factitious'
parts.context: At the end of his essay Huxley turns from Gladstone to the wider question. ('Factitious' means artificial, manufactured.)
parts.plain: Huxley says: the supposed war between science and religion is invented, on one side by religious people who confuse their theology with religion itself, and on the other by scientists who forget that science can only deal with what can be clearly understood; beyond that, they must admit imagination, hope and ignorance.

commentary.on: The antagonism between science and religion, about which we hear so much, appears to me to be purely factitious
commentary.text: From 'Darwin's bulldog' this is a striking sentence. Huxley does not think science and religion are natural enemies. The conflict, he says, is manufactured by people on both sides who overstep their limits.

commentary.on: short-sighted scientific people who forget that science takes for its province only that which is susceptible of clear intellectual comprehension
commentary.text: Huxley warns scientists, too: science has limits. Beyond what it can measure lies a realm of 'imagination, hope and ignorance'. The modern sceptic often forgets this half of Huxley.

parts.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
parts.work: The Interpreters of Genesis and the Interpreters of Nature
parts.title: Do justly, love mercy
parts.context: Huxley quotes the prophet Micah (6:8), in the King James Version. The cut before this passage leaves out a paragraph in which Huxley speaks of 'Semitic and Aryan races', in the racial language of his time, which we do not reproduce.
parts.plain: Huxley says: the Hebrew prophets' idea of religion, summed up in Micah's 'do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God', is as great an achievement as Greek art or Aristotle's science. No scientific discovery can touch it. The prophet would have been astonished to be asked whether God also required belief in the exact accuracy of Genesis's account of creation.

commentary.on: And what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
commentary.text: Huxley, the agnostic, quotes the Bible with deep admiration. For him, Micah's verse is the heart of religion, and no science can refute it.

commentary.on: Will the progress of research prove that justice is worthless and mercy hateful
commentary.text: Huxley's point: science can tell us the order of fossils, but not whether justice and mercy are good. Those questions lie outside its 'province'.

commentary.on: an implicit belief in the accuracy of the cosmogony of Genesis
commentary.text: 'Cosmogony' means an account of how the world began. Huxley's real target is the demand that believers accept Genesis as accurate natural history. That, he thinks, is no part of true religion.

parts.author: Thomas Henry Huxley
parts.work: The Interpreters of Genesis and the Interpreters of Nature
parts.title: False science in the name of religion
parts.context: Huxley's last word.
parts.plain: Huxley says: science is not the enemy of religion. It is the enemy of old pagan survivals and bad philosophy that have attached themselves to religion, and I hope it will always go on freeing people from false science taught in the name of religion.

commentary.on: The antagonism of science is not to religion, but to the heathen survivals and the bad philosophy under which religion herself is often well-nigh crushed.
commentary.text: So Huxley's case, at full strength, is this: Genesis read as science is false, and science should free people from it. What he does not claim is that science disproves God or the religion of the prophets. Keep that distinction in mind for the lecture.
