sessions.practice: Live it this week: keep one promise that costs you something, and make it a promise you could easily have got out of.
sessions.reflect: Is there a promise of God, or a hope, that you find hard to believe because you cannot yet see any sign of it?
takeaways: In the covenant ceremony only God passes between the pieces: he binds himself to the promise.
Abram trusted God's promise with no evidence, and God credited it to him as righteousness.
Paul and James both use Abraham; the churches still differ on faith and works, though Lutherans and Catholics agreed much in 1999.

sessions.title: The other son
sessions.line: A slave woman, a boy in the desert, and the God who sees.
sessions.plain: Sarai cannot have children, so she gives her Egyptian slave, Hagar, to Abram to bear a child for her. Hagar has a son, Ishmael, but is driven out, twice. Both times, God finds her in the desert. This session asks the question every child asks about choosing: what about the ones who are not chosen? It is also the beginning of the story of Islam, which traces itself to Ishmael.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 and 2 showed God choosing one family and binding himself to his promise. But choosing one means not choosing others. Here, for the first time, we meet someone outside the line of the promise, and see how God treats her.
answers: Who were Hagar and Ishmael, and why were they sent away?
If God chose Isaac, did he abandon Ishmael?
How do Islam and Christianity each read the story of Hagar?
How should we read a story that includes slavery and cruelty?
sessions.finding: Choosing one family does not mean abandoning others: the God of Abraham sees the slave woman, hears her son, and blesses him too, and the story makes us feel for the one who was not chosen.

paras: God chose Abraham by grace, for the sake of every family on earth (session 1), and bound himself to his promise by covenant: Abraham's trust, not his merit, was counted as righteousness (session 2). But there is still no son.
background.key: Chosen by grace; a promise God guarantees; still no son.

paras: This session's story happens between the stars of Genesis 15 and the new names of Genesis 17. Abram is 85, Sarai is 75, and they have waited ten years in Canaan. Sarai decides to help the promise along.

In the ancient Near East a childless wife could give her slave woman to her husband to bear a child that would legally count as the wife's. The Laws of Hammurabi, from Babylon about 1750 BC, regulate exactly this situation (laws 144–147), including what happens if the slave then puts on airs and claims equality with her mistress: she may be returned to slavery but not sold. Marriage contracts found at Nuzi, in northern Iraq, from the fifteenth century BC, also require it. To Abram and Sarai's neighbours, nothing about the plan was strange.
background.key: A childless wife giving her slave to bear a child was a known custom, regulated in Hammurabi's laws.

paras: Hagar is an Egyptian, perhaps acquired during the visit to Egypt in Genesis 12, though Genesis doesn't say. She is a slave: she has no say in what is done with her body. Slavery in the ancient world was usually through debt, war or purchase, and it was everywhere; the Bible's own laws later regulate and limit it, and its stories, like this one, show its cruelty.
Hagar matters far beyond Genesis. In Islam she is Hajar, the mother of Ishmael (Ismail), and every pilgrim to Mecca re-enacts her search for water.
background.key: Hagar is an Egyptian slave with no say over her body; in Islam she is Hajar, honoured mother of Ishmael.

paras: The main reading has four parts: Hagar's first flight (16), the birth of Isaac (21:1–7), Hagar and Ishmael driven out (21:8–21), and Paul's reading of the story (Galatians 4), which shows how differently a story can be used.

The comparison is from the Qur'an: Abraham's prayer for the son he settled 'in an unfruitful valley, nigh to thy holy house', and Abraham and Ishmael building the Kaaba in Mecca. They show how the story continues for a quarter of the world's people.
background.key: Hagar's two flights, Isaac's birth, Paul's allegory, and the Qur'an's Ishmael.

before: Who acts in this story, and who is acted on? Notice who speaks and who doesn't.
What does God promise Hagar and her son?
In the comparison, where does the Qur'an place Ishmael?
sessions.readWhy: The story of the son who was not chosen, in four parts: Hagar's first flight, Isaac's birth, Hagar and Ishmael driven out, and how Paul read it.

paras: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.
Sarai said to Abram, “See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.” Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
Sarai, Abram’s wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to Abram her husband to be his wife.
He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.
Sarai said to Abram, “This wrong is your fault. I gave my servant into your bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, she despised me. May Yahweh judge between me and you.”
But Abram said to Sarai, “Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.” Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face.
Yahweh’s angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain on the way to Shur.
He said, “Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?”
She said, “I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “I will greatly multiply your offspring, that they will not be counted for multitude.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Behold, you are with child, and will bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction.
He will be like a wild donkey among men. His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him. He will live opposed to all of his brothers.”
She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,” for she said, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?”
Therefore the well was called Beer Lahai Roi. Behold, it is between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore a son for Abram. Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.
Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken.
Sarah conceived, and bore Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.
Abraham called his son who was born to him, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac.
Abraham circumcised his son, Isaac, when he was eight days old, as God had commanded him.
Abraham was one hundred years old when his son, Isaac, was born to him.
Sarah said, “God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.”
She said, “Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? For I have borne him a son in his old age.”
The child grew and was weaned. Abraham made a great feast on the day that Isaac was weaned.
Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, mocking.
Therefore she said to Abraham, “Cast out this servant and her son! For the son of this servant will not be heir with my son, Isaac.”
The thing was very grievous in Abraham’s sight on account of his son.

God said to Abraham, “Don’t let it be grievous in your sight because of the boy, and because of your servant. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice. For your offspring will be named through Isaac.
I will also make a nation of the son of the servant, because he is your child.”

Abraham rose up early in the morning, and took bread and a container of water, and gave it to Hagar, putting it on her shoulder; and gave her the child, and sent her away. She departed, and wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba.
The water in the container was spent, and she put the child under one of the shrubs.
She went and sat down opposite him, a good way off, about a bow shot away. For she said, “Don’t let me see the death of the child.” She sat opposite him, and lifted up her voice, and wept.
God heard the voice of the boy.
The angel of God called to Hagar out of the sky, and said to her, “What troubles you, Hagar? Don’t be afraid. For God has heard the voice of the boy where he is.
Get up, lift up the boy, and hold him with your hand. For I will make him a great nation.”
God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She went, filled the container with water, and gave the boy a drink.
God was with the boy, and he grew. He lived in the wilderness, and as he grew up, became an archer.
He lived in the wilderness of Paran. His mother got a wife for him out of the land of Egypt.
Tell me, you that desire to be under the law, don’t you listen to the law?
For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the servant, and one by the free woman.
However, the son by the servant was born according to the flesh, but the son by the free woman was born through promise.
These things contain an allegory, for these are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children to bondage, which is Hagar.
For this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia, and answers to the Jerusalem that exists now, for she is in bondage with her children.
But the Jerusalem that is above is free, which is the mother of us all.
For it is written,

“Rejoice, you barren who don’t bear.
Break out and shout, you who don’t travail.
For the desolate have more children than her who has a husband.”
Now we, brothers, as Isaac was, are children of promise.
But as then, he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now.
However what does the Scripture say? “Throw out the servant and her son, for the son of the servant will not inherit with the son of the free woman.”
So then, brothers, we are not children of a servant, but of the free woman.

parts.title: The God who sees
parts.context: Abram has lived in Canaan for ten years. Sarai, still childless, makes a plan.

commentary.on: Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.
commentary.text: Sarai's plan was legal and normal. Notice that it repeats an old pattern: in Genesis 3, a woman takes and gives to her husband, and he listens to her voice. Here 'Abram listened to the voice of Sarai'. Human beings trying to secure God's promise their own way.

commentary.on: When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.
commentary.text: Exactly what Hammurabi's laws foresaw. The slave who can bear a child feels herself above the free woman who can't. Everyone in this triangle behaves badly.

commentary.on: Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.
commentary.text: Abram washes his hands of the woman carrying his child. Sarai 'dealt harshly with her', using a Hebrew verb later used for Egypt's oppression of the Israelites (Exodus 1:11–12). The irony is deliberate: the ancestors of Israel oppress an Egyptian slave, before Egyptians oppress Israel.

commentary.on: Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?
commentary.text: The first time in the Bible that 'the angel of Yahweh' appears, it is not to Abram but to a runaway Egyptian slave in the desert. He calls her by name. No one else in the story has.

commentary.on: Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands.
commentary.text: A hard command, and readers have always found it so. Why send her back? The likeliest answer in the story is survival: a pregnant woman alone in the desert would die. The promises that follow are the reason to return.

commentary.on: You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction.
commentary.text: Ishmael means 'God hears'. The boy's very name tells the story: God heard a slave woman's misery. Hagar receives a promise of countless descendants, like Abram's.

commentary.on: She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,”
commentary.text: Hagar is the only person in the whole Bible who gives God a name. 'El Roi': the God who sees me. The one person in the story whom nobody sees, a foreign slave, is the one who sees God and is seen by him.

parts.title: Isaac: laughter
parts.context: Fourteen years later, after God has renewed the covenant and given new names (Genesis 17) and promised a son to Sarah (Genesis 18, which you will read in the next session), the promise is kept.

commentary.on: Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken.
commentary.text: The sentence says the same thing twice, on purpose: 'as he had said… as he had spoken'. After twenty-five years, God keeps his word exactly.

commentary.on: Abraham was one hundred years old when his son, Isaac, was born to him.
commentary.text: The age is the point. This child is not the product of planning or custom, like Ishmael, but of a promise. Paul will call Isaac the son 'born through promise' (Galatians 4:23).

commentary.on: God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.
commentary.text: Isaac's name, Yitzhak, means 'he laughs'. Both Abraham and Sarah had laughed in disbelief when the son was promised (17:17; 18:12). Now the laughter of disbelief becomes the laughter of joy.

parts.title: Driven out
parts.context: A few years later, when Isaac is weaned, perhaps aged two or three, Ishmael is about sixteen.

commentary.on: Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian, whom she had borne to Abraham, mocking.
commentary.text: The Hebrew word, metzahek, is a play on Isaac's name: 'laughing' or 'playing'. It may mean that Ishmael mocked Isaac, or only that he was playing, or 'Isaac-ing', acting as an heir. Sarah does not even name him: he is 'the son of Hagar the Egyptian'.

commentary.on: Cast out this servant and her son!
commentary.text: Sarah wants Ishmael removed as a rival heir. Under ancient law, a slave's son freed with his mother lost his claim to inherit, so this may also be an act of freeing them. But it is a freedom that drives them into the desert.

commentary.on: The thing was very grievous in Abraham’s sight on account of his son.
commentary.text: Abraham loves Ishmael. Genesis says so plainly: 'his son'. God tells him to do as Sarah says, but adds a promise: Ishmael too will be a nation, 'because he is your child'.

commentary.on: Don’t let me see the death of the child.
commentary.text: One of the most painful moments in the Bible. The water is gone. A mother puts her son under a bush and sits a bowshot away so she will not have to watch him die.

commentary.on: God heard the voice of the boy.
commentary.text: Ishmael's name again: 'God hears'. The boy is not part of the covenant line, and God hears him anyway. Hagar weeps, but it is the boy's voice God answers.

commentary.on: God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water.
commentary.text: The well was there; she could not see it. The God who sees opens her eyes. Ishmael grows up in the wilderness of Paran, an archer, and his mother finds him a wife from her own country, Egypt. Genesis 25:9 adds a moving detail: when Abraham died, 'Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him' together.

parts.title: Paul's allegory
parts.context: Paul again, writing to Gentile Christians who were being told to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. He turns the story of Hagar and Sarah into an allegory, a story in which each figure stands for something else, to make his argument.

commentary.on: These things contain an allegory, for these are two covenants.
commentary.text: Paul says openly that he is reading the story as an allegory. Hagar, the slave, stands for the covenant made at Mount Sinai and the law; Sarah, the free woman, for the new covenant of the promise.

commentary.on: For this Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
commentary.text: A surprising move. Paul links Hagar with Sinai, where the law was given, and with Arabia, where Ishmael's descendants lived. In ordinary Jewish thinking, the Jews were Sarah's children and the law their glory. Paul reverses it, to argue that those who rely on the law are, in his allegory, slaves.

commentary.on: Now we, brothers, as Isaac was, are children of promise.
commentary.text: Paul's point: Gentile believers, who were never part of Abraham's bloodline, are like Isaac, born by God's promise, not by human effort.

commentary.on: Throw out the servant and her son, for the son of the servant will not inherit with the son of the free woman.
commentary.text: Paul quotes Sarah's words as Scripture. Many readers today are uneasy: the allegory takes no notice of Hagar's suffering or of God's care for her and Ishmael, and it was later used against Jews. Paul's purpose was to defend the freedom of Gentile Christians; but his reading is one use of the story, not the whole of it.

paras:
ABRAHAM said, "O Lord make this land secure, and turn aside me and my children from serving idols:
For many men, O my Lord, have they led astray. But whosoever shall follow me, he truly shall be of me; and whosoever shall disobey me. . . . Thou truly art Gracious, Merciful.
O our Lord! verily I have settled some of my offspring in an unfruitful valley, nigh to thy holy house; O our Lord, that they may strictly observe prayer! Make thou therefore the hearts of men to yearn toward them, and supply them with fruits that they may be thankful.
O our Lord! thou truly knowest what we hide and what we bring to light; nought on earth or in heaven is hidden from God. Praise be to God who hath given me, in my old age, Ismael and Isaac! My Lord is the hearer of prayer.

And when Abraham, with Ismael, raised the foundations of the House, they said, "O our Lord! accept it from us; for thou art the Hearer, the Knower.
O our Lord! make us also Muslims, and our posterity a Muslim people; and teach us our holy rites, and be turned towards us, for thou art He who turneth, the Merciful.

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: Abraham's prayer for the valley
parts.context: This sura is named after Abraham. Here he prays for Mecca, the 'land' he asks God to make secure, and for the son he left there. The 'holy house' is the Kaaba, the cube-shaped shrine at the centre of Mecca, towards which Muslims pray. Muslim tradition tells that Abraham left Hagar and the baby Ishmael in this valley; Hagar ran seven times between two hills, Safa and Marwa, looking for water, until the spring of Zamzam burst out.
parts.plain: Abraham prays: make this land safe, and keep me and my children from serving idols. I have settled some of my children in a barren valley near your holy house, so that they may pray; make people's hearts love them, and give them food. Praise God who gave me, in my old age, Ishmael and Isaac.

commentary.on: turn aside me and my children from serving idols
commentary.text: Abraham's first prayer is the one you met in session 1: no idols. In Islam, Mecca was founded as a place of pure worship of the one God, which later generations corrupted with idols until Muhammad cleansed it.

commentary.on: verily I have settled some of my offspring in an unfruitful valley, nigh to thy holy house
commentary.text: Here the desert where Hagar and Ishmael were sent becomes the valley of Mecca. What Genesis tells as an expulsion, the Islamic tradition tells as a settling, by God's command, at the place of his house. Every year, pilgrims on the Hajj walk seven times between Safa and Marwa, remembering Hagar's search for water, and drink from the well of Zamzam.

commentary.on: Praise be to God who hath given me, in my old age, Ismael and Isaac!
commentary.text: Both sons, named together, with thanks. Notice that Ishmael comes first, as the elder. In the Qur'an, both are prophets.

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: Building the House
parts.context: The Qur'an's longest sura. These verses describe Abraham and Ishmael raising the foundations of the Kaaba together.
parts.plain: Abraham and Ishmael built the foundations of God's house, and prayed: accept this from us; make us people who submit to you, and our descendants too; teach us how to worship, and forgive us.

commentary.on: And when Abraham, with Ismael, raised the foundations of the House
commentary.text: Father and son, together, building God's house. The son Genesis sends away is, in the Qur'an, his father's partner in founding the central shrine of the faith.

commentary.on: O our Lord! make us also Muslims, and our posterity a Muslim people
commentary.text: 'Muslim' means 'one who submits' to God. For Islam, Abraham and Ishmael were Muslims in this original sense, long before Muhammad. So Islam does not see itself as a new religion, but as a return to the faith of Abraham.

compare.author: The Qur'an
compare.why: In Islam, the son who was sent away is not a side character. Ishmael, Ismail in Arabic, is a prophet and the ancestor of the Arabs and of Muhammad. Read two short passages from the Qur'an: Abraham's prayer for the son he settled in the desert, and Abraham and Ishmael building the Kaaba, the shrine at Mecca.
compare.title: Ishmael in the Qur'an

paras: Read the Hagar stories again and count who sees whom. Sarai and Abram look at Hagar as a means to an end: a womb, then a problem. No one in the household calls her by her name; she is 'my servant', 'your maid', 'this servant'. Then, in the desert, the angel calls her 'Hagar', asks where she is going, and listens to her answer. She names God 'the God who sees me'.

This is the first thing the story says about the unchosen: God sees them. The covenant goes through Isaac, but God's care does not stop at the covenant's edge. Ishmael's name, 'God hears', says the same. The story was told and kept by Abraham's descendants through Isaac, and they told it with sympathy for the son who was sent away.
sections.key: The household sees Hagar as a means; God sees her as a person, and hears her son.

paras: Does God's choice of Isaac mean the rejection of Ishmael? Genesis says no. Ishmael receives promises almost as large as Isaac's: a great nation, countless descendants, twelve princes (17:20). He is circumcised with Abraham (17:23–26), so he bears the covenant's sign. God is 'with the boy' (21:20). What he does not receive is the covenant role: to be the line through which the promise to all nations is carried.

That distinction, between being loved and being given a particular task, is one of the keys to the whole journey. The Jewish scholar Jon Levenson puts it this way: in Genesis, chosenness is real and often painful, but the unchosen are not damned; they are part of the story, and frequently treated with great tenderness.
sections.key: Ishmael is loved, blessed and protected; what he is not given is the covenant role of carrying the promise.

paras: The same story is read in remarkably different ways. Paul used it as an allegory of law and freedom. Jewish tradition identified Ishmael with the Arabs, and later rabbis were sometimes hostile, sometimes sympathetic; one midrash says Abraham secretly visited Ishmael in the desert. Islam places Hagar and Ishmael at the centre of its holiest rites.

In recent decades many Christian readers, especially women, have read the story from Hagar's side. The American theologian Delores Williams, in Sisters in the Wilderness (1993), saw in Hagar the experience of Black women in America: enslaved, used for their bodies, driven out, and met by God in the wilderness, who gave them not freedom at once but survival and a future.

rows: Abraham's beloved son, blessed but not the covenant heir
A story of chosen and unchosen, both under God's care
An Egyptian slave who sees God and is seen
Ancestor of the Arab peoples; sometimes a rival, sometimes a penitent (some rabbis said he repented)
Explains Israel's relation to its neighbours
Some rabbis identified her with Keturah, whom Abraham later married (Genesis 25:1)
In Paul, the son 'born according to the flesh'
Paul's allegory of law and promise (Galatians 4); modern readers from Hagar's side
In Paul, the covenant of slavery; for many today, the God who sees the oppressed
Ismail, a prophet; builder with Abraham of the Kaaba; ancestor of Muhammad
The founding of Mecca and the Hajj
Hajar, honoured mother; her search for water is re-enacted by every pilgrim

sections.key: Paul made Hagar an allegory; the rabbis linked Ishmael with the Arabs; Islam honours Hajar and Ismail at Mecca; many readers today read from Hagar's side.

paras: This story contains slavery, sexual use of a woman who could not refuse, jealousy and expulsion. Genesis does not approve of what Abram and Sarai do; it simply tells it, and lets the reader see the cost. Its sympathy is plainly with Hagar and the boy.

We should also say what the story does not settle. It does not tell us whether God approved of the slavery that frames it; later biblical law limits slavery and commands care for the foreigner and the runaway slave (Deuteronomy 23:15–16), and the New Testament's 'neither slave nor free' (Galatians 3:28) became, in time, part of the case against it. It is fair to ask why God tells Hagar to return and later tells Abraham to listen to Sarah. Readers have answered: for survival, for the promise's sake, or as the hard limits of a world God works within rather than approves. The question deserves to be held, not hurried.
sections.key: Genesis tells Hagar's story without approving its cruelty; its sympathy is with her, and the hard questions remain fair ones.

paras: The story of the two sons does not end with the expulsion. When Abraham dies 'at a good old age', Genesis records: 'Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him in the cave of Machpelah' (25:9). The two half-brothers, separated as boys, stand together at their father's grave.

Today that grave, in Hebron, is one of the most contested places on earth, divided between a synagogue and a mosque. The one image Genesis leaves us of the two sons together is of them burying their father in peace.
sections.key: Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham together: the story ends with the brothers side by side.

refs: Laws of Hammurabi §§144–147, trans. L. W. King (1910); the Nuzi marriage contract (HSS 5 67), in J. B. Pritchard, Ancient Near Eastern Texts (3rd ed. 1969).
Qur'an 14:35–41; 2:124–129; 37:100–101. Hajar, Safa and Marwa, and Zamzam: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Prophets (hadith 3364).
Jon D. Levenson, The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son (1993) and Inheriting Abraham (2012).
Rabbinic traditions: Genesis Rabbah 61:4 (Hagar as Keturah); Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer 30 (Abraham visits Ishmael).
Delores S. Williams, Sisters in the Wilderness (1993); Phyllis Trible, Texts of Terror (1984), chapter 1.

debate.question: How should we read the story of Hagar and Ishmael?

positions.name: A story of the promise
positions.who: Most traditional Jewish and Christian readers
positions.view: The story's main point is that God keeps his promise his own way, through Isaac, not through human schemes; Ishmael is blessed, but the covenant line is Isaac's.
positions.evidence: Genesis 17:19–21; 21:12; the contrast between the planned son and the promised son.

positions.name: A story of the God who sees
positions.who: Phyllis Trible; Delores Williams; many readers today
positions.view: The story's heart is Hagar: used, abused and driven out by the family of promise, and met by God in the wilderness. It judges the chosen family and shows God's care for the oppressed.
positions.evidence: Hagar alone names God; God appears to her first; the angel calls her by name; Ishmael means 'God hears'.

positions.name: A story of two peoples
positions.who: Islamic tradition; many historians of religion
positions.view: The story is the founding of two lines of Abraham's descendants, both blessed; Ishmael's line is not a footnote but its own great story, centred on Mecca.

debate.agree: All agree that God hears Ishmael and blesses him, and that the story does not hide the suffering of Hagar.

look.why: Hagar was an Egyptian, and when she found her son a wife, she went back to Egypt for her (Genesis 21:21). Sanford Robinson Gifford, an American landscape painter, saw this Egyptian town on the Nile in 1869 and painted it in 1874, in hazy desert light.
points: A dirt path winds through gold-green grass towards a town on low hills.
Tiny people walk on the path, and one rides a horse.
In the town, flat-topped buildings and one domed building with two slender minarets, among palm trees.
A low sun blazes over rocky mountains on the left.
To the right, people sit near a white tent, with horses and smaller animals grazing.

music.why: John Newton, once a slave-ship captain, wrote 'Amazing Grace' after his conversion: 'I once was lost, but now am found, was blind, but now I see'. Hagar's God opens blind eyes; Newton's song came out of the slave trade.

think.why: Hagar was a slave. Ask how the Bible that contains her story became, over centuries, part of the case against slavery.

learn.why: The only time in the Bible a person names God: the God who sees.

check.q: Why might Sarai's plan to have a child through Hagar have seemed reasonable to her neighbours?
options: Because Hagar had asked to become Abram's wife
Because Hagar was Abram's first wife
Because God had told her to
Because ancient laws and contracts, such as Hammurabi's, recognised a childless wife giving her slave to bear a child that counted as hers
check.why: It was a known and regulated custom.

check.q: What is the significance of Hagar naming God 'El Roi'?
options: It means 'God of Abraham'
It was the usual Egyptian name for God
It shows Hagar worshipped another god
It is the only time a person in the Bible gives God a name, and it is a foreign slave whom no one else in the story sees
check.why: The unseen woman is the one who sees God and is seen.

check.q: Which statement about Ishmael in Genesis is accurate?
options: God rejects him and promises him nothing
He never meets Isaac again
He becomes the covenant heir instead of Isaac
He is blessed, promised a great nation and twelve princes, and circumcised, but the covenant line passes through Isaac
check.why: He is loved and blessed; what he is not given is the covenant role. He buries Abraham with Isaac.

check.q: In Galatians 4, Paul links Hagar with Mount Sinai. Why is this surprising?
options: Because Hagar is never mentioned again after Genesis
Because Sinai is where Abraham bound Isaac
Because Paul identifies Hagar with the Gentile Christians he is defending
Because Sinai, where the law was given, was the glory of the Jews, Sarah's descendants; Paul reverses the usual identification to argue for Gentile freedom
check.why: Paul's allegory turns the expected reading upside down for his argument.

check.q: What does Hagar's search for water mean in Islam?
options: Pilgrims on the Hajj walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa in memory of it, and drink from the well of Zamzam
Pilgrims drink from the wells of Beersheba
It is remembered by fasting during Ramadan
It explains why Muslims pray five times a day
check.why: Hajar's search is part of the central pilgrimage of Islam.

check.q: Why does the Hebrew word for what Ishmael was doing (Genesis 21:9) matter?
options: It is a play on Hagar's name
It shows Ishmael was mocking Sarah's old age
It proves he was attacking Isaac
It is a play on Isaac's name ('laughing' or 'playing') and may mean only that he was playing, or acting as an heir, so the reason for the expulsion is ambiguous
check.why: Metzahek echoes Yitzhak; translators differ between 'mocking' and 'playing'.

tutorial.question: What does the story of Hagar and Ishmael show about God's choosing?
tutorial.approach: Tell the two stories (Genesis 16 and 21) briefly. Then ask what God does for Hagar and Ishmael, and what he does not give them. Compare Paul's allegory with the Islamic tradition and with readings from Hagar's side. End by saying how the story answers the question 'what about the ones not chosen?'
strong: Explains the ancient custom behind Sarai's plan.
Notices that God appears first to Hagar, calls her by name, and that she names God.
Distinguishes between being blessed and being given the covenant role.
Explains Paul's allegory and its limits.
Describes Hagar and Ishmael's place in Islam.
Faces the story's troubling elements honestly.

reading.title: Texts of Terror
reading.why: Its first chapter reads Hagar's story with great care and feeling.

reading.author: Delores S. Williams
reading.title: Sisters in the Wilderness
reading.why: Hagar and the experience of Black women in America.

reading.author: Jon D. Levenson
reading.title: The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son
reading.why: On chosen and unchosen sons in Genesis.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: notice one person who is usually overlooked, at work, at school, in your street, and talk to them by name.
sessions.reflect: Have you ever felt like the one who was not chosen? What would it mean to be seen by God there?
takeaways: Sarai's plan was a legal custom, and everyone in the triangle behaves badly; Genesis's sympathy is with Hagar.
God sees Hagar and hears Ishmael: he is blessed and protected, though the covenant line passes through Isaac.
Paul made the story an allegory; Islam honours Hajar and Ismail at Mecca; Isaac and Ishmael bury Abraham together.

sessions.title: Can you argue with God?
sessions.line: Three strangers at the tent door, and a man who bargains for a city.
sessions.plain: Three strangers arrive at Abraham's tent in the heat of the day, and he runs to welcome them. They turn out to be God and two angels. They promise Sarah a son, then turn towards Sodom, a city so wicked that God is about to destroy it. And Abraham does something astonishing: he argues with God, and God lets him. This session asks what the chosen family is chosen for, and whether a person may argue with God.
sessions.why: Session 3 showed that God's choosing does not mean abandoning the unchosen. Now Genesis says, in God's own words, what Abraham is chosen for: 'to do righteousness and justice'. We see what that looks like, in welcome for strangers and in a plea for a wicked city.
answers: Who were the three visitors, and why does the story make so much of hospitality?
What is Abraham chosen for?
Can a person argue with God, and does God ever change his mind?
What was the sin of Sodom?
Is God bound by justice, or is whatever God does just by definition?
sessions.finding: The family is chosen for justice and blessing towards others: Abraham welcomes strangers and pleads for a wicked city, and God welcomes the argument, because he too is bound by the justice he asks of people.

paras: God chose Abraham by grace, for all the families of the earth (session 1); he bound himself to his promise by covenant (session 2); and he saw and blessed Hagar and Ishmael, who were not the covenant line (session 3). Now Abraham is ninety-nine, newly renamed, and Sarah is still childless.
background.key: Chosen by grace, held by God's oath, and the unchosen not abandoned.

paras: Abraham is living by the 'oaks of Mamre', near Hebron, in the hills south of Jerusalem. Far below, to the east, lies the Dead Sea, the lowest place on earth, and somewhere near it the 'cities of the plain', Sodom and Gomorrah. No one knows exactly where they were; several sites around the south and north-east of the Dead Sea have been proposed.

Abraham's nephew Lot lives in Sodom. Years before, when their flocks grew too large to share pasture, Abraham let Lot choose the land he wanted, and Lot chose the rich, well-watered plain by Sodom (Genesis 13). Genesis added then: 'the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners against Yahweh'.

timeline.text: Abraham and Lot part; Lot settles near Sodom
Abraham rescues Lot from raiding kings
New names; Abraham aged 99
The three visitors; Abraham pleads for Sodom
Sodom destroyed; Lot rescued
Isaac born

background.key: Abraham lives at Mamre, in the hills; Lot lives in Sodom, on the rich plain by the Dead Sea.

paras: In the ancient world there were no hotels and few inns. A traveller depended on the kindness of strangers for food, water and safety, and a host was bound by sacred duty to protect his guests. Greeks called it xenia, guest-friendship, protected by Zeus himself, who was believed to travel in disguise to test it; the whole of Homer's Odyssey turns on hosts who honour their guests and suitors who abuse them.
So when strangers arrive in a story, the first hearers sat up. How would they be treated? The answer told you who the host really was.
background.key: Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty, and stories of strangers tested the host.

paras: The main reading has three parts: the visitors at Abraham's tent (18:1–15), Abraham's argument with God for Sodom (18:16–33), and the destruction of the city and Lot's rescue (19:15–17, 24–29).

The comparison is from the Roman poet Ovid: the story of Baucis and Philemon, an old couple who welcome two disguised gods when everyone else turns them away. It is strikingly like Genesis 18–19, and it shows what the ancient world shared, and what Genesis adds.
background.key: Welcome, argument, judgement and rescue; and a Roman story of gods in disguise.

before: How does Abraham treat the strangers? Count the things he does.
Why does God decide to tell Abraham his plan?
What does Abraham appeal to when he argues? Where does he stop, and why?
sessions.readWhy: Abraham's welcome, his argument with God, and the judgement on Sodom, in three parts.

paras: Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day.
He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth,
and said, “My lord, if now I have found favor in your sight, please don’t go away from your servant.
Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
I will get a piece of bread so you can refresh your heart. After that you may go your way, now that you have come to your servant.”
They said, “Very well, do as you have said.”
Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, “Quickly prepare three seahs of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.”
Abraham ran to the herd, and fetched a tender and good calf, and gave it to the servant. He hurried to dress it.
He took butter, milk, and the calf which he had dressed, and set it before them. He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.
They asked him, “Where is Sarah, your wife?”
He said, “There, in the tent.”
He said, “I will certainly return to you at about this time next year; and behold, Sarah your wife will have a son.”
Sarah heard in the tent door, which was behind him.
Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing.
Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”
Yahweh said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh, saying, ‘Will I really bear a child when I am old?’
Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
Then Sarah denied it, saying, “I didn’t laugh,” for she was afraid.
He said, “No, but you did laugh.”
The men rose up from there, and looked toward Sodom. Abraham went with them to see them on their way.
Yahweh said, “Will I hide from Abraham what I do,
since Abraham will surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth will be blessed in him?

For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice; to the end that Yahweh may bring on Abraham that which he has spoken of him.”
Yahweh said, “Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous,
I will go down now, and see whether their deeds are as bad as the reports which have come to me. If not, I will know.”
The men turned from there, and went toward Sodom, but Abraham stood yet before Yahweh.
Abraham came near, and said, “Will you consume the righteous with the wicked?
What if there are fifty righteous within the city? Will you consume and not spare the place for the fifty righteous who are in it?

May it be far from you to do things like that, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked. May that be far from you. Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?”
Yahweh said, “If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare the whole place for their sake.”
Abraham answered, “See now, I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord, although I am dust and ashes.
What if there will lack five of the fifty righteous? Will you destroy all the city for lack of five?”
He said, “I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there.”
He spoke to him yet again, and said, “What if there are forty found there?”
He said, “I will not do it for the forty’s sake.”
He said, “Oh don’t let the Lord be angry, and I will speak. What if there are thirty found there?”
He said, “I will not do it if I find thirty there.”
He said, “See now, I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord. What if there are twenty found there?”
He said, “I will not destroy it for the twenty’s sake.”
He said, “Oh don’t let the Lord be angry, and I will speak just once more. What if ten are found there?”
He said, “I will not destroy it for the ten’s sake.”
Yahweh went his way, as soon as he had finished communing with Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place.
When the morning came, then the angels hurried Lot, saying, “Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be consumed in the iniquity of the city.”
But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand, his wife’s hand, and his two daughters’ hands, Yahweh being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city.
It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”
Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky.
He overthrew those cities, all the plain, all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew on the ground.
But Lot’s wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
Abraham went up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before Yahweh.
He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and saw that the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace.
When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in which Lot lived.

parts.title: Three men at the tent door
parts.context: Midday at Mamre. Genesis tells the reader at once who the visitor is ('Yahweh appeared'); Abraham sees only three travellers.

commentary.on: as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day
commentary.text: The hottest hour, when nobody travels and everybody rests. Abraham is ninety-nine and recently circumcised. Every detail makes what he does next more remarkable.

commentary.on: he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth
commentary.text: An old man running, in the heat, to strangers, and bowing to the ground. He does not know who they are. He treats unknown travellers as honoured guests.

commentary.on: I will get a piece of bread so you can refresh your heart.
commentary.text: He promises 'a piece of bread', then provides a feast: cakes from about twenty litres of fine flour, a tender calf, butter and milk. Jewish tradition admired this: say little, do much (Mishnah Avot 1:15).

commentary.on: He stood by them under the tree, and they ate.
commentary.text: The host stands and serves while the guests eat. Hebrews 13:2 has this scene in mind: 'some have entertained angels without knowing it'.

commentary.on: Sarah laughed within herself
commentary.text: Sarah, listening behind the tent door, laughs at the promise of a son. She is long past childbearing. Her laughter, like Abraham's in chapter 17, becomes the boy's name: Isaac, 'he laughs'.

commentary.on: Is anything too hard for Yahweh?
commentary.text: The question at the centre of the passage, and of the whole promise. The angel Gabriel says almost the same words to Mary in Luke 1:37.

parts.title: The Judge of all the earth
parts.context: The visitors set off towards Sodom, and Abraham walks with them, as a good host would. Two of the 'men' go on; the third, Yahweh, stays.

commentary.on: Will I hide from Abraham what I do
commentary.text: God decides to tell Abraham his plan. He is treating Abraham as a friend, or as a prophet, one who is let into God's counsel (compare Amos 3:7). Abraham is meant to have a say.

commentary.on: that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice
commentary.text: Here, in God's own words, is what Abraham is chosen for: to teach his children 'righteousness and justice'. The chosen family is meant to be a school of justice for the world. This verse is the purpose behind the promise.

commentary.on: Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great
commentary.text: 'The cry' is the word for the scream of the oppressed, used of the Israelites crying out in Egypt (Exodus 3:7). Someone in Sodom is crying for help. God goes 'down to see', as at Babel: he investigates before he judges.

commentary.on: Will you consume the righteous with the wicked?
commentary.text: Abraham steps forward ('came near') and asks a moral question of God. He does not plead for Lot by name. He pleads for the principle: it is wrong to kill the innocent with the guilty.

commentary.on: Shouldn’t the Judge of all the earth do right?
commentary.text: One of the boldest sentences in the Bible. Abraham holds God to God's own justice. He assumes there is a right that even the Judge of the whole earth must do, and that God will want to be reminded of it.

commentary.on: although I am dust and ashes
commentary.text: Boldness and humility together. Abraham knows he is a creature of dust, as Genesis 2 said, and still speaks. This is the pattern of prayer in the Bible: honest, persistent, reverent.

commentary.on: What if ten are found there?
commentary.text: Fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten. Each time God agrees at once. Abraham stops at ten, perhaps the smallest group that counts as a community. The question the passage leaves is: would ten good people be enough to save a city? God says yes.

parts.title: Fire and rescue
parts.context: Between the last passage and this one, the two angels reach Sodom in the evening. Lot, sitting at the city gate, insists that they stay in his house and makes them a meal, as Abraham did. That night every man in the city, 'young and old', surrounds the house and demands that the guests be brought out so that they can rape them (19:4–5). Lot refuses, and, horribly, offers his own daughters instead; the angels strike the mob blind (19:8–11). At dawn they tell Lot to flee.

commentary.on: But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand
commentary.text: Lot cannot bring himself to leave the city he chose. The angels have to drag him and his family out by the hand. Genesis adds: 'Yahweh being merciful to him'. Lot is rescued not because he is righteous, but by mercy.

commentary.on: Then Yahweh rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah sulfur and fire from Yahweh out of the sky.
commentary.text: Not ten righteous people were found. Many have suggested a natural cause, such as an earthquake igniting the bitumen and gas of the Dead Sea region, which is rich in both (Genesis 14:10 mentions its tar pits). Genesis presents it as God's judgement.

commentary.on: But Lot’s wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
commentary.text: She looked back at what she was leaving, and was caught in it. The salt formations around the Dead Sea gave the story a visible landmark; Jesus says, 'Remember Lot's wife' (Luke 17:32).

commentary.on: He looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the plain, and saw that the smoke of the land went up as the smoke of a furnace.
commentary.text: Abraham returns to the place where he argued with God and looks down at the smoke. No words. He lost the argument, because there were not ten. But the next verse says why Lot lived.

commentary.on: God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow
commentary.text: Lot was saved because God 'remembered Abraham'. Abraham's prayer did not save the city, but it was not wasted. This is the first answer to the question of the passage: intercession, praying for others, matters to God.

paras: “And that thou mayst the less doubt {of this}, there is upon the Phrygian hills, an oak near to the lime tree, enclosed by a low wall. I, myself, have seen the spot; for Pittheus sent me into the land of Pelops, once governed by his father, {Pelops}. Not far thence is a standing water, formerly habitable ground, but now frequented by cormorants and coots, that delight in fens. Jupiter came hither in the shape of a man, and together with his parent, the grandson of Atlas, {Mercury}, the bearer of the Caduceus, having laid aside his wings. To a thousand houses did they go, asking for lodging and for rest. A thousand houses did the bolts fasten {against them}. Yet one received them, a small one indeed, thatched with straw, and the reeds of the marsh. But a pious old woman {named} Baucis, and Philemon of a like age, were united in their youthful years in that {cottage}, and in it, they grew old together;

and by owning their poverty, they rendered it light, and not to be endured with discontented mind. It matters not, whether you ask for the masters there, or for the servants; the whole family are but two; the same persons both obey and command. When, therefore, the inhabitants of heaven reached this little abode, and, bending their necks, entered the humble door, the old man bade them rest their limbs on a bench set {there}; upon which the attentive Baucis threw a coarse cloth. Then she moves the warm embers on the hearth, and stirs up the fire they had had the day before, and supplies it with leaves and dry bark, and with her aged breath kindles it into a flame; and brings out of the house faggots split into many pieces, and dry bits of branches, and breaks them, and puts them beneath a small boiler. Some pot-herbs, too, which her husband has gathered in the well-watered garden, she strips of their leaves.

“There is {now} a short pause; the fire {then} sends up the warm repast; and wine kept no long time, is again put on; and {then}, set aside for a little time, it gives place to the second course. Here are nuts, {and} here are dried figs mixed with wrinkled dates, plums too, and fragrant apples in wide baskets, and grapes gathered from the purple vines. In the middle there is white honey-comb. Above all, there are welcome looks, and no indifferent and niggardly feelings. In the meanwhile, as oft as Baucis and the alarmed Philemon behold the goblet, {when} drunk off, replenish itself of its own accord, and the wine increase of itself, astonished at this singular event, they are frightened, and, with hands held up, they offer their prayers, and entreat pardon for their entertainment, and their want of preparation. There was a single goose, the guardian of their little cottage, which its owners were preparing to kill for the Deities, their guests. Swift with its wings, it wearied them, {rendered} slow by age, and it escaped them a long time, and at length seemed to fly for safety to the Gods themselves. The immortals forbade it to be killed, and said, ‘We are Divinities, and this impious neighbourhood shall suffer deserved punishment. To you it will be allowed to be free from this calamity; only leave your habitation, and attend our steps, and go together to the summit of the mountain.’

“They both obeyed; and, supported by staffs, they endeavoured to place their feet {on the top} of the high hill. They were {now} as far from the top, as an arrow discharged can go at once, {when} they turned their eyes, and beheld the other parts sinking in a morass, {and} their own abode alone remaining. While they were wondering at these things, {and} while they were bewailing the fate of their {fellow countrymen}, that old cottage of {theirs}, {too} little for even two owners, was changed into a temple. Columns took the place of forked stakes, the thatch grew yellow, and the earth was covered with marble; the doors appeared carved, and the roof to be of gold. Then, the son of Saturn uttered such words as these with benign lips: ‘Tell us, good old man, and thou, wife, worthy of a husband {so} good, what it is you desire?’ Having spoken a few words to Baucis, Philemon discovered their joint request to the Gods: ‘We desire to be your priests, and to have the care of your temple; and, since we have passed our years in harmony, let the same hour take us off both together;

and let me not ever see the tomb of my wife, nor let me be destined to be buried by her.’ Fulfilment attended their wishes. So long as life was granted, they were the keepers of the temple; and when, enervated by years and old age, they were standing, by chance, before the sacred steps, and were relating the fortunes of the spot, Baucis beheld Philemon, and the aged Philemon saw Baucis, {too}, shooting into leaf. And now the tops of the trees growing above their two faces, so long as they could they exchanged words with each other, and said together, ‘Farewell! my spouse;’ and at the same moment the branches covered their concealed faces. The inhabitants of Tyana still shew these adjoining trees, made of their two bodies. Old men, no romancers, (and there was no reason why they should wish to deceive me) told me this. I, indeed, saw garlands hanging on the branches, and placing {there} some fresh ones {myself}, I said, ‘The good are the {peculiar} care of the Gods, and those who worshipped {the Gods}, are {now} worshipped {themselves}.’”

parts.author: Ovid
parts.title: The gods in disguise
parts.context: Ovid (43 BC–AD 17) was the great poet of Augustus's Rome. His Metamorphoses, 'Transformations', is a long poem of myths in which people are changed into other things. In this story an old man, Lelex, tells it to prove that the gods can do anything. Jupiter is the king of the gods (Zeus to the Greeks), and 'the grandson of Atlas', Mercury, is his messenger. Phrygia is in what is now central Turkey. This is Henry Riley's literal prose translation of 1851; words in curly brackets are ones he added to make the sense clear. The '…' marks a cut, in which the old couple prepare and serve the meal.
parts.plain: The story says: Jupiter and Mercury came to Phrygia disguised as men, asking for shelter. A thousand houses shut their doors. One little cottage, owned by a poor, pious old couple, Baucis and Philemon, let them in and gave them everything they had. When the wine kept refilling itself, the couple realised their guests were gods. The gods drowned the neighbourhood in a marsh, saved the couple, and turned their cottage into a temple. Asked what they wanted, the couple asked to serve as priests and to die at the same moment, and at the end of their lives they were turned into two trees growing side by side.

commentary.on: To a thousand houses did they go, asking for lodging and for rest. A thousand houses did the bolts fasten
commentary.text: Like Sodom, a whole neighbourhood fails the test of hospitality. In both stories the gods, or God, come down in human form to see for themselves how strangers are treated.

commentary.on: by owning their poverty, they rendered it light
commentary.text: Baucis and Philemon are poor, where Abraham is rich. But they give in the same spirit: everything they have, and gladly. Ovid lingers lovingly over the details of their humble meal, as Genesis does over Abraham's.

commentary.on: behold the goblet, {when} drunk off, replenish itself of its own accord
commentary.text: The miracle that reveals the guests, like the visitors' knowledge of Sarah's laughter in Genesis 18. Christian readers have thought of Jesus turning water into wine at Cana.

commentary.on: this impious neighbourhood shall suffer deserved punishment
commentary.text: Here is the clearest parallel: the inhospitable neighbourhood is destroyed and the good hosts led up a mountain to safety, as Lot was told to flee to the mountains. But notice what is missing. Baucis and Philemon do not plead for their neighbours. No one argues that the innocent should be spared. That is Abraham's distinctive act.

commentary.on: let the same hour take us off both together
commentary.text: Their one wish is for each other: to serve the gods together and to die together. It is one of the most tender pictures of marriage in ancient literature.

commentary.on: The good are the {peculiar} care of the Gods
commentary.text: The moral of Ovid's tale: the gods care for the good. Genesis shares that conviction, but it goes further: God cares for the wicked city enough to listen to a plea for it, and his justice is something a man can appeal to.

compare.author: Ovid
compare.why: The Roman poet Ovid tells of two gods who wander in disguise looking for hospitality, are turned away by a thousand houses, and are welcomed by one poor old couple. The parallels with Genesis 18–19 are striking: welcome, a feast, a revelation, a destroyed neighbourhood and the hosts saved. Read it, and look for what is the same and what is different.
compare.title: Baucis and Philemon

paras: Who were the three men? Genesis says 'Yahweh appeared to him' and then that Abraham saw three men; later two of them, called angels, go to Sodom, while Yahweh stays with Abraham. Jewish tradition says they were three angels, each with one task: one to announce Isaac's birth, one to destroy Sodom, one to heal Abraham (Talmud, Bava Metzia 86b). Many early Christians saw a hint of the Trinity, and the most famous Orthodox icon, Andrei Rublev's Trinity (painted in Russia in the early fifteenth century), shows the three visitors seated at Abraham's table as Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

Either way the lesson is the same, and the New Testament draws it: 'Don't forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it' (Hebrews 13:2). Jesus goes further: 'I was a stranger, and you took me in' (Matthew 25:35). In the Bible, how you treat a stranger is how you treat God.

rows: Three angels, each with one task, with God present (Bava Metzia 86b)
Hospitality is a holy duty; Abraham is its model
A sign of the Holy Trinity, as in Rublev's icon
God himself comes as a guest; communion at his table
Usually God (perhaps the Son before his birth as a man) with two angels; some see a hint of the Trinity
Welcome the stranger, for Christ comes in the stranger (Matthew 25:35)

sections.key: Abraham welcomes strangers who turn out to be God and angels; in the Bible, how you treat a stranger is how you treat God.

paras: This session gives the clearest answer yet to the journey's question. Why one family? Genesis 18:19 says it in God's own words: 'that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice'. Abraham is chosen so that a family, and later a people, will learn and practise justice, and so become a blessing to the nations.

Then, immediately, Abraham shows what that means. Faced with a city about to be destroyed, a city that is not his, and that has wronged strangers, he does not gloat. He pleads for it. The chosen man's first act of justice is to speak up for others.
sections.key: Genesis 18:19: Abraham is chosen to teach 'righteousness and justice', and his first act is to plead for others.

paras: Abraham is the first of a long line of people in the Bible who argue with God. Moses argues God out of destroying Israel after the golden calf (Exodus 32:11–14), and 'Yahweh turned away from the evil which he said he would do'. Job demands an answer for his suffering. The Psalms are full of complaint: 'How long, Yahweh?' (Psalm 13). Jesus himself prays in Gethsemane, 'if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me' (Matthew 26:39).

Jewish tradition has a name for this boldness: chutzpah towards heaven, which the Talmud says 'is effective' (Sanhedrin 105a). The Jewish writer Elie Wiesel, who survived Auschwitz, wrote a play, The Trial of God (1979), in which people put God on trial for a massacre, and kept faith while doing it. Christian teaching has put it more quietly: prayer is not informing God of what he does not know, but sharing in his care for the world. Does God change his mind? The Bible says both that he does not change (Malachi 3:6) and that he relents when people repent or plead (Jonah 3:10). Most theologians read the second as God's unchanging mercy meeting a changed situation.
sections.key: From Abraham and Moses to Job, the Psalms and Gethsemane, the Bible lets people argue with God, and God listens.

paras: Abraham's question, 'Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?', raises one of philosophy's oldest puzzles. In Plato's dialogue Euthyphro, written in the early fourth century BC, Socrates asks: is something good because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is good? If good is simply whatever God commands, then 'God is good' means nothing. If God commands things because they are good, then goodness seems to stand above God.

Abraham assumes the second, at least in the sense that God's justice is real and recognisable, and that a human being can appeal to it. Jewish and Christian thinkers have usually answered the puzzle this way: goodness is neither above God nor arbitrary, but is God's own nature; God's commands come from who he is, and he cannot act against it. That is why Abraham can appeal to God against a threatened injustice. It is also why the next session's story is so hard.
sections.key: Abraham assumes God's justice is real and can be appealed to; the usual answer to Euthyphro is that goodness is God's own nature.

paras: The argument ends at ten. The idea behind it, that a few righteous people can save a whole community, runs through the Bible. Jeremiah is told to search Jerusalem for a single person who does justice, 'then I will pardon her' (Jeremiah 5:1). Isaiah's suffering servant bears the sins of many (Isaiah 53). Paul says that through one man's obedience 'many will be made righteous' (Romans 5:19).

Jewish tradition developed a beautiful legend from it: that in every generation there are at least thirty-six hidden righteous people, unknown even to themselves, for whose sake the world is kept in being (Talmud, Sanhedrin 97b and Sukkah 45b). Every ordinary good person might be one of them.
sections.key: A few righteous people can save many: from Abraham's ten to the thirty-six hidden righteous of Jewish legend.

refs: Genesis 13; 18–19; Exodus 32:11–14; Jeremiah 5:1; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Jonah 3:10; Malachi 3:6; Matthew 25:35; Luke 17:32; Romans 5:19; Hebrews 13:2; Jude 7; Acts 14:11–12.
Talmud: Bava Metzia 86b (three angels); Sanhedrin 105a (chutzpah towards heaven); Sanhedrin 97b and Sukkah 45b (thirty-six righteous); Sanhedrin 109a–b (the cruelty of Sodom); Mishnah Avot 1:15.
Andrei Rublev, The Trinity (early fifteenth century), Tretyakov Gallery, Moscow.
Elie Wiesel, The Trial of God (1979); Plato, Euthyphro 10a.
Ovid, Metamorphoses VIII.618–724, trans. H. T. Riley (1851); Homer, Odyssey, on xenia.
Catechism of the Catholic Church 2357 (citing Genesis 19:1–29); Robert Gagnon, The Bible and Homosexual Practice (2001); Robert Alter, Genesis (1996), notes on chapter 19.

debate.question: What was the sin of Sodom?

positions.name: Injustice and cruelty to the poor and the stranger
positions.who: Ezekiel 16:49–50; the Talmud; many Jewish commentators
positions.view: Sodom's sin was arrogance, greed and cruelty: it was rich and refused to help the poor or welcome strangers. The 'cry' God heard was the cry of its victims.
positions.evidence: Ezekiel 16:49, 'pride, fullness of bread, and prosperous ease… she also didn't strengthen the hand of the poor and needy'; the Talmud's stories of Sodom's laws against charity (Sanhedrin 109a–b).

positions.name: Sexual violence against guests
positions.who: Many modern scholars across traditions
positions.view: The story's sin is the attempted gang rape of strangers who are under a host's protection: violence, humiliation and the total violation of hospitality. The story says nothing about loving relationships.
positions.evidence: Genesis 19:4–9, where 'all the people from every quarter' demand the guests; the parallel story in Judges 19.

positions.name: Sexual immorality, including same-sex acts
positions.who: Jude 7; Philo; most of the Christian tradition; the Catechism of the Catholic Church
positions.view: The story condemns the city's violence and inhospitality, and also its sexual immorality, including sex between men; this is how many Jewish and Christian writers read it from the first century onwards.
positions.evidence: Jude 7, 'given themselves over to sexual immorality and gone after strange flesh'; the long tradition of interpretation; Catechism 2357.

debate.agree: All agree that the men of Sodom attempted violent sexual assault on strangers, that the city was unjust and inhospitable, and that the story holds up Abraham's welcome and his plea for the city as the opposite of Sodom.

look.why: Albrecht Dürer painted this small panel in the late 1490s, on the back of a painting of the Virgin and Child. Lot and his daughters walk away from the burning cities, carrying what they could save, with their eyes cast down. The story's dark sequel (19:30–38) is not shown.
points: Lot, an old man with a long grey beard, walks in front, in a royal-blue fur-lined coat and a turban with a crown.
He carries a stick with a water flask over his shoulder and a basket of silver in his other hand.
His two daughters follow, one carrying a small chest and two sticks, the other balancing a blue pack on her head.
Far behind them, a shadowy figure walks away along the path towards the cliffs.
In the distance, flames and plumes of black and pink smoke rise from a town by the water, and another town burns on the horizon.

music.why: Thomas Tallis's motet for forty voices (about 1570) sets a prayer from the book of Judith: 'I have never put my hope in any other but you, O God of Israel… who forgives all the sins of humankind in their suffering'. Forty voices pleading as one: an intercession.

think.why: Abraham appeals to a justice God himself must keep. Ask whether morality needs God, and what the Euthyphro dilemma really shows.

learn.why: Abraham's question to God, the boldest sentence in Genesis.

check.q: Why does God decide to tell Abraham what he plans to do to Sodom (Genesis 18:17–19)?
options: Because Lot was Abraham's nephew
Because Abraham is chosen to teach his descendants 'righteousness and justice', and so is treated as a friend who shares in God's counsel
Because Abraham asked him
Because God needed Abraham's permission
check.why: Verse 19 gives the reason: the purpose of Abraham's calling is justice.

check.q: What does Abraham appeal to in his argument for Sodom?
options: His own righteousness
God's love for Lot
The promise that all nations would be blessed through him
The principle that the Judge of all the earth must not kill the righteous with the wicked
check.why: He holds God to God's own justice, and never mentions Lot.

check.q: What is the most important difference between Ovid's story of Baucis and Philemon and Genesis 18–19?
options: In Ovid the hosts are rich
In Ovid the gods are not in disguise
In Ovid nobody pleads for the inhospitable neighbourhood; in Genesis Abraham argues with God to spare the wicked city
In Ovid the gods punish the hosts for their poverty
check.why: Both share the ancient pattern of hospitality tested; only Genesis has the intercession.

check.q: Why was Lot rescued, according to Genesis 19:16 and 19:29?
options: Because of God's mercy, and because God remembered Abraham
Because he was one of the ten righteous
Because he had shown hospitality, which earned his rescue
Because the angels needed him to guide them
check.why: Lot lingered and was dragged out; he was saved by mercy and by Abraham's prayer.

check.q: Which statement best describes the evidence about the sin of Sodom?
options: The Bible never explains it
The Bible mentions only sexual sin
The Bible mentions only lack of charity
Genesis describes attempted sexual violence against guests; Ezekiel stresses pride and neglect of the poor; Jude stresses sexual immorality; interpreters weigh these differently
check.why: All three strands are in the Bible; the traditions emphasise them differently.

check.q: Abraham's question 'Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?' bears on the Euthyphro dilemma. How?
options: It proves that morality has nothing to do with God
It assumes that God's justice is real and recognisable, not merely whatever God happens to do, so a person can appeal to it
It shows that whatever God does is just by definition
It shows that Abraham was testing God's power
check.why: Abraham treats justice as something God himself keeps; the usual answer is that goodness is God's nature.

tutorial.question: What does Genesis 18–19 teach about what Abraham was chosen for?
tutorial.approach: Start with Abraham's hospitality and compare it with Lot's and with Sodom's. Then use 18:19 to say what Abraham is chosen for. Analyse the argument: what Abraham appeals to, and how God responds. Compare Ovid's Baucis and Philemon. End with what the story suggests about prayer and about God's justice.

Quotes 18:19 and explains its importance for the journey's question.
Analyses Abraham's appeal to God's justice and its humility ('dust and ashes').
Notes that Lot is saved because God remembered Abraham.
Compares Ovid fairly: shared pattern, distinctive intercession.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: welcome a stranger properly: someone new at work, a neighbour you have never spoken to, a visitor at church. Offer them something, and listen.
sessions.reflect: For whom would you be willing to argue with God?
takeaways: Abraham welcomes strangers who turn out to be God and angels; in the Bible, how you treat a stranger is how you treat God.
God says why Abraham was chosen: to teach 'righteousness and justice'. Abraham's first act of justice is to plead for a wicked city.
God welcomes the argument: his justice is real and can be appealed to. Lot is saved because God remembered Abraham.

sessions.title: The unthinkable: the binding of Isaac
sessions.line: God asks Abraham to sacrifice his son. The case against, at full strength.
sessions.plain: At last Abraham has the son he was promised. Then God tells him to take Isaac up a mountain and offer him as a sacrifice. Abraham goes. At the last moment an angel stops his hand, and a ram is offered instead. Many readers find this the most disturbing story in the Bible: what kind of God asks this, and what kind of father obeys? This session lets the objection speak first, at full strength, and then sets out how Jews, Christians and Muslims have read the story.
sessions.why: Sessions 1 to 4 showed God choosing Abraham by grace, binding himself by oath, caring for the unchosen, and inviting Abraham to argue for justice. Now comes the story that seems to contradict all of it. If Abraham could argue for Sodom, why doesn't he argue for his son? It is the strongest objection to the God of Abraham, and it belongs here, once you know the story well enough to weigh it.
answers: What exactly happens in Genesis 22?
How could a good God ask a father to kill his son?
Why doesn't Abraham argue, as he did for Sodom?
Was child sacrifice common in the ancient world, and is the story against it?
How do Jews, Christians and Muslims each read the story?
Does the objection succeed?
sessions.finding: The binding of Isaac is the strongest objection to Abraham's God, and it is real: no reading removes its horror; but in all three faiths it ends with the knife stopped and the son given back, and both Jewish and Christian teaching insist that no one may ever use it to harm another.

paras: God chose Abraham by grace, for all the families of the earth (session 1). He bound himself to the promise by oath (session 2). He saw and blessed Hagar and Ishmael (session 3). He told Abraham he was chosen for 'righteousness and justice', and welcomed his argument for Sodom (session 4). Then Isaac was born, the son of laughter, when Abraham was a hundred, and Ishmael was sent away.
background.key: Chosen by grace, held by oath, the unchosen cared for, and Abraham chosen for justice; at last, Isaac.

paras: Here is the objection in its plainest form. If God commanded a father to kill his child, God is a monster. If Abraham was willing to do it, Abraham is a fanatic, and the story praises him. And whatever the story meant once, it has been used since, by people who heard a voice telling them to kill.

Philosophers have pressed this since the Enlightenment. In 1798 Immanuel Kant, the greatest philosopher of his age, argued that Abraham should have answered the voice: I am quite certain that I must not kill my innocent son; I can never be as certain that you, who command it, are God. Robert Ingersoll, the most famous American sceptic of the nineteenth century, put it in one sentence: 'The boy was not consulted.' You will read Ingersoll in this session's comparison.
background.key: The objection: a God who commands a father to kill his son is a monster, and a father who obeys is a fanatic.

paras: Jews call this story the Akedah, Hebrew for 'the binding', because Isaac is bound but not sacrificed. Christians often call it the sacrifice of Isaac. Muslims tell it of Ibrahim and his son, usually understood to be Ismail, and remember it at the greatest festival of the year, Eid al-Adha, the Feast of the Sacrifice.

The place is 'the land of Moriah'. Later the Bible says Solomon built the Temple in Jerusalem 'on Mount Moriah' (2 Chronicles 3:1). So Jewish tradition places the Akedah on the Temple Mount, where today the Dome of the Rock stands; Islamic tradition, which places the sacrifice near Mecca, honours the same rock as the place of Muhammad's night journey.
background.key: The Akedah, 'the binding': for Jews on the Temple Mount; for Muslims near Mecca, remembered at Eid al-Adha.

paras: The main reading is the whole of Genesis 22:1–19, in three parts: the command and the journey, the altar, and the promise renewed. Then one passage from the New Testament (Hebrews 11:17–19) shows how early Christians read it.
The comparison has two parts. First, Robert Ingersoll, making the case against in his own words. Second, the Qur'an's telling, in which the son is asked, and consents.
background.key: Genesis 22 in three parts, Hebrews' reading, Ingersoll's case against, and the Qur'an's telling.
