What does Abraham tell the servants, and what does he tell Isaac? Are they lies, or faith?
In the comparison, what is Ingersoll's strongest point? And how does the Qur'an's version differ from Genesis?
sessions.readWhy: The hardest story in Genesis, read slowly in three parts, then as early Christians read it.

paras: After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, “Abraham!”
He said, “Here I am.”
He said, “Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”

Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey; and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went to the place of which God had told him.
On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place far off.
Abraham said to his young men, “Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go over there. We will worship, and come back to you.”
Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. He took in his hand the fire and the knife. They both went together.
Isaac spoke to Abraham his father, and said, “My father?”
He said, “Here I am, my son.”
He said, “Here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?”
Abraham said, “God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.” So they both went together.
They came to the place which God had told him of. Abraham built the altar there, and laid the wood in order, bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar, on the wood.
Abraham stretched out his hand, and took the knife to kill his son.
Yahweh’s angel called to him out of the sky, and said, “Abraham, Abraham!”
He said, “Here I am.”
He said, “Don’t lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him. For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.”

Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and saw that behind him was a ram caught in the thicket by his horns. Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt offering instead of his son.
Abraham called the name of that place “Yahweh Will Provide”. As it is said to this day, “On Yahweh’s mountain, it will be provided.”
Yahweh’s angel called to Abraham a second time out of the sky,
and said, “ ‘I have sworn by myself,’ says Yahweh, ‘because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son,

that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your offspring greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your offspring will possess the gate of his enemies.
All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.’ ”
So Abraham returned to his young men, and they rose up and went together to Beersheba. Abraham lived at Beersheba.
By faith, Abraham, being tested, offered up Isaac. Yes, he who had gladly received the promises was offering up his one and only son,
to whom it was said, “Your offspring will be accounted as from Isaac,”
concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead. Figuratively speaking, he also did receive him back from the dead.

parts.title: The command and the journey
parts.context: Isaac is now a boy, or a young man; Genesis does not say his age. Abraham lives at Beersheba, in the south. Moriah is about three days' walk to the north.

commentary.on: After these things, God tested Abraham
commentary.text: The narrator tells us at once what Abraham does not know: this is a test. The reader is never in suspense about God's purpose. That does not make the story easier, but it frames everything that follows.

commentary.on: He said, “Here I am.”
commentary.text: In Hebrew, hineni: I am here, I am ready, I am listening. Abraham says it three times in this chapter: to God, to Isaac, and to the angel. He is fully present to each of them.

commentary.on: Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love
commentary.text: The command tightens like a noose, one phrase at a time: your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love. Ishmael has gone; Isaac is all that is left of the promise. This is the first time the word 'love' appears in the Bible: a father's love for his son.

commentary.on: Offer him there as a burnt offering
commentary.text: A burnt offering was the most complete sacrifice: the whole animal burned on the altar for God. The command is not only to kill Isaac but to give him up entirely.

commentary.on: Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey
commentary.text: No reply. No argument. The man who bargained for Sodom says nothing for his son. Genesis gives us actions only: he rises, saddles, splits wood, goes. Three days of silence. The great literary critic Erich Auerbach said this story is 'fraught with background': everything that matters is left unsaid.

commentary.on: We will worship, and come back to you.
commentary.text: 'We will come back', not 'I will'. Is Abraham lying to the servants, hoping, or trusting that God will somehow give Isaac back? Hebrews will say the third.

commentary.on: Here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?
commentary.text: The only words Isaac speaks in the story, and the most painful in it. He is carrying the wood for his own sacrifice.

commentary.on: God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.
commentary.text: Abraham's answer can be read two ways, and perhaps is meant to be. It is an evasion that spares the boy; or it is faith: God will see to it. In Hebrew there is no comma, and some Jewish readers have heard it as 'God will provide the lamb: my son'. 'So they both went together'.

parts.title: The altar
parts.context: Father and son reach the mountain alone.

commentary.on: bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar, on the wood
commentary.text: This is the 'binding', the Akedah. If Isaac was a young man and Abraham over a hundred, Isaac could not have been bound unless he let himself be. Jewish tradition drew exactly that conclusion: Isaac consented.

commentary.on: Abraham stretched out his hand, and took the knife to kill his son.
commentary.text: The story does not spare us. The knife is raised. Everything Abraham was promised is about to die by his own hand.

commentary.on: Don’t lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him.
commentary.text: The heart of the story, for many readers. The God who asked for the sacrifice forbids it. In a world where some peoples sacrificed children to their gods, the God of Abraham stops the knife.

commentary.on: For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me.
commentary.text: 'Fear God' in the Bible means reverence and total trust, not terror. The test showed that Abraham trusted God more than he trusted his own hold on the promise. That is what the story claims, and what the objection disputes.

commentary.on: saw that behind him was a ram caught in the thicket by his horns
commentary.text: A substitute: the ram dies 'instead of his son'. The idea of substitution, one life given in place of another, runs from here through Israel's sacrifices to the Christian reading of the cross.

commentary.on: Abraham called the name of that place “Yahweh Will Provide”.
commentary.text: In Hebrew, Yahweh yireh, from the same verb as Abraham's answer to Isaac: 'God will provide' (literally, 'God will see'). Remember Hagar's 'God who sees'. Twice in Abraham's story, at the edge of a child's death, God sees and provides.

parts.title: The promise sworn
parts.context: The angel calls a second time.

commentary.on: I have sworn by myself
commentary.text: The only time in the stories of Abraham that God swears an oath by himself. The promise, already guaranteed in Genesis 15, is now sworn on God's own being.

commentary.on: All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.
commentary.text: The promise of Genesis 12:3 returns: all the nations. The test does not cancel the purpose of the family; it renews it.

commentary.on: So Abraham returned to his young men
commentary.text: Abraham returns. Isaac is not mentioned. Some rabbis asked where he was; one midrash says he went to study, another that he was taken to paradise to heal. The next chapter tells of Sarah's death. God never speaks to Abraham again in Genesis.

parts.title: How the early Christians read it
parts.context: The chapter on faith again, from session 1.

commentary.on: concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead
commentary.text: Hebrews reads Abraham's 'we will come back' as faith in resurrection. Abraham reasoned that God, who had promised descendants through Isaac, must be able to give Isaac back even from death.

commentary.on: Figuratively speaking, he also did receive him back from the dead.
commentary.text: Hebrews sees the story as a figure, a picture in advance, of resurrection. Early Christians went further and saw Isaac carrying the wood up the hill as a figure of Christ carrying his cross to Golgotha.

paras: Abraham was commanded to offer his son Isaac as a sacrifice, and he intended to obey. The boy was not consulted.

And the next we find Him talking to Abraham, and with Abraham He makes a contract. And how did He do it? "I will bless them that bless thee, and curse them that curse thee." Fine contract for a God. And thereupon He made certain promises to Abraham--promised to give him the whole world, all the nations round about, and that his seed should be as the sands of the sea. Never kept one of His promises--not one. He made the same promises to Isaac, and broke every one. Then He made them all over to Jacob, and broke every one; made them again to Moses, and broke them all. Never said a word about anybody behaving themselves--not a word.

I want him to answer; and when he answers he will say he does not believe the Bible is inspired. That is what he will say, and he holds these old worthies in the same contempt that I do. Suppose he should act like Abraham. Suppose he should send some woman out into the wilderness with his child in her arms to starve, would he think that mankind ought to hold up his name forever, for reverence.

Robert Collyer says that we should read and scan every word of the Old Testament with reverence; that we should take this book up with reverential hands. I deny it. We should read it as we do every other book, and everything good in it, keep it and everything that shocks the brain and shocks the heart, throw it away. Let us be honest.

And he said, "Verily, I repair to my Lord who will guide me:
O Lord give me a son, of the righteous."
We announced to him a youth of meekness.
And when he became a full-grown youth,
His father said to him, "My son, I have seen in a dream that I should sacrifice thee; therefore, consider what thou seest right."
He said, "My father, do what thou art bidden; of the patient, if
God please, shalt thou find me."
And when they had surrendered them to the will of God, he laid him down upon his forehead:
We cried unto him, "O Abraham!
Now hast thou satisfied the vision." See how we recompense the righteous.
This was indeed a decisive test.
And we ransomed his son with a costly victim,
And we left this for him among posterity,
"PEACE BE ON ABRAHAM!"
Thus do we reward the well-doers,
For he was of our believing servants.
And we announced Isaac to him-a righteous Prophet-

parts.author: Robert G. Ingersoll
parts.ref: Robert G. Ingersoll, from three lectures
parts.title: The boy was not consulted
parts.context: Robert Green Ingersoll (1833–1899) was an American lawyer, Civil War colonel and the most popular orator of his day, known as 'the Great Agnostic'. These extracts come from three different lectures, marked off by '…'. In the first he lists the Bible's treatment of children. In the second he mocks God's covenant with Abraham. In the last two, from 1879, he challenges Robert Collyer, a famous Chicago minister who had said the Old Testament should be read with reverence.
parts.plain: Ingersoll says: Abraham was told to sacrifice Isaac and meant to do it, and nobody asked the boy. God's covenant with Abraham was a bargain of favouritism, blessing and cursing, and its promises were never kept. Would any decent minister today send a woman and her child into the desert to starve, as Abraham did, and expect to be honoured for it? We should read the Bible like any other book: keep what is good, and throw away whatever shocks the mind and the heart.

commentary.on: The boy was not consulted.
commentary.text: Ingersoll's whole objection in five words. Whatever the story means for Abraham and God, Isaac is treated as a thing to be offered. A modern reader's first sympathy is with the child, and Ingersoll will not let it be explained away.

commentary.on: Fine contract for a God.
commentary.text: Ingersoll attacks the idea of choosing itself: a God who takes sides, blesses one family and curses its enemies is a tribal god, not the God of all. This is the scandal of particularity, the journey's question, at its sharpest.

commentary.on: Suppose he should send some woman out into the wilderness with his child in her arms to starve
commentary.text: Ingersoll brings in Hagar and Ishmael from session 3. His argument is a test any reader can apply: if a man did this today, we would call it cruelty, not faith. Why should Abraham be different?

commentary.on: We should read it as we do every other book
commentary.text: This is Ingersoll's alternative: the Bible has no special authority; read it, keep the good and reject the shocking. It is the position of most secular readers today. Notice that it assumes we already know what is good, which is itself a question (session 4's Euthyphro).

parts.author: The Qur'an
parts.title: The son consents
parts.context: The Qur'an's telling of the sacrifice. It does not name the son; most Muslims hold that he was Ishmael (Ismail), because Isaac's birth is announced only afterwards, in the last line here. Rodwell's translation, 1861.
parts.plain: The Qur'an says: Abraham prayed for a son and was given a gentle boy. When the boy was old enough, Abraham told him: I have seen in a dream that I must sacrifice you; what do you think? The son said: Father, do as you are commanded; God willing, you will find me patient. When both had submitted and Abraham laid him down, God called out: you have fulfilled the vision. It was a clear test, and God ransomed the son with a great sacrifice.

commentary.on: My son, I have seen in a dream that I should sacrifice thee; therefore, consider what thou seest right.
commentary.text: The great difference from Genesis: Abraham tells his son and asks his view. In the Qur'an, the boy is consulted. Ingersoll's objection is answered within this telling of the story itself.

commentary.on: My father, do what thou art bidden
commentary.text: The son consents. He is patient and willing, a model of submission (islam) to God, and so he too is a prophet. The test is of both father and son.

commentary.on: And when they had surrendered them to the will of God
commentary.text: 'Surrendered' here translates the verb from which the words islam and Muslim come. This story is, for Islam, the perfect picture of what submission to God means.

commentary.on: And we ransomed his son with a costly victim
commentary.text: The ram, or 'a great sacrifice'. At Eid al-Adha, Muslims who can afford it sacrifice a sheep, goat or cow, and share the meat with family, neighbours and the poor, remembering the ransom.

commentary.on: This was indeed a decisive test.
commentary.text: Like Genesis ('God tested Abraham'), the Qur'an frames the story as a test that was never meant to end in death.

compare.author: Robert G. Ingersoll and The Qur'an
compare.ref: Robert G. Ingersoll, from three lectures
compare.why: First, the objection in the words of Robert Ingersoll, the great American sceptic of the nineteenth century, who lectured to packed halls on the 'mistakes of Moses'. Then the Qur'an's version of the story, which differs in a way that bears directly on Ingersoll's objection.
compare.title: The case against, and another telling

paras: Let the objection have its full force first. It has three parts.

First, the moral argument. Kant put it with great precision in The Conflict of the Faculties (1798). We can be certain that killing an innocent child is wrong. We can never be equally certain that a voice which tells us to do it comes from God. So a good person must always refuse; and a God who asked it would not be good. Second, the human argument, Ingersoll's: the story treats Isaac as an object, and Hagar and Ishmael before him. Third, the argument from consequences. People have killed in obedience to voices they took for God's, and the story has been used to honour unconditional obedience. In 1918 the soldier-poet Wilfred Owen, killed a week before the Armistice, rewrote the story as the First World War: the angel tells the old man to offer the ram instead, 'But the old man would not so, but slew his son, / And half the seed of Europe, one by one.'
No honest reading can make this story comfortable. The question is not whether it disturbs us, but what it is saying.
sections.key: Kant: we can never be surer that a voice is God's than that killing a child is wrong. Ingersoll: the boy was not consulted. Owen: the old men slew their sons.

paras: In the world of Genesis, the sacrifice of children to gods was not unthinkable; it was known. The Bible records that Mesha, king of Moab, sacrificed his eldest son on the city wall during a siege (2 Kings 3:27). Its laws forbid giving children to the god Molech (Leviticus 18:21), and the prophets condemn Israelites who burned their children in the valley of Hinnom, 'which I didn't command, nor did it come into my mind' (Jeremiah 7:31). Child sacrifice among the Phoenicians and at Carthage is reported by Greek and Roman writers and debated by archaeologists.

Read against that background, many scholars hear the story's climax as its point: Abraham's God, unlike the gods of his neighbours, does not want children's blood. 'Don't lay your hand on the boy.' The Jewish scholar Jon Levenson has warned that this is too simple. The story praises Abraham's willingness, and Israel's law still said 'the firstborn of your sons you shall give to me' (Exodus 22:29), though he was always to be redeemed, bought back, by an animal (Exodus 34:20). So the story does not simply reject the idea that a child belongs to God. It transforms it: the child belongs to God, and God gives him back.
sections.key: Child sacrifice was known in Abraham's world; the story ends with God forbidding it, though, as Levenson notes, it transforms rather than simply rejects the idea that the firstborn belongs to God.

paras: The most famous modern reading is by the Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard, in Fear and Trembling (1843), written under the pen-name Johannes de Silentio, 'John of Silence'. Kierkegaard refused to make the story easy. Preachers, he complained, talk about Abraham's faith on Sunday as if it were simple, when anyone who really understood what Abraham did would be appalled.

In our own words, his argument runs like this. In ordinary ethics, the duty of a father to his son is absolute; by that standard, Abraham is a murderer. If Abraham is great, there must be something higher than ethics: a relation of the single individual to God that cannot be explained or justified to anyone else. Kierkegaard called this the 'teleological suspension of the ethical'. And Abraham's faith was not resignation, giving Isaac up, but something stranger: he believed, at the same moment, that he would lose Isaac and that he would have him back. That is why he is silent: he cannot explain. Kierkegaard does not say we should imitate Abraham. He says that if we cannot understand him, we should stop pretending that faith is easy.
sections.key: Kierkegaard: either Abraham is a murderer, or faith is a relation to God beyond ethics; Abraham believed he would lose Isaac and receive him back.

sections.h: How the three faiths read it
paras: Each faith has made this story central, and each reads it in its own way.

In Judaism the Akedah is read in synagogue on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, and the ram's horn, the shofar, is blown. The Talmud has God say: 'Blow before me a ram's horn, so that I may remember for you the binding of Isaac' (Rosh Hashanah 16a). A midrash makes Isaac thirty-seven years old and willing; Josephus, in the first century, made him twenty-five. In the massacres of Jewish communities during the First Crusade (1096), martyrs who died rather than be forcibly baptised were remembered as new Akedahs. Christians read it at the Easter Vigil, the night before Easter, and see in it a figure of Christ: the beloved only son, the wood carried up the hill, 'God will provide the lamb' (John 1:29), and a Father who 'didn't spare his own Son' (Romans 8:32). For Christians the difference is decisive: at Moriah God stopped the knife; at Golgotha, they believe, God himself gave his Son. Muslims remember it at Eid al-Adha: a willing son, a father's submission, and God's ransom.

paras: Does the objection succeed? Here are the best replies, and what remains after them.

First, the story is told as a test whose outcome God intended: the reader is told so in the first verse, and the command is withdrawn. Second, its last word is a prohibition: the knife is stopped, and the later prophets say God never willed such a thing. Third, in the Qur'an, and in Jewish tradition, the son is consulted and consents, which answers Ingersoll in part. Fourth, Jewish and Christian teaching both agree with Kant on the practical point: no one may ever appeal to this story to harm another person. Genesis 22 is told as a unique event in the founding of the covenant, not as a rule; the rule is Jeremiah's, 'nor did it come into my mind'.

What remains is real. The story still shows God asking, and Abraham willing. Some readers, Jewish and Christian, conclude that Abraham failed the test by not arguing, as he had for Sodom, and note that God never speaks to him again. Others conclude, with Kierkegaard, that the story's purpose is to unsettle us. Either way, you are not asked to find it easy. You are asked to read it whole: the command, the silence, the stopped hand, the ram, and the God who provides.
sections.key: The best replies: a test, a prohibition, a consenting son, and a unique event never to be imitated; what remains is the story's real and intended difficulty.
