debate.question: Did Abraham pass the test?

positions.name: Yes: faith beyond understanding
positions.who: Hebrews 11; Kierkegaard; much of Jewish, Christian and Islamic tradition
positions.view: Abraham trusted that God would keep his promise even through Isaac's death, and his willingness to give God everything is the model of faith and submission.
positions.evidence: 'We will come back to you' (22:5); 'God will provide' (22:8); Hebrews 11:19; Qur'an 37:103–105, 'thou hast satisfied the vision'.

positions.name: No: he should have argued
positions.who: Some modern Jewish and Christian readers
positions.view: The test was whether Abraham would protest, as he did for Sodom. His silence was a failure; God stopped him, never spoke to him again, and Sarah died in the next chapter.
positions.evidence: The contrast with Genesis 18; God's silence towards Abraham after Genesis 22; midrashim linking Sarah's death to the Akedah.

positions.name: The question is wrong
positions.who: Kant; Ingersoll; many secular readers
positions.view: No good God would set such a test, and no one can know a voice commanding murder is God's. The story should be read as a relic of an age of child sacrifice, not as a model.
positions.evidence: The moral certainty that killing an innocent is wrong; Jeremiah 7:31; the harm done by obedience to 'divine' voices.

debate.agree: All agree the story is meant to disturb, that it ends with the child spared, and that no one should ever use it to justify harming another person.

look.why: Early Christians saw Isaac, carrying the wood for his own sacrifice up the hill, as a figure of Christ carrying his cross. Cornelis van Poelenburch, a Dutch painter working in Italy, painted this crowded scene in the early 1620s.
points: A crowd surges out of a ruined stone fortress on the right.
Near the front, a man in a lilac-purple robe kneels under the crossbeam of a wooden cross, with a ring of thorns on his head, looking back over his shoulder at us.
A bare-chested man in red breeches pulls on the rope tied to the cross.
A woman in blue and yellow holds out a white cloth; another, in rose-pink and azure blue, stands with her fingers interlaced.
Two bound men walk ahead with their heads down, and a soldier in armour rides a rearing horse.

music.why: 'O Sacred Head, Now Wounded', the great Passion chorale that Bach used again and again in his St Matthew Passion. It is sung in Holy Week, the week before Easter, when Christians read the binding of Isaac beside the death of Christ (Genesis 22 is one of the readings of the Easter Vigil).

think.why: The binding of Isaac is the Bible's most extreme picture of a test. Ask how the traditions understand God's relation to suffering and to trials.

learn.why: Abraham's answer to Isaac, on the way up the mountain: 'God will provide'.

listen.why: A famous sceptic and a former prime minister debate whether religion is a force for good. Listen for how each handles the charge that faith licenses terrible acts.

check.q: Why does it matter that Genesis 22 begins 'God tested Abraham'?
options: It shows that Abraham knew it was a test
It means Isaac was not really in danger
It means God did not know how Abraham would respond
It tells the reader from the start that God's purpose was to test, not to have Isaac killed, though Abraham does not know it
check.why: The reader knows what Abraham doesn't; the story's horror is real for him.

check.q: What is the force of Kant's argument against Abraham?
options: That Abraham misheard the command
That we can be more certain that killing an innocent child is wrong than that any voice commanding it is God's, so we must always refuse
That only the community, not an individual, can interpret a divine command
That obedience to God must always come before ethics
check.why: Kant's is an argument from comparative certainty.

check.q: How does the Qur'an's telling bear on Ingersoll's objection that 'the boy was not consulted'?
options: In the Qur'an the son is named as Isaac
In the Qur'an Abraham tells his son of the dream and asks his view, and the son consents
In the Qur'an an angel warns the son first
In the Qur'an the son is killed
check.why: Sura 37:102: 'consider what thou seest right'.

check.q: What is Jon Levenson's caution about reading the story simply as a rejection of child sacrifice?
options: That the story praises Abraham's willingness and that Israel's law still held the firstborn belonged to God, to be redeemed by a substitute, so the story transforms the idea rather than simply rejecting it
That the story is really about the Temple, not about Isaac
That child sacrifice never existed
That Genesis 22 is a later addition
check.why: Exodus 22:29 and 34:20 show the firstborn belonging to God and redeemed.

check.q: What, in Kierkegaard's reading, made Abraham's faith different from resignation?
options: He believed, at the same moment, that he would lose Isaac and that he would receive him back
He knew the angel would stop him
He refused to go
He gave Isaac up completely and expected nothing
check.why: Resignation gives up; faith also expects to receive back, 'by virtue of the absurd', in Kierkegaard's phrase.

check.q: Which reply to the objection do Jewish and Christian teaching both share with Kant?
options: That the story shows obedience must come before conscience
That no one may ever appeal to this story to justify harming another person
That the story should be removed from the Bible
That the story is only a myth and has no authority
check.why: Jeremiah 7:31; the story is a unique event, not a rule.

tutorial.question: Is the binding of Isaac a story of faith or of fanaticism?
tutorial.approach: State the objection fairly, using Kant, Ingersoll and Owen. Then read the story closely: the test, the silence, the 'we will come back', the stopped hand, the ram. Set out the ancient background of child sacrifice and Levenson's caution. Compare the Jewish, Christian and Islamic readings and Kierkegaard's. Then give your own judgement, and say what remains unresolved.
strong: States the objection at full strength, in its best advocates' terms.
Reads the text closely, including 'God tested', 'Here I am', 'we will come back' and 'God will provide'.
Explains the background of child sacrifice and the stopped hand, with Levenson's nuance.
Sets out Kierkegaard's reading accurately.
Compares the three faiths' readings, including the Qur'an's consenting son.
Reaches a judgement, and is honest about what remains troubling.

reading.author: Søren Kierkegaard
reading.title: Fear and Trembling
reading.why: Short, passionate and unsettling; read it slowly.

reading.author: Jon D. Levenson
reading.title: The Death and Resurrection of the Beloved Son
reading.why: The best scholarly study of the Akedah in Judaism and Christianity.

reading.author: Shalom Spiegel
reading.title: The Last Trial
reading.why: Jewish legends of the Akedah, including those in which Isaac dies and is raised.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: let someone who depends on you, a child, a parent, a colleague, have a real say in a decision that affects them.
sessions.reflect: What would you never give up, even for God? And what does that tell you about what you trust most?
takeaways: The objection is real: Kant says no voice is surer than the wrongness of killing a child; Ingersoll that the boy was not consulted.
The story ends with the knife stopped and a ram given instead; in its world, that was a 'no' to child sacrifice, though it transforms more than it rejects.
Jews remember Isaac's binding at Rosh Hashanah, Christians see in it a figure of Christ, Muslims celebrate a consenting son at Eid al-Adha; all agree it may never be used to harm another.

sessions.title: Wrestling with God: Jacob
sessions.line: A cheat, a ladder to heaven, a fight in the dark, and a brother's embrace.
sessions.plain: Abraham's grandson Jacob is a cheat. He tricks his twin brother Esau out of his rights as the elder son and deceives his blind father to steal his blessing. Then he runs for his life. Yet God chooses him, meets him in a dream of a stairway to heaven, and twenty years later wrestles with him all night by a river. Jacob comes out limping, with a new name, Israel, and goes to meet the brother he wronged. This session asks why God chooses people like Jacob, and whether such people can change.
sessions.why: Session 5 faced the hardest story about Abraham and his son. Now the promise passes to the next generations: from Isaac to his son Jacob. If the chosen are chosen for justice, as session 4 found, why is the next one a liar and a thief? And what happens to the brother who was passed over?
answers: Who were Jacob and Esau, and how did Jacob cheat his brother?
Why would God choose a cheat?
What happened at Bethel and at the river Jabbok, and who did Jacob wrestle with?
Where does the name Israel come from?
'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated': is God unfair? How do the churches understand election?
sessions.finding: The promise passes not to the deserving but to a cheat, who is chosen by grace, wounded and renamed by God, and reconciled with the brother he wronged: God's choosing does not leave people as it finds them.

paras: God chose Abraham by grace for the sake of all families (session 1), bound himself to the promise (session 2), cared for the unchosen Hagar and Ishmael (session 3), and chose Abraham to teach justice, welcoming his argument for Sodom (session 4). Then came the hardest story, the binding of Isaac, whose objection is real (session 5).
background.key: Grace, covenant, care for the unchosen, a calling to justice, and the hardest test.

paras: After the binding, Sarah dies and Abraham buries her at Hebron (Genesis 23). He sends his servant back to his family's homeland to find a wife for Isaac, and the servant meets Rebekah at a well (Genesis 24): this session's painting shows that scene. Abraham dies, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him (Genesis 25).

Isaac is the quietest of the patriarchs; almost his only story is that, like his father, he passes his wife off as his sister (Genesis 26). Rebekah, like Sarah, cannot have children for many years. Then she has twins, Esau and Jacob. Their story fills the next ten chapters.

timeline.text: Sarah dies; Rebekah is found for Isaac
Abraham dies; Jacob and Esau born
Jacob steals Esau's blessing and flees
Jacob's dream at Bethel
Twenty years with his uncle Laban in Haran; marries Leah and Rachel
Jacob wrestles at the Jabbok, and meets Esau
Joseph (session 7)

background.key: Isaac marries Rebekah; their twins, Esau and Jacob, fill the next ten chapters.

paras: Two things belonged to the eldest son in Abraham's world. The birthright was a double share of the inheritance and the position of head of the family. The blessing was the father's solemn last words, believed to shape the son's future, and it could not be taken back once spoken.

Jacob gets both from Esau: the birthright by a bargain, the blessing by a trick. Jacob's name sounds like the Hebrew for 'heel', because he was born holding his twin's heel, and also like 'he cheats' or 'he supplants'.
background.key: The birthright was the eldest son's inheritance; the blessing, his father's last words. Jacob takes both.

paras: The main reading follows Jacob's life in four parts: the twins and the birthright (25:21–34), the stolen blessing (27:30–38), the dream at Bethel (28:10–22), and the night of wrestling and the meeting with Esau (32:22–33:10).

The comparison has two later readings of Jacob: the prophet Hosea, who uses him as a warning and an example, and Paul, who uses the twins to argue about God's choosing, in words that have troubled readers ever since.
background.key: Jacob's life in four scenes; then Hosea and Paul on what it means.

before: Who is to blame for the stolen blessing: Jacob, Rebekah, Isaac or Esau?
What does God say to Jacob at Bethel? Is there any rebuke?
What does Jacob ask for at the Jabbok, and how is it different from what he did before?
sessions.readWhy: Jacob's life in four scenes: the bargain, the trick, the dream and the wrestling.

paras: Isaac entreated Yahweh for his wife, because she was barren. Yahweh was entreated by him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.
The children struggled together within her. She said, “If it is like this, why do I live?” She went to inquire of Yahweh.
Yahweh said to her,

“Two nations are in your womb.
Two peoples will be separated from your body.
The one people will be stronger than the other people.
The elder will serve the younger.”
When her days to be delivered were fulfilled, behold, there were twins in her womb.
The first came out red all over, like a hairy garment. They named him Esau.
After that, his brother came out, and his hand had hold on Esau’s heel. He was named Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when she bore them.
The boys grew. Esau was a skillful hunter, a man of the field. Jacob was a quiet man, living in tents.
Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.
Jacob boiled stew. Esau came in from the field, and he was famished.
Esau said to Jacob, “Please feed me with some of that red stew, for I am famished.” Therefore his name was called Edom.
Jacob said, “First, sell me your birthright.”
Esau said, “Behold, I am about to die. What good is the birthright to me?”
Jacob said, “Swear to me first.”
He swore to him. He sold his birthright to Jacob.
Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew. He ate and drank, rose up, and went his way. So Esau despised his birthright.
As soon as Isaac had finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had just gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, Esau his brother came in from his hunting.
He also made savory food, and brought it to his father. He said to his father, “Let my father arise, and eat of his son’s venison, that your soul may bless me.”
Isaac his father said to him, “Who are you?”
He said, “I am your son, your firstborn, Esau.”
Isaac trembled violently, and said, “Who, then, is he who has taken venison, and brought it to me, and I have eaten of all before you came, and have blessed him? Yes, he will be blessed.”
When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried with an exceedingly great and bitter cry, and said to his father, “Bless me, even me also, my father.”
He said, “Your brother came with deceit, and has taken away your blessing.”

He said, “Isn’t he rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times. He took away my birthright. See, now he has taken away my blessing.” He said, “Haven’t you reserved a blessing for me?”
Isaac answered Esau, “Behold, I have made him your lord, and all his brothers I have given to him for servants. I have sustained him with grain and new wine. What then will I do for you, my son?”
Esau said to his father, “Do you have just one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, my father.” Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.
Jacob went out from Beersheba, and went toward Haran.
He came to a certain place, and stayed there all night, because the sun had set. He took one of the stones of the place, and put it under his head, and lay down in that place to sleep.
He dreamed and saw a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven. Behold, the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.
Behold, Yahweh stood above it, and said, “I am Yahweh, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac. I will give the land you lie on to you and to your offspring.

Your offspring will be as the dust of the earth, and you will spread abroad to the west, and to the east, and to the north, and to the south. In you and in your offspring, all the families of the earth will be blessed.
Behold, I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go, and will bring you again into this land. For I will not leave you, until I have done that which I have spoken of to you.”
Jacob awakened out of his sleep, and he said, “Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn’t know it.”
He was afraid, and said, “How awesome this place is! This is none other than God’s house, and this is the gate of heaven.”
Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put under his head, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil on its top.
He called the name of that place Bethel, but the name of the city was Luz at the first.
Jacob vowed a vow, saying, “If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and clothing to put on,
so that I come again to my father’s house in peace, and Yahweh will be my God,
then this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, will be God’s house. Of all that you will give me I will surely give a tenth to you.”
He rose up that night, and took his two wives, and his two servants, and his eleven sons, and crossed over the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them, and sent them over the stream, and sent over that which he had.
Jacob was left alone, and wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day.
When he saw that he didn’t prevail against him, the man touched the hollow of his thigh, and the hollow of Jacob’s thigh was strained as he wrestled.
The man said, “Let me go, for the day breaks.”
Jacob said, “I won’t let you go unless you bless me.”
He said to him, “What is your name?”
He said, “Jacob”.
He said, “Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.”
Jacob asked him, “Please tell me your name.”
He said, “Why is it that you ask what my name is?” He blessed him there.
Jacob called the name of the place Peniel; for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.”
The sun rose on him as he passed over Peniel, and he limped because of his thigh.
Therefore the children of Israel don’t eat the sinew of the hip, which is on the hollow of the thigh, to this day, because he touched the hollow of Jacob’s thigh in the sinew of the hip.
Jacob lifted up his eyes, and looked, and, behold, Esau was coming, and with him four hundred men. He divided the children between Leah, Rachel, and the two servants.
He put the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children after, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear.
He himself passed over in front of them, and bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
Jacob said, “Please, no, if I have now found favor in your sight, then receive my present at my hand, because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God, and you were pleased with me.

parts.title: Twins
parts.context: Isaac and Rebekah have waited twenty years for a child. Rebekah's pregnancy is so painful that she asks God why.

commentary.on: The children struggled together within her.
commentary.text: The brothers fight before they are born. The whole of their story is in this sentence.

commentary.on: Two nations are in your womb.
commentary.text: The twins are also two peoples: Jacob is Israel, and Esau is Edom, Israel's neighbour and rival to the south-east of the Dead Sea. Much of the story is about how two related peoples came to be what they were.

commentary.on: The elder will serve the younger.
commentary.text: God's word before the boys are born, before either has done anything good or bad. This reverses the ancient rule that the eldest inherits. Again and again in Genesis the younger son is preferred: Abel, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Ephraim. God's choosing does not follow human rank.

commentary.on: his hand had hold on Esau’s heel. He was named Jacob.
commentary.text: Ya'akov, from akev, 'heel'. Jacob grabs from birth. Esau later makes the pun bitter: 'Isn't he rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times.'

commentary.on: Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob.
commentary.text: Each parent has a favourite. Favouritism will poison this family for two more generations: Jacob will favour Joseph, with terrible results.

commentary.on: First, sell me your birthright.
commentary.text: Jacob takes advantage of a hungry man. He does not offer stew; he sells it, for the whole inheritance.

commentary.on: So Esau despised his birthright.
commentary.text: The narrator does not let Esau off: he valued a meal over his future. Both brothers are at fault, in different ways.

parts.title: The stolen blessing
parts.context: Years later Isaac is old and blind. He tells Esau to hunt and make him his favourite food, so that he can bless him before he dies. Rebekah overhears, cooks two young goats, dresses Jacob in Esau's clothes and puts the goatskins on his hands and neck, because Esau is hairy. Isaac is suspicious ('The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau'), but gives Jacob the blessing (27:1–29). Then Esau comes in.

commentary.on: Isaac trembled violently
commentary.text: In Hebrew, 'trembled with a very great trembling'. The old man realises what has happened, and that the blessing cannot be taken back.

commentary.on: he cried with an exceedingly great and bitter cry
commentary.text: Genesis does not hurry past Esau's pain. Centuries later, in the book of Esther, the same words describe Mordecai's cry (Esther 4:1); Jewish commentators saw it as a debt the descendants of Jacob would pay. The story makes us feel for the brother who was cheated.

commentary.on: Isn’t he rightly named Jacob? For he has supplanted me these two times.
commentary.text: Esau's bitter pun. The cheat lives up to his name.

commentary.on: Do you have just one blessing, my father?
commentary.text: The most painful question in the chapter. Isaac does give Esau a blessing (27:39–40), a lesser one: he will live by the sword, serve his brother, and one day break free. Edom did later rebel against Judah and become independent (2 Kings 8:20–22).

commentary.on: Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.
commentary.text: Esau's weeping ends the scene. Then he plans to kill his brother when their father dies (27:41), and Rebekah sends Jacob away to her brother Laban in Haran. She never sees him again.

parts.title: A stairway to heaven
parts.context: Jacob flees north, alone, towards Haran, where Abraham's family still lives: back along the road his grandfather came. He stops for the night in the hill country.

commentary.on: He took one of the stones of the place, and put it under his head
commentary.text: A fugitive with a stone for a pillow, with nothing: no family, no home, a brother who wants him dead. This is where God meets him.

commentary.on: He dreamed and saw a stairway set upon the earth, and its top reached to heaven.
commentary.text: 'Jacob's ladder', though the word probably means a stairway or ramp, like the stepped sides of a ziggurat. Remember Babel's tower, 'whose top reaches to the sky'. There, people tried to build up to heaven. Here, heaven opens downward, uninvited, to a man who deserves nothing.

commentary.on: I am Yahweh, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac.
commentary.text: There is no rebuke for the stolen blessing. God simply gives Jacob the promises of Abraham: land, descendants 'as the dust of the earth', and the blessing of 'all the families of the earth'. The promise passes by grace, again.

commentary.on: Behold, I am with you, and will keep you, wherever you go
commentary.text: The promise Jacob most needs, alone on the road: God's presence, not tied to any place. It is the promise that Jesus gives at the end of Matthew's Gospel: 'I am with you always' (Matthew 28:20).

commentary.on: Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn’t know it.
commentary.text: One of the great sentences of spiritual experience. God was there before Jacob noticed. Jacob calls the place Bethel, 'house of God'.

commentary.on: If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go
commentary.text: Jacob's answer is a bargain: if you do this, then you will be my God. He is still the dealer of the stew and the birthright. God accepts him as he is, and waits.

parts.title: The wrestling and the embrace
parts.context: Twenty years later. Jacob has served his uncle Laban, been cheated by him (given Leah instead of Rachel as his bride, 29:25), married both sisters, had eleven sons and grown rich. Now he is coming home, and he hears that Esau is coming to meet him with four hundred men. He is terrified, prays, for once humbly, for help (32:9–12), and sends gifts ahead. The night before the meeting, he is by the river Jabbok, east of the Jordan.

commentary.on: Jacob was left alone, and wrestled with a man there until the breaking of the day.
commentary.text: Alone in the dark, before the day he most fears, Jacob is attacked by 'a man'. The story never says who he is. By the end, Jacob is sure he has met God.

commentary.on: I won’t let you go unless you bless me.
commentary.text: The heart of the story. The man who stole a blessing by trickery now asks for one, openly, holding on in pain. Jacob has stopped grabbing and started asking. This is the change the whole of his life has been leading to.

commentary.on: What is your name?
commentary.text: The last time Jacob was asked his name, by his blind father, he lied: 'I am Esau your firstborn' (27:19). Now he has to say who he really is: 'Jacob', the heel-grabber, the cheat. Only then does he receive a new name.

commentary.on: Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel; for you have fought with God and with men, and have prevailed.
commentary.text: Israel probably means 'God strives' or 'he strives with God'. The whole people will take this name. They are named after a man who wrestled with God and would not let go: a people defined by their struggle with God, not their ease with him.

commentary.on: I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved.
commentary.text: Jacob names the place Peniel, 'face of God'. He leaves wounded: 'he limped because of his thigh'. He has won a blessing, but not unscathed. Meeting God changes how you walk.

commentary.on: Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept.
commentary.text: The brother Jacob feared comes with four hundred men, and runs to embrace him. Esau has forgiven. Jesus uses almost exactly these words for the father in the parable of the prodigal son, who 'ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him' (Luke 15:20), which you will read in the next session.

commentary.on: because I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God
commentary.text: The night before, Jacob saw God's face and lived. Now he sees it again in the forgiving face of the brother he wronged. The two meetings are one story: reconciled with God, reconciled with his brother.

read.ref: Genesis 25:21–34; Genesis 27:30–38; Genesis 28:10–22; Genesis 32:22–32; Genesis 33:1–4; Genesis 33:10

paras:
In the womb he took his brother by the heel;
and in his manhood he contended with God.

even Yahweh, the God of Armies;
Yahweh is his name of renown!

Therefore turn to your God.
Keep kindness and justice,
and wait continually for your God.
Not only so, but Rebekah also conceived by one, by our father Isaac.
For being not yet born, neither having done anything good or bad, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him who calls,
it was said to her, “The elder will serve the younger.”
Even as it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
What shall we say then? Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be!
For he said to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”
So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy.

parts.title: Hosea: he wept, and begged
parts.context: Hosea was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century BC, before it was destroyed by Assyria. He accuses the people, the descendants of Jacob, of deceit like their ancestor's, and calls them to return.

commentary.on: In the womb he took his brother by the heel
commentary.text: Hosea knows the story of the twins and the heel. Jacob's grasping is Israel's grasping: the prophet holds up the ancestor as a mirror.

commentary.on: he wept, and made supplication to him
commentary.text: A detail Genesis does not give: at the Jabbok Jacob wept and begged for the blessing. For Hosea, Jacob did not win by strength but by tears and pleading.

commentary.on: Keep kindness and justice,
commentary.text: Hosea's conclusion: be like the changed Jacob, not the grasping one. 'Kindness and justice' echoes what Abraham was chosen to teach (Genesis 18:19).

parts.title: Paul: not of works, but of him who calls
parts.context: In Romans 9–11 Paul wrestles with a painful question: why have most of his fellow Jews not believed in Jesus? Has God's promise failed? He answers that God's promise was never simply to all of Abraham's physical descendants, and he points to Isaac and Ishmael, and Jacob and Esau.

commentary.on: being not yet born, neither having done anything good or bad
commentary.text: Paul's point is the timing. God chose Jacob before the twins were born, so the choice could not have been a reward for anything Jacob did. Election is 'not of works, but of him who calls'.

commentary.on: Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.
commentary.text: Paul quotes the prophet Malachi (1:2–3), who was speaking of the two nations, Israel and Edom, centuries later. 'Hated' in this Hebrew idiom means 'not chosen' or 'loved less': Genesis 29:30–31 says Jacob 'loved Rachel more than Leah', and then that 'Leah was hated'. It describes a choice, not an emotion.

commentary.on: Is there unrighteousness with God? May it never be!
commentary.text: Paul raises the objection himself: isn't this unfair? His answer is that God's choosing is mercy, and no one has a claim on mercy. Whether that answer satisfies has been argued for two thousand years, as the lecture shows.

compare.why: Two later readings. The prophet Hosea, in the eighth century BC, uses Jacob's story to call Israel back to God. The apostle Paul uses the twins to argue that God's choosing is free, in a passage that has been fought over more than almost any other.
compare.title: What later writers made of Jacob

paras: Genesis never says that Jacob was right to cheat. It shows instead what his cheating cost. He stole the blessing by disguising himself with goatskins, in the dark of his father's blindness. Twenty years later his uncle Laban cheats him the same way, swapping his bride in the dark of the wedding night, and Jacob cries, 'Why then have you deceived me?' (29:25). Later still his own sons deceive him with a goat's blood on Joseph's coat (37:31), which you will meet in the next session.

This is how Genesis does moral teaching: not by stating rules, but by showing consequences. Jacob is chosen by grace, but grace does not shield him from what he has done. He lives twenty years in exile and never sees his mother again. When Pharaoh asks his age, he answers: 'The days of the years of my life have been few and evil' (47:9).
sections.key: Jacob deceives with a goat in the dark, and is deceived the same way twice: Genesis teaches by showing what wrong costs.

paras: If God chose people for their virtue, Esau, open, generous, quick to forgive, might seem the better choice. Genesis says plainly that the choice came first, before either boy had done anything (25:23). The reason is not in Jacob.

That is the third time the journey has met the same pattern. Abraham lied in Egypt; Isaac lied in Gerar; Jacob cheats his brother. The family is not chosen because it is good. It is chosen so that God can do something good through it, and in it. Jacob's story shows the second part: the cheat at Bethel becomes the man at the Jabbok who asks instead of grabbing, tells the truth about his name, and bows to the ground seven times before the brother he wronged. Being chosen did not leave him as he was.
sections.key: The choice comes before either twin has done anything; being chosen changes Jacob from a grasper to a man who asks and is reconciled.

paras: Genesis calls him 'a man', and then has Jacob say he has seen God face to face. Hosea calls him an angel. Readers have answered in different ways. Some Jewish interpreters said it was Esau's guardian angel, so that Jacob had to wrestle with his brother in the spirit before he could meet him in the flesh (Genesis Rabbah 77:3). Many early Christians, such as Justin Martyr in the second century, said it was the Word of God, the Son, appearing before his birth as a man. Many modern readers see the story as deliberately mysterious: a night struggle with God, and with oneself.

Charles Wesley's great hymn on the story, 'Come, O thou Traveller unknown' (1742), takes Jacob's part and will not let go until the stranger tells his name: the answer, in the last verse, is 'Thy nature and thy name is Love'. Isaac Watts is reported to have said it was worth all the verses he himself had written.
sections.key: A man, an angel, Esau's angel, the Word, or God: the wrestler is left mysterious; Wesley's hymn hears the answer 'Love'.

paras: The name given at the Jabbok becomes the name of a people, and today of a state. It is worth noticing what kind of name it is. Israel is not 'God's favourite' or 'the righteous'. It is 'he struggles with God'. The people of the Bible are named after a night of wrestling, a blessing won in tears, and a limp.

Esau's people, the Edomites, also have a place in the story. They are Israel's 'brother' (Deuteronomy 23:7: 'You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother'), and a whole chapter of Genesis records Esau's family (Genesis 36). The two nations were often at war; prophets such as Obadiah condemned Edom for violence against 'your brother Jacob'. But the brothers' embrace at the Jabbok stands at the head of it all.
sections.key: 'Israel' means 'he strives with God'; Edom is Israel's brother, and the brothers' embrace comes first.

paras: 'Election' is the theologians' word for God's choosing. Paul's use of Jacob and Esau in Romans 9 made it one of the great disputes in Christian history. Is God's choice of some people arbitrary? Does it mean others are rejected for ever?

Most Jewish thinkers have understood the election of Israel as a calling to a task, not a privilege: Amos has God say 'I have only chosen you of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all of your sins' (Amos 3:2). Many Christian scholars today read Romans 9 the same way, as about peoples and their roles in history, not about individuals' eternal destiny; Paul's argument ends with 'all Israel will be saved' (11:26) and with God having 'mercy on all' (11:32).

rows: God freely chooses individuals for salvation, before they are born, for reasons in himself alone; Calvin added that he passes over others
Passed over by God's free decision; still responsible for his own choices
God chooses those he foreknows will believe; or he chooses a people in Christ, open to all
Not damned in advance; free to respond
Predestination is real and a mystery, but no one is predestined to evil; grace and freedom work together (Council of Orange, 529; Trent, 1547)
His fate was not fixed by Jacob's election
God foreknows but does not override freedom; election is a calling to serve, and God wills all to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4)
Israel is chosen for a task, to keep the covenant and be a light to the nations; the righteous of every nation have a share in the world to come

sections.key: In Romans 9 'hated' means 'not chosen'; Reformed Christians stress God's free choice of individuals, others stress foreknowledge, freedom or election as a calling, and Judaism sees election as a task.

refs: Genesis 25–33; 36; 47:9; Hosea 12:2–6; Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9–11; Amos 3:2; Deuteronomy 23:7; Obadiah 10; 2 Kings 8:20–22; Matthew 28:20; Luke 15:20.
Genesis Rabbah 77:3 (the angel of Esau); Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 125–126.

Charles Wesley, 'Wrestling Jacob' ('Come, O thou Traveller unknown'), in Hymns and Sacred Poems (1742); the Watts remark is reported in John Wesley's obituary tribute to his brother, Minutes of Conference (1788).

Augustine, To Simplician I.2 (396); John Calvin, Institutes III.21–24 (1559); Jacobus Arminius, Declaration of Sentiments (1608); Council of Orange (529), conclusion; Council of Trent, Session VI, canon 17; Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 and Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2 (the righteous of the nations).
N. T. Wright, Paul and the Faithfulness of God (2013), on Romans 9–11; Robert Alter, Genesis (1996).

debate.question: Why did God choose Jacob rather than Esau?

positions.name: Free grace
positions.who: Augustine; Calvin; Reformed theology
positions.view: God chose Jacob before birth, for reasons in himself alone, to show that salvation is by grace and not by merit. No one deserves to be chosen, so no one is wronged.
positions.evidence: Genesis 25:23; Romans 9:11–16, 'not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy'.

positions.name: A calling for history
positions.who: Many modern scholars; much Jewish tradition; the Orthodox
positions.view: The choice is of a people for a role in God's purposes, not of one person for heaven and another for hell. Esau is loved and blessed; Jacob is given the task of carrying the promise.
positions.evidence: 'Two nations are in your womb' (25:23); Malachi speaks of nations; Romans 11:32, God's 'mercy on all'; Deuteronomy 23:7.

positions.name: Foreknowledge
positions.who: Arminius; John Wesley; many Catholic and Orthodox theologians
positions.view: God chose Jacob knowing what he would become and how he would respond; election respects freedom.
positions.evidence: Romans 8:29, 'whom he foreknew'; Jacob's change at the Jabbok; 1 Timothy 2:4.

debate.agree: All agree that Jacob did not earn his election, that God's choosing is mercy, and that Esau is not left without blessing.

look.why: This painting shows Jacob's mother, Rebekah, years before he was born: Abraham's servant has travelled back to Haran to find a wife for Isaac, and meets her at a well, where she waters his camels (Genesis 24). Paolo Veronese and his workshop painted it in Venice in the 1580s. Rebekah is the one who plans the stolen blessing, and the one who later sends Jacob away to safety in that same country.
points: A woman in a salmon-pink skirt and gold-veiled bodice stands at the stone ledge of a well, light falling on her face.
In front of her, a man kneels and holds up a handful of gold coins or jewellery: the servant's gifts.
Beside him, a balding, grey-bearded man with a staff leans towards her and gestures to the gold.
On the left, a man reaches for the reins of two camels; another camel drinks from a copper vessel in the lower right.
In the distance, a town of white buildings lines the horizon under a sky streaked with blue, grey and mauve.

music.why: Bob Dylan's 1981 song is a man's prayer at a moment of reckoning, looking back over his own failures and finding that he is known and held all the same. It is Jacob's night at the Jabbok in a modern key.

think.why: Jacob is changed slowly, over twenty years, through exile, struggle and prayer. Ask whether, and how, people really change.

learn.why: Jacob at the Jabbok: the grasper who learns to ask.

check.q: What does the oracle 'the elder will serve the younger' (Genesis 25:23), given before the twins' birth, show?
options: That Esau was wicked from birth
That Jacob was older
That God's choice did not depend on anything either twin had done, and that it reversed the usual rule of the eldest inheriting
That Rebekah made it up
check.why: Paul builds his argument in Romans 9 on exactly this timing.

check.q: How does Genesis show that Jacob's deceit was wrong, without ever saying so?
options: Isaac curses Jacob when he discovers the trick
Jacob is deceived in the same way, in the dark, by Laban, and later by his own sons with a goat's blood, and lives twenty years in exile
God refuses to speak to Jacob until he repents
Esau takes the blessing back by force
check.why: Genesis teaches by consequences: the deceiver is deceived.

check.q: Why is the question 'What is your name?' at the Jabbok so significant?
options: Because Jacob had to give his name to receive Esau's forgiveness
Because the last time Jacob was asked who he was, he lied ('I am Esau'); now he must admit he is Jacob, the cheat, before he is renamed
Because the man did not know Jacob
Because asking a name was a challenge to wrestle
check.why: Confession comes before the new name.

check.q: In Malachi 1:2–3 and Romans 9:13, what does 'Esau I hated' most probably mean?
options: That God felt hatred for the man Esau
That Esau was condemned to hell
That God did not choose Esau (or Edom) for the covenant role; Genesis 29:30–31 uses 'hated' of Leah, whom Jacob 'loved less'
That Esau was punished for selling his birthright
check.why: A Hebrew idiom of preference; the readings of its consequences differ.

check.q: What links Jacob's night at the Jabbok with his meeting with Esau?
options: In both he sees a 'face of God': God's at Peniel, and God's in the forgiving face of his brother (33:10)
Both happen at Bethel
In both he sends gifts ahead to win favour
In both he wins a fight
check.why: Reconciliation with God and with his brother are one story.

check.q: Which of these is the most accurate statement about election in the traditions?
options: The Orthodox teach double predestination
All Christians agree with Calvin's view of predestination
Reformed theology stresses God's free choice of individuals; Arminians and many Catholics and Orthodox stress foreknowledge and freedom; much Jewish thought sees election as a calling to a task
Judaism teaches that only Jews can be saved
check.why: The traditions differ sharply; Judaism holds that the righteous of all nations have a share in the world to come.

tutorial.question: Why does God choose Jacob, and what does his story show about how God's choosing works?
tutorial.approach: Tell Jacob's story through its four scenes. Show how Genesis judges his deceit by its consequences. Explain what changes at the Jabbok, and how the meeting with Esau completes it. Then set out the debate about election from Romans 9, with the main traditions' views, and give your own.
strong: Explains the oracle and why the choice comes before birth.
Shows how Jacob's deceit is repaid (Laban, his sons).
Notes that God gives the promise at Bethel without rebuke.
Explains the change at the Jabbok: asking, confessing his name, the new name, the limp.
Connects the Jabbok with Esau's embrace and 'the face of God'.
Sets out the views of election fairly, including the meaning of 'hated'.

reading.author: Marilynne Robinson
reading.title: Reading Genesis
reading.why: A novelist's luminous reading of Genesis, with much on Jacob and Esau and on grace.

reading.author: Jonathan Sacks
reading.title: Covenant and Conversation: Genesis
reading.why: A former Chief Rabbi's essays on each week's reading; his pieces on Jacob are outstanding.

reading.author: Walter Brueggemann
reading.title: Genesis (Interpretation commentary)
reading.why: A theologically rich commentary, strong on the Jacob cycle.

sessions.practice: Live it this week: take the first step towards someone you have wronged, or who has wronged you: a message, a call, an apology. You don't have to resolve everything; just go towards them.
sessions.reflect: What is the name you would have to admit to, before you could receive a new one?
takeaways: Jacob takes Esau's birthright and blessing; Genesis judges him by consequences: he is deceived in turn and lives twenty years in exile.
God gives him the promise at Bethel by grace; at the Jabbok he wrestles, asks, confesses his name, and is renamed Israel.
Esau runs to embrace him; 'Esau I hated' means 'not chosen', and the traditions read election very differently.

sessions.title: Forgiveness, and the verdict: Joseph
sessions.line: A favourite son sold by his brothers, a slave who rules Egypt, and the words that end Genesis.
sessions.plain: Jacob's favourite son, Joseph, is sold into slavery in Egypt by his jealous brothers. Years later, after prison and a rise to power, he is ruler of Egypt in a great famine, and his brothers come to buy food, not knowing him. He tests them, then reveals himself and forgives them, saying: 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive'. This session reads the end of Genesis, and then gives the journey's verdict: why does the story turn on one family?
sessions.why: Session 6 ended with brothers reconciled. Now the last generation of Genesis repeats the old wrongs, favouritism and betrayal, and the story ends with forgiveness. With the whole family story in view, we can at last answer the journey's question.
answers: Who was Joseph, and why did his brothers sell him?
How does Joseph forgive his brothers, and do they change?
Is there evidence for the Joseph story in Egypt?
What does 'God meant it for good' mean? Does God cause evil?
So, why does the Bible's story turn on one family?
sessions.finding: The family's story ends in forgiveness, and in God bringing good out of evil 'to save many people alive': the chosen family, flawed throughout, becomes in Joseph a blessing to Egypt and the world, which is what it was chosen for.

paras: Six sessions have followed one family. God chose Abraham by grace, for the sake of all the families of the earth (1), and bound himself to the promise by oath (2). He saw and blessed the unchosen Hagar and Ishmael (3). He chose Abraham to teach justice, and welcomed his plea for Sodom (4). The binding of Isaac gave the strongest objection, which is real (5). The promise passed to Jacob, a cheat, who was changed and reconciled with Esau (6).
background.key: Grace, covenant, care for the unchosen, justice, the hardest test, and a cheat changed.

paras: Jacob had twelve sons by four women: his wives Leah and Rachel and their servants Bilhah and Zilpah. He loved Rachel most, and she died giving birth to her second son, Benjamin. Her first son, Joseph, became Jacob's favourite, and Jacob gave him a special robe, the famous 'coat of many colours'.

The story of Joseph fills Genesis 37 to 50, the longest single story in the book, and it is told with the skill of a novel. Between this session's passages Joseph is sold to an Egyptian official, Potiphar; resists the seductions of Potiphar's wife and is falsely accused and imprisoned; interprets the dreams of Pharaoh's officials and then of Pharaoh himself, who dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones; and is made ruler of all Egypt to store grain in seven years of plenty against seven years of famine.

timeline.text: Joseph's dreams; his brothers sell him
Judah and Tamar
Potiphar, prison, Pharaoh's dreams; Joseph rules Egypt
The famine; the brothers come to Egypt and are tested
'I am Joseph'
Jacob's family moves to Egypt; Jacob blesses his sons and dies
Joseph forgives his brothers again; Joseph dies

background.key: Joseph is sold, rises to rule Egypt, and saves his family in a famine; it is the longest story in Genesis.

paras: The main reading has four parts: the dreams and the jealousy (37:3–11), the sale (37:18–28), 'I am Joseph' (45:1–15), and the last scene between the brothers, with Joseph's death (50:15–26).

The comparison is the parable Jesus told of a father and two sons (Luke 15). It is the New Testament's great story of forgiveness, and it uses the words of Esau's embrace from the last session. Read it with Joseph in mind: two families, a son lost and found, and a brother who cannot forgive.
background.key: Joseph's story in four scenes; then the parable of the prodigal son.

before: Who is to blame for the brothers' hatred? Look at what Jacob does, and what Joseph says.
When Joseph reveals himself, what reason does he give for not being angry?
In the parable, which son is most like Joseph's brothers?
sessions.readWhy: The last story of Genesis in four scenes: jealousy, betrayal, revelation and forgiveness.

paras: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a tunic of many colors.
His brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, and they hated him, and couldn’t speak peaceably to him.
Joseph dreamed a dream, and he told it to his brothers, and they hated him all the more.
He said to them, “Please hear this dream which I have dreamed:
for behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and also stood upright; and behold, your sheaves came around, and bowed down to my sheaf.”
His brothers asked him, “Will you indeed reign over us? Will you indeed have dominion over us?” They hated him all the more for his dreams and for his words.
He dreamed yet another dream, and told it to his brothers, and said, “Behold, I have dreamed yet another dream: and behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to me.”

He told it to his father and to his brothers. His father rebuked him, and said to him, “What is this dream that you have dreamed? Will I and your mother and your brothers indeed come to bow ourselves down to you to the earth?”
His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind.
They saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to kill him.
They said to one another, “Behold, this dreamer comes.
Come now therefore, and let’s kill him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, ‘An evil animal has devoured him.’ We will see what will become of his dreams.”
Reuben heard it, and delivered him out of their hand, and said, “Let’s not take his life.”
Reuben said to them, “Shed no blood. Throw him into this pit that is in the wilderness, but lay no hand on him”—that he might deliver him out of their hand, to restore him to his father.
When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped Joseph of his tunic, the tunic of many colors that was on him;
and they took him, and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty. There was no water in it.

They sat down to eat bread, and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and saw a caravan of Ishmaelites was coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing spices and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, “What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?
Come, and let’s sell him to the Ishmaelites, and not let our hand be on him; for he is our brother, our flesh.” His brothers listened to him.
Midianites who were merchants passed by, and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. The merchants brought Joseph into Egypt.

Then Joseph couldn’t control himself before all those who stood before him, and he called out, “Cause everyone to go out from me!” No one else stood with him, while Joseph made himself known to his brothers.
He wept aloud. The Egyptians heard, and the house of Pharaoh heard.
Joseph said to his brothers, “I am Joseph! Does my father still live?”
His brothers couldn’t answer him; for they were terrified at his presence.
Joseph said to his brothers, “Come near to me, please.”
They came near. He said, “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.
Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.
For these two years the famine has been in the land, and there are yet five years, in which there will be no plowing and no harvest.
God sent me before you to preserve for you a remnant in the earth, and to save you alive by a great deliverance.
So now it wasn’t you who sent me here, but God, and he has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his house, and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
Hurry, and go up to my father, and tell him, ‘This is what your son Joseph says, “God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me. Don’t wait.
You shall dwell in the land of Goshen, and you will be near to me, you, your children, your children’s children, your flocks, your herds, and all that you have.
There I will provide for you; for there are yet five years of famine; lest you come to poverty, you, and your household, and all that you have.” ’
Behold, your eyes see, and the eyes of my brother Benjamin, that it is my mouth that speaks to you.
You shall tell my father of all my glory in Egypt, and of all that you have seen. You shall hurry and bring my father down here.”
He fell on his brother Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.
He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.
When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,

‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.” ’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.
Joseph said to his brothers, “I am dying, but God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.”
Joseph took an oath from the children of Israel, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.”
So Joseph died, being one hundred ten years old, and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.

parts.title: The coat and the dreams
parts.context: Joseph is seventeen, keeping the flocks with his older half-brothers, and has already brought his father a bad report of them (37:2).

commentary.on: Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children
commentary.text: The family sin again. Isaac preferred Esau and Rebekah Jacob; now Jacob, who suffered from favouritism, practises it. Notice that the narrator calls him 'Israel', the name of the whole people: what happens in this family happens to the nation.

commentary.on: he made him a tunic of many colors
commentary.text: The famous coat. The Hebrew phrase is rare; it may mean a long robe with sleeves, the dress of someone who does not do manual work. Either way, it marks Joseph out as the heir.

commentary.on: and they hated him, and couldn’t speak peaceably to him
commentary.text: 'Couldn't speak peaceably', literally 'couldn't speak to him for shalom'. They could not even say hello. Hatred begins in silence.

commentary.on: the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowed down to me
commentary.text: Joseph's dreams are true, as the story will show, but telling them is foolish. He is seventeen, spoilt and tactless. Genesis is fair to the brothers: Joseph helped make them hate him.

commentary.on: His brothers envied him, but his father kept this saying in mind.
commentary.text: Envy, the sin of Cain against Abel, is back. Jacob 'kept this saying in mind', as Mary later 'kept all these sayings' about her son (Luke 2:19, 51).

parts.title: Sold
parts.context: Jacob sends Joseph, wearing his coat, to check on his brothers, who are with the flocks far to the north at Dothan.

commentary.on: Behold, this dreamer comes.
commentary.text: Literally 'this master of dreams'. They see him coming from far off, by the coat. They plan murder before he arrives.

commentary.on: We will see what will become of his dreams.
commentary.text: The irony at the heart of the story: by trying to destroy the dreams, they will make them come true.

commentary.on: Shed no blood. Throw him into this pit
commentary.text: Reuben, the eldest, tries to save Joseph by stealth. He means well, but he lacks the courage to stand against the others openly.

commentary.on: They sat down to eat bread
commentary.text: One of the coldest details in the Bible. They throw their brother into a dry pit and sit down to a meal. Years later, they will remember 'the distress of his soul, when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen' (42:21).

commentary.on: for he is our brother, our flesh
commentary.text: Judah's argument is not compassion but profit: why kill him when you can sell him? 'He is our brother' is said while selling him. But remember Judah. He will change more than anyone.

commentary.on: sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver
commentary.text: Ishmael's descendants carry Abraham's great-grandson down to Egypt. Twenty shekels of silver was the price of a slave in Mesopotamian records of the early second millennium BC; later the price rose (Exodus 21:32 sets thirty), a detail some scholars use to date the story's background early. Christians later noticed that Judas, whose name is the Greek form of Judah, sold Jesus for silver.

parts.title: I am Joseph
parts.context: More than twenty years later. Joseph, now in his late thirties, is vizier of Egypt. The famine has driven his brothers to Egypt to buy grain; they bow before him without recognising him, as his dream foretold. Joseph tests them. He accuses them of spying, keeps one brother hostage, demands that they bring Benjamin, Rachel's other son, and then plants his silver cup in Benjamin's sack so that Benjamin will be made his slave. Will they abandon Rachel's son, as they once abandoned him? Judah steps forward and offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place, so that their father will not die of grief (44:18–34). That is the moment Joseph breaks.

commentary.on: Then Joseph couldn’t control himself before all those who stood before him
commentary.text: The powerful ruler loses control. He sends everyone out, so that his brothers' shame will be private, and weeps so loudly that all Egypt hears it.

commentary.on: I am Joseph! Does my father still live?
commentary.text: Three words in Hebrew, 'I am Joseph', after twenty years. His first question is about his father.

commentary.on: I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt.
commentary.text: He names the wrong plainly: 'whom you sold'. Forgiveness in Genesis does not pretend that nothing happened.

commentary.on: for God sent me before you to preserve life
commentary.text: Joseph's reason for not being angry. He sees the whole story from above: the brothers' crime was real, but God has woven it into a plan to save lives. He says it three times: 'God sent me'.

commentary.on: He kissed all his brothers, and wept on them. After that his brothers talked with him.
commentary.text: Remember 37:4: they 'couldn't speak peaceably to him'. Now, at last, 'his brothers talked with him'. The silence of hatred is broken.

parts.title: Am I in the place of God?
parts.context: Seventeen years later. Jacob has brought the whole family to Egypt, blessed his sons, and died, and they have buried him in Abraham's tomb at Hebron. Now the brothers are afraid: was Joseph only being kind for their father's sake?

commentary.on: It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.
commentary.text: Guilt does not believe in forgiveness. Seventeen years later, the brothers still cannot believe they are forgiven. They send a message, possibly invented, claiming that Jacob asked Joseph to forgive them.

commentary.on: Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
commentary.text: Joseph weeps because they still do not trust him. Being forgiven can be harder to accept than being punished.

commentary.on: Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
commentary.text: The key to Joseph's forgiveness. Judgement and revenge belong to God, not to him. To forgive is to refuse to take God's place.

commentary.on: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive
commentary.text: The most important sentence in the Joseph story, and perhaps in Genesis. One act, two intentions. The brothers meant evil, and it was evil. God meant good, and brought good out of it. Their guilt is not cancelled; it is overruled. 'To save many people alive': not only Jacob's family but Egypt and the nations who came to Egypt for grain.

commentary.on: God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.
commentary.text: Genesis ends with the family in Egypt and a promise still waiting. Joseph makes them swear to carry his bones home. In the book of Exodus, four hundred years later, Moses does (Exodus 13:19). The promise to Abraham is not finished; its next chapter is the Exodus.

commentary.on: they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt
commentary.text: The last words of Genesis. The book that began with God's breath giving life to Adam ends with a coffin in Egypt: a family saved, but a people not yet free.

paras: He said, “A certain man had two sons.
The younger of them said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of your property.’ He divided his livelihood between them.
Not many days after, the younger son gathered all of this together and traveled into a far country. There he wasted his property with riotous living.
When he had spent all of it, there arose a severe famine in that country, and he began to be in need.
He went and joined himself to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed pigs.
He wanted to fill his belly with the husks that the pigs ate, but no one gave him any.
But when he came to himself he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger!
I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight.
I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.” ’
“He arose, and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
“But the father said to his servants, ‘Bring out the best robe, and put it on him. Put a ring on his hand, and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf, kill it, and let’s eat, and celebrate;
for this, my son, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’ Then they began to celebrate.
“Now his elder son was in the field. As he came near to the house, he heard music and dancing.
He called one of the servants to him, and asked what was going on.
He said to him, ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and healthy.’
But he was angry, and would not go in. Therefore his father came out, and begged him.
But he answered his father, ‘Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.
But when this your son came, who has devoured your living with prostitutes, you killed the fattened calf for him.’
“He said to him, ‘Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
But it was appropriate to celebrate and be glad, for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.’ ”

parts.title: The son who came home
parts.context: Luke's Gospel, written in the later first century. The parable is usually called 'the prodigal son'; 'prodigal' means wasteful.

commentary.on: there arose a severe famine in that country
commentary.text: Like Joseph's brothers, the younger son is driven by famine. Hunger brings him to himself, as it brought the brothers to Egypt and, in the end, to the truth.

commentary.on: I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in your sight.
commentary.text: He rehearses his confession, as the brothers rehearsed theirs. Like them, he expects at best to be a servant: 'Make me as one of your hired servants', as they said, 'we are your servants'.

commentary.on: But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
commentary.text: Almost the exact words of Esau's embrace of Jacob (Genesis 33:4), and of Joseph falling on his brothers' necks. In Jesus' story, the one who runs is the father, and for Christians the father is God. The forgiveness the brothers of Genesis learned to give each other is, in the parable, the very nature of God.

commentary.on: for this, my son, was dead, and is alive again. He was lost, and is found.
commentary.text: Jacob thought Joseph was dead and found him alive (Genesis 45:26–28). The father says the same of his son. Christians hear resurrection in it.

parts.title: The brother who stayed outside
parts.context: The parable does not end with the feast. There is an elder son.

commentary.on: But he was angry, and would not go in.
commentary.text: The elder brother is the Bible's oldest problem: the one who resents the favour shown to another, like Cain, like Esau, like Joseph's brothers. He has done nothing wrong, and he cannot forgive.

commentary.on: Therefore his father came out, and begged him.
commentary.text: The father goes out to the elder son as he ran out to the younger. He loves both. Neither son is unchosen.

commentary.on: for this, your brother, was dead, and is alive again
commentary.text: 'This your son', the elder said; 'this, your brother', the father answers. The parable ends with a question, not an answer: will he go in? It is the question Genesis asked of every pair of brothers.

compare.why: Jesus told this parable to people who were grumbling that he welcomed sinners (Luke 15:1–2). It is the New Testament's great story of forgiveness, and it is full of echoes of Genesis: a younger son, a famine, a far country, a father who runs to embrace, and an elder brother who cannot rejoice. Read it in two parts.
compare.title: A father and two sons

paras: Joseph's forgiveness is not quick, and it is not cheap. He tests his brothers for months. Why? Because he needs to know whether they have changed. The test is precise: he puts them in the same position as before, with the power to abandon Rachel's other son and go home. And Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph, offers to become a slave himself so that Benjamin can go free (44:33).

That is the turning point. The brothers have repented, not in words only, but in an act that reverses their old one. Only then does Joseph reveal himself. Genesis shows forgiveness as a journey with several stages: the wrong named plainly ('whom you sold'), the wrongdoer changed, the injured person refusing revenge ('am I in the place of God?'), and a new relationship ('his brothers talked with him'). Jewish tradition calls this teshuvah, repentance or 'return'; its classic test, in Maimonides' laws of repentance, is facing the same situation again and choosing differently.
sections.key: Joseph tests his brothers; Judah offers himself for Benjamin; only then does Joseph reveal himself: forgiveness meets repentance.

paras: 'You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.' This sentence has become the Bible's clearest statement of providence: God's guiding of history, even through human wickedness. It does not say the brothers' act was good, or that God made them do it. It says God was at work in and through what they freely did, to bring good from it. Paul says the same in Romans 8:28: 'all things work together for good for those who love God'.

Augustine put it famously: God judged it better to bring good out of evil than to allow no evil at all (Enchiridion 27). Thomas Aquinas taught that God permits evil for the sake of a greater good, but never wills it in itself. Calvin stressed that God governs every event, even the wicked acts of people, while they remain guilty. Many people find this the hardest part of faith: was every suffering 'meant'? Genesis does not say that. It says that Joseph, looking back from the end, could see God's hand in his story. It is a confession made after the event, not an explanation offered to someone in the pit.
sections.key: 'God meant it for good' is the Bible's clearest picture of providence: God brings good out of evil without making evil good.

paras: Is there evidence for Joseph? Egyptian records do not mention him, and we should not expect them to name a foreign official. What archaeology does show is that Semitic people from Canaan lived in Egypt in large numbers in the early second millennium BC. A painting in the tomb of the official Khnumhotep II at Beni Hasan (about 1890 BC) shows a group of 'Asiatics' arriving in Egypt in bright, patterned clothes. At Avaris in the Nile Delta, excavations have uncovered a large Canaanite town from about 1800 BC; later its people, the Hyksos, ruled northern Egypt for about a century (about 1650–1550 BC).

Some details fit early Egypt, such as the price of a slave. Others, such as the Egyptian names Zaphenath-paneah and Asenath, are of a type most common in the first millennium BC, which led the scholar Donald Redford to argue that the story was written then. There is also an Egyptian story, the Tale of Two Brothers (about 1200 BC), in which a married woman tries to seduce a young man and then accuses him, as Potiphar's wife does Joseph. Most scholars think the Joseph story is a carefully crafted narrative using Egyptian colour; how much history lies behind it is debated.
sections.key: Semitic people did live in Egypt, as at Avaris and in the Beni Hasan painting; Joseph himself is unattested, and the story's details point to different dates.

paras: Joseph is loved in all three Abrahamic faiths. The Qur'an gives him a whole chapter, Sura 12, which calls his story 'one of the most beautiful of narratives'; it is the only sura told as one continuous story. In it Joseph (Yusuf) is a prophet, and Jacob trusts all along that his son is alive. Christians, from the early Church Fathers on, have seen Joseph as a figure of Christ: the beloved son, rejected by his brothers, sold for silver, brought down to the pit and raised to the right hand of power, who forgives those who betrayed him and feeds the world. In the twentieth century the German novelist Thomas Mann retold the story in a four-volume novel, Joseph and His Brothers (1933–43), written in exile from Nazi Germany: a humane, ironic Joseph whose gift is to feed the hungry nations.

rows: Yosef ha-tzaddik, 'Joseph the righteous', who resisted temptation and forgave
Repentance and forgiveness; God's hidden hand; the descent into Egypt that leads to the Exodus
A figure of Christ, betrayed, sold, raised and forgiving
God brings good out of evil; the rejected one becomes the saviour
Yusuf, a prophet; Sura 12, 'one of the most beautiful of narratives'
Patience (sabr) and trust in God through suffering

sections.key: All three faiths love Joseph: Judaism's righteous one, Christianity's figure of Christ, Islam's patient prophet.

paras: We can now answer the journey's question. Why does the Bible's story turn on one family?

Not because they were better than others. Every generation fails: Abraham lies, Sarah and Abraham drive out Hagar, Jacob cheats, the brothers sell Joseph. They are chosen by grace (session 1). Not to keep the blessing for themselves: they are chosen so that 'all the families of the earth' will be blessed (12:3), and taught 'righteousness and justice' (18:19, session 4). Not at the expense of the others: God sees Hagar, hears Ishmael, blesses Esau (sessions 3 and 6). And the promise depends on God, who swore it by himself (sessions 2 and 5).

The objection is real. A God who chooses one family can look like a God of favourites, as Ingersoll said, and the eighteenth-century German thinker Gotthold Lessing asked how truths that matter to everyone could hang on the accidents of one people's history: theologians call this the 'scandal of particularity'. The Bible's answer, in Genesis, is that God works in history the way history works: through real people, in one place and time, starting small. The universal is reached through the particular, as a whole field is sown from a handful of seed.

And Genesis ends by showing it happen. Joseph, the son of the chosen family, sold by his brothers, becomes the man through whom 'all countries came into Egypt, to Joseph, to buy grain' (41:57), and he saves 'many people alive'. For the first time, the promise to Abraham is visibly kept: through one family, the nations are blessed. Christians believe it is kept fully in Jesus, 'the son of Abraham' (Matthew 1:1), through whom Abraham's family is opened to every nation; Jews, that it continues in the covenant people and in a world one day healed; Muslims, that it was renewed in Muhammad, descendant of Ishmael. All three agree that it began with one man who left home on the strength of a promise.
sections.key: One family, chosen by grace, for the sake of all; flawed throughout, held by God's promise; and in Joseph, for the first time, a blessing to the nations.

refs: Genesis 37–50; Exodus 13:19; 21:32; Luke 15; Romans 8:28; Matthew 1:1; Acts 7:9–16.

Augustine, Enchiridion 27; Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.19.9 and I.22.2; John Calvin, Institutes I.18; Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 2:1.
Qur'an 12; Ambrose, On Joseph (about 388); Thomas Mann, Joseph and His Brothers (1933–43).
